**1.21.13**  "You are all nectar, O god; you are Soma, supremely worshipped. You are the muhūrta, and the tithi; you are the lava, and the kṣaṇa."

**1.21.14**  "You are the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, the kalā, kāṣṭhā, truṭi, years, seasons, months, nights, and days."

**1.21.15**  "You are the earth at her best with mountains and forests; you are the sky, luminous with the sun, free of darkness. You are the great ocean, filled with timi and timiṅgila fish, with great waves, many makaras, and a home for fish."

**1.21.16**  "You are great glory — so you are ever worshipped by the wise and by the great ṛṣis with joyful hearts. Praised, you drink the soma at sacrifices, and the havis offered with the vaṣaṭ call for the welfare of beings."

**1.21.17**  "You are ever worshipped here by the brāhmaṇas for the sake of fruit; you are sung of in the Vedic ancillaries, O flood of incomparable strength. For your sake the twice-born lords, devoted to sacrifice, master the Vedic ancillaries together with all the Vedas."

**1.22.1**  Suta said: Thus praised by Kadrū, the blessed Harivāhana covered the entire sky with masses of dark-blue clouds.

**1.22.2**  Those clouds, blazing with lightning, released abundant water and roared incessantly against one another in the sky as if competing.

**1.22.3**  The sky seemed to be packed solid with those most wondrous rain-clouds, which poured forth incomparable water ceaselessly with a tremendous roar.

**1.22.4**  The sky seemed to dance with the manifold surging waves of rain, and the firmament was filled with the resounding peal of thunder.

**1.22.5**  The nāgas were filled with the greatest joy when Vāsava rained down; and the earth too was flooded with water on every side.

**1.23.1**  Suta said: Carried by Suparṇa, they quickly reached that place, which was encircled by the waters of the ocean and resounded with the cries of flocks of birds.

**1.23.2**  It was covered with rows of trees bearing varied fruits and flowers, enclosed by lovely mansions, and adorned with lotus pools as well.

**1.23.3**  It was embellished with lakes of clear water of variegated beauty, and fanned by holy breezes carrying divine fragrances.

**1.23.4**  It was beautified by sandal-wood trees that touched the sky with their fragrance, and which, shaken by the wind, were showering down rains of blossoms.

**1.23.5**  The showers of flowers and water seemed to be scattered over the nāgas assembled there; the place was heart-gladdening, holy, beloved of gandharvas and apsarases, resonant with the calls of many birds, lovely, and a source of delight for the sons of Kadrū.

**1.23.6**  Having reached that forest, the serpents sported there with joy, and they also addressed the mighty Suparṇa, that best of birds.

**1.23.7**  "Carry us to yet another island, most beautiful, with abundant water. For you, O sky-ranger, while flying, behold many lovely regions."

**1.23.8**  Reflecting on this, the bird then spoke to his mother Vinatā: "What is the reason, Mother, that I must do what the serpents say?"

**1.23.9**  Vinatā said: "I have become the slave of my ignoble sister, O best of birds — a false wager was contrived by the serpents through treachery."

**1.23.10**  Suta said: When the reason had been told by his mother, the sky-traveler, pained by that sorrow, spoke these words to the serpents:

**1.23.11**  "By fetching what, or by knowing what, or by what act of valor here, may I be freed from slavery to you? Tell me truly, O tongue-flickering ones."

**1.23.12**  Hearing him, the serpents replied: "Bring us the amṛta by your power; then will your freedom from slavery come to pass, O sky-traveler."

**1.24.1**  Suta said: Thus addressed by the serpents, Garuḍa then spoke to his mother: "I go to fetch the amṛta. I wish to know what I should eat on the way."

**1.24.2**  Vinatā said: "In a secluded part of the ocean's bosom is the supreme dwelling of the Niṣādas. After eating many thousands of them, bring back the amṛta."

**1.24.3**  "But you must never under any circumstance entertain the thought of killing a brāhmaṇa. A brāhmaṇa is not to be slain by any living being, for he is inviolable and without equal."

**1.24.4**  "When angered, a vipra becomes fire, the sun, poison, and a weapon. The vipra is the foremost among all creatures in receiving food, the best of the varṇas, a father, a teacher."

**1.24.5**  Garuḍa said: "Please tell me, Mother, since I ask — by what auspicious signs would I recognize a brāhmaṇa? You ought to explain this to me properly."

**1.24.6**  Vinatā said: "Son, whoever, once swallowed and lodged in your throat, burns like a live coal — like a swallowed hook — him you should know to be a bull among brāhmaṇas."

**1.24.7**  Suta said: And Vinatā, from maternal love for her son, spoke these words to him — knowing his incomparable might — accompanied by a benediction.

**1.24.8**  "May the wind protect your wings, and the moon your back, my son. May fire protect your head, and the sun your entire being."

**1.24.9**  "And I, my son, am ever devoted to your peace and well-being. Go by an unobstructed path, dear child, to the accomplishment of your purpose."

**1.24.10**  Then, having heard his mother's words, he spread his wings and soared into the sky; and the powerful one approached the Niṣādas, hungry as great Death itself at the end of time.

**1.24.11**  Driving those Niṣādas together then, he stirred up a great dust reaching to the sky, dried up the waters in the ocean's bosom, and shook the mountains standing nearby.

**1.24.12**  Then the king of birds opened his enormous mouth, blocking the path of the Niṣādas; and the Niṣādas rushed headlong toward the mouth of that devourer of serpents.

**1.24.13**  Into that gaping mouth of immense size they flew by the thousands, like birds flying into the sky, bewildered by the swirling dust-laden wind, like trees shaken by a great gale in the forest.

**1.24.14**  Then the bird, scorcher of enemies, swift and mighty, closed his mouth — slaying those who eat fish of many kinds — hungry, that lord of sky-travellers, at that moment.

**1.25.1**  Sūta said: A brahmin along with his wife had reached Garuḍa's throat. Garuḍa — blazing like a flaming coal — spoke to him as he flew through the sky.

**1.25.2**  "O best of twice-born, come out quickly from my open mouth. A brahmin is never to be slain by me, not even one who is always given to wicked deeds."

**1.25.3**  As Garuḍa spoke thus, the brahmin addressed him: "This Niṣādī woman is my wife — let her come out together with me."

**1.25.4**  Garuḍa said: "Take this Niṣādī woman too and fly out swiftly. Sustain yourself well — you have not yet been digested by my fierce energy."

**1.25.5**  Sūta said: Then that brahmin came out, accompanied by the Niṣādī woman. Having praised Garuḍa, he departed to his desired destination.

**1.25.6**  When that brahmin had departed with his wife, the king of birds spread his wings and soared into the sky with the speed of thought.

**1.25.7**  Then he saw his father and, being questioned, told his father: "I have been sent by the serpents; I am resolved to fetch soma. I shall bring it this very day for the sake of freeing my mother from bondage."

**1.25.8**  "I was also instructed by my mother to eat Niṣādas. Yet I found no satisfaction even after devouring them by the thousands."

**1.25.9**  "Therefore, O blessed one, O lord, point out to me another food that I may eat and thereafter be capable of fetching the amṛta."

**1.25.10**  Kaśyapa said: "There was once a great sage named Vibhāvasu, exceedingly wrathful. He had a younger brother named Supratīka, great in his austerities."

**1.25.11**  "That great sage did not wish to hold wealth in common with his brother; Supratīka kept insisting on a partition, again and again."

**1.25.12**  "And his brother Vibhāvasu said to Supratīka: 'Many people desire to make a partition out of delusion, always. Once separated, they no longer regard one another, deluded by wealth.'"

**1.25.13**  "'Knowing those fools absorbed in self-interest, separated and each with his own wealth, enemies in the guise of friends then drive them further apart.'"

**1.25.14**  "'And others, knowing them to be divided, fall upon the gaps between them. The destruction of the divided is immeasurable and comes about swiftly.'"

**1.25.15**  "'Therefore the wise do not commend partition for those bound together under the teaching of a guru, who would come to be suspicious of one another.'"

**1.25.16**  "'Since you cannot be restrained and you desire to divide the wealth, therefore, O Supratīka, you shall become an elephant.'"

**1.25.17**  "Cursed thus, Supratīka then spoke to Vibhāvasu: 'You too shall become a tortoise that moves beneath the waters.'"

**1.25.18**  "Thus, through mutual curses, Supratīka and Vibhāvasu, their minds foolish on account of wealth, came to assume the forms of an elephant and a tortoise."

**1.25.19**  "Even though they had taken birth in animal wombs through the fault of their anger, they were devoted to mutual hatred, both proud of their extraordinary strength."

**1.25.20**  "These two with their great bodies, pursuing old enmity, dwell in that lake. One of them, the magnificent great elephant, now approaches."

**1.25.21**  "Hearing the trumpeting sound of the elephant, the tortoise, that great-bodied one who rests beneath the water, rises up, churning the entire lake."

**1.25.22**  "Seeing the tortoise, the elephant with its entwined trunk plunges into the water — mighty, with the force of its tusks, trunk, tail, and feet."

**1.25.23**  "As the elephant churns that lake filled with many fish, the tortoise too raises its head and comes forward mightily, eager for battle."

**1.25.24**  "The elephant stands six yojanas tall and is twice that in length; the tortoise is three yojanas in height and ten yojanas in circumference."

**1.25.25**  "These two, maddened for battle and each seeking victory over the other — make swift use of them and accomplish your desired goal."

**1.25.26**  Sūta said: Having heard his father's words, the sky-soarer of terrible speed seized the elephant with one talon and the tortoise with the other.

**1.25.27**  Then that great bird soared high into the sky and, reaching the sacred ford called Ālambatīrtha, he approached the trees of the gods.

**1.25.28**  Terrified, those divine trees with their golden branches trembled, struck by the wind of his wings, thinking, "Let him not break us."

**1.25.29**  Seeing those trees shaking their limbs — trees whose fruits fulfil all desires, with incomparably beautiful forms — the sky-ranger approached others.

**1.25.30**  He approached those great and radiant trees, their branches set with vaiḍūrya gems, bearing golden and silver fruits, surrounded by the waters of the ocean.

**1.25.31**  There, the Rohiṇa tree — exceedingly grown and very great — spoke to that best of birds as he came swooping with the speed of thought:

**1.25.32**  "This great branch of mine extends one hundred yojanas. Alight on this branch and devour these two — the elephant and the tortoise."

**1.25.33**  Then, swiftly swooping upon that tree frequented by thousands of birds, the best of birds — his body like a mountain — shook it with great speed and broke that branch, thickly covered with dense leaves.

**1.26.1**  Sūta said: The moment Garuḍa, so mighty, touched it with his feet, that branch of the tree snapped — and he caught hold of it as it broke.

**1.26.2**  Gazing and smiling at that broken great branch, he then saw the Vālakhilya sages hanging from it, head downward.

**1.26.3**  Out of fear of causing their destruction, the lord of birds swooped down, seized the branch in his beak out of concern for them, and flew gently, threading his way through the mountains.

**1.26.4**  Thus he flew over many regions, carrying the elephant and tortoise, out of compassion for the Vālakhilyas, yet found no place to set down.

**1.26.5**  Going to Gandhamādana, the foremost and imperishable of mountains, he there saw Kaśyapa, his father, standing in austerity.

**1.26.6**  His father too beheld that bird of divine form, endowed with splendour, heroism, and strength, swift as the mind and the wind.

**1.26.7**  He resembled a mountain peak, like Brahmā's staff raised on high — inconceivable, unrecognisable in form, terrifying to all beings.

**1.26.8**  He bore within him a valour like magic, like a blazing fire raised aloft — not to be assailed, not to be conquered by gods, dānavas, or rākṣasas.

**1.26.9**  He was a cleaver of mountain peaks, a drainer of river waters, a terrible churner of the worlds, dreadful to behold as Death itself.

**1.26.10**  Seeing him arrive and knowing his intention, the blessed Kaśyapa then spoke these words:

**1.26.11**  "Son, do not act rashly; do not bring sudden pain upon yourself. May the Vālakhilyas who feed on rays of light and who are fiercely wrathful not burn you."

**1.26.12**  Then Kaśyapa, for the sake of his son, appeased those Vālakhilyas who had perfected their austerities, pointing to this reason:

**1.26.13**  "O wealth-of-austerity sages, Garuḍa's undertaking is for the benefit of all living beings. He desires to accomplish a great deed — you should grant him your permission."

**1.26.14**  Thus addressed by the blessed one, those sages agreed. Releasing the branch, those ascetics then made for the sacred Himavat mountain.

**1.26.15**  Then, when they had departed, the son of Vinatā — his face still occupied by the branch held in his beak — questioned his father Kaśyapa.

**1.26.16**  "O blessed one, where shall I release this tree branch? Let the blessed one tell me of a region free from brahmins."

**1.26.17**  Then Kaśyapa pointed out to him a mountain devoid of people, its ravines sealed by snow, inaccessible even to the mind of others.

**1.26.18**  Entering the vast hollow of that mountain with the speed of thought, Tārkṣya flew swiftly, bearing the branch along with the elephant and tortoise.

**1.26.19**  Not even a hundred large or small leather thongs could encircle that great branch of the tree which the bird had seized and carried away.

**1.26.20**  Then Garuḍa, best among fliers, covered a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas in no very great time.

**1.26.21**  Reaching that mountain in a mere moment, following his father's words, the sky-ranger released that great branch there with a resounding crash.

**1.26.22**  Struck by the wind of his wings, the king of mountains trembled; the trees, shaken all together, showered down a rain of flowers.

**1.26.23**  And the peaks of that mountain shattered on all sides — those peaks of jewels and gold, which adorned the great mountain.

**1.26.24**  Many of the trees, struck by that branch, shone with their golden blossoms like clouds lit by lightning.

**1.26.25**  Those trees, blazing with golden blossoms and mingled with the minerals of the mountain, shone there, reflecting the rays of the sun.

**1.26.26**  Then, alighting on the peak of that mountain, Garuḍa — best of birds — devoured both the elephant and the tortoise.

**1.26.27**  Then he launched himself from the summit of the mountain peak with the speed of thought. Thereupon ill omens arose among the gods, portending fear.

**1.26.28**  Indra's beloved thunderbolt blazed with anguish, and a heavenly meteor with smoke and flame fell from the sky.

**1.26.29**  And so too the weapons of the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas in their entirety, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and whatever other hosts of gods — each one's weapon turned against the others.

**1.26.30**  Something unprecedented even in the war of gods and asuras then occurred: violent thundering winds blew, and meteors fell on every side.

**1.26.31**  Even the cloudless sky roared with tremendous sound, and the god who is the divine dispenser of rain rained down blood.

**1.26.32**  The garlands of the gods withered, their splendours grew dim; dreadful portent-clouds rained down much blood, and dust rose up to assail their crowns.

**1.26.33**  Then Śatakratu, greatly agitated with fear, seeing these dreadful omens together with the gods, spoke thus to Bṛhaspati:

**1.26.34**  "Why, O blessed one, have these terrible great omens arisen? And I see no enemy in battle who could challenge us."

**1.26.35**  Bṛhaspati said: "Through your transgression, O Devendra, and through your carelessness, O Śatakratu, a wondrous being has arisen through the austerities of the Vālakhilyas."

**1.26.36**  "The son of the sage Kaśyapa and of Vinatā, a flyer, powerful and capable of assuming any form, has arrived with intent to steal the soma."

**1.26.37**  "This bird, the foremost of the mighty, is capable of stealing the soma. I consider him capable of everything — he could even accomplish what is thought impossible."

**1.26.38**  Sūta said: Having heard these words, Śakra addressed the guardians of the amṛta: "A bird of great heroism and strength is here set on stealing the soma."

**1.26.39**  "I am alerting you so that he may not carry it off by force. Bṛhaspati has told me that his strength is matchless."

**1.26.40**  Hearing these words, the gods were astonished and took up their effort; they stood surrounding the amṛta, and Indra the thunderbolt-wielder, Śatakratu, stood among them.

**1.26.41**  Those high-minded ones wore their most precious armour — golden and variegated, set with vaiḍūrya gems —

**1.26.42**  — and they raised up manifold weapons of terrible appearance, innumerable, sharp and keen of point and edge, by the thousands.

**1.26.43**  Everywhere blazing with sparks and flames, emitting smoke — discs, iron clubs, tridents, and battle-axes —

**1.26.44**  — and various sharp spears, and bright swords, in forms that matched their own bodies, and maces fierce to behold —

**1.26.45**  — armed with those radiant weapons, adorned with divine ornaments, those shining hosts of gods stood free from all impurity.

**1.26.46**  Those gods — of incomparable strength, heroism, and splendour — their minds set on guarding the amṛta, destroyers of the cities of the asuras, shone with bodies blazing like kindled fire.

**1.26.47**  Thus that excellent battle-array of the gods — crowded with hundreds of thousands of iron clubs, shining within the expanse of the sky as if it were the sun's own radiance — blazed forth in glory.

**1.27.1**  Śaunaka said: What was Mahendra's offence, and what was his blunder, O son of a sūta? And how was Garuḍa born through the austerities of the Vālakhilyas?

**1.27.2**  And how did the lord of birds become the son of the twice-born Kaśyapa? How did he become unassailable by all beings, and how did he become invincible?

**1.27.3**  And how did that sky-traveller move freely at will and possess strength at will? I wish to hear all this, if it is recorded in the Purāṇa.

**1.27.4**  The Sūta said: What you ask me about is indeed a subject treated in the Purāṇa. O twice-born, hear from me as I recount it all in brief.

**1.27.5**  When the progenitor Kaśyapa was performing a sacrifice desiring a son, the seers, the gods, and the Gandharvas all rendered him assistance.

**1.27.6**  For the fetching of firewood, Śakra was assigned by Kaśyapa, along with the Vālakhilya sages and whatever other hosts of divinities were present.

**1.27.7**  Śakra, the mighty lord, easily lifted a load of firewood equal in size to a mountain, commensurate with his own strength, and bore it forward without much effort.

**1.27.8**  Then on the path he saw the tiny sages, as small as a thumb-joint at the belly, all together carrying a single stalk of a palāśa leaf.

**1.27.9**  Those ascetic-wealthy ones, as though dissolved into their own limbs, without food, afflicted with fatigue, with feeble strength, were struggling in water flooded even in a cow's hoofprint.

**1.27.10**  Seized with pride and intoxicated by his own might, Purandara laughed at them all and quickly leaped over them with contempt, dishonoring them.

**1.27.11**  Then those sages, utterly seized by rage and deeply angered, undertook a great deed that would strike terror into Śakra.

**1.27.12**  Those brāhmaṇas of intense austerity poured oblations into the sacred fire according to rule, with mantras both high and low, for a particular purpose — hear what that was.

**1.27.13**  "Let there arise another Indra of all the gods — one possessed of strength at will and movement at will, one who strikes fear into the king of the gods" — so vowed those keepers of their vows.

**1.27.14**  "Let one who is a hundredfold superior to Indra in heroism and prowess, swift as thought, and formidable, now come into being through the fruit of our austerities" — thus they spoke.

**1.27.15**  Learning of this, the king of the gods, Śatakratu, greatly distressed, went for refuge to Kaśyapa of sharpened vow.

**1.27.16**  Having heard of the king of the gods' plight, the progenitor Kaśyapa approached the Vālakhilyas and inquired about the completion of their ritual act.

**1.27.17**  Those truth-speakers replied to him, "So be it." Then the progenitor Kaśyapa spoke these conciliatory words to them.

**1.27.18**  "This Indra has been appointed over the three worlds by Brahmā's command, and you too, O wealthy in austerities, have been striving for the sake of Indra."

**1.27.19**  "O best of beings, you ought not render Brahmā's word false; nor do I intend to make your resolve come to naught."

**1.27.20**  "Let this one become Indra of the winged beings, supremely powerful and courageous; and let your grace be shown to the king of the gods who now supplicates you."

**1.27.21**  Thus addressed by Kaśyapa, the Vālakhilyas, wealthy in austerities, replied after duly honoring that best of sages and progenitor.

**1.27.22**  "This undertaking of ours all together was for the sake of Indra, O Progenitor; and your desired undertaking is for the sake of offspring."

**1.27.23**  "So let this fruit-bearing act be accepted by you, and arrange things here as you see to be the greatest good."

**1.27.24**  At this very time, the goddess Vinatā — the auspicious, beautiful daughter of Dakṣa, that illustrious one who was desirous of sons —

**1.27.25**  — having performed austerities and being devoted to her vow, having bathed and purified herself in the puṃsavana rite, approached her husband. Then Kaśyapa spoke to her.

**1.27.26**  "This undertaking of yours, O goddess, shall bear the fruit you desired; you will give birth to two heroic sons, lords of the three worlds."

**1.27.27**  "Born through the austerities of the Vālakhilyas and from my own intention likewise, your two highly fortunate sons shall be worshipped throughout the worlds."

**1.27.28**  The venerable Mārīca then spoke to her again: "This embryo of great and auspicious potency must be carried with all care and without negligence."

**1.27.29**  "One of them, that heroic sky-ranger honoured throughout the worlds, possessed of strength at will, shall exercise the lordship of Indra over all winged creatures."

**1.27.30**  Then the progenitor, pleased, spoke to Śatakratu: "These two birds shall be your brothers and allies."

**1.27.31**  "No harm shall come to you from these two, O Purandara. Let your anxiety depart, O Śakra; you yourself shall remain Indra."

**1.27.32**  "And you must never again despise the knowers of Brahman, nor out of arrogance dishonor those whose words are venomous and who are provoked to fierce anger."

**1.27.33**  Thus addressed, Indra departed free of anxiety to heaven, and Vinatā too had her purpose accomplished and became joyful.

**1.27.34**  She gave birth to two sons — Aruṇa and Garuḍa. Of the two, Aruṇa was deformed and became the forerunner of the Sun.

**1.27.35**  Garuḍa was consecrated as Indra of the winged beings. O joy of the Bhṛgu line, hear now of this great deed of his.

**1.28.1**  The Sūta said: Then, O best of the twice-born, when that event had thus unfolded, Garutmān, the lord of birds, swiftly advanced against the gods.

**1.28.2**  Seeing him of such overwhelming strength, they trembled on all sides; and yet they struck one another even while wielding all their weapons.

**1.28.3**  There was present one of immeasurable spirit, blazing like lightning and fire, named Bhauvana, of very great heroism, the guardian of the Soma.

**1.28.4**  Wounded by that lord of birds with his wings, beak, and talons, he fought an incomparable battle for a moment and then was slain in combat.

**1.28.5**  The sky-traveller stirred up a great mass of dust with the wind of his wings, darkened the worlds so they were without light, and with it scattered the gods.

**1.28.6**  Enveloped in that dust, the gods fell into confusion; the guardians of the nectar, shrouded by the dust, could not see him.

**1.28.7**  Thus Garuḍa threw the abode of the three heavens into turmoil, and with blows of his wings and beak he tore the gods asunder.

**1.28.8**  Then the thousand-eyed god quickly urged on the Wind: "Disperse this rain of dust — that is your task, O Wind."

**1.28.9**  Then the mighty Wind swiftly blew away that dust. Once the darkness had cleared, the gods assailed the bird.

**1.28.10**  The powerful bird roared aloud with the sound of a great storm-cloud, terrifying all beings even while being assailed by the hosts of gods; and the lord of birds, of great heroism and slayer of enemy heroes, soared upward.

**1.28.11**  Soaring up and hovering above the gods in the midair, all the armoured gods showered him with weapons of every kind from below.

**1.28.12**  With axes, iron clubs, spears, and maces together with Vāsava, and also with blazing discuses with sharp edges resembling the sun in form.

**1.28.13**  Though struck on all sides by discharges of every kind of weapon and waging a most tumultuous battle, the lord of birds did not waver.

**1.28.14**  Roaring as if filling the sky, the valiant son of Vinatā flung the gods in every direction with his wings and chest.

**1.28.15**  Those gods, thus hurled away and tormented by Garuḍa, fled; wounded by his talons and beak, they bled profusely.

**1.28.16**  The Sādhyas along with the Gandharvas fled to the east; the Vasus fled to the south along with the Rudras, all driven away by the lord of birds.

**1.28.17**  The Ādityas fled to the western quarter, the Nāsatyas to the north, repeatedly glancing back and fighting against the one of great might.

**1.28.18**  With the hero Aśvakranda, with the bird Reṇuka, with the valiant Krathana, and with the sky-traveller Tapana —

**1.28.19**  — and with Ulūka and Śvasana, and with the bird Nimeṣa, and with Praruja and Praliha — with all these he waged battle.

**1.28.20**  With tips of his wings, talons, and beak the son of Vinatā tore them apart, infuriated like Śiva with his Pināka bow at the end of an age, possessed of great might.

**1.28.21**  Those beings of great heroism and great energy, lacerated in many ways by him, shone like dense storm clouds raining torrents of blood.

**1.28.22**  Having left all those beings deprived of their lives, the best of birds, advancing for the sake of the nectar, saw fire blazing on all sides.

**1.28.23**  It was enveloping the sky on all sides with its great flames, scorching like the fierce-rayed sun, terrible, fanned by the wind.

**1.28.24**  Then the swift and great-souled Garuḍa, having made ninety times ninety mouths, drank up rivers with those mouths and returned again with great speed.

**1.28.25**  That scorcher of enemies, the chariot of feathers, extinguished the blazing fire with those rivers. Then, wishing to enter and having quenched the fire, he assumed a different, small form.

**1.29.1**  The Sūta said: Becoming made of pure gold, blazing brilliantly with rays of light, the bird forcefully entered like a current of water rushing into the ocean.

**1.29.2**  He saw near the nectar a wheel rimmed with razor-sharp blades, whirling ceaselessly, of keen edge, made of iron.

**1.29.3**  Blazing with the radiance of fire and sun, terrible, a cutter-down of those who would steal the Soma — that device of most terrible form had been skillfully constructed by the gods.

**1.29.4**  The sky-traveller, perceiving the gaps in it, began to revolve; contracting his body in an instant, he darted through the spaces between the spokes.

**1.29.5**  Below the wheel, in that place, were two serpents of most fearsome kind — their tongues like lightning, their faces blazing, their eyes blazing — shining with the radiance of a blazing fire.

**1.29.6**  Those best of serpents, possessed of poison in their very gaze, of great heroism, perpetually enraged, and swift — he saw them stationed there for the very purpose of guarding the nectar.

**1.29.7**  Their eyes always inflamed, their gaze forever unwinking — whomever even one of the two looked upon would instantly be reduced to ashes.

**1.29.8**  Suparṇa swiftly blinded the eyes of the two with dust; his own form unseen, he then assailed them on all sides.

**1.29.9**  Mounting upon the bodies of the two, the sky-ranger, son of Vinatā, swiftly cut them down in the middle; then he rushed toward the Soma.

**1.29.10**  That powerful and heroic son of Vinatā then tore out the nectar, and having shattered the device, he leaped upward with great speed.

**1.29.11**  Without drinking the nectar, the powerful bird, swiftly grasping it, departed without fatigue — that sky-traveller who was able to obscure the brilliance of the sun.

**1.29.12**  Then in the sky the son of Vinatā met Viṣṇu; Nārāyaṇa was pleased with him for that act of freedom from greed.

**1.29.13**  The imperishable god said to that sky-traveller, "I am a granter of boons." That sky-ranger chose: "May I always dwell above you."

**1.29.14**  And he spoke these words to Nārāyaṇa once more: "May I be free from old age and immortal even without the nectar."

**1.29.15**  Having received those two boons, Garuḍa said to Viṣṇu: "I also grant a boon to you; let the Blessed Lord choose as well."

**1.29.16**  Kṛṣṇa chose the mighty Garutmān as his mount; and the Blessed Lord made him his banner, saying to him: "You shall abide above me."

**1.29.17**  Chasing the bird, Indra struck him on the body with his vajra — that sky-ranger, that enemy of the gods, who was carrying away the nectar by force.

**1.29.18**  Thus struck by the vajra, Garuḍa, the best of fliers, spoke to Indra with a laugh and with gentle words:

**1.29.19**  "I shall honor the sage from whose bones the vajra was made; and I shall show honour to the vajra itself and to you as well, O Śatakratu."

**1.29.20**  "I now shed a single feather the end of which you shall never find; for the fall of the vajra has never caused me any pain at any time."

**1.29.21**  There all living beings, astonished, spoke at that time upon beholding that beautiful bird: 'Let this be Suparṇa.'

**1.29.22**  And seeing that marvel, Sahasrākṣa, the destroyer of cities, reflecting that this bird is a great being, addressed him.

**1.29.23**  'I wish to know the strength that is supreme and unsurpassed in you, and I desire an eternal friendship with you, O best of birds.'

**1.30.1**  Garuḍa said: 'Let there be friendship between you and me, O god, as you wish, O Purandara. But know my strength to be great and truly unbearable.'

**1.30.2**  'Indeed, the virtuous do not commend self-praise of one's own strength, nor the recounting of one's own virtues by oneself, O Śatakratu.'

**1.30.3**  'But since you, O friend, treating me as a friend have asked me, I shall tell you; for that which is mixed with self-praise ought not to be spoken without reason.'

**1.30.4**  'This broad earth with its mountains and forests, and this ocean with its forests, and you yourself clinging here — all this with a single sinew of my wing, O Śakra —'

**1.30.5**  '— or all the worlds gathered together with their stationary and moving beings, I could carry without fatigue. Know this to be my great strength.'

**1.30.6**  The Sūta said: To that hero who had spoken thus, O Śaunaka, the diadem-wearer, best of the glorious, the lord Indra, benefactor of all beings, replied.

**1.30.7**  'Let this supreme and eternal friendship of mine be accepted now. You have no need of the Soma; give the Soma to me — for those from whom you would give it would trouble us.'

**1.30.8**  Garuḍa said: 'For a certain reason I am carrying this Soma. I will not give it to anyone whatsoever to take away.'

**1.30.9**  'But wherever I myself set it down, O Sahasrākṣa, then you swiftly take it away, O lord of the thirty gods.'

**1.30.10**  Śakra said: 'I am pleased by this speech you have spoken here, O born-of-an-egg. Whatever boon you desire from me, take it, O best of birds.'

**1.30.11**  The Sūta said: Thus addressed, he replied thus, remembering the sons of Kadrū, and also recalling the deception done regarding his mother's enslavement.

**1.30.12**  'I am master of all, and I shall fulfil your request as well. O Śakra, may the mighty serpents become my food.'

**1.30.13**  Having said 'So be it,' the slayer of demons then followed him, saying to him: 'I shall take the Soma once it is set down.'

**1.30.14**  Then Suparṇa came swiftly to his mother's side, and then addressed all the serpents thus, with great joy.

**1.30.15**  'This amṛta I have brought I shall place on the kuśa grass for you. Having bathed and performed auspicious rites, then eat it, O serpents.'

**1.30.16**  'And this mother shall be a slave no longer; from this day let her be free to me. The word I gave to you has been fulfilled.'

**1.30.17**  Then the serpents went to bathe, having replied to him 'So be it.' And Śakra, snatching up the amṛta, returned again to the triple heaven.

**1.30.18**  Then the serpents, desiring the Soma, came to that spot — having bathed, performed their recitations, joyful, and having performed auspicious rites.

**1.30.19**  The serpents, knowing that it had been taken away and that it was a mere semblance, and that this was the place where the Soma had been, then licked the kuśa grass.

**1.30.20**  Thereupon, by that act, the tongues of the serpents became forked. And those blades of kuśa grass, from the touch of the amṛta, became sacred.

**1.30.21**  Then Suparṇa, supremely joyful, having sported with his mother in that forest — the devourer of serpents, greatly honoured by the birds, his glory unblemished — made Vinatā rejoice.

**1.30.22**  Whoever constantly hears this tale or recites it in an assembly of leading brāhmaṇas shall, without doubt, attain the triple heaven, gaining merit through the glorification of the great-souled lord of birds.

**1.31.1**  Śaunaka said: 'The cause of the curse on the serpents, and of the mother and her son, and of Vinatā, O son of a Sūta, you have narrated.'

**1.31.2**  'The granting of boons by the husband to Kadrū and Vinatā, and also the names of the two birds born of Vinatā, have been told by you.'

**1.31.3**  'But the names of the serpents you do not recite, O son of a Sūta. We wish to hear the principal names as well.'

**1.31.4**  The Sūta said: 'Because of the great number of names of the serpents, O wealth of asceticism, I shall not recite all of them. Hear from me only the principal ones.'

**1.31.5**  Śeṣa was born first, then Vāsuki; and Airāvata, Takṣaka, and Karkoṭaka and Dhanaṃjaya.

**1.31.6**  Kāliya and Maṇināga, and the serpent Apūraṇa, and also the serpent Piñjaraka, then Elāpatra and Vāmana.

**1.31.7**  The two serpents Nīla and Anīla, and also Kalmāṣa and Śabala, and Āryaka and Ādika, and also the serpent Śalapotaka.

**1.31.8**  Sumanomukha and Dadhimukha, and also Vimalapiṇḍaka; Āpta and also Koṭanaka, Śaṅkha and Vālaśikha as well.

**1.31.9**  Niṣṭhyūnaka, Hemaguha, Nahuṣa and Piṅgala, Bāhyakarṇa and Hastipada, and also Mudgarapiṇḍaka.

**1.31.10**  Kambala and Aśvatara, and also the serpent Kālīyaka, and the two serpents Vṛtta and Saṃvartaka, and two known as the Padmas.

**1.31.11**  The serpent Śaṅkhanaka, and also another named Sphaṇḍaka; the great serpent Kṣemaka and the serpent Piṇḍāraka as well.

**1.31.12**  Karavīra, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, Eḷaka, Bilvapāṇḍuka, Mūṣakāda, Śaṅkhaśiras, Pūrṇadaṃṣṭra, and Haridraka.

**1.31.13**  Aparājita, Jyotika the serpent, and Śrīvaha; Kauravya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Puṣkara, and also Śalyaka.

**1.31.14**  Virajā, Subāhu, and the mighty Śālipiṇḍa, Hastibhadra, Piṭharaka, Mukhara, and Koṇavāsana.

**1.31.15**  Kuñjara, Kurara, and also the serpent Prabhākara, Kumuda and Kumudākṣa, Tittiri and Halika, and both Karkara and Akarkara, and Kuṇḍodara and Mahodara.

**1.31.16**  These serpents have been named in order of prominence, O best of twice-born. Because of the great number of names, the others have not been recited.

**1.31.17**  The offspring of these, and the lineages of those offspring — regarding them I do not speak, O best of twice-born, deeming them to be without number.

**1.31.18**  Many thousands, millions, and tens of millions here — truly impossible to count — are the serpents, O wealth of asceticism.

**1.32.1**  Śaunaka said: 'Indeed the serpents were born, O dear one, mighty and unapproachable. But having come to know that curse, what did they do next?'

**1.32.2**  The Sūta said: Among them, the blessed Śeṣa of great renown, abandoning Kadrū, undertook vast austerities, living on air, with restrained vows.

**1.32.3**  Reaching Gandhamādana, and Badarī, intent on asceticism; at Gokarṇa, in the forest of Puṣkara, and on the slopes of the Himālayas.

**1.32.4**  In those various holy tīrthas and sacred shrines, living in solitude, disciplined, constantly, with his senses conquered.

**1.32.5**  The Grandfather beheld him practising terrible austerities — the lord, his flesh, skin, and sinews withered, wearing matted locks and bark garments.

**1.32.6**  The Grandfather spoke to him, holding to truth, as he performed austerities: 'What is this you are doing, Śeṣa? Ensure the well-being of living creatures.'

**1.32.7**  'For with your fierce austerity you cause affliction to living creatures, O sinless one. Tell me your desire, O Śeṣa — that which has long been lodged in your heart.'

**1.32.8**  Śeṣa said: 'All my brothers from the same mother are of dull mind. I have no desire to live with them — may Your Honour consent to this.'

**1.32.9**  'They constantly envy one another like enemies; therefore I practise austerity, thinking: may I not see them.'

**1.32.10**  'They constantly do not endure Vinatā and her son, and our other brother Vainateya, O Grandfather.'

**1.32.11**  'They hate him exceedingly, and he too is of very great strength, by virtue of the boon from his father, the great-souled Kaśyapa.'

**1.32.12**  'Therefore I, having undertaken austerity, shall abandon this body — so that even after death there may be no association with them for me.'

**1.32.13**  Brahmā said: 'I know, O Śeṣa, the conduct of all your brothers. And from the fault of your mother there is indeed great danger for your brothers.'

**1.32.14**  'And a remedy has already been arranged here beforehand, O serpent. For all of your brothers, you ought not to grieve.'

**1.32.15**  'And choose a boon from me, O Śeṣa, whatever you desire. For I will grant you a boon today; my pleasure in you is supreme.'

**1.32.16**  'By good fortune your mind is fixed on dharma, O best of serpents. Therefore may your mind be firmly stable in dharma even more.'

**1.32.17**  Śeṣa said: 'This very thing is the boon I desire today, O Great-grandfather: may my mind delight in dharma, in tranquillity, and in austerity, O Lord.'

**1.32.18**  Brahmā said: 'I am pleased by this self-restraint and tranquillity of yours, O Śeṣa. But this task must be done by you, by my command, for the welfare of living beings.'

**1.32.19**  'This earth adorned with mountains and forests, with its oceans, with its towns and cities — O Śeṣa, support it properly as it trembles, so that it may be steady.'

**1.32.20**  Śeṣa said: 'As the god, the granter of boons, the lord of beings, the lord of the earth, the lord of the world commands, so shall I hold the earth steady. Place it upon my head, O Lord of beings.'

**1.32.21**  Brahmā said: 'Go beneath the earth, O best of serpents — she herself will give you an opening. By you holding this earth up, a great favour will be done for me, O Śeṣa.'

**1.32.22**  The Sūta said: Having said 'So be it,' he entered the opening. That lord of the earth, the foremost of the best of serpents, stands there, bearing on his head this goddess Earth, grasping her with her ocean-rim on all sides.

**1.32.23**  Brahmā said: 'You are Śeṣa, O best of serpents, the god of dharma. You alone bear this earth with your infinite coils encompassing it all — even as I do, even as Balabhit does.'

**1.32.24**  The Sūta said: Thus the serpent Ananta, powerful in might, dwells beneath the earth, holding the earth alone, the mighty one, by Brahmā's command.

**1.32.25**  And the blessed Grandfather, best of the immortals, then granted Suparṇa, the son of Vinatā, as a friend to Ananta.

**1.33.1**  The Sūta said: Having heard that curse from their mother, the best of serpents, Vāsuki, began to think: 'How may this curse not come to pass?'

**1.33.2**  Then he took counsel on all sides with his brothers led by Airāvata — those who were devoted to dharma.

**1.33.3**  Vāsuki said: 'This curse as declared you all know, O sinless ones. For the sake of release from that curse, having deliberated, let us strive.'

**1.33.4**  'For all curses there is a counter-remedy; yet there may be no release for those who have been cursed by their own mother, O serpents.'

**1.33.5**  'Upon hearing that we were cursed in the presence of the Imperishable, the Immeasurable, and Truth itself, a trembling arises in my heart.'

**1.33.6**  'Surely this our complete destruction has been proclaimed. For that imperishable god did not restrain her as she cursed.'

**1.33.7**  'Therefore let us deliberate here on the welfare of the serpents, so that it may be for all of us; let not this time pass us by.'

**1.33.8**  'Even while deliberating we may perceive a means for deliverance — just as the gods once found the hidden fire that had entered a cave.'

**1.33.9**  'Such that that sacrifice may not take place, or such that it may be defeated — the sacrifice of Janamejaya that is the instrument of the serpents' destruction.'

**1.33.10**  The Sūta said: Saying 'So be it,' all those sons of Kadrū assembled together and made a compact there — skilled in the wisdom of counsel.

**1.33.11**  Some of the serpents there said: 'Let us become foremost brāhmaṇas and beg Janamejaya, saying: may your sacrifice not take place.'

**1.33.12**  But other serpents there, fancying themselves learned, said: 'All of us shall become his trusted ministers, well esteemed.'

**1.33.13**  He will ask us to determine the purpose in all matters; there we shall offer our counsel so that the sacrifice may be averted.

**1.33.14**  Knowing us, who are well esteemed, to be the best among the wise, that king will clearly ask us for the sake of the sacrifice — and we shall say: no.

**1.33.15**  Showing many terrible faults pertaining to the next world and to this one, with reasons and grounds, we shall argue that the sacrifice should not take place.

**1.33.16**  Or, whoever shall be the officiating priest at that rite — one who knows the ritual procedure of the serpent sacrifice and is devoted to serving the king's interest —

**1.33.17**  Let some serpent go and bite him; he shall die. When that performer of the sacrifice is slain, the rite shall not proceed.

**1.33.18**  And whatever other priests versed in the serpent sacrifice shall serve as his officiants — we shall bite them all; thus the deed will be accomplished.

**1.33.19**  Then other serpents of righteous soul deliberated there: "This is foolishness on your part — the slaying of a brahmin is not a thing of merit."

**1.33.20**  "For calm in adversity, rooted properly in right conduct, is the highest good; but dominance of unrighteousness would destroy the entire world."

**1.33.21**  Other serpents then said: "Becoming clouds with lightning, we shall quench the blazing sacrificial fire with rain."

**1.33.22**  "Or let other excellent serpents go by night and swiftly steal the ladles and sacrificial vessels from the heedless attendants — thus the obstruction will be accomplished."

**1.33.23**  "Or let serpents at that sacrifice, in hundreds and thousands, bite all the people — thus terror will come about."

**1.33.24**  "Or let the serpents defile the prepared food with their own urine and excrement, destroying all the food."

**1.33.25**  Others said there: "Let us become his priests; we will obstruct the sacrifice — let fees be given." And having come under our sway, he will act as we desire.

**1.33.26**  Others said there: "Let us seize the king while he is sporting in the water, bring him home, and bind him — thus the rite shall not take place."

**1.33.27**  Other serpents who were doers of good deeds said there: "Let us quickly seize and bite him — thus the deed will be accomplished. When he is dead, the root of our misfortunes will be severed."

**1.33.28**  "This indeed is the final counsel agreed upon by all; or as you, O lord, may think best — let that be arranged quickly."

**1.33.29**  Having spoken thus, they all looked toward Vāsuki, the lord of serpents; and Vāsuki too, having reflected, spoke to those serpents.

**1.33.30**  "This final counsel of yours is not what I consider should be done, O serpents; none of these plans of all the serpents pleases me."

**1.33.31**  "But what is to be arranged here for the benefit of all of you — I am greatly tormented by this, since both the merits and the defects rest with me."

**1.34.1**  The Sūta said: Having heard the words of all of them — the various proposals — and having heard the speech of Vāsuki, Elāpatra spoke thus.

**1.34.2**  "That sacrifice will not fail to take place; nor will that king be otherwise — Janamejaya the Pāṇḍava descendant, from whom comes our great fear."

**1.34.3**  "A man who is struck by fate, O king, must take shelter in fate alone — there is no other recourse in that matter."

**1.34.4**  "This fear of ours is thus from fate, O best of serpents; let us take shelter in fate alone in this matter — and hear my words."

**1.34.5**  "When the curse was being uttered, I heard those words at that time, seated in fear on our mother's lap, O best of serpents."

**1.34.6**  "O best among serpents, O lord of great splendor, the gods, afflicted with grief, approached the Grandfather, saying 'The fierce ones, the fierce ones!'"

**1.34.7**  The gods said: "Who indeed, having obtained beloved sons, would curse them thus, O Grandfather, except Kadrū of fierce nature — before you, O god of gods?"

**1.34.8**  "And you too uttered the words 'So be it' to her speech, O Grandfather — this we wish to understand: what is the reason why she was not restrained?"

**1.34.9**  Brahman said: "Many serpents are fierce, of terrible might, and overflowing with venom; wishing for the welfare of living beings, I did not restrain her at that time."

**1.34.10**  "Those that bite, the vile ones that walk in evil and overflow with venom — their destruction will come; but not those who walk in righteousness."

**1.34.11**  "And the reason for the deliverance of those serpents from that great fear — hear that now, when the time has come."

**1.34.12**  "In the clan of the Yāyāvaras, a great wise sage shall arise, famed as Jaratkāru, of brilliant energy, with subdued senses."

**1.34.13**  "His son, born of Jaratkāru, of great austerity, named Āstīka, shall stop that sacrifice at that time; and there the serpents who shall be righteous will be released."

**1.34.14**  The gods said: "That chief of sages, O god, Jaratkāru of great austerity — upon whom shall that mighty one, valiant in power, beget his great-souled son?"

**1.34.15**  Brahman said: "Upon a maiden of the same name as himself, O gods — that best of twice-born, that mighty one, shall beget an offspring equal in valor."

**1.34.16**  Elāpatra said: "'So be it,' the gods said to that Grandfather; and having spoken thus, the gods departed, and so did that divine Grandfather."

**1.34.17**  "I thus foresee this, O Vāsuki: your sister who is known as Jaratkāru — give her to him."

**1.34.18**  "To the sage of holy vows who will come begging like a mendicant, give her for the pacification of the serpents' fear — this deliverance I heard of."

**1.35.1**  The Sūta said: O best of twice-born, having heard the words of Elāpatra, all the serpents, with rejoicing hearts, honored him saying "Well said, well said!"

**1.35.2**  From that time forward Vāsuki carefully guarded that maiden Jaratkāru, his sister; and he experienced the greatest joy.

**1.35.3**  Then no very great time seemed to pass before all the gods and asuras churned the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa.

**1.35.4**  There the serpent Vāsuki, best among the mighty, served as the rope; and having completed that labor, they approached the Grandfather.

**1.35.5**  The gods together with Vāsuki then said to the Grandfather: "O blessed one, this Vāsuki, afraid of the curse, is greatly tormented."

**1.35.6**  "You should remove this mental anguish arising from his mother's curse, O god — he who desires the welfare of his kinsmen."

**1.35.7**  "For this king of serpents has always been helpful and dear to us; show your grace, O lord of gods, and quench the fever of his mind."

**1.35.8**  Brahman said: "That which was declared to him long ago by the serpent Elāpatra — that very word was dispensed by my own mind, O immortals."

**1.35.9**  "Let this lord of serpents carry out that word which has come to its appointed time; the evil ones will perish, but not those who walk in righteousness."

**1.35.10**  "That twice-born Jaratkāru, devoted to fierce austerity, has been born; let this one give him his sister Jaratkāru at the proper time."

**1.35.11**  "What was spoken at that time by the serpent Elāpatra, O gods — that is for the benefit of the serpents; it is so and not otherwise."

**1.35.12**  The Sūta said: Hearing these words of the Grandfather, that lord of serpents then stationed many serpents, always engaged, to watch over Jaratkāru.

**1.35.13**  "When the mighty Jaratkāru wishes to choose a wife, come quickly and inform me — that will be for our good."

**1.36.1**  Śaunaka said: "O son of the Sūta, you have mentioned the name Jaratkāru — I wish to hear about that great-souled sage."

**1.36.2**  "For what reason is this name Jaratkāru renowned on earth? You should properly explain the derivation of the name Jaratkāru."

**1.36.3**  The Sūta said: "'Jara' they call a terrible wasting away; 'kāru' denotes the body — he had such a body; and that wise one, little by little,

**1.36.4**  wore it away through fierce austerity — therefore he is called Jaratkāru, O brahmin; and likewise Vāsuki's sister."

**1.36.5**  Thus addressed, the righteous-souled Śaunaka laughed, and having acknowledged Ugraśravas, said "Well answered."

**1.36.6**  The Sūta said: Then, for a great length of time, that sage of sharpened vow, the wise one devoted to austerity, did not desire a wife.

**1.36.7**  That great-souled one, practicing upward retention of seed, absorbed in austerity, devoted to sacred study, free from fear and weariness, wandered over the whole earth; and he did not desire a wife even in his mind.

**1.36.8**  Then, at another time that arrived, there was a king renowned as Parīkṣit, the upholder of the Kaurava lineage.

**1.36.9**  Just as the mighty-armed Pāṇḍu, the foremost archer on earth, was fond of hunting — so was his great-grandfather of old.

**1.36.10**  Piercing deer, boars, hyenas, buffaloes, and other various forest creatures, that lord of the earth wandered about.

**1.36.11**  Once, having wounded a deer with a straight-jointed arrow, he gave chase into the dense forest, bow in hand.

**1.36.12**  Just as the blessed Rudra, having wounded the sacrifice-deer in the sky, followed after it with bow in hand, searching here and there.

**1.36.13**  For a deer once wounded by him does not go away alive into the forest; but this was surely a portent of his going to heaven — the deer that was wounded and vanished on that king Parīkṣit.

**1.36.14**  Led far away by that deer, that lord of the earth, exhausted and suffering from thirst, came upon a sage in the forest.

**1.36.15**  He was seated in the cow-pasture, largely consuming the foam flowing from the mouths of calves drinking milk.

**1.36.16**  Running swiftly toward that sage of sharpened vow, the king, raising his bow and afflicted with hunger and fatigue, asked him.

**1.36.17**  "Ho there, O brahmin! I am the king Parīkṣit, son of Abhimanyu. A deer I wounded has gone missing — have you perhaps seen it?"

**1.36.18**  That sage, observing his vow of silence, said nothing at all to him; so the angry king placed a dead serpent on his shoulder with the tip of his bow.

**1.36.19**  Lifting it up with the tip of his bow, he looked at him, but spoke not a word to him — neither auspicious nor inauspicious.

**1.36.20**  That king, having cast off his anger, and distressed at seeing him in that condition, went to the city; the sage remained sitting just as he was.

**1.36.21**  He had a young son of sharp energy and great austerity, named Śṛṅgī, of great wrath, hard to appease, and of mighty vows.

**1.36.22**  He regularly attended upon the supreme lord Brahman, the divine one devoted to the welfare of all beings, with complete self-restraint; and having been given leave by that Brahman, he went home.

**1.36.23**  O best of twice-born, as he was coming, he was addressed in jest by a playful, laughing friend — the son of a sage named Kṛśa, who was extremely hot-tempered, wrathful, and like venom, the sage's son.

**1.36.24**  "Your father, though so energetic and such an ascetic, carries a corpse on his shoulder — do not be so proud, O Śṛṅgī."

**1.36.25**  "Do not speak any such words to the sons of sages — to the accomplished ones, the knowers of Brahman, the ascetics such as we are."

**1.36.26**  "Where is your self-importance now? Where are such words of yours, born of arrogance — you whose father you shall see carrying a corpse like that?"

**1.37.1**  The Sūta said: Thus addressed, that energetic Śṛṅgī, filled with anger, hearing that his teacher was carrying a dead thing, was consumed with fury.

**1.37.2**  Looking at that Kṛśa and suppressing a kind reply, he asked: "How is it that my father is today a carrier of a dead thing?"

**1.37.3**  Kṛśa said: "Dear friend, the king Parīkṣit, while ranging about on a hunt, today hung a dead serpent on your father's shoulder."

**1.37.4**  Śṛṅgī said: "What wrong did my father do to that evil-souled king? Tell me truthfully, O Kṛśa — and witness the power of my austerity."

**1.37.5**  Kṛśa said: That king Parīkṣit, son of Abhimanyu, having gone out hunting, chased a deer alone after wounding it with a feathered arrow.

**1.37.6**  Not finding the deer as he roamed that great forest, the king, upon seeing your father, questioned him — though he was one who did not speak.

**1.37.7**  Him standing there motionless as a post, the king — exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue — questioned your father again and again about the lost deer.

**1.37.8**  But he, bound by his vow of silence, did not answer him at all; and the king, with the tip of his bow, placed a dead serpent upon his shoulder.

**1.37.9**  O Śṛṅgin, your father sits just so even now, steadfast in his vow; and that king has returned to his own city, Gajāhvaya.

**1.37.10**  The Sūta said: Hearing this, the son of the sage stood as though he had struck the sky, his eyes red with rage, blazing as it were with wrath.

**1.37.11**  Seized by anger, that brilliant one then cursed the king, touching water and overpowered by the force and violence of his fury.

**1.37.12**  Śṛṅgin said: That sinful king who has thrown a dead serpent upon the shoulder of my aged father while he was in distress —

**1.37.13**  — that wicked one, Takṣaka the foremost of serpents, venomous-fanged, of fierce brilliance, urged on by the power of my words in great fury,

**1.37.14**  shall conduct him from this day to the abode of Yama within seven nights — this despiser of brahmins, this disgrace to the Kurus.

**1.37.15**  The Sūta said: Having thus cursed the king in his anger, Śṛṅgin went to his father, who sat in that grove still bearing the dead serpent.

**1.37.16**  Seeing his father with the dead serpent still upon his shoulder, Śṛṅgin was filled with grief and anger anew.

**1.37.17**  From grief he shed tears and spoke these words to his father: "Father, having heard of this insult inflicted upon you by that wicked one —

**1.37.18**  — by King Parīkṣit, I have in my fury cursed that king with the terrible curse he deserves, the lowest of the Kuru line.

**1.37.19**  On the seventh day, Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents, shall conduct that wretch to the dreadful abode of Vaivasvata.

**1.37.20**  His father addressed him, so filled with anger, and said: O brahmin, you have not done what is pleasing to me, my son; this is not the dharma of ascetics.

**1.37.21**  We dwell in the realm of that king; we are properly protected by him. Therefore I do not approve of his being harmed.

**1.37.22**  For such as we are, we must always forgive a king acting in any manner, my son — for dharma when destroyed destroys in return; of this there is no doubt.

**1.37.23**  If the king did not protect us, we would suffer greatly; we would not be able to practise dharma in peace and comfort, my son.

**1.37.24**  Being protected by kings who act according to the scriptures, we practise abundant dharma, and they too receive a rightful share of that dharma.

**1.37.25**  Parīkṣit in particular protects us even as his great-grandfather did; he protects his subjects as a king ought to protect them.

**1.37.26**  By him — wearied today, hungry and fatigued, an ascetic — this was done without knowing my vow. Of this there is no doubt.

**1.37.27**  Therefore this wrong act has been rashly committed by you out of childishness; for the king in no way deserves a curse from us, my son.

**1.38.1**  Śṛṅgin said: Whether this was rashness, father, or a wrong deed done, whether it pleases you or not — the word I have spoken is not false.

**1.38.2**  It shall not be otherwise, father — this I tell you. I do not speak falsehood even in jest; how much less when pronouncing a curse.

**1.38.3**  Śamīka said: I know you, my son, to be of fierce power and true speech; you have never spoken what is untrue — this too shall not prove false.

**1.38.4**  Nevertheless, a son, however grown, must always be instructed by his father, so that he may become endowed with virtues and attain great fame.

**1.38.5**  How much more so when you are but a child, though formed by asceticism, O lord. And indeed the anger of great souls who are powerful grows exceedingly.

**1.38.6**  So I see that you, O best upholder of dharma, must be spoken to, considering both your filial status and your youth, as well as this rashness of yours.

**1.38.7**  Therefore, be possessed of calmness, live subsisting on forest food, and abandon this anger — do not thus forsake dharma.

**1.38.8**  For anger destroys the dharma that ascetics have accumulated through suffering; and those bereft of dharma do not attain the desired goal.

**1.38.9**  Serenity alone is the cause of perfection for ascetics who possess forbearance; both this world and the next belong to those endowed with forbearance.

**1.38.10**  Therefore conduct yourself always with forbearance as your nature, with senses conquered; through forbearance you shall attain worlds next to that of Brahman.

**1.38.11**  But I, resorting to calmness, shall do what can be done today — I shall send a messenger to the king this very day.

**1.38.12**  "You have been cursed by my son, a child of immature understanding, O king, who was provoked to indignation upon witnessing this insult to me inflicted by you."

**1.38.13**  The Sūta said: Having given these instructions to his disciple, that great ascetic of good vows, moved by compassion, sent him to King Parīkṣit.

**1.38.14**  Having enjoined him to convey greetings and also to recount the entire matter, he sent the disciple named Gauramukha, a virtuous and composed man.

**1.38.15**  Quickly approaching the king, the enhancer of the Kuru line, and first being announced by the doorkeepers, he entered the royal palace.

**1.38.16**  After being duly honoured by the king, the brahmin Gauramukha, having rested, related everything in full to the king — the terrible message of Śamīka just as it was spoken — in the presence of the ministers.

**1.38.17**  "There lives in your realm, O king of kings, a sage named Śamīka — one of supreme righteous soul, self-restrained, calm, and of great austerity.

**1.38.18**  O tiger among men, O best of the Bharatas, a serpent robbed of life was placed by you on his shoulder with the tip of your bow. He himself forgave your act, but his son could not endure it.

**1.38.19**  You have been cursed by him, O king, without his father's knowledge: Takṣaka shall be your death within seven nights.

**1.38.20**  'Protect yourself in this matter,' he said again and again; yet it cannot be made otherwise by anyone at all.

**1.38.21**  For he could not restrain his son overcome by anger; therefore I have been sent by him for your welfare, O king.

**1.38.22**  Hearing that terrible news, the king, delight of the Kurus, was tormented with remorse for having committed that wrong — the king of great penance.

**1.38.23**  And hearing that the great sage had been observing a vow of silence, the king's heart was again burned with grief.

**1.38.24**  Recognising too the compassionate nature of Śamīka, he was tormented yet further for having committed that offence against the sage.

**1.38.25**  For the king did not grieve so much upon hearing of his impending death as he — who was like an immortal — lamented having committed that deed.

**1.38.26**  The king then sent Gauramukha back with the message: "May the revered one be gracious to me."

**1.38.27**  And as soon as Gauramukha had departed, the king, with an agitated mind, deliberated with his ministers.

**1.38.28**  Having decided, together with his ministers, and being expert in the essence of counsel, he had a palace built on a single pillar, well-guarded.

**1.38.29**  He stationed guards there, as well as physicians with medicines, and brahmins accomplished in mantras, on all sides.

**1.38.30**  Residing there, he conducted all affairs of state, learned in dharma, and guarded on all sides together with his ministers.

**1.38.31**  But on the seventh day arriving, O best of brahmins, the learned Kāśyapa came to treat that king.

**1.38.32**  For it had come to his hearing that today Takṣaka, foremost of serpents, would conduct that best of kings to the abode of Yama.

**1.38.33**  Thinking to himself: "I shall cure him after he is bitten by the lord of serpents — in that I shall find both profit and merit," he went forth.

**1.38.34**  But the king of serpents Takṣaka saw Kāśyapa going along the road with single-pointed mind, and assuming the form of a brahmin of advanced age,

**1.38.35**  the lord of serpents addressed Kāśyapa, foremost of sages: "Where does the venerable one hasten, and what task does he wish to accomplish?"

**1.38.36**  Kāśyapa said: Takṣaka, foremost of serpents, will today burn with his blazing power the king Parīkṣit, born of the Kuru lineage, the subduer of foes.

**1.38.37**  Him, bitten by that lord of serpents whose energy equals fire, that king of boundless might, the upholder of the Pāṇḍava lineage — I go, dear one, in haste to cure forthwith.

**1.38.38**  Takṣaka said: I am that Takṣaka, O brahmin; I shall burn that lord of the earth. Turn back — you are not able to cure one bitten by me.

**1.38.39**  Kāśyapa said: O serpent, it is my firm conviction that I shall cure that king after he has been bitten by you, relying on the power of my knowledge.

**1.39.1**  Takṣaka said: If you are able to cure one bitten by me here, then revive this tree that I have bitten, O Kāśyapa.

**1.39.2**  Display the utmost power of your mantras and exert yourself; I shall burn this banyan tree before your eyes, O foremost of brahmins.

**1.39.3**  Kāśyapa said: Bite, O king of serpents, whatever tree you have in mind; I shall revive it after you have bitten it, O serpent.

**1.39.4**  The Sūta said: Thus addressed by the great-souled Kāśyapa, that foremost of serpents, the lord of serpents, approached and bit a banyan tree.

**1.39.5**  That tree, bitten by him of great brilliance, immediately burst into flames on all sides, suffused with the venom of the poison-fanged serpent.

**1.39.6**  Having burned that tree, the serpent again addressed Kāśyapa: "Make the effort, O best of brahmins; revive this lord of the forest."

**1.39.7**  Then, the tree having been reduced to ash by the power of the king of serpents, Kāśyapa gathered all the ash and spoke these words:

**1.39.8**  "Behold the power of my knowledge upon this lord of the forest, O king of serpents; I shall revive it before your eyes, O serpent."

**1.39.9**  Then that blessed and learned Kāśyapa, best of brahmins, revived the tree that had been reduced to a heap of ash, by means of his knowledge.

**1.39.10**  He caused it first to sprout, then to bear two leaves, then to put forth foliage and branches, and then to become a full tree once again.

**1.39.11**  Seeing the tree restored to life by the great-souled Kāśyapa, Takṣaka said: "O brahmin, this is exceedingly wondrous in you.

**1.39.12**  O lord of brahmins, you who could neutralise the venom of one like me — what purpose do you seek to gain by going there, O treasury of austerity?

**1.39.13**  Whatever fruit you desire to obtain from that best of kings, I myself will give you that, even if it be difficult to obtain.

**1.39.14**  For in the case of a king whose life is waning, overwhelmed by a brahmin's curse, even your best efforts may meet with uncertain success, O brahmin.

**1.39.15**  And then your fame, blazing and renowned throughout the three worlds, would vanish from here like a sunbeam robbed of its rays.

**1.39.16**  Kāśyapa said: I go there in desire of wealth — give me that, O serpent; then I shall return home, O best of serpents.

**1.39.17**  Takṣaka said: I will give you today more than whatever wealth you would seek from that king — turn back, O foremost of brahmins.

**1.39.18**  The Sūta said: Hearing the words of Takṣaka, that brilliant and wise Kāśyapa, best of brahmins, reflected deeply about the king.

**1.39.19**  That brilliant one endowed with divine knowledge, having understood that the king, the descendant of Pāṇḍu, had then exhausted his span of life, the sage Kāśyapa turned back — having obtained from Takṣaka as much wealth as he desired.

**1.39.20**  When that great-souled Kāśyapa had turned away at that moment, Takṣaka swiftly went to the city named after the serpents — Hastināpura.

**1.39.21**  And as he went, Takṣaka heard that the lord of the earth was being carefully protected by means of charms, antidotes, and poison-neutralizing medicines.

**1.39.22**  He then reflected: "By what stratagem of illusion can I deceive this king? What means might there be?"

**1.39.23**  Then the serpent Takṣaka, taking fruits, leaves, and water, sent other snakes in the guise of ascetics to the king.

**1.39.24**  Takṣaka said: "Go to the king calmly, on the pretext of a mission, and have the king accept these — fruits, leaves, and water."

**1.39.25**  The Sūta said: Those snakes, instructed by Takṣaka, did exactly so — they presented to the king darbha grass, water, and fruits.

**1.39.26**  The mighty king of kings accepted all of it, and having attended to their business, he said to them: "You may go."

**1.39.27**  When those snakes in the disguise of ascetics had departed, the lord of men spoke to his ministers and friends.

**1.39.28**  "Let all of you eat these sweet fruits that the ascetics have brought — together with me."

**1.39.29**  Then the king along with his minister went to take the fruits. In the fruit taken by the king there appeared a tiny worm — small, dark-eyed, and copper-colored, O Śaunaka.

**1.39.30**  Taking it up, that foremost of kings said to his ministers: "The sun is setting; today I no longer have any fear of poison."

**1.39.31**  "Let that sage's words prove true — let this little worm bite me, becoming Takṣaka by name; in that way the prophecy shall be fulfilled."

**1.39.32**  And those ministers followed his lead, driven by fate. Having spoken thus, that king of kings placed the little worm on his neck, laughed aloud, and swiftly he who was near death lost consciousness.

**1.39.33**  Still laughing, he was coiled by Takṣaka in serpent form, who had emerged from that very fruit — the one that had been presented to the king.

**1.40.1**  The Sūta said: Seeing him thus encoiled by the serpent, all the ministers, their faces gone pale, wept, overwhelmed with grief.

**1.40.2**  Hearing that cry, those ministers fled in all directions, and they saw the wondrous serpent moving through the sky.

**1.40.3**  Overwhelmed with sorrow, they saw Takṣaka, that foremost of serpents, of lotus-like radiance, streaking across the sky as if parting it in two.

**1.40.4**  Then, as the serpent's venom set the palace ablaze and it burned, they abandoned it in fear and fled in all directions; and it fell like a tree struck by lightning.

**1.40.5**  When the king was slain by the power of Takṣaka, the pure brahmin who was the royal chaplain, and likewise all the ministers of that king, performed all the rites for the other world.

**1.40.6**  All the people of the city assembled and made his young son king — that hero of the Kurus whom they called the destroyer of enemies: Janamejaya.

**1.40.7**  Even as a child, that foremost of kings, noble-minded and pre-eminent among the bulls of the Kuru line, governed the kingdom together with those ministers and the royal priest, just as his valiant great-grandfather had done.

**1.40.8**  Then the ministers of that king, seeing him as the scorcher of enemies, approached the Kāśi king Suvarṇavarman and sued for Vapuṣṭamā on his behalf.

**1.40.9**  Then that king, having examined the match by dharmic standards, gave Vapuṣṭamā to that hero of the Kurus; and the hero, having obtained her, was filled with joy, and never again set his mind on any other woman.

**1.40.10**  The valiant one sported with a cheerful heart in lakes full of blooms and in forests; that best of kings disported himself just as Purūravas of old had done upon obtaining Urvaśī.

**1.40.11**  And Vapuṣṭamā too, having obtained that excellent and handsome lord of the earth as husband, delighted him with her love; that beauty of the inner quarters was his joy in all his hours of pleasure.

**1.41.1**  The Sūta said: At this very time, the sage Jaratkāru of great austerities, who had no fixed home, wandered over the entire earth, sleeping wherever evening found him.

**1.41.2**  Of great splendor, practising a severe vow of initiation impossible for the undisciplined, he wandered among sacred tirthas, bathing at each holy site.

**1.41.3**  Living on air alone, taking no food, the sage drying up day by day — he saw his ancestors hanging head-downward in a pit.

**1.41.4**  They were clinging to a clump of vīraṇa grass of which only a single stalk remained, and a rat that lived in the burrow below was slowly gnawing at that stalk.

**1.41.5**  Those without food, emaciated and wretched, hanging in the pit and longing for rescue — he approached those miserable ones, himself appearing wretched, and addressed them.

**1.41.6**  "Who are you, clinging to this clump of vīraṇa grass, now weak because its roots are being eaten by the rat that dwells in the burrow?"

**1.41.7**  "Even the one root of this vīraṇa clump that still remains here, this rat is slowly taking away with its sharp teeth."

**1.41.8**  "Because so little remains, even this will be severed before long; then you will fall head-downward into this very pit."

**1.41.9**  "Seeing you hanging head-downward and fallen into this dire calamity, grief has arisen in me. What good may I do for you?"

**1.41.10**  "Tell me without delay whether I can rescue you from this calamity with a quarter, or a third, or even half of my austerities."

**1.41.11**  "Or perhaps all of you may cross over this difficulty by means of the whole of my austerities — let it be arranged as you wish."

**1.41.12**  The ancestors said: You are a prosperous celibate student who desires to save us here; but, O foremost of brahmins, this cannot be removed by austerity alone.

**1.41.13**  "We have the fruit of our austerities, O son, O best among the eloquent; but, O brahmin, we are falling into an impure hell because our lineage is dying out."

**1.41.14**  "As we hang here, O son, understanding does not come to us — we do not recognize you, though your valor is renowned in the world."

**1.41.15**  "You are prosperous and greatly blessed; out of compassion you have come and grieve for us who are pitiable and deeply pained. Hear who we are, O brahmin."

**1.41.16**  "We are the sages called the Yāyāvaras, of sharp vows; we have fallen from the meritorious worlds into this place because our line is dying, O lord."

**1.41.17**  "Our meritorious austerities are being destroyed, for we have no thread of lineage. There is one thread left to us today, yet it is as good as gone."

**1.41.18**  "He who is the kinsman of the wretched in our family is himself unfortunate — known as Jaratkāru, versed in the Vedas and their auxiliaries, self-controlled, great-souled, of excellent vows, and of very great austerities."

**1.41.19**  "By his greed for austerity we have been brought to this calamity. He has no wife, no son, no kinsman whatsoever."

**1.41.20**  "That is why we hang in this pit, our senses lost, like those without a protector. You, having seen our plight, should speak to him on our behalf so that we may have a guardian."

**1.41.21**  "'Your fathers hang wretched and head-downward in a pit — take a wife and beget offspring, O lord.' For you alone, O wealth of austerity, remain as the single thread of our lineage."

**1.41.22**  "This clump of vīraṇa grass to which you see us clinging, O brahmin — this was our family-stalk, the one that was to have enlarged our line."

**1.41.23**  "These roots of this plant that you see here, O brahmin — these are our lineage-threads, O son, consumed by time."

**1.41.24**  "And that root of it which you see half-gnawed away — to that we all cling; he too is the sole one, and he has taken to austerity."

**1.41.25**  "The rat you see, O brahmin — that is mighty Time itself; it slowly gnaws and wears away that one devoted to austerities — Jaratkāru, the witless, small-minded one, whose mind is consumed by his greed for austerity."

**1.41.26**  "For his austerity will not save us, O noble one — we whose roots are cut, who are utterly fallen, whose minds are struck by Time; behold us, destined for hell as though we were evildoers."

**1.41.27**  "When we have fallen here along with the forefathers before us, he too, cut off by Time, will then go to hell."

**1.41.28**  "Austerity, or sacrifice, or whatever other great purification there may be — none of it equals progeny: such is the opinion of the good, O son."

**1.41.29**  "Having seen this, O son, you should speak to the ascetic Jaratkāru; and what you have seen here must be told to him in full."

**1.41.30**  "So that he may take a wife and beget sons — in that manner, O brahmin, you must address him on our behalf, that we may have a guardian."

**1.42.1**  The Sūta said: Hearing this, Jaratkāru, overwhelmed with pain and sorrow, spoke to his own ancestors in a voice choked with tears out of grief.

**1.42.2**  "I am that very Jaratkāru — the sinful son who is your offspring. Mete out your punishment to me, the ill-doer, the undisciplined one."

**1.42.3**  The ancestors said: O son, by good fortune you have arrived at this place by chance. But why, O brahmin, have you not taken a wife?

**1.42.4**  Jaratkāru said: This thought, O fathers, has always revolved in my heart: as an upward-semened celibate I would convey this body to the next world.

**1.42.5**  "But having seen you hanging thus like birds, O forefathers, my mind has been turned away from celibacy."

**1.42.6**  "I will do what you wish and take a wife — there is no doubt in this — if ever I shall find a maiden who shares my name."

**1.42.7**  "And she who is freely offered, as if in alms — I will accept her; but one whom I would have to maintain, her I will not take."

**1.42.8**  "If I can find such a match, I will enter householder life; otherwise I will not — this is my truth, O forefathers."

**1.42.9**  The Sūta said: Having thus spoken to his ancestors, the sage wandered the earth; yet he found no wife, O Śaunaka, for people said: "This one is too old."

**1.42.10**  When he had fallen into despondency, yet urged on by his ancestors as well, he went into a forest and cried out loudly in deep anguish.

**1.42.11**  "Whatever beings there are in this place — moving or unmoving, or those that are hidden — let them hear my words."

**1.42.12**  "My ancestors, though I abide in fierce austerity, urge me in their distress: 'Take a wife.' Desiring to do what is dear to them, I speak."

**1.42.13**  "I wander the entire earth seeking a maiden given as alms for the purpose of establishing a household; I am a poor man, of a sorrowful nature, set to this task by my ancestors."

**1.42.14**  "Whatever being has a maiden among those I have here proclaimed — let them give her to me as I roam in all directions."

**1.42.15**  "Let them give me that maiden who shares my name and who is offered as if in alms, and whom I will not have to maintain — give me that maiden."

**1.42.16**  Then the serpents who were attentive to Jaratkāru's affairs took that intelligence and reported it to Vāsuki.

**1.42.17**  Hearing their report, that lord of serpents took that maiden adorned with ornaments and went with her into the forest, to the vicinity of that sage.

**1.42.18**  There Vāsuki, the king of serpents, offered that maiden to that great-souled one as if in alms; but O brahmin, he did not accept her.

**1.42.19**  He thought her name was not the same as his; and with the question of maintenance unresolved, being one who stood in a state of liberation, he was of two minds about accepting.

**1.42.20**  Then he asked the name of the maiden, O joy of the Bhṛgu line, and he said to Vāsuki: "I will not maintain her."

**1.43.1**  The Sūta said: Then Vāsuki spoke these words to the sage Jaratkāru: "This maiden is your namesake — she is my sister, endowed with austerities."

**1.43.2**  "I will maintain your wife — accept her, O foremost of twice-born; and I will protect her with all my power, O treasure of austerity."

**1.43.3**  When the serpent had promised "I will maintain my sister," Jaratkāru then went to the dwelling of the serpent.

**1.43.4**  There, that foremost knower of mantras, great in austerity, of mighty vows, righteous-souled, took her hand according to the prescribed rites preceded by sacred formulas.

**1.43.5**  Then, taking his wife and praised by great sages, he went to the bright dwelling sanctioned by the lord of serpents.
