**1.43.6**  There a bed was prepared, covered with splendid coverings; and there Jaratkāru dwelt together with his wife.

**1.43.7**  That best of men made a covenant with his wife there: "What is displeasing to me must never be done, nor ever spoken."

**1.43.8**  "For if you displease me, I shall abandon you and leave this house of yours. Take to heart this word I have now spoken."

**1.43.9**  Then the sister of the serpent lord, deeply agitated and filled with great sorrow, said to him: "So be it."

**1.43.10**  And that illustrious woman, ever wishing to please him, tended her difficult-tempered husband by every cautious and discreet means.

**1.43.11**  Then once, after her purificatory bath at the proper season, the sister of Vāsuki duly approached her husband, the great sage.

**1.43.12**  Then within her a child was conceived, blazing like fire, endowed with great ascetic power, brilliant as Vaiśvānara; and it grew like the moon in the bright fortnight.

**1.43.13**  Then after some days Jaratkāru of great austerity, resting his head in her lap, fell into deep sleep as though exhausted.

**1.43.14**  And while that foremost of brahmins slept, the sun moved toward its setting mountain at the close of the day, O brahmin; then Vāsuki's sister, that wise woman, became fearful of a lapse in religious duty and began to reflect.

**1.43.15**  "Would it be right for me to wake my husband, or not? He is righteous yet difficult-tempered — how can I not offend him?"

**1.43.16**  "Either the wrath of this righteous man, or else a lapse in his religious duty — a lapse in religious duty is certainly the graver of the two": thus she resolved in her mind.

**1.43.17**  "If I wake him, he will certainly be angry; but if the twilight prayer is missed, there will certainly be a breach of his religious duty."

**1.43.18**  Having thus resolved in her mind, that serpent-woman Jaratkāru, the sweet-spoken one, gently addressed the reclining sage of blazing austerity in these words.

**1.43.19**  "Arise, O greatly blessed one — the sun is setting. O lord, touch water and observe the twilight worship, you who are strict in your vows."

**1.43.20**  "This is the hour when the fire-sacrifice is kindled, both lovely and awesome; and now the twilight prayer begins in the western quarter, O master."

**1.43.21**  Thus addressed, the venerable Jaratkāru of great austerity, his lips quivering, spoke these words to his wife.

**1.43.22**  "This is an insult you have offered me, O serpent-woman. I will not stay with you any longer; I shall go the way I came."

**1.43.23**  "For it is my firm conviction that while I sleep, the sun Vibhāvasu has no power to set at its proper time, O fair-thighed one."

**1.43.24**  "Nor would it please anyone who has been insulted to remain here — least of all one of righteous conduct such as I, of my disposition."

**1.43.25**  When Jaratkāru was thus addressed by her husband, Vāsuki's sister spoke with a trembling heart in that dwelling.

**1.43.26**  "It was not out of disrespect that I woke you; I did this so that there might be no breach of your religious duty, O brahmin."

**1.43.27**  Thus addressed by his wife, the great sage Jaratkāru of mighty austerity, seized by anger and resolved to abandon the serpent-woman, spoke.

**1.43.28**  "My word does not speak falsehood — I shall depart, O serpent-woman. For this was the covenant I made with you from the beginning."

**1.43.29**  "I have dwelt here in happiness, O auspicious one. Tell your brother, O timid one: 'That venerable one has departed from here.' And after I have gone, you too should not grieve."

**1.43.30**  Thus addressed, the blameless-limbed Jaratkāru, overwhelmed with worry and grief, replied to her husband Jaratkāru.

**1.43.31**  With a voice choked with tears, a face pale and dry, eyes brimming with tears, hands folded in supplication, that woman of fair limbs steadied herself with composure though her heart was trembling.

**1.43.32**  "O knower of dharma, you should not abandon me who am without fault, who stands firm in dharma, who is ever devoted to your welfare and happiness."

**1.43.33**  "And the purpose for which I was given to you, O best of twice-born ones — if I have not achieved that, what will Vāsuki say to wretched me?"

**1.43.34**  "The offspring longed for from you for the sake of my kinsmen who are oppressed by their mother's curse, O excellent one — that too has not yet come to be seen."

**1.43.35**  "Through the gaining of offspring from you, wellbeing would come to my kinsmen; let not this union with you be fruitless for me, O twice-born one."

**1.43.36**  "Wishing the welfare of my kinsmen, O venerable one, I entreat you — having planted in me this child whose form is not yet manifest, O best of men, how can you, being a great soul, wish to abandon me who am without fault?"

**1.43.37**  Thus addressed, the sage Jaratkāru, wealth of austerity, spoke an apt and fitting word to his wife.

**1.43.38**  "This child exists within you, O fortunate one, comparable to Vaiśvānara — a seer of supreme righteousness, versed in the Vedas and all their branches."

**1.43.39**  Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled great sage Jaratkāru, firmly resolved, departed again for severe austerities.

**1.44.1**  The Sūta said: As soon as her husband had departed, Jaratkāru quickly came to her brother and told him the truth of what had happened, O wealth of austerity.

**1.44.2**  Then that foremost of serpents, having heard the deeply grievous news, spoke to his dejected sister, himself more dejected still.

**1.44.3**  "You know, dear one, what purpose was to be served and the reason you were given — whether a son would be born to you from him for the welfare of the serpents."

**1.44.4**  "That valiant one will surely rescue us from the serpent sacrifice — so did the grandfather formerly tell me, together with the gods."

**1.44.5**  "Is there indeed a child in you from that best of sages, O fortunate one? I do not want the act of marriage of that wise one to have been fruitless."

**1.44.6**  "Indeed it is not proper for me to question you on such a matter; but because the urgency of the task is paramount, I have thus pressed you."

**1.44.7**  "Knowing the difficult nature of your husband, that most austere one, I will not go after him — for he might curse me."

**1.44.8**  "Tell me, dear one, everything your husband did. Remove this terrible thorn that has long been lodged in my heart, O dear one."

**1.44.9**  Then Jaratkāru, thus addressed, replied with words comforting the afflicted Vāsuki, lord of serpents.

**1.44.10**  "When I asked him for the sake of offspring, that great soul of mighty austerity said 'it exists,' pointing to my womb, and then he departed."

**1.44.11**  "Even in casual speech I do not recall him ever saying anything false — how then, O king, would he speak falsely in a matter of such consequence?"

**1.44.12**  "You must not grieve regarding the purpose, O serpent lord — your nephew will be born, blazing with the radiance of fire and sun."

**1.44.13**  "Having said this to me, O brother, my husband went to the forest of austerities; therefore let this great sorrow that lodges in your mind depart."

**1.44.14**  Having heard this, that lord of serpents Vāsuki accepted his sister's words with great joy, saying "So be it."

**1.44.15**  That foremost of serpents honored his sister born of the same womb with comforting words, gifts, and fitting reverence.

**1.44.16**  Then that child of mighty radiance, brilliant as the sun, grew in the womb — like the moon risen in the bright fortnight in the sky, O foremost of twice-born ones.

**1.44.17**  In due time, O brahmin, that sister of the serpent gave birth to a boy who resembled the embryo of a god, the remover of his father's and mother's fear.

**1.44.18**  And he grew up there in the dwelling of the serpent king; he mastered the Vedas along with their branches from the Bhārgava, the son of Cyavana.

**1.44.19**  Even as a boy he observed his vows, endowed with wisdom, courage, and virtue; and his name became known throughout the worlds as Āstīka.

**1.44.20**  Because his father departed for the forest saying 'it exists' even while he was still in the womb, therefore his name became celebrated as Āstīka.

**1.44.21**  While still a boy he moved about there, that one of boundless intellect, carefully guarded and protected in the house of the serpent king.

**1.44.22**  Growing up like the venerable lord of the gods, the trident-bearer, the bestower of gold, he filled all those serpents with joy.

**1.45.1**  Śaunaka said: What king Janamejaya then asked his ministers regarding his father's passing to heaven — tell me that again in full.

**1.45.2**  The Sūta said: Listen, O brahmin, to how the ministers, being questioned by the king, all narrated the death of Parīkṣit.

**1.45.3**  Janamejaya said: You gentlemen know how my father conducted himself and how that greatly renowned one met his death in due time.

**1.45.4**  "For having heard from you the full account of my father's life and conduct, I shall pursue what is good and never what is contrary to it."

**1.45.5**  The Sūta said: Then the ministers, questioned by that great-souled one, those learned men versed in all dharma, spoke their words to king Janamejaya.

**1.45.6**  "Your father was righteous-souled, great-souled, a protector of his subjects — hear how that great soul conducted himself here."

**1.45.7**  "That king, knowing dharma, protected the four social orders established in their own duties, ruling righteously — as though dharma incarnate."

**1.45.8**  "That glorious one of incomparable valor protected this noble earth; he had no enemies, nor did he hate anyone — equal to all beings, he was like Prajāpati himself."

**1.45.9**  "Brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, each established in their proper duties and contented in mind, O king, were well governed by that king."

**1.45.10**  "He cared for widows, the helpless, the wretched, and the disabled; that fair-looking one was like a second moon to all beings."

**1.45.11**  "His people were content and well-fed; that glorious king was true of speech and firm in valor; he was a student of the science of archery under Śāradvatī's son."

**1.45.12**  "Your father was dear to Govinda, O Janamejaya, and that greatly renowned one was dear to all the world."

**1.45.13**  "When the Kurus were all but extinct, he was born of Uttarā; through him, that mighty son of Saubhadra's line, Parīkṣit came to be."

**1.45.14**  "Skilled in royal dharma and statecraft, endowed with every virtue, that king had conquered his senses, was self-possessed, intelligent, and attended upon by elders."

**1.45.15**  "Master of the six categories, of great intellect, supremely versed in policy and dharma — your father protected these subjects for sixty years, then met his fated end, which could not be turned aside, through a serpent."

**1.45.16**  "Then you, O best of men, rightfully obtained this kingdom that has come down through the Kuru lineage — you were born noble, a protector of all beings, even as a child."

**1.45.17**  Janamejaya said: In this family there never was a king who was not a benefactor and beloved of his subjects — as one sees by looking at the great conduct of our forefathers who were utterly devoted to right conduct.

**1.45.18**  "How did such a father of mine meet his death? Tell me truly; I wish to hear it in full."

**1.45.19**  The Sūta said: Thus urged by the king, all those ministers, devoted to the welfare of their lord, spoke the full account to the king.

**1.45.20**  "Your father, O king, was always fond of the hunt, like the greatly blessed Pāndu — the foremost of bow-bearers in battle — entrusting all royal affairs entirely to us."

**1.45.21**  "Once, while roaming the forest, he pierced a deer with an arrow, and after wounding it, he swiftly pursued that deer into the dense jungle."

**1.45.22**  "Going on foot, sword belted at his side, quiver of arrows strapped on, your father could not find the deer that had vanished in the thicket."

**1.45.23**  "Exhausted, advanced in years, sixty years old and feeling the weight of age, and hungry, he spotted a sage close by in the great forest."

**1.45.24**  That king, best among kings, questioned the sage who was bound by a vow of silence; but the sage did not say anything to him, even though he was being asked.

**1.45.25**  Then the king, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, came immediately under the sway of anger toward that sage who stood like a post, observing his vow of silence, calm and quiet.

**1.45.26**  Indeed the king did not understand that the sage was observing a vow of silence; possessed by anger, your father insulted him.

**1.45.27**  Lifting a dead serpent from the ground with the tip of his bow, he placed it on the shoulder of that pure-souled one, O best of the Bharatas.

**1.45.28**  But that wise sage said nothing to him — neither good nor ill — he remained just as he was, neither angry, carrying the serpent on his shoulder.

**1.46.1**  The ministers said: Then that king, O best of kings, having placed the serpent on the shoulder of the sage — emaciated as he was from hunger — returned again to his own city.

**1.46.2**  But that sage had a son, born of a cow, of great fame, named Śṛṅgī, of great radiance, fierce in energy, and extremely wrathful.

**1.46.3**  The sage had gone to pay homage to Brahman; having paid his respects and been given leave, Śṛṅgī went there, and at that point he heard from a friend that his father had been insulted by your father in that manner.

**1.46.4**  That his father was carrying on his shoulder a dead serpent placed there by your father, O Janamejaya, O tiger among the Kurus — the father who had done no wrong.

**1.46.5**  A great ascetic, the foremost of sages, O king, one who had conquered the senses, pure, and engaged in wondrous action,

**1.46.6**  whose soul blazed with austerity, who was restrained in his own limbs, of auspicious conduct, of auspicious speech, perfectly steadfast and free from greed,

**1.46.7**  not petty, without envy, aged, abiding in the vow of silence, a refuge for all beings — such a one had been wronged by your father.

**1.46.8**  Having heard this, he cursed your father, filled with fury — the son of the sage, of great radiance, though a boy yet superior to elders.

**1.46.9**  Quickly touching water, he spoke these words in rage, blazing as it were with his fiery energy, directed against your father:

**1.46.10**  "He who placed a dead serpent on my innocent teacher — Takṣaka the serpent, in wrath, shall lay him low with his venom within seven nights from now. Wicked man, behold the power of my austerity!"

**1.46.11**  Having spoken thus, he went to where his father was; and having seen his father, he reported to him that curse.

**1.46.12**  And that tiger among sages also sent a messenger to your father: "You have been cursed by my son — be on your guard, O lord of the earth; Takṣaka, O great king, will lay you low with his venom."

**1.46.13**  Hearing those terrible words, your father, O Janamejaya, was on his guard, terrified of Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents.

**1.46.14**  Then when the seventh day arrived, the brahmarṣi Kāśyapa wished to go to the king's presence.

**1.46.15**  Then Takṣaka, lord of serpents, saw Kāśyapa and spoke to him as he was hurrying on his way: "Where does your honour go in such haste, and what deed does he intend to perform?"

**1.46.16**  Kāśyapa said: There where the king, best of the Kurus, known as Parīkṣit, is to be burned by the serpent Takṣaka — that is where I am going, O twice-born one.

**1.46.17**  I go to him quickly to cure him at once of his affliction; one protected by me — the serpent shall not harm him.

**1.46.18**  Takṣaka said: Why do you wish to revive the one bitten by me? Tell me your desire — I will grant it to you today; go to your own home.

**1.46.19**  The ministers said: He replied to him that he was going there out of desire for wealth; and Takṣaka, honouring that great-souled one, addressed him with conciliatory words:

**1.46.20**  "Whatever wealth you desire from that king, take even more than that from me and turn back, O sinless one."

**1.46.21**  Thus addressed by the serpent, Kāśyapa, best among two-footed beings, having received from Takṣaka as much wealth as he desired, turned back.

**1.46.22**  After the brahmin departed, Takṣaka, approaching in disguise, that king — best of kings, your righteous father —

**1.46.23**  though he was on guard in his palace, burned him with the fire of his venom; then you, O tiger among men, were consecrated to victory.

**1.46.24**  All this, seen and heard by us in full, O best of kings, we have related to you in its entirety — this most terrible thing.

**1.46.25**  Having heard of this overthrow of the king, O best of rulers, and of this sage Uttaṅka as well, decide now what is to follow.

**1.46.26**  Janamejaya said: I wish to hear this — what was then the conversation between the lord of serpents and Kāśyapa in the lonely forest wilderness.

**1.46.27**  By whom was it seen and heard, and how did it reach your ears? Having heard it, I shall then resolve upon a course of action to destroy the serpents.

**1.46.28**  The ministers said: Listen, O king, as to how this was told to us before — the encounter on the road between the lord of twice-born ones and the lord of serpents.

**1.46.29**  On that tree, O lord of the earth, some man had previously climbed in search of firewood, to gather dry branches from the forest tree; the serpent and the twice-born one did not notice him sitting there in that tree.

**1.46.30**  He was reduced to ashes along with that very tree; but by the power of the twice-born one, O best of kings, he was restored to life together with the forest tree.

**1.46.31**  He went and reported to this city, O best of kings, all that had happened — the entire account of Takṣaka and the twice-born one.

**1.46.32**  This has been told to you, O king, exactly as it occurred and as we heard it; having heard it, O tiger among kings, do now as you desire.

**1.46.33**  The Sūta said: Having heard the words of the ministers, king Janamejaya was tormented with grief; afflicted with sorrow, he wrung his hands.

**1.46.34**  Repeatedly he exhaled long hot sighs; the lotus-eyed king shed tears continuously from both eyes; and the lord of the earth, overwhelmed with grief and sorrow, spoke:

**1.46.35**  "Having heard these words of yours regarding my father's passage to heaven, my resolve is firm — hear what it is from me.

**1.46.36**  I think that retribution must follow immediately against the wicked-souled Takṣaka, by whom my father was harmed.

**1.46.37**  For had that wicked one, after fulfilling the words of the sage Śṛṅgin and burning the king, gone away — surely my father would be alive.

**1.46.38**  What would have been lost to him if that king had lived, by the grace of Kāśyapa and by the good counsel of the ministers?

**1.46.39**  But he, out of delusion, turned away Kāśyapa, the best of twice-born ones, who had come to revive the invincible king.

**1.46.40**  This is a great transgression by the wicked-souled Takṣaka — that he gave wealth to the brahmin so that the king might not be revived.

**1.46.41**  Doing what is dear to Uttaṅka, what is greatly dear to myself, and dear to all of you — I shall take vengeance for my father."

**1.47.1**  The Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that glorious king, approved by his ministers, O brahmin, then undertook the vow for the snake sacrifice — that tiger of the Bharatas, king Pārikṣita Janamejaya.

**1.47.2**  Having summoned the household priest and the sacrificial priests, the lord of the earth, gifted in speech, uttered words that were purposeful and apt:

**1.47.3**  "That evil-minded Takṣaka who harmed my father — how I may retaliate against him: tell me that, gentlemen.

**1.47.4**  Is the method known to you by which I may bring Takṣaka, the serpent, together with his kinsmen, into the blazing fire?

**1.47.5**  Just as my father was formerly burned by him with the fire of venom, so too do I wish to burn that wicked serpent."

**1.47.6**  The priests said: There exists, O king, a great sacrifice ordained by the gods for your purpose; it is known as the Sarpasatra — the snake sacrifice — and is spoken of in the Purāṇas, O king.

**1.47.7**  "You and no other are the one to perform that sacrifice, O lord of men" — so the Purāṇic authorities declare; and that rite is within our knowledge."

**1.47.8**  The Sūta said: Thus addressed, that royal seer imagined the serpent Takṣaka already entered into the blazing mouth of the fire god, O good one.

**1.47.9**  Then the king, knower of sacred formulas, said to those brahmins: "I shall perform that sacrifice — let the materials be assembled for me."

**1.47.10**  Then those priests of his, O best of twice-born ones, measured out the ground according to scripture for the purpose of establishing the sacrificial site; all of them were knowers of sacred science, their minds reaching the highest wisdom.

**1.47.11**  It was endowed with supreme prosperity, delightful, thronged with multitudes of twice-born ones, abundantly rich in wealth and grain, well laid out by the officiating priests.

**1.47.12**  Having properly constructed the desired sacrificial ground according to rule, they then initiated the king for the attainment of the snake sacrifice.

**1.47.13**  And there had arisen previously at that snake sacrifice a great portent — a sign that an obstacle to the sacrifice would come.

**1.47.14**  When the sacrificial ground was being laid out, the master-builder, endowed with intelligence and learned in the science of architecture, spoke these words:

**1.47.15**  Thus spoke the master-builder, the versed narrator of Purāṇas at that time: "In the place and at the time when this measuring was initiated, owing to a brahmin being the cause, this sacrifice will not be completed."

**1.47.16**  Having heard this, the king said to the doorkeeper before the time of his initiation: "Let no one unknown to me enter here."

**1.47.17**  Then the work of the snake sacrifice began according to rule, and the officiating priests went about properly, each in his own assigned duty.

**1.47.18**  Having put on dark garments, their eyes reddened by smoke, they poured oblations with sacred formulas into the well-kindled fire.

**1.47.19**  Causing the minds of all serpents to tremble, they summoned all the snakes there into the mouth of fire.

**1.47.20**  Then the serpents fell into the blazing sacrificial fire, writhing pitifully, calling out to one another.

**1.47.21**  Some wriggling, others hissing, others coiling — they entered the fire of many colours head-first and tail-first repeatedly.

**1.47.22**  White ones, black ones, and blue ones — old and young alike — uttering terrible cries, they fell into the blazing fire.

**1.47.23**  In this way hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions of serpents were helplessly destroyed, O best of twice-born ones.

**1.47.24**  Some were there like elephants with their trunks, others with limbs like elephant trunks, others like maddened elephants — all of great body and great strength.

**1.47.25**  Many of various sizes, of diverse colours, teeming with venom, terrible, like iron clubs, great serpents of great strength — all fell into the fire, tormented by the rod of their mother's words.

**1.48.1**  Śaunaka said: At that snake sacrifice of the wise king Janamejaya, descendant of the Pāṇḍavas, who were the officiating priests — the greatest of sages?

**1.48.2**  Who were the attending sages at that dreadful snake sacrifice — so exceedingly producing despair, in that great terror for the serpents?

**1.48.3**  You ought to relate everything in detail, dear one — for you are known as knowledgeable in the procedure of the snake sacrifice, O son of the Sūta.

**1.48.4**  The Sūta said: Come, I shall tell you here the names of the wise men who were the officiating priests and attending sages of that king at that time.

**1.48.5**  There the Hotā priest was the brahmin Caṇḍabhārgava, born in the lineage of Cyavana, renowned as the best among knowers of the Veda.

**1.48.6**  The Udgātā was the aged and learned brahmin Kautsāryajaimini; the Brahman priest was Śārṅgarava, and the Adhvaryu was Bodhapiṅgala.

**1.48.7**  Among the attending sages was Vyāsa, accompanied by his sons and disciples; Uddālaka; Śamaṭhaka; and Śvetaketu as the fifth.

**1.48.8**  Asita and Devala; Nārada and Parvata likewise; Ātreya; the twice-born Kuṇḍajaṭhara; and Kuṭighaṭa as well.

**1.48.9**  Vātsya; the aged Śrutaśravā, devoted to austerity and self-study; Kahoḍa; Devaśarmā; Maudgalya; and Śamasaubhara.

**1.48.10**  These and many other Brahmanas of keen vows were the assembly-members at the snake-sacrifice of the son of Parikshit.

**1.48.11**  As the priests were offering oblations at that great rite, the snake-sacrifice, terrible serpents fell there, striking terror into all living creatures.

**1.48.12**  Streams of fat and marrow flowed from the serpents; and continuously, day and night, a tumultuous smell of burning rose from those that were being consumed.

**1.48.13**  The sound of those serpents falling and of those hovering in the sky was heard incessantly, as they were consumed with great intensity by the fire.

**1.48.14**  But Takshaka, that lord of serpents, hearing that king Janamejaya had been consecrated, fled to the abode of Indra, the Destroyer of Pura.

**1.48.15**  Then, having told everything that had come to pass, that best of serpents, terror-stricken and conscious of his offence, sought refuge with Indra, the Destroyer of Pura.

**1.48.16**  Indra, greatly pleased, said to him: "O Takshaka, O lord of serpents, you have nothing to fear here from that snake-sacrifice under any circumstances."

**1.48.17**  "The Grandsire was formerly propitiated by me on your behalf; therefore you have nothing to fear — let the fever of your mind depart."

**1.48.18**  Thus reassured by him, that best of serpents then dwelt in Shakra's mansion, joyful and at ease.

**1.48.19**  As serpents fell ceaselessly into the fire, Vasuki, with his retinue much reduced, was greatly distressed and burned with anguish.

**1.48.20**  A terrible stupor seized Vasuki, lord of serpents; his heart reeling, he spoke thus to his sister:

**1.48.21**  "My limbs burn, dear sister; the directions are unclear to me; I am as if sinking in confusion, and my mind seems to whirl."

**1.48.22**  "My vision spins exceedingly, and my heart seems to burst; today I shall fall helplessly into that blazing fire."

**1.48.23**  "That sacrifice of Parikshit's son is proceeding with intent to destroy us; clearly I too must go to the abode of the king of the dead."

**1.48.24**  "This is the moment for which you, my sister, were given in marriage to Jaratkaru long ago — protect us now together with all our kindred."

**1.48.25**  "The Grandsire himself previously told me that Astika would indeed stop that sacrifice when it was proceeding with the best of serpents as its victim."

**1.48.26**  "Therefore, dear child, speak today to your own son, that youth revered by the elders, that foremost knower of the Vedas, for the liberation of me and my servants."

**1.49.1**  The Suta said: Then Jaratkaru, the female serpent, summoning her own son, spoke these words at the bidding of Vasuki, king of serpents:

**1.49.2**  "I was given to your father, my son, by my brother for a purpose; that moment has now arrived — do what is required of you accordingly."

**1.49.3**  Astika said: "For what purpose were you given to my father by my maternal uncle? Tell me the truth of it — having heard, I shall act accordingly."

**1.49.4**  The Suta said: Then she, the sister of the king of serpents, Jaratkaru, composed and well-wishing toward her kindred, told him this:

**1.49.5**  "The mother of all the serpents without exception is known as Kadru; by her, angered, were her sons cursed — hear the reason for that."

**1.49.6**  "Ucchaihshravas, that king of horses — because you did not make him falsely mine in the wager made for Vinata's sake, my sons, for the sake of enslaving her."

**1.49.7**  "'At Janamejaya's sacrifice, the fire whose charioteer is the wind shall burn you; meeting dissolution there, you shall go to the world of the dead.'"

**1.49.8**  "And the Grandsire of the world himself, seeing her who had thus cursed, spoke the words 'So be it' and approved of it."

**1.49.9**  "And Vasuki, hearing that word of the Grandsire at the time the nectar was being churned, O dear one, sought the refuge of the gods."

**1.49.10**  "And all the gods, having attained the peerless nectar and their purpose fulfilled, with my brother at their head, approached Prajapati."

**1.49.11**  "All the gods together propitiated the Grandsire along with king Vasuki, that the curse might not take effect."

**1.49.12**  "'This Vasuki, king of serpents, is distressed on account of his kinsmen; let not this curse from his mother come to pass, O Lord.'"

**1.49.13**  "Brahma said: 'A twice-born one born to Jaratkaru from the wife named Jaratkaru whom he shall obtain will deliver the serpents from the curse.'"

**1.49.14**  Jaratkaru said: "Hearing this speech, Vasuki, lord of serpents, gave me, O one equal to the immortals, to your father, the great-souled one, even before the time came; therein you were born of me."

**1.49.15**  "This is that moment now arrived — you must rescue us from fear; you must rescue my brother as well from the fire."

**1.49.16**  "That act of mine would not be in vain — that I was given to your wise father for the sake of liberation. What do you think, my son?"

**1.49.17**  The Suta said: Thus addressed, having said "So be it," Astika then spoke to his mother and, as if reviving Vasuki, who was burning with sorrow:

**1.49.18**  "I will rescue you, O Vasuki, O best of serpents, from that curse, O great being — this I tell you truly."

**1.49.19**  "Be of easy mind, O serpent — there is no fear for you. I shall strive in such a way that what is beneficial will come about. My speech has never spoken untruth even in play — how then otherwise?"

**1.49.20**  "Going to that best of kings, the consecrated Janamejaya, I shall today please him with words full of auspicious praise, O maternal uncle, in such a way that the king's sacrifice will be brought to a close, O noble one."

**1.49.21**  "O lord of serpents, O great-minded one, place all trust in me — your mind ought never to prove false in regard to me."

**1.49.22**  Vasuki said: "Astika, I reel all around; my heart is bursting; I do not recognise the directions, crushed as I am by the rod of Brahma's curse."

**1.49.23**  Astika said: "You must not grieve in any way, O best of serpents — I will destroy your fear that has arisen from the blazing fire."

**1.49.24**  "I will destroy the great and terrible rod of Brahma's curse, equal in energy to the fire of dissolution — mother, you must not fear in any way."

**1.49.25**  The Suta said: Then, having removed the terrible anguish of mind from Vasuki and bearing it upon his own limbs, he set forth with great haste.

**1.49.26**  That foremost of twice-born men, Astika, went to Janamejaya's sacrifice, endowed with all its qualities, for the liberation of the lords of serpents.

**1.49.27**  Going there, Astika beheld that excellent sacrificial ground surrounded by many assembly-members of a brilliance equal to the sun and fire.

**1.49.28**  Stopped there at the gate by the doorkeepers as he sought to enter, that best of twice-born men, that foremost among the twice-born, praised the sacrifice in order to gain admittance.

**1.50.1**  Astika said: "The sacrifice of Soma, the sacrifice of Varuna, the sacrifice of Prajapati performed at Prayaga — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bharatas, O son of Parikshit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

**1.50.2**  "The sacrifice of Shakra is said to be one hundred in number; another equally counted is verily a hundred — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bharatas, O son of Parikshit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

**1.50.3**  "As was the sacrifice of Yama and of Harishmedha, as was the sacrifice of king Rantideva — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bharatas, O son of Parikshit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

**1.50.4**  "The sacrifice of Gaya, the sacrifice of king Shashabindu, and the sacrifice of king Vaishravana — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bharatas, O son of Parikshit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

**1.50.5**  "The sacrifice of Nriga and that of Ajamidha, as was the sacrifice of king Dasharathi — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bharatas, O son of Parikshit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

**1.50.6**  "We have heard of the sacrifice in heaven of the son of the gods, the sacrifice of king Yudhishthira, the descendant of Ajamidha — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bharatas, O son of Parikshit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

**1.50.7**  "The sacrifice of Krishna, the son of Satyavati, wherein he himself performed the rites — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bharatas, O son of Parikshit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

**1.50.8**  "For these ones here of a brilliance like the sun and fire are seated as at the rite of the Slayer of Vritra; no knowledge exists today to fully comprehend them — what is given to them can never in any way be lost."

**1.50.9**  "There is no equal to Dvaipayana as a priest anywhere in the worlds — this is my firm conviction. For his disciples walk this earth as officiant priests, all skilled in their respective rites."

**1.50.10**  "Vibhavasu, Chitrabhanu, the great-souled one, bearer of golden seed, all-consumer, dark-pathed, with flame spiralling rightward, blazing — the god who is the eater of oblations desires this offering of yours."

**1.50.11**  "There is no other king found in this world of the living equal to you as a protector of subjects; I am always glad at heart by your steadfastness — you are either the king Dharmaraja or Yama himself."

**1.50.12**  "As Shakra, the thunderbolt-wielding Indra himself, is protector in this world, so are you here the protector of subjects; you are esteemed by us as the lord of men in this world — and there is none other than you who is master of this sacrifice."

**1.50.13**  "Equal to Khatvanga, Nabhaga, and Dilipa, of prowess comparable to Yayati and Mandhata, of energy matching the brilliance of the Adityas — you shine, O Suvarata, like Bhishma."

**1.50.14**  "Your composure is as firm as Valmiki's; your anger is as restrained as Vasishtha's; your lordship I deem equal to that of Indra; and your radiance shines like Narayana's."

**1.50.15**  "As Yama you know the determination of dharma; as Krishna you are endowed with every virtue; as Shri is the abode of the Vasus, so are you the repository of sacrifices."

**1.50.16**  "In strength you are equal to Dambhodbhava; like Rama you are versed in weapons and missiles; in energy you are equal to Aurva and Trita; you are hard to look upon as the sun, or like Bhagiratha."

**1.50.17**  The Suta said: Thus praised, all of them — the king, the assembly-members, the priests, and the bearer of oblations — were pleased. Seeing the contented gestures of all of them, king Janamejaya then spoke:

**1.51.1**  Janamejaya said: "This boy speaks like an elder; this is no boy — he is an elder in my estimation. I wish to grant him a boon — O Brahmanas, assembled together, permit me this."

**1.51.2**  The assembly-members said: "Even a Brahmin boy is always worthy of honour from kings, whether unlearned or learned. He deserves all wishes from you properly today — and let Takshaka come quickly to us."

**1.51.3**  The Suta said: As the boon-granting king was about to speak, offering a boon to the twice-born youth, the Hota then said with a heart not excessively joyful: "Choose a boon" — for Takshaka had not yet come to the rite.

**1.51.4**  Janamejaya said: "May all of you strive with your utmost power that this rite of mine be completed and that Takshaka comes quickly to us — for he is my enemy."

**1.51.5**  The officiating priests said: "As the scriptures tell us, and as the fire itself indicates — O king, Takshaka is in the mansion of Indra, oppressed by fear."

**1.51.6**  The Suta said: "Just as the great-souled Suta Lohitaksha, the Puranic bard, had known this beforehand and told the king when asked at that time — even as the Brahmanas declare it, so is this the case, O lord of men."

**1.51.7**  "'Drawing on the Purana, I tell you this: Indra gave him that boon, O king: "Dwell here in my presence, well protected — the fire shall not burn you."'"

**1.51.8**  Hearing this, the consecrated king, burning with ardour, sat urging the Hota on at the time of the rite; the Hota, alert, offered with mantras — and thereupon Indra himself came in person.

**1.51.9**  Having mounted his celestial vehicle, the great and glorious one was praised by all the gods, accompanied also by Balahaka spirits, by the Vidyadharas and by hosts of Apsaras.

**1.51.10**  That serpent, hidden in Indra's upper garment, could find no safety, agitated by fear; then the king, versed in spells, again spoke words in anger, desiring the end of Takshaka:

**1.51.11**  "O Brahmanas, if that serpent Takshaka is in the mansion of Indra, then hurl him together with Indra himself into the fire."

**1.51.12**  The officiating priests said: "Takshaka is indeed coming quickly under your power, O king; his great cry is heard, roaring terribly out of fear."

**1.51.13**  "Surely that serpent has been released by the thunder-bearer; fallen from Indra's embrace, his body loosened by the mantras, that lord of serpents comes whirling through the sky, having lost consciousness, breathing violent breaths."

**1.51.14**  "This rite of yours is proceeding according to rule, O lord of kings, O master. Now you should grant a boon to this foremost of twice-born men."

**1.51.15**  Janamejaya said: "O immeasurable one, fitting your youth and handsome form, I grant you a boon as is proper. Choose whatever rests in your heart as desired — I shall bestow it on you even if it be ungrantable."

**1.51.16**  The Suta said: As the lord of serpents Takshaka was on the verge of falling into the fire, seizing this interval, Astika then urged his request, saying: "This is the moment."

**1.51.17**  "If you grant me a boon, O Janamejaya, this is my choice: let this sacrifice of yours cease, and let no more serpents fall here."

**1.51.18**  The Suta said: Thus addressed, the king, son of Parikshit, O Brahmin, was then not altogether of a rejoicing mind, and spoke these words to Astika:

**1.51.19**  Janamejaya said: Gold, silver, cows, and whatever else you may desire, O lord — all that I would give you as a boon, O brahmin; let my sacrifice not be turned back.

**1.51.20**  Āstīka said: Gold, silver, and cows — none of these do I choose from you, O king. Let this sacrifice of yours be stopped; may there be welfare for our mother's kin.

**1.51.21**  The Sūta said: Thus addressed by Āstīka, the king, son of Parīkṣit, then spoke again and again to Āstīka, saying, 'Choose among those who speak the best boon.'

**1.51.22**  He said: Choose another boon, good fortune to you, O best of the twice-born. But that son of the Bhṛgu line asked for no other boon.

**1.51.23**  Then all the learned members of the assembly who were versed in the Vedas together spoke to that king: Let the brahmin receive his boon.

**1.52.1**  Śaunaka said: Those serpents that fell into the fire in this snake sacrifice — I wish to hear the names of all of them, O son of the Sūta.

**1.52.2**  The Sūta said: Many thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions — they cannot be fully enumerated because of their great number, O best of Veda-knowers.

**1.52.3**  Yet as I remember them, hear from me the names of the chief serpents that were offered into the sacred fire, as I speak them.

**1.52.4**  Learn from me first, by way of eminence, those born in Vāsuki's lineage — dark, red, white, terrible, of great bodies, and fierce with venom.

**1.52.5**  Koṭika, Mānasa, Pūrṇa, Saha, Paila, Halīsaka, Picchila, Koṇapa, Cakra, Koṇavega, and Prakālana —

**1.52.6**  Hiraṇyavāha, Śaraṇa, Kakṣaka, and Kāladantaka — these serpents born of Vāsuki entered the sacrificial fire.

**1.52.7**  Those born in the lineage of Takṣaka I will now declare; hear them: Pucchaṇḍaka, Maṇḍalaka, Piṇḍabhettā, and Rabheṇaka —

**1.52.8**  Ucchikha, Surasa, Draṅga, Balaheḍa, Virohaṇa, Śilīśalakara, Mūka, Sukumāra, and Pravepana —

**1.52.9**  Mudgara, Śaśaromā, Sumanā, and Vegavāhana — these serpents born of Takṣaka entered the sacrificial fire.

**1.52.10**  Pārāvata, Pāriyātra, Pāṇḍara, Hariṇa, Kṛśa, Vihaṃga, Śarabha, Moda, Pramoda, and Saṃhatāṅgada —

**1.52.11**  These from the lineage of Airāvata entered the sacrificial fire. Now hear from me the serpents born in the lineage of Kauravya, O best of the twice-born.

**1.52.12**  Aiṇḍila, Kuṇḍala, Muṇḍa, Veṇiskandha, Kumāraka, Bāhuka, Śṛṅgavega, Dhūrtaka, and the pair Pāta and Pātara —

**1.52.13**  Hear in detail the serpents born in the lineage of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as I enumerate them, O brahmin — swift as the wind and fierce with venom.

**1.52.14**  Śaṅkukarṇa, Piṅgalaka, Kuṭhāramukha, Mecaka, Pūrṇāṅgada, Pūrṇamukha, Prahasa, Śakuni, and Hari —

**1.52.15**  Āmāhaṭha, Komaṭhaka, Śvasana, Mānava, Vaṭa, Bhairava, Muṇḍavedāṅga, Piśaṅga, and Udrapāraga —

**1.52.16**  Ṛṣabha, Vegavān, Piṇḍāraka, Mahāhanu, Raktāṅga, Sarvasāraṅga, Samṛddha, and the pair Pāṭa and Rākṣasa —

**1.52.17**  Varāhaka, Vāraṇaka, Sumitra, Citravediha, Parāśara, Taruṇaka, Maṇiskandha, and Āruṇi —

**1.52.18**  Thus have I enumerated these fame-enhancing serpents, O brahmin — the chief ones principally; not all of them, given their great multitude.

**1.52.19**  The sons and grandsons of these, and the whole succession of their offspring who entered the blazing fire — they cannot be fully counted.

**1.52.20**  Those with seven heads, those with two heads, and others with five heads — terrible, bearing the venom of the fires of time — were offered by the hundreds of thousands.

**1.52.21**  Of vast body and great might, towering like mountain peaks, a yojana in length and breadth, or stretching two yojanas in extent —

**1.52.22**  Able to assume any form at will, moving wherever they wished, fierce with the venom of blazing fire — they were burned in that great sacrifice, crushed by the rod of Brahman's curse.

**1.53.1**  The Sūta said: We have heard of yet another most wonderful thing concerning Āstīka, when the king, son of Parīkṣit, was plying him with boons.

**1.53.2**  When the serpent slipped from Indra's hand and remained suspended in mid-air, King Janamejaya became deeply anxious.

**1.53.3**  Though the fire was burning fiercely and offerings were being made in the proper manner, Takṣaka, tormented by fear, did not fall into the fire.

**1.53.4**  Śaunaka said: Why, O Sūta, did the collection of mantras of those wise brahmins fail to work, so that Takṣaka did not then fall into the fire?

**1.53.5**  The Sūta said: As that best of serpents slipped from Indra's hand and was losing consciousness, Āstīka raised his voice three times, calling out: Stop! Stop!

**1.53.6**  Then that serpent remained stationary in the sky, its heart trembling — just as a man might stand still when caught within a circle of cattle.

**1.53.7**  Then the king, strongly urged by the members of the assembly, spoke: Let it be so, as Āstīka has spoken, as he desires.

**1.53.8**  Let this rite be concluded; let the serpents be free from harm; let this Āstīka be pleased; and let the words of the Sūta prove true.

**1.53.9**  Then a cry of rejoicing arose; and when the boon was granted to Āstīka, it likewise came to rest — the sacrifice stopped.

**1.53.10**  That sacrifice of the king, the son of Pāṇḍu's line, the son of Parīkṣit — and King Janamejaya of the Bharata race was pleased.

**1.53.11**  To the officiating priests and the assembled members of the council who had gathered there, he gave wealth in hundreds and thousands.

**1.53.12**  To Lohitākṣa the Sūta, and likewise to the architect, the mighty king gave a great gift — it was he who had foretold at the very start of the sacrifice that it would be stopped.

**1.53.13**  Saying, 'This brahmin was the omen,' he gave him abundant wealth; then he performed the concluding ablution in accordance with the prescribed ritual.

**1.53.14**  The king, his heart pleased, sent Āstīka — the wise one, pleased and fulfilled in his purpose — home with great honor.

**1.53.15**  And he said to him: You must come again; you shall be a member of my council at the great horse sacrifice.

**1.53.16**  Saying 'So be it,' Āstīka departed joyfully, having accomplished an incomparable purpose and having satisfied the king.

**1.53.17**  He went, supremely glad, approached his mother and his maternal uncle, embraced them, and reported to them everything that had transpired.

**1.53.18**  Hearing this, the serpents who had gathered there, freed from delusion and rejoicing, were filled with delight toward Āstīka; and they spoke to him: Choose whatever boon you desire.

**1.53.19**  Again and again they all said to him on every side: What shall we do today that is dear to you, O wise one? We are pleased, and all of us have been saved; what desire shall we fulfill for you today, dear child?

**1.53.20**  Āstīka said: May those in the world — brahmins, ordinary men, and others too — who with pure hearts morning and evening recite this account of mine have no fear from you whatsoever.

**1.53.21**  The Sūta said: And addressed by them with pure hearts, their nephew was told: This is true; we who act thus with joy shall certainly fulfill every desire of yours, O nephew, being ever inclined to it.

**1.53.22**  May Āstīka, born of Jaratkāru from Jaratkārvā, of great renown, firm in his vow of truth, protect me from serpents.

**1.53.23**  Whoever remembers Asita, Ārtimanta, and Sunītha — whether by day or by night — shall have no fear of serpents.

**1.53.24**  The Sūta said: Having freed the serpents from the snake sacrifice, that best of twice-born, righteous in soul, went in time to his appointed end, blessed with sons and grandsons.

**1.53.25**  Thus has the tale of Āstīka been recounted to you by me faithfully; one who narrates it has no fear from serpents anywhere.

**1.53.26**  Having heard this most righteous tale of Āstīka — the meritorious story of the poet Āstīka, O brahmin, his glorious career from the very beginning —

**1.53.27**  Śaunaka said: The great tale has been told to me by you in full, O son of the Sūta, my dear — from the lineage of Bhṛgu onward; I am pleased with you for that.

**1.53.28**  And I shall question you further, O delight of the Sūta; tell me also again the story composed by Vyāsa.

**1.53.29**  During the intervals of that most difficult of rites — the snake sacrifice of those great souls — according to proper procedure, among the members of the council, O great poet —

**1.53.30**  Whatever wonderful stories arose and in what matters they were told truly — I wish to hear these from you, O Sūta, for you are indeed discerning.

**1.53.31**  The Sūta said: During the intervals of the rite, the twice-born men told stories rooted in the Vedas; but Vyāsa always narrated the great tale, the Mahābhārata.

**1.53.32**  Śaunaka said: The tale of the Mahābhārata, that account glorifying the Pāṇḍavas — when Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was questioned by Janamejaya —

**1.53.33**  He recited it in due form during those intervals of the rite; that sacred story I truly wish to hear in proper order.

**1.53.34**  Narrate it — that story born from the ocean of the great seer's mind, whose deeds are holy — O best among the righteous; I am never satiated, O son of the Sūta.

**1.53.35**  The Sūta said: Very well, I shall tell you that great and excellent story — the Mahābhārata as composed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana — from the very beginning.

**1.53.36**  Enjoy it as I narrate it, O brahmin of supreme understanding; in recounting it, joy of mind arises within me here as well.

**1.54.1**  The Sūta said: Having heard that Janamejaya had consecrated himself for the snake sacrifice, the learned seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana then came to him.

**1.54.2**  The one whom Kālī — still a maiden — bore on the island in the Yamunā from Parāśara, son of Śakti, that grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas —

**1.54.3**  Who, even as soon as he was born, instantly grew in body by the power of his will, and mastered the Vedas with all their ancillary branches and histories — that one of great glory —

**1.54.4**  Whom no one could surpass in austerity, nor in the study of the Vedas, nor by vows, nor by fasting, nor by birth, nor by ardor —

**1.54.5**  Who divided the one Veda into four — he, the best of those who know the Vedas, knower of the far and near, a brahmin seer, a poet, firm in the vow of truth, and pure —

**1.54.6**  Who fathered Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vidura as well, extending the lineage of Śāntanu — he of holy fame and great glory —

**1.54.7**  He entered the sacrificial hall of Janamejaya the royal seer at that time, accompanied by disciples who had mastered the Vedas and all their branches.

**1.54.8**  There he saw King Janamejaya seated, surrounded by many members of the assembly — like Puraṃdara surrounded by the gods.

**1.54.9**  And also with consecrated kings from various countries, and with officiating priests equal to the gods, skilled in the spreading of the sacrificial ground.

**1.54.10**  Janamejaya the royal seer, best of the Bharatas, seeing that seer arrive, rose swiftly with his retinue out of joy.

**1.54.11**  With the approval of the assembly members, the mighty king arranged a golden seat for him — just as Indra would for Bṛhaspati.

**1.54.12**  When he had taken his seat there — the bestower of boons, honored by the hosts of divine seers — the foremost of kings honored him with acts prescribed by scripture.

**1.54.13**  Water for washing the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, the guest offering, and a cow — all in due order — he presented to Kṛṣṇa, his grandfather, as was worthy of him.

**1.54.14**  Having received that honor from Janamejaya, the Pāṇḍava's descendant, and having given permission for the cow, Vyāsa was pleased at that time.

**1.54.15**  Having thus honored that great-grandfather with care, the king sat near him with a joyful heart and inquired after his welfare.

**1.54.16**  The blessed one in turn, seeing the king, communicated his well-being, was honored by all the assembly members, and honored the assembly members in return.

**1.54.17**  Then Janamejaya, after that best of twice-born had been duly honored by all the assembly members, thereafter addressed him with folded hands.

**1.54.18**  You have been a direct witness of the Kurus and the Pandavas; I wish to hear their deeds narrated by you, O brahmin.

**1.54.19**  How did the split arise between those whose deeds were beyond reproach? And how did that great war come to pass — the war that put an end to so many living beings?

**1.54.20**  Tell me all of this in full, concerning all those forefathers whose minds were possessed by fate, O Blessed One, for you are skilled in such telling.

**1.54.21**  Hearing those words, Krsna Dvaipayana then instructed his disciple Vaishampayana, who was seated nearby.

**1.54.22**  Narrate to him in full how the split between the Kurus and the Pandavas came about in former times — everything that you have heard from me.

**1.54.23**  That bull among brahmins, having received the command of his guru, then narrated the entire ancient history.

**1.54.24**  To that king, to the members of the assembly, and to all the kshatriyas gathered there, he then told the story of the rift and the destruction of the kingdom of the Kurus and Pandavas.

**1.55.1**  Vaishampayana spoke: Having first bowed to my guru with mind, intellect, and concentrated thought, and having honoured all the brahmins and other learned persons present —

**1.55.2**  — I shall now set forth in full the teaching of Vyasa, the great sage renowned throughout all the worlds, the wise one of immeasurable splendour.

**1.55.3**  O king, you are a worthy vessel to hear this Bharata tale; the eagerness to speak on behalf of my guru urges me on with joy, as it were.

**1.55.4**  Hear, O king, how the rift between the Kurus and the Pandavas came about: the exile arising from the dice game over the kingdom, and all that followed.

**1.55.5**  And how the war came about — the war that laid waste to the earth — all of that I shall recount to you who ask, O bull of the Bharata line.

**1.55.6**  When their father had died, those heroes returned from the forest to their own dwelling, and in no great time became learned in both the Veda and the bow.

**1.55.7**  Seeing the Pandavas endowed with beauty, valour, and vigour, approved of by the citizens, and bearing glory and renown, the Kurus could not endure them.

**1.55.8**  Then the cruel Duryodhana, together with Karna and Shakuni son of Subala, undertook various schemes to suppress and banish them.

**1.55.9**  That wicked son of Dhritarashtra then administered poison to Bhima; but the hero Vrikodara digested it along with his food.

**1.55.10**  Then, binding the sleeping Vrikodara at Pramanakoți and hurling Bhima into the waters of the Ganga, he returned to the city.

**1.55.11**  When Kaunteya awoke, he snapped his bonds and arose, O great king — Bhimasena, free of all distress.

**1.55.12**  He also had him bitten all over his body by venomous black serpents while he slept; yet that slayer of foes did not die.

**1.55.13**  In each and every one of those acts of harm, the great-minded Vidura was ever watchful in rescuing and countering them.

**1.55.14**  Just as Indra, dwelling in heaven, ever brings welfare to the living world, so too did Vidura ever bring welfare to the Pandavas.

**1.55.15**  But when, despite all manner of concealed and open stratagems, he could not kill those who were protected by fate and divine will —

**1.55.16**  — then, having taken counsel with his ministers headed by Vrisha and Duhshasana, and having obtained Dhritarashtra's permission, he ordered the house of lac.

**1.55.17**  He had the Pandavas of boundless might housed there, and then, when they were off guard, he set fire to them with a conflagration.

**1.55.18**  But by Vidura's counsel a tunnel had been prepared beforehand; by this means he delivered them, and they, freed, fled in fear.

**1.55.19**  Then in the dreadful great forest, Bhimasena of fearsome might, enraged, slew on the earth the rakshasa named Hidimba.

**1.55.20**  Then those heroes, scorchers of foes, having set out together for the city of Ekachakra, went there in the guise of brahmins, accompanied by their mother.

**1.55.21**  There, for the sake of a brahmin, they slew the mighty Baka, and then, in the company of brahmins, they departed for the city of the Panchalas.

**1.55.22**  There, having won Draupadi and resided for the full period of a year, those tamers of enemies returned to Hastinapura, now known for who they were.

**1.55.23**  They were addressed by King Dhritarashtra son of Shantanu: "My dear sons, why should there be conflict between you and your brothers? We have thought of a dwelling for you at Khandavaprastha."

**1.55.24**  "Therefore, setting aside your anger, go to Khandavaprastha to dwell there — a land endowed with populated territories and well-laid broad roads."

**1.55.25**  At the word of those two, they departed, taking all manner of gems and jewels, along with all their friends and well-wishers, for the city of Khandavaprastha.

**1.55.26**  There they dwelt, O king, for many years, bringing other kings under their dominion by the might of their arms.

**1.55.27**  Ever foremost in dharma, devoted to vows of truth, alert and diligent, forbearing, yet blazing with power against their enemies — such were they in those days.

**1.55.28**  The mighty Bhimasena conquered the eastern quarter; the heroic Arjuna, the northern; and Nakula likewise conquered the western.

**1.55.29**  Sahadeva, slayer of enemy heroes, conquered the southern quarter; and together they brought the entire earth under their sway.

**1.55.30**  With five Pandavas resplendent as the sun, and with the sun itself blazing, the earth shone as if lit by six suns — the Pandavas of true valour.

**1.55.31**  Then, on account of a certain circumstance, King Yudhishthira the Dharmaraja sent his brother Dhananjaya to the forest.

**1.55.32**  He dwelt in the forest for a full year and one month, and then at some point went to Hrishikesha at Dvaravati.

**1.55.33**  There Bibhatsu obtained as wife the lotus-eyed Subhadra, the younger sister of Vasudeva, she of auspicious speech.

**1.55.34**  Subhadra, delighted, was united with the Pandava Arjuna just as Shachi is with great Indra, or as Sri is united with Krishna.

**1.55.35**  And Bibhatsu, that Kaunteya, together with Vasudeva, satisfied the fire — the carrier of oblations — in the Khandava forest, O best of kings.

**1.55.36**  For Partha, with Keshava as companion in his endeavours, bore no excessive burden — even as Vishnu is with his allies in the slaying of foes.

**1.55.37**  Agni also gave to Partha the supreme bow Gandiva, two inexhaustible quivers with arrows, and a chariot marked with the monkey-banner.

**1.55.38**  Bibhatsu rescued there the great asura Maya, and he in turn fashioned a divine assembly hall filled with every kind of gem.

**1.55.39**  In that hall, the dull-witted and most evil-minded Duryodhana conceived his covetousness; and thereafter, with Shakuni son of Subala, he cheated Yudhishthira at dice.

**1.55.40**  He sent them to the forest for twelve years, and for the thirteenth year to live unrecognized within the kingdom — thus thirteen years in all.

**1.55.41**  Then in the fourteenth year, when they sought their rightful property, they did not obtain it, O great king, and so the war began.

**1.55.42**  Having then destroyed everything and slain King Duryodhana, the Pandavas recovered the kingdom, now emptied of most of its people.

**1.55.43**  Such was the ancient story of those whose deeds were beyond reproach: the rift, the destruction of the kingdom, and the victory — O best of conquerors.

**1.56.1**  Janamejaya spoke: You have narrated in summary, O best of brahmins, the entire Mahabharata — the great story of the deeds of the Kurus.

**1.56.2**  But as you narrate this tale of wondrous import, O sinless one, an exceeding great curiosity has arisen in me to hear it at length.

**1.56.3**  You, sir, should narrate this again in full detail; for I am not satisfied, listening to the great deeds of the ancestors.

**1.56.4**  For the cause cannot have been trivial — those who know dharma, the Pandavas, killed men who were in principle inviolable, and yet they are praised by all people.

**1.56.5**  For what reason did those tigers among men, though capable and themselves without fault, endure the afflictions inflicted upon them by the wicked?

**1.56.6**  How was it that Vrikodara, mighty of arm, with the strength of ten thousand elephants, could restrain his anger even while suffering great torment, O best of brahmins?

**1.56.7**  How was it that Draupadi the dark one, being tormented by the wicked, chaste as she was and possessed of terrible eyes, did not burn the sons of Dhritarashtra?

**1.56.8**  How did the two Parthas and the two sons of Madri, passing over the transgression at the dice game, follow that tiger among men even as he was being cheated by the wicked?

**1.56.9**  How was it that Yudhishthira, the foremost of those who uphold dharma, the son of Dharma himself, a knower of dharma, who deserved no such thing, could endure the utmost affliction?

**1.56.10**  And how did Dhananjaya, the Pandava with Krishna as his charioteer, single-handedly shooting arrows, send all those vast armies to the world of the fathers?

**1.56.11**  Tell me all of this as it truly occurred, O wealth of asceticism, and whatever those great chariot-warriors did on each occasion.

**1.56.12**  Vaishampayana spoke: I shall now set forth in full the teaching of Vyasa, the great sage of great soul worshipped throughout all the worlds, the one of immeasurable splendour.

**1.56.13**  For this collection of a hundred thousand verses of meritorious deeds has been expounded here by the son of Satyavati, that one of boundless might.

**1.56.14**  The learned man who has this recited, and the person who hears it — they, having attained the abode of Brahman, shall reach a state equal to that of the gods.

**1.56.15**  This is equal to the Vedas, most sacred, most excellent; this Purana is the foremost of all things worth hearing, and it is praised by the seers.

**1.56.16**  In this most meritorious history, artha, dharma, and ultimate wisdom are taught in their entirety.

**1.56.17**  One who, knowing this Veda of Krishna, has it recited to those who are not petty-minded, who are given to charity, devoted to truth, and not unbelievers, shall attain the highest good.

**1.56.18**  Even the sin incurred by the killing of an embryo is undoubtedly shed — even a most hardened man, upon hearing this history.

**1.56.19**  This history named Jaya should be heard by one who desires victory; he shall conquer the entire earth and vanquish his enemies as well.

**1.56.20**  This is the best rite for obtaining a male child; this is a great rite of blessing; it should be heard many times by the queen and the crown prince alike.

**1.56.21**  This is a sacred treatise on wealth; this is the supreme treatise on dharma; this is declared to be the treatise on liberation, by Vyasa of boundless intellect.

**1.56.22**  Some relate it even now; others will relate it hereafter; there are sons who are eager to serve, and attendants who do whatever is pleasing.

**1.56.23**  All the sin committed by body, by speech, and by mind — a person who always hears this swiftly sheds all of it.

**1.56.24**  Those who listen without envy to the great birth-narrative of the Bharatas shall have no fear of disease — how then could they fear the world beyond?

**1.56.25**  This, which confers prosperity, renown, long life, heaven, and merit, was composed by Krishna Dvaipayana, who desired to bestow merit.

**1.56.26**  He composed it to spread the fame throughout the world of the great-souled Pandavas, and of the other kshatriyas of abundant wealth and splendour.

**1.56.27**  Just as the blessed ocean and the mountain Himavat are both renowned as treasuries of gems, so the Bharata is called a treasury of gems.

**1.56.28**  The learned man who has this recited to brahmins here on the occasion of the parvan days — his sins shaken off, heaven won — he attains the state of Brahman.

**1.56.29**  And one who has even a single verse of this recited to brahmins at a shraddha ceremony — that shraddha of his shall remain inexhaustible, and shall fully reach his ancestors.

**1.56.30**  Whatever sin a person commits unknowingly in the course of a day — all of that dissolves simply upon hearing this narrative called the Mahabharata.

**1.56.31**  The great birth of the Bharatas is called the Mahābhārata; he who knows its etymology is freed from all sins.

**1.56.32**  Rising early each day for three years, the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana composed this excellent narrative, the Mahābhārata.

**1.56.33**  Whatever here concerns dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, O bull of the Bharatas — that is found elsewhere too; but what is not here is nowhere else.

**1.57.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a king named Rājoparicara, steadfast in dharma, a lord of the earth; though firm in his vows, he once set out for the hunt.

**1.57.2**  At Indra's instruction, Vasu, the joy of the Paurava line, that lord of the earth, took possession of the pleasant Cedi kingdom, worthy of acquisition.

**1.57.3**  To him who had laid aside his weapons and was dwelling in an hermitage delighting in austerity, the god himself — the wielder of the thunderbolt — came in person to that lord of the earth.

**1.57.4**  Reflecting that this king was worthy of Indra's station through his austerity, Indra gently turned him away from his penance in person.

**1.57.5**  Indra said: Let not dharma be confounded upon the earth, O lord of the earth — protect it; for dharma, when upheld, sustains the entire world.

**1.57.6**  Guard the dharma of the world, ever diligent and composed; yoked to dharma, you will thereby win blessed and eternal worlds.

**1.57.7**  Dwelling on earth while I dwell in heaven, become my friend and dear companion; inhabit that region which is the udder of the earth, O lord of men.

**1.57.8**  That land is rich in cattle, holy, stable, abounding in wealth and grain, easy to defend, pleasant, and endowed with the enjoyable gifts of the earth.

**1.57.9**  This region surpasses all others, richly furnished with riches and gems; the earth there is full of wealth — dwell among the Cedis, O lord of the Cedis.

**1.57.10**  The people of that realm are virtuous in character, easily contented, and righteous; there is no false speech even in casual talk, much less otherwise.

**1.57.11**  Men devoted to the welfare of their elders do not divide property from their fathers; they do not yoke lean cattle to the plough, and they do not allow the feeble to starve.

**1.57.12**  All the social orders always abide in their own dharma in the Cedi realm, O giver of honour; nothing that occurs in the three worlds is unknown to you.

**1.57.13**  A great divine crystal aerial chariot, fit for the enjoyment of the gods, moving through the sky — a flying vehicle given by me — shall attend upon you.

**1.57.14**  You alone among all mortals, mounted on the finest of aerial chariots, shall move on high like an embodied god.

**1.57.15**  I give you the Vaijayantī garland of unfading lotuses, which shall protect you unwounded by weapons in battle.

**1.57.16**  This very mark shall be yours, O lord of men — known as the Indra-garland, auspicious, matchless, and great.

**1.57.17**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The slayer of Vṛtra also gave him a bamboo staff, meant for bestowing desired gifts and protecting the righteous.

**1.57.18**  In honour of that staff of Indra, the lord of the earth had it planted in the ground once a year had passed.

**1.57.19**  From that time forward, even to this day, O king, the planting of the staff is performed by the best of kings just as he established it.

**1.57.20**  The next day too the staff is raised by kings, decked with boxes, fragrant unguents, garlands, and ornaments; wreathed with garlands and festoons it is duly honoured according to rule.

**1.57.21**  And the blessed Śaṃkara is worshipped here in a comic form, assumed by himself out of affection for the great-souled Vasu.

**1.57.22**  Seeing this auspicious worship, done by the gods and by Vasu the foremost of kings, the mighty Mahendra spoke with delight.

**1.57.23**  Those men and kings who shall worship my festival and celebrate it joyfully as the lord of the Cedis has done —

**1.57.24**  — for them, together with their kingdoms, there shall be prosperity and victory, and their realm shall be flourishing and joyful.

**1.57.25**  Thus was the great king Vasu honoured with affection by the great-souled Mahendra, the bounteous one, O lord of men.

**1.57.26**  Those men who shall always celebrate Indra's festival — just as they are purified by great gift-bestowing sacrifices with gifts of land and the like, so also are they purified by the Indra-festival.

**1.57.27**  Thus duly honoured by the bounteous Indra, Vasu the lord of the Cedis governed the earth from Cedi with righteousness, and that lord of the earth celebrated the Indra-festival out of love for Indra.

**1.57.28**  He had five sons of great valour and boundless energy, and that emperor consecrated his sons over various kingdoms.

**1.57.29**  The renowned great warrior Bṛhadratha king of Magadha, Pratyagraha, Kuśāmba who is called Maṇivāhana, Macchilla, Yadu, and the warrior Aparājita —

**1.57.30**  These were the sons of that royal sage of abundant lustre, O king; those five Vāsava kings settled countries and cities with their own names and founded eternal separate dynasties.

**1.57.31**  Dwelling in the crystal aerial palace given by Indra, that great-souled king was attended upon by Gandharvas and Apsarases; thus his name became celebrated as Rājoparicara — the king who roams above.

**1.57.32**  The mountain Kolāhala, endowed with consciousness and overcome by desire, blocked the river Śuktimatī that flowed past his city.

**1.57.33**  Vasu struck that mountain Kolāhala with his foot; the river escaped through the cleft made by that blow.

**1.57.34**  The mountain had begotten a pair in that river; delighted at her release, the river presented them to the king.

**1.57.35**  The male child born there — that best of royal sages, Vasu the giver of wealth, made him a subduer-of-foes commander of the army; the king took the beloved girl, named Girikā, as his wife.

**1.57.36**  His wife Girikā, desiring a son, duly informed him that her fertile season had come; she had bathed, performed the puṃsavana rite, and was pure.

**1.57.37**  On that very day the ancestors spoke to him with affection — to that best of kings, the finest of the wise — saying: "Slay deer for us."

**1.57.38**  Not transgressing that command of the ancestors, the king went forth to hunt, yet, filled with desire, he kept thinking only of Girikā — she who was supremely beautiful, a very second Śrī made manifest.

**1.57.39**  As he roamed in that lovely forest his seed fell; the moment it fell the lord of the earth caught it on a leaf.

**1.57.40**  He caught it thinking: "My seed must not fall in vain; and the fertile season of my wife must not pass fruitless," so resolved the lord.

**1.57.41**  Having deliberated thus and pondered again and again, the best of kings, ascertaining that the seed must not be wasted —

**1.57.42**  — and reckoning the moment right for conveying the seed to his chief queen, he consecrated that seed with mantras; then, knowing the subtle truth of dharma and purpose, he discerned a swift hawk nearby and addressed it.

**1.57.43**  "For my sake, dear one, carry this seed swiftly to my home and deliver it to Girikā, for today is her fertile time."

**1.57.44**  Taking it, the hawk at once soared up swiftly and flew off at the greatest speed through the sky.

**1.57.45**  Another hawk, seeing that hawk coming, immediately rushed at it, suspecting that it carried meat.

**1.57.46**  The two then fought beak-to-beak in the sky; as they struggled the seed fell — and fell into the waters of the Yamunā.

**1.57.47**  There a celebrated celestial nymph named Adrikā, transformed into a fish by a brahmin's curse, was living in the Yamunā.

**1.57.48**  Adrikā, in the form of a fish, swiftly approached and swallowed that seed which had fallen from the hawk's talons — the seed of Vāsava's descendant.

**1.57.49**  Some time later, fishermen caught that fish; and when the tenth month had arrived, O best of the Bharatas, they drew from her belly a human pair — one female, one male.

**1.57.50**  Thinking it a wonder, they reported to the king: "O king, these two human beings were born from the body of a fish."

**1.57.51**  Of the two, Rājoparicara took the male; he became the righteous king named Matsya, true to his word.

**1.57.52**  The Apsarā was freed from her curse in an instant, as the blessed one had previously told her: "O fair one, after entering an animal womb and giving birth to two humans, you shall be released from the curse."

**1.57.53**  Then, after giving birth to those two and being cut open by the fisherman, she abandoned the fish form, regained her divine form, and that excellent Apsarā went on her way along the path of Siddhas, sages, and Cāraṇas.

**1.57.54**  The daughter, born of that fish and smelling of fish, endowed with beauty and character, adorned with all virtues — the king gave her to a fisherman saying: "Let her be yours."

**1.57.55**  She became known by the name Satyavatī; living with the fisherman-killer, she smelled of fish for some time, though she was sweet-smiled.

**1.57.56**  While she was ferrying her father's boat on the water in service to him, Parāśara, wandering on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, saw her.

**1.57.57**  Seeing her — supremely beautiful, desired even by the Siddhas, and lovely to behold — that wise and learned bull among sages desired her, that maiden of Vāsava's line, and resolved to act.

**1.57.58**  She said: "Look, revered sir — on both banks stand sages who can see us both; how could our union take place?"

**1.57.59**  Addressed thus by her, the blessed and mighty sage created a mist by which that entire region became as if enveloped in darkness.

**1.57.60**  Seeing the mist conjured by the great sage, the intelligent girl was amazed and spoke, abashed.

**1.57.61**  "Know me, revered sir, as a maiden ever under my father's authority; by union with you my maidenhood would be defiled, O sinless one."

**1.57.62**  "And with my maidenhood defiled, O best of twice-born, how shall I be able to go home? Nor can I bring myself to remain at home, O wise one. Considering all this, revered sir, do whatever is best thereafter."

**1.57.63**  To her who spoke thus, the delighted foremost of sages said: "After granting me my desire, you shall remain a maiden still."

**1.57.64**  "Choose also a boon, timid one, whatever you desire, O beautiful lady; for my grace has never before been granted in vain, O sweet-smiled one."

**1.57.65**  Addressed thus, she chose as her boon a supreme fragrance of the body; and the blessed and mighty sage granted her the desire of her heart.

**1.57.66**  Then, having obtained her boon and delighted, adorned with the virtues of womanhood, she united with that sage of wondrous deeds.

**1.57.67**  From this her name Gandhavatī became celebrated on earth; people on earth could smell her fragrance from a yojana away.

**1.57.68**  Thus she became also widely known by the name Yojanagandha — "she whose fragrance reaches a yojana"; and the blessed Parāśara departed to his own abode.

**1.57.69**  Thus Satyavatī, overjoyed at obtaining that excellent boon, instantly conceived upon her union with Parāśara, and on an island in the Yamunā she gave birth; the mighty son of Parāśara was born.

**1.57.70**  He paid his respects to his mother, then set his mind on austerity; he said to her: "When you remember me, I shall appear to you in times of need."

**1.57.71**  Thus was Dvaipāyana born to Satyavatī from Parāśara; as that child was set down on an island (dvīpa) he became known as Dvaipāyana.

**1.57.72**  Knowing how dharma recedes step by step from age to age, and observing the lifespan and capacity of mortals age by age —

**1.57.73**  — wishing to confer benefit on Brahma and on the brahmins, he divided the Vedas; and because of that dividing (vyāsa) he is remembered as Vyāsa.

**1.57.74**  He taught the Vedas — with the Mahābhārata as the fifth — to Sumanta, Jaimini, Paila, and his own son Śuka.

**1.57.75**  The mighty, greatest, boon-granting Vyāsa also taught Vaiśaṃpāyana; by them the saṃhitās of the Bhārata were published separately.

**1.57.76**  Likewise Bhīṣma, son of Śāntanu, of boundless splendour, was born from Gaṅgā through the power of the Vasus — of great valour and great renown.

**1.57.77**  The ancient sage who was impaled on a spike — though no thief — out of suspicion of theft: he became celebrated as Aṇīmāṇḍavya, of very great renown.

**1.57.78**  That great seer, summoning Dharma of old, said this: 'In my childhood I pierced a little bird with a reed-stalk.'

**1.57.79**  That sin I remember, O Dharma — no other evil do I remember. Why then has not my austerity, which is equal to a thousand, conquered it here?

**1.57.80**  Since the slaying of a brahmin is graver than the slaying of all other beings, therefore, on account of this sin, you shall be born in a shudra womb.

**1.57.81**  By that curse, Dharma himself was born in a shudra womb — learned, in the form of Vidura, a righteous body free from sin.

**1.57.82**  Sanjaya, resembling a sage, was born as a charioteer's son from Gavalgana. And from the Sun, in the maiden daughter of Kunti, was born Karna the great warrior, bearing congenital armor, his face radiant with earrings.

**1.57.83**  For the benefit of the worlds, Vishnu, revered by the world, the greatly glorious one, manifested himself from Vasudeva through Devaki.

**1.57.84**  That god, without beginning or end, is the maker and lord of the universe — the unmanifest, imperishable Brahman, the primal cause, of the nature of that which is beyond qualities.

**1.57.85**  He is the imperishable Self, the supreme source of Nature, the Cosmic Person, the maker of the universe, the union with pure being, the eternal and imperishable.

**1.57.86**  Infinite, immovable, divine, the Swan, Narayana the lord, the Sustainer, unaging, eternal — they call him the supreme and imperishable.

**1.57.87**  That all-pervading Person, the maker, the grandfather of all beings, was born among the Andhaka-Vrishnis for the purpose of upholding righteousness.

**1.57.88**  Satyaki and Kritavarma, both of great valor, skilled in all weapons and expert in missiles, devoted followers of Narayana, were born from Satyaka and Hridika respectively, both masters of arms.

**1.57.89**  The seed spilled from Bharadvaja developed in a vessel; from that severe-ascetic great seer's seed, Drona was born.

**1.57.90**  From Sharadvan of the Gautama line, a pair was born from a clump of reeds — the mother of Ashvatthama and Kripa the mighty. Ashvatthama was then born from Drona, the foremost among bearers of weapons.

**1.57.91**  Likewise Dhrishtadyumna too, directly blazing like fire, was born from the sacred fire when a Vedic rite was being performed — the valiant hero, born with a bow, destined to destroy Drona.

**1.57.92**  Likewise from the sacrificial altar was born Krishna (Draupadi) as well — radiant, auspicious, resplendent of form, bearing a most exquisite beauty.

**1.57.93**  Nagnajit, a pupil of Prahlada, became Subala; his offspring, destroyers of dharma, were born due to the wrath of the gods.

**1.57.94**  The son of the king of Gandhara became Shakuni, the son of Subala; and the mother of Duryodhana — both were born, those two knowers of worldly affairs.

**1.57.95**  From Krishna-Dvaipayana (Vyasa) were born Dhritarashtra, lord of men, and the mighty Pandu as well, in the field of Vichitraveerya.

**1.57.96**  From Pandu were born five sons equal to gods, each from different mothers of two wives; the eldest among them in virtue was Yudhishthira.

**1.57.97**  Yudhishthira was born from Dharma, Vrikodara (Bhima) from the wind god; from Indra was born the glorious Dhananjaya (Arjuna), foremost among all bearers of weapons.

**1.57.98**  The twin pair, endowed with beauty, were born from the Ashvins — Nakula and Sahadeva, devoted to the service of their elders.
