**1.57.99**  Likewise a hundred sons were born to the wise Dhritarashtra — headed by Duryodhana, and Yuyutsu, and Karana (Vikarna) likewise.

**1.57.100**  Abhimanyu was born from Arjuna through Subhadra — the nephew of Vasudeva, the grandson of the great-souled Pandu.

**1.57.101**  From the five Pandavas through Krishna (Draupadi) were born five princes, endowed with beauty and skilled in all weapons.

**1.57.102**  Prativindhya from Yudhishthira, Sutasoma from Vrikodara (Bhima), Shrutakirti from Arjuna, and Shatanika the son of Nakula.

**1.57.103**  Likewise from Sahadeva came the valiant Shrutasena; and from Bhima through Hidimba in the forest was born Ghatotkacha.

**1.57.104**  Shikhandin was born from Drupada — a girl who attained sonhood, whom the yaksha Sthuna made into a man out of desire to please.

**1.57.105**  In that conflict of the Kurus, hundreds of thousands of kings assembled, about to fight in battle.

**1.57.106**  Their names in their entirety cannot be reckoned — it is not possible to count them even in tens of thousands of years. But the chief ones have been named here, by whom this narrative is woven together.

**1.58.1**  Janamejaya said: O brahmin, those who have been named, and others who have not been fully named — I wish to hear about all of them properly, and about the other illustrious kings.

**1.58.2**  For what purpose were these great warriors, equal to gods, born here upon the earth — that, O greatly blessed one, you ought to explain to me fully.

**1.58.3**  Vaishampayana said: This is indeed a secret of the gods, O king — so we have heard. Yet I shall tell it to you, after bowing to the Self-born (Brahma).

**1.58.4**  Having made the earth devoid of kshatriyas twenty-one times in the past, Jamadagni's son (Parashurama) practiced austerities on Mount Mahendra, the greatest of mountains.

**1.58.5**  Then, when the world had been made devoid of kshatriyas by the descendant of Bhrigu, O king, the kshatriya women approached brahmin men seeking to conceive.

**1.58.6**  With them those brahmins of disciplined vows came together, O tiger among men, in the proper fertile season, not out of desire, nor out of season.

**1.58.7**  From those brahmins those kshatriya women conceived by the thousands; then they gave birth, O king, to kshatriyas honored for their valor — both boys and girls — for the replenishment of the kshatriya order.

**1.58.8**  Thus that kshatriya order, born from ascetic brahmins upon kshatriya women, prospered in righteousness, endowed with very long life; and all four social orders at that time were foremost in brahminic virtue.

**1.58.9**  They approached women only in the proper season, not out of desire, nor out of season; likewise the other creatures, even those of animal birth, would approach their mates in season then, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.58.10**  Then those subjects grew in righteousness, living for hundreds of thousands of years, devoted to the vow of dharma, O protector of the earth; men were entirely free from mental anguish and physical disease.

**1.58.11**  Then the kshatriya order again ruled over this earth bounded by the ocean, traversed in its entirety with the gait of a great elephant, with its mountains, forests, and groves.

**1.58.12**  When the kshatriya order again governed this wealth-bearing earth by dharma, the social orders headed by the brahmins attained supreme joy.

**1.58.13**  The lords of men, having cast away the faults born of desire and anger, administered punishment to those deserving punishment in accordance with dharma, and thus protected their subjects.

**1.58.14**  While the kshatriya order was thus devoted to dharma, the thousand-eyed one of a hundred sacrifices (Indra) rained sweetly in the right place and season, nourishing the subjects.

**1.58.15**  In that age, O lord of men, no child died in infancy; nor did any male know a woman before reaching youth.

**1.58.16**  Thus, O bull of the Bharatas, this earth bounded by the ocean was abundantly filled with long-lived subjects.

**1.58.17**  The kshatriyas performed great sacrifices with abundant fees; and the brahmins studied the Vedas along with their supplementary texts and the Upanishads.

**1.58.18**  The brahmins did not sell sacred knowledge in those days, O king; nor did they recite the Vedas in the proximity of those equal to shudras.

**1.58.19**  The vaishyas caused cultivation by means of oxen; they did not yoke a cow to the plough, nor did they keep thin-bodied animals alive for labor.

**1.58.20**  Men did not milk cows with suckling calves that were still drinking the froth-milk; nor did merchants sell goods with false weights in those days.

**1.58.21**  Men, O tiger among men, performed deeds imbued with righteousness, keeping dharma always in view, devoted to dharma.

**1.58.22**  All the social orders were absorbed in their own proper duties, O lord of men; thus in that age, O tiger among men, dharma did not diminish anywhere.

**1.58.23**  Cows gave birth in due season, and women likewise, O bull of the Bharatas; trees bore flowers and fruits in their seasons.

**1.58.24**  Thus when the Krita age was proceeding properly in those days, O king, the entire earth was abundantly filled with many living beings.

**1.58.25**  Then, as the human world flourished, O bull of the Bharatas, the asuras were born in the fields of kings, O foremost of men.

**1.58.26**  For the daityas, having been repeatedly defeated in battle by the Adityas and deprived of their sovereignty, came to be born here upon the earth.

**1.58.27**  Desiring divinity here and endowed with proud minds, O lord, the asuras were born among human beings on earth, in this and that creature.

**1.58.28**  Among cattle, among horses, O king of kings, among donkeys, camels, and buffaloes, among carnivorous creatures, among elephants and deer as well —

**1.58.29**  — by those who had been born here and those still being born, O guardian of the earth, this earth could no longer bear herself by her own strength.

**1.58.30**  Then certain kings were born endowed with great strength — sons of Diti and of Danu, fallen from that higher world to this one.

**1.58.31**  Powerful and arrogant, bearing various forms, those crushers of foes roamed over this earth bounded by the ocean.

**1.58.32**  They oppressed brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras alike; they oppressed all other creatures as well with their power.

**1.58.33**  Terrifying and slaying these various groups of beings, they wandered over the earth in all directions, O king, by the hundreds of thousands.

**1.58.34**  Assaulting great sages dwelling in their hermitages here and there, those enemies of brahmins, intoxicated with pride of valor and drunk with the intoxication of power —

**1.58.35**  — this earth, thus oppressed by those great asuras swollen with might and power, O protector of the earth, approached Brahma.

**1.58.36**  For neither the wind, O king, nor the nagas, nor the mountains were able to bear this earth that had been forcibly overrun by the danavas.

**1.58.37**  Then the earth, O protector of the earth, weighed down by her burden and afflicted by fear, went for refuge to the god who is the grandfather of all beings.

**1.58.38**  She saw the god Brahma, the imperishable maker of the worlds, surrounded by the greatly blessed gods, twice-born ones, and great seers.

**1.58.39**  Being praised by gandharvas and apsarases engaged in the work of eulogizing, filled with joy — she approached and paid reverence to him.

**1.58.40**  Then the earth, seeking refuge, presented her petition to him in the presence of all the world-guardians, O descendant of Bharata.

**1.58.41**  But the purpose of that earth's visit had already been known beforehand, O king, to the Self-born one of supreme nature, the one seated on the highest.

**1.58.42**  For how would the creator of the universe fail to know, O descendant of Bharata, the innermost thoughts of all worlds — of gods and asuras — without exception?

**1.58.43**  To her, O great king, spoke the lord of the earth, the all-pervading one, the source of all beings, the lord, the auspicious one, the Lord of Creatures (Brahma).

**1.58.44**  For the purpose for which you have come into my presence, O holder of wealth, for that purpose I shall set all the celestial ones to work.

**1.58.45**  Having said this and dismissed the earth, O king, Brahma the god, the creator of beings, himself gave instructions to all the wise ones.

**1.58.46**  He said: 'To remove the burden of this earth, be born separately, each in a portion, upon this very earth, for opposition against the asuras.'

**1.58.47**  Likewise, having assembled the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, the blessed one said this excellent word to them all: 'Be born as you please among human beings, each through your own portion.'

**1.58.48**  Then Indra and all the others, having heard the word of their divine preceptor — true, purposeful, and beneficial — accepted it then.

**1.58.49**  Then all of them, having resolved to go to the earth through their own portions, approached Narayana the destroyer of foes at Vaikuntha.

**1.58.50**  He who holds discus and mace in hand, clad in yellow, dark of radiance, lotus-naveled, destroyer of the foes of the gods, with broad and beautiful oblique eyes —

**1.58.51**  — to that Purushottama (Supreme Person), Indra, for the purification of the earth, said: 'Descend through a portion of yourself.' And Hari replied to him: 'So be it.'

**1.59.1**  Vaishampayana said: Then Indra, together with Narayana, made an agreement to descend to earth from heaven, accompanied by the gods, each taking a partial incarnation.

**1.59.2**  And Shakra himself, having instructed all the heaven-dwellers, departed once again from the abode of Narayana.

**1.59.3**  For the destruction of the enemies of the immortals and for the welfare of all the worlds, those heaven-dwellers descended in succession from heaven to this earth.

**1.59.4**  Then, O tiger among kings, those heaven-dwellers were born at will in the lineages of brahmarshis and in the royal families of earthly sages.

**1.59.5**  They slew danavas and rakshasas, gandharvas and nagas, and many other man-eating beings in great numbers.

**1.59.6**  But the danavas, rakshasas, gandharvas, and nagas — those mighty ones — could not slay them even in childhood, O best of the Bharatas.

**1.59.7**  Janamejaya said: Of the assemblies of gods and danavas, of gandharvas and apsaras, of all humans, and also of yakshas and rakshasas —

**1.59.8**  I wish to hear truly, from the very beginning, the complete origin of all these, and of all living beings in their entirety — for you know all things.

**1.59.9**  Vaishampayana said: Well then, I shall tell you — having bowed to the Self-born — the origin and dissolution of the worlds, beginning with the gods, completely and correctly.

**1.59.10**  The six great sages known as the mind-born sons of Brahma are: Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.

**1.59.11**  Kashyapa is the son of Marichi, and from Kashyapa were born these offspring. The thirteen highly blessed daughters of Daksha gave birth to these creatures.

**1.59.12**  Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kala, Anayus, Simhika, Muni, Krodha, Prava, Arishta, Vinata, and Kapila —

**1.59.13**  — and Kadru, O tiger among men, these daughters of Daksha, O Bharata: the offspring — sons and grandsons — of these ladies, endowed with might, is without end.

**1.59.14**  From Aditi were born the twelve Adityas, lords of the worlds. I shall name them for you, O king, O Bharata.

**1.59.15**  Dhata, Mitra, Aryama, Shakra, Varuna, and Amsha; Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pusha, and Savita the tenth —

**1.59.16**  — Tvashta the eleventh, and Vishnu is declared the twelfth. He, the last-born of all the Adityas, surpasses them all in virtues.

**1.59.17**  Diti had but one son, remembered as Hiranyakashipu. These five sons of that great-souled one were known by the following names:

**1.59.18**  Prahlada was the eldest among them, then Samhrada next; Anuhlada was the third, and after him came Shibi and Bashkala.

**1.59.19**  Prahlada had three sons known everywhere, O Bharata: Virochana, Kumbha, and Nikumbha, all renowned.

**1.59.20**  Virochana had one son, the mighty Bali; and Bali's famous son was the great asura named Bana.

**1.59.21**  Danu had forty sons known everywhere, O Bharata; the eldest among them was the king Viprachitti, of great renown.

**1.59.22**  Shambara, Namuchi, the renowned Puloma; Asiloma, Keshi, and the danava Durjaya —

**1.59.23**  — Ayahshira, Ashvashira, and the mighty Ayahshanku; Gaganamurdha, the swift Ketuman —

**1.59.24**  — Svarbhanu, Ashva, Ashvapati, Vrishaparva and Ajaka; Ashvagrīva, Sukshma, and the great asura Tuhunda —

**1.59.25**  — Isripa, Ekachakra, Virupaksha, Hara and Ahara; Nichandra, Nikumbha, Kupatha, and Kapatha —

**1.59.26**  — Sharaba, Shalaba, and also the pair Surya and Chandrama: thus are the danavas of Danu's lineage enumerated. But those two — Surya and Chandrama — are indeed remembered as belonging to the gods.

**1.59.27**  And these ten bull-like danavas, famous in their lineage, full of vitality and mighty in strength, are the sons of Danu, O great king.

**1.59.28**  Ekaksha, the heroic Mritapa, Pralamba and Naraka; Vatapi, Shatrutapana, and the great asura Shatha —

**1.59.29**  — Gavishtha, Danayu, and the danava Dirghajihva. Their sons and grandsons are remembered as innumerable, O Bharata.

**1.59.30**  Simhika bore the son Rahu, the afflicting force of moon and sun; also Suchandra, the moon-slayer, and Chandravimardana.

**1.59.31**  The offspring — sons and grandsons — of this cruel-natured woman are without end; the host called Krodhavasha, of cruel deeds and destroyer of enemies.

**1.59.32**  Anayus had four bull-like asura sons: Vikshara, Bala, Vira, and the great asura Vritra.

**1.59.33**  The renowned sons of Kala, resembling Death itself in their striking power, are known on earth as mighty in valor among the danavas, afflicting their foes.

**1.59.34**  Vinashana, Krodha, Hanta the other son of Krodha, and likewise Krodhashatru — these are renowned as the Kaleyas.

**1.59.35**  Shukra, son of the sage Bhrigu, became the preceptor of the asuras. The four famous sons of Ushanas were officiant priests for the asuras.

**1.59.36**  Tvashtavara, Atri, and two others — performers of sacred rites — blazing in splendor equal to the sun, and powerful enough to illuminate Brahma's world.

**1.59.37**  Thus has this origin of lineages been told to you — of the vigorous asuras and the gods — as I have heard it in the Purana.

**1.59.38**  The offspring of these beings — qualities included — cannot be fully enumerated in its entirety, O lord of the earth; it is without end.

**1.59.39**  Tarkshya, Arishtanemi, and likewise Garuda and Aruna; Aruni and Varuni — these are remembered as the sons of Vinata.

**1.59.40**  Shesha, Ananta, Vasuki, the serpent Takshaka, Kurma, and Kulika — these mighty sons of Kadru are the Kadruveyas.

**1.59.41**  Bhimasena, Ugrasena, Suparna, and Varuna; Gopati, Dhritarashtra, and Suryavarchas the seventh —

**1.59.42**  — Puravin, Arkaparna, and the renowned Prayuta; the celebrated Bhima and Chitraratha, known as all-knowing and self-controlled —

**1.59.43**  — and Shalishira, O king, Pradyumna the fourteenth, Kali the fifteenth, and Narada the sixteenth — thus are these divine gandharvas, the Mauneyas, enumerated.

**1.59.44**  Now I shall name other beings, O Bharata. Prava gave birth to: the blameless Anuvasham, Anunam, Aruna, Priya, Anupa, Subhaga, and Bhasi.

**1.59.45**  Siddha, Purna, Barhi, the greatly renowned Purnasha, Brahmachari, Ratiguṇa, and Suparna the seventh —

**1.59.46**  — Vishvavasu, Bhanu, and Suchandra the tenth: thus are these divine gandharvas, the sons of Prava, enumerated.

**1.59.47**  This lineage of the apsaras, known for its auspicious qualities — the highly blessed goddess Prava bore it long ago, as received from the divine sages.

**1.59.48**  Alambusa, Mishrakeshi, Vidyutparna, Tulanagha, Aruna, Rakshita, Rambha, and likewise Manorama —

**1.59.49**  — Asita, Subahu, Suvrata, Subhuja, Supriya, and Atibahu; and the renowned Haha, Huhu, and Tumburu are remembered as the four foremost gandharvas.

**1.59.50**  Amrita, brahmanas, cows, gandharvas, and apsaras — these are celebrated in the Purana as the offspring of Kapila.

**1.59.51**  Thus has the origin of all beings been told to you by me, counted out correctly, and likewise that of the gandharvas and apsaras.

**1.59.52**  Of serpents and of suparnas, of the Rudras and the Maruts, of cows and of brahmanas — of the glorious ones of meritorious deeds.

**1.59.53**  This account is life-prolonging, meritorious, and enriching; it is pleasant to hear, should always be listened to, and should be narrated with a heart free from envy.

**1.59.54**  Whoever recites this lineage of great souls with discipline in the presence of brahmanas and gods gains abundant progeny, prosperity, and renown, and after death an excellent destination.

**1.60.1**  Vaishampayana said: The six great sages, known as the mind-born sons of Brahma, are well known. The eleven supremely mind-born sons of Sthanu (Shiva) are also renowned.

**1.60.2**  Mrigavyadha, Sharva, the greatly renowned Nirrti; Ajaikapat, Ahirbudhnya, and Pinaki the scorcher of foes —

**1.60.3**  — Dahana, Ishvara, Kapali of great splendor, Sthanu, and the lord Bhava: these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.

**1.60.4**  Marichi, Angiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu — these six are the mighty great-sage sons of Brahma.

**1.60.5**  Angiras had three sons renowned everywhere in the world: Brihaspati, Utathya, and Samvarta — all firm in their vows.

**1.60.6**  Atri had many sons, O lord of men — all knowers of the Vedas, perfected, tranquil-souled great sages, as is told.

**1.60.7**  Rakshasas came from Pulastya, as did vanaras and kinnaras. From Pulaha came deer, lions, tigers, and kimpurushas.

**1.60.8**  Kratu's sons are equal to Kratu himself in power, companions of birds in flight, renowned throughout the three worlds, and wholly devoted to the vow of truth.

**1.60.9**  Daksha, the blessed sage, was born from the right thumb of Brahma, O protector of the earth — the best of those who have sons.

**1.60.10**  From Brahma's left thumb was born the wife of that great-souled one; and the sage himself fathered fifty daughters upon her.

**1.60.11**  All those daughters, faultless-limbed and lotus-eyed, the Prajapati appointed as putrikas (daughters serving as sons), since he had no sons.

**1.60.12**  He gave ten to Dharma, twenty-seven to Soma (the moon), by divine rule, O king, and thirteen to Kashyapa.

**1.60.13**  Learn from me the names of those wives of Dharma as I recite them: Kirti, Lakshmi, Dhrti, Medha, Pushti, Shraddha, and Kriya —

**1.60.14**  — Buddhi, Lajja, and Mati: these are the ten wives of Dharma. These are the gateways of Dharma appointed by the Self-born.

**1.60.15**  The twenty-seven wives of Soma are celebrated in the world; engaged in guiding time, wives of the moon, of pure vows, all connected to the nakshatras, established in the order of the world's journey.

**1.60.16**  The grandfather Muni is a god; his son is the Prajapati (Dharma). That one had eight Vasus as sons — I shall speak of them in detail.

**1.60.17**  Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Aha, Anila, Anala, Pratyusha, and Prabhasa — these are remembered as the eight Vasus.

**1.60.18**  Dhara is the son of Dhumra, and similarly Dhruva is a knower of Brahma. Soma is the son of Manasvinī; from Shvasa came Shvasana (Anila, the wind).

**1.60.19**  Aha is the son of Rata; Hutashana (fire) is the son of Shandilya. Pratyusha and Prabhasa are remembered as the two sons of Prabhata.

**1.60.20**  The sons of Dhara are Dravina and Hutahavyavaha (carrier of oblations). The son of Dhruva is the blessed Kala, who brings about the dissolution of the worlds.

**1.60.21**  Soma's son is Varcha, by whom the radiant are born. From Manohara were born Shishira, Prana, and Ramana.

**1.60.22**  The sons of Aha are remembered as Jyoti, Shrama, Shanta, and Muni. The son of Agni (Anala) is the glorious Kumara, who dwells in the shara-grass forest.

**1.60.23**  His sons are Shakha, Vishakha, and Naigamesha born from his back. Because the Krittikas adopted him, he is remembered as Karttikeya.

**1.60.24**  Shiva is the wife of Anila (the wind god); her son is Purojava. Avijnatagati is the other — these are the two sons of Anila.

**1.60.25**  Pratyusha's son is known as the sage named Devala. Devala also had two sons — patient and wise.

**1.60.26**  Brihaspati's sister, a noble woman, a celibate ascetic, accomplished in yoga, roams the entire world unattached — she is the wife of Prabhasa, the eighth of the Vasus.

**1.60.27**  The greatly blessed Viśvakarmā was born — the Prajāpati of crafts, the maker of thousands of works of art, the carpenter of the thirty gods.

**1.60.28**  He is the maker of all ornaments, the foremost among artisans, who fashioned the celestial aerial chariots of the gods.

**1.60.29**  Men live by the craft of that great-souled one, and they worship the imperishable Viśvakarmā without ceasing.

**1.60.30**  Bursting through the right breast of Brahmā in human form, the blessed Dharma issued forth — he who brings happiness to all the worlds.

**1.60.31**  He has three excellent sons, delightful to all beings — Śama (Tranquility), Kāma (Desire), and Harṣa (Joy) — who by their radiance sustain the worlds.

**1.60.32**  Rati (Delight) is the wife of Kāma; Prāpti (Attainment) is the consort of Śama; and Nandī (Bliss) is the wife of Harṣa — in whom the worlds are established.

**1.60.33**  Kaśyapa is the son of Marīci; from Kaśyapa were born the gods and the asuras, O tiger among kings — he is indeed the progenitor of the worlds.

**1.60.34**  Tvāṣṭrī, the greatly blessed wife of Savitṛ, assuming the form of a mare, gave birth in the sky to both the Aśvins.

**1.60.35**  Aditi has exactly twelve sons, headed by Indra, O lord of men; the youngest of them is Viṣṇu, in whom the worlds are established.

**1.60.36**  These are the thirty-three gods. I shall now declare to you their lineages, their factions, their clans, and their groups.

**1.60.37**  Know the Bhārgavas as belonging to the other faction of the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, the Vasus, and the Viśvedevas as well.

**1.60.38**  The mighty Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, and likewise Aruṇa, and the blessed Bṛhaspati — these are reckoned among the Ādityas.

**1.60.39**  Know the Guhyakas, all medicinal herbs, and animals as belonging to the Aśvins. O king, this host of gods has been proclaimed to you in order; a person who recites this list is freed from all sins.

**1.60.40**  The blessed Bhṛgu issued forth by splitting open the heart of Brahmā. The son of Bhṛgu is Kavi, the wise one; Śukra is the son of Kavi, and he became a planet (graha).

**1.60.41**  Appointed by the Self-born (Brahmā) for the regulation of the life-journey of the three worlds, governing rain and drought, fear and safety, he courses through the universe.

**1.60.42**  He became the teacher of Yoga, of great intellect, the preceptor of the Daityas and also of the gods — supremely wise, observing celibacy and firm in his vows.

**1.60.43**  When that Bhārgava was appointed by the Lord for the welfare of the worlds, Bhṛgu sired another blameless son.

**1.60.44**  That son was Cyavana, blazing with ascetic power, righteous in soul and wise — he who fell from the womb in anger for the liberation of his mother, O Bhārata.

**1.60.45**  Āruṣī, the daughter of Manu, became the wife of that wise one (Cyavana). From her was born the greatly renowned Aurva, ripping through the thigh — endowed with mighty austerity, great radiance, and all virtues even as a child.

**1.60.46**  Ṛcīka was the son of Aurva; from him was born Jamadagni. The great-souled Jamadagni had four sons.

**1.60.47**  Rāma was the youngest of them, yet endowed with qualities not of the least — skilled in all weapons and missiles, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, and master of himself.

**1.60.48**  Aurva had a hundred sons, headed by Jamadagni; from them arose thousands of descendants — this is the expansion of the Bhṛgu lineage.

**1.60.49**  Brahmā has two other sons by whose marks the world is governed — Dhātā and Vidhātā, who dwell together with Manu.

**1.60.50**  The auspicious goddess Lakṣmī, dwelling in the lotus, is the sister of those two. Her mind-born sons are the horses that move through the sky.

**1.60.51**  The eldest wife of Varuṇa, a goddess, was born from Śukra (Śukrā). Know her son to be Bala (Strength), and also Surā (Wine), the delight of the gods.

**1.60.52**  Among the creatures who hungered for food and who fell to devouring one another, Adharma (Unrighteousness) arose there — the destroyer of all beings.

**1.60.53**  His wife is Nirṛti; from her the Nairṛta Rākṣasas arise. She has three sons, ever given to wicked deeds: Bhaya (Fear), Mahābhaya (Great Fear), and Mṛtyu (Death), the ender of beings.

**1.60.54**  The goddess Tāmrā gave birth to five daughters, renowned throughout the world: Kākī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī.

**1.60.55**  Kākī gave birth to owls; Śyenī bore hawks; Bhāsī brought forth vultures and kites, O lord of the people.

**1.60.56**  Dhṛtarāṣṭrī — that spirited one — gave birth to swans, royal swans, and chakravāka birds in full, blessings to you.

**1.60.57**  O knower of righteousness, Śukī — high-minded, endowed with auspicious qualities, honored by all marks of excellence — gave birth only to parrots.

**1.60.58**  Krodhavaśā also gave birth to nine daughters of her own: Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Hari, and Bhadramanā —

**1.60.59**  — and Mātaṅgī, Śārdūlī, Śvetā, Surabhī endowed with all auspicious marks, and the illustrious Surasā.

**1.60.60**  All deer are the offspring of Mṛgī, O son of the best of men. From Mṛgamandā came bears, sṛmaras (a deer species), and yaks.

**1.60.61**  From Bhadramanā was born the great serpent Airāvata as her son; Airāvata's son is the divine elephant Mahāgaja.

**1.60.62**  The offspring of Harī are the lions and the swift monkeys; the golāṅgūlas too — blessings to you — are called the children of Harī.

**1.60.63**  And Śārdūlī gave birth to lions, tigers, and leopards, O Bhārata — all of them, O greatly fortunate one, without doubt.

**1.60.64**  The offspring of Mātaṅgī are the mātaṅgas (elephants), O lord of men. And Śvetā gave birth to the swift directional elephant called Śveta.

**1.60.65**  Likewise, O king, Surabhī gave birth to two daughters — blessings to you — Rohiṇī and the illustrious Gandharvī. From Rohiṇī were born cattle, and from Gandharvī her sons were horses.

**1.60.66**  Surasā gave birth to nāgas, O king, and Kadrū brought forth serpents. Analā also gave birth to seven trees bearing round fruits. Śukī is the daughter of Analā, and Surasā is the daughter of Kadrū.

**1.60.67**  Śyenī, the wife of Aruṇa, gave birth to Saṃpāti and likewise Jaṭāyu — two mighty, powerful sons. And Vinatā's two famous sons are Garuḍa and Aruṇa.

**1.60.68**  Thus has the origin of all these great beings been fully proclaimed by me, O lord of men, O best of the wise.

**1.60.69**  Having properly heard this, a person is purified of sin, attains omniscience, and finds the highest path.

**1.61.1**  Janamejaya said: O blessed one, I wish to hear truly about the births and deeds of all these great-souled beings — gods, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all other beings —

**1.61.2**  — how they were born among men, and their deeds, in proper order.

**1.61.3**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O lord of men, I shall tell you in full about those heavenly beings and also the dānavas who were born among humans — them first.

**1.61.4**  He who was known as Vipracitti, the bull among dānavas — he was born among men as the famous Jarāsaṃdha, the bull among men.

**1.61.5**  He who, O king, is remembered as Hiraṇyakaśipu, son of Diti — he was born in the human world as Śiśupāla, the bull among men.

**1.61.6**  He who was famed as Saṃhrāda, the younger brother of Prahrāda — he was born as the renowned Śalya, the bull of the Bāhlīkas.

**1.61.7**  The radiant Anuhrāda, who was known as the lastborn, became famed as Dhṛṣṭaketu, a lord among men.

**1.61.8**  He who, O king, was celebrated as the Daitya named Śibi — he was widely known as Druma and was a king on earth.

**1.61.9**  He among them who was the excellent asura named Bāṣkala — he was known as Bhagadatta and was a lord among men.

**1.61.10**  Ayaḥśirā, Aśvaśirā, the valiant Ayaḥśaṅku, Gaganamūrdhā, and Vegavān as the fifth —

**1.61.11**  — these five valiant great asuras were born, O king, as great-souled ones among the Kekayas, the very best of royal bulls.

**1.61.12**  He who was otherwise known as the glorious Ketumān — he became known on earth as Amitaujā, a king.

**1.61.13**  He who was the glorious great asura known as Svarbhānu — he became known as Ugrasena, the fierce-actioned lord of men.

**1.61.14**  He who was the glorious great asura known as Aśva — he became the king named Aśoka, of mighty valor and prowess.

**1.61.15**  He who was the younger brother of that one, O king, remembered as the Daitya Aśvapati — he became the king Hārdikya, the bull among men.

**1.61.16**  He who was the glorious great asura known as Vṛṣaparvan — he became known on earth as Dīrghaprajña, a king.

**1.61.17**  He who was the younger brother of Vṛṣaparvan, O king — Ajaka — became known on earth as Malla, a king.

**1.61.18**  He who was the powerful great asura known as Aśvagrīva — he became known on earth as Rocamāna, a king.

**1.61.19**  He who was celebrated, O king, as Sūkṣma, the wise and the famous — he became known on earth as Bṛhanta, a king.

**1.61.20**  He who was known as Tuhuṇḍa, the foremost among asuras — he became known as Senābindu, a lord of men.

**1.61.21**  He among those asuras named Isṛpā, who was supreme in strength — he became the king named Pāpajit on earth, renowned for his valor.

**1.61.22**  He who was known as the great asura Ekacakra — he became renowned on earth as Prativindhya.

**1.61.23**  The Daitya Virūpākṣa, a great asura of variegated warfare — he was known on earth as Citravarman and was a king.

**1.61.24**  He who was the heroic foremost of dānavas, Hara (or Arihara) — he was born as the bull among men known as Suvāstu.

**1.61.25**  Ahara, of great radiance, the destroyer of the enemy's side — he became the king renowned on earth as Bāhlīka.

**1.61.26**  He who was the foremost asura known as Nicandra Candravaktra — the glorious Muñjakeśa was that king on earth.

**1.61.27**  Nikumbha, unvanquished in battle, of great intellect, was born on earth as the best of kings, remembered as Devādhipa.

**1.61.28**  He among those Daityas who was the great asura named Śarabha — he became the royal sage named Paurava here among men.

**1.61.29**  He who was the second among those asuras, named Śalabha — he became the lord of men known as Bāhlīka Prahrāda.

**1.61.30**  Candra, the foremost of Diti's sons, comparable to the lord of stars, became the royal sage named Ṛṣika, the best of kings.

**1.61.31**  He who was known as Mṛtapā, the foremost of asuras — know that king as the lord of the western marshlands, O best of kings.

**1.61.32**  Gaviṣṭha, of great radiance, who was celebrated as a great asura — he became known on earth as Drumasena, a king.

**1.61.33**  He who was the glorious great asura known as Mayūra — he became renowned as Viśva and was a lord of the earth.

**1.61.34**  He who was the younger brother of that one, known as Suparṇa — he became known on earth as Kālakīrti, a king.

**1.61.35**  He among them who was celebrated as the pre-eminent asura Candrahanta — he became the royal sage named Śunaka, a lord of men.

**1.61.36**  He who was named the great asura Vināśana of the moon — he became the royal sage named Jānaki, a lord of men.

**1.61.37**  He who was called Dīrghajihva, the bull among dānavas, O descendant of the Kurus — he became known on earth as the Kāśirāja, lord of the earth.

**1.61.38**  The demon Siṃhī gave birth to that Graha who oppresses the moon and sun; he became known among men as King Krātha.

**1.61.39**  The foremost among the four sons of Anāyus was the powerful demon Vikṣara; that radiant one became King Vasumitra among men.

**1.61.40**  The second after Vikṣara, O lord of men, was a great demon who became king renowned as the lord of Pāṃsurāṣṭra.

**1.61.41**  He who was known as Balavīra, that foremost of demons, became the king called the lord of Pauṇḍramatsyaka among men.

**1.61.42**  He who was widely renowned as Vṛtra, that great demon, O king, became the royal sage known as Maṇimān, a lord of men.

**1.61.43**  The demon who was Vṛtra's younger brother, known as Krodhahantā, became the king on earth widely renowned as Daṇḍa.

**1.61.44**  He who was known as Krodhavardhana became the lord of men known as Daṇḍadhāra.

**1.61.45**  The sons of Kālakā — eight of them were born as lords of men, O tiger among kings, with valor equal to a tiger.

**1.61.46**  Among the Magadhas, the illustrious Jayatsena was king; he was the foremost of those eight sons of Kālakā, that great demon.

**1.61.47**  The second among them, illustrious as Indra's steed, became the lord of men known as Aparājita, the unconquered.

**1.61.48**  The third, O great king, was a great demon of mighty arms who was born on earth as the lord of the Niṣādas, of fearsome valor.

**1.61.49**  He who is listed as the fourth among them became known on earth as Śreṇimān, the foremost of royal sages.

**1.61.50**  The fifth, who was the foremost great demon among them, became known here as Mahaujā, the scourge of foes.

**1.61.51**  The sixth, who was the wise great demon among them, became known on earth as Abhīru, the foremost of royal sages.

**1.61.52**  From that same group, the king Samudrasena was born, renowned across the sea-girdled earth, versed in the truth of righteousness and worldly gain.

**1.61.53**  Named Bṛhan, the eighth of those sons of Kālakā, O king, was a scorcher of foes, righteous in soul and devoted to the welfare of all beings.

**1.61.54**  The demonic host known as the Krodhavaśas, which I have enumerated for you, O king — from them were born heroes here on earth as lords of men.

**1.61.55**  Nandika, Karṇaveṣṭa, Siddhārtha, Kīṭaka, Suvīra, Subāhu, Mahāvīra, and Bāhlika —

**1.61.56**  Krodha, Vicitya, Surasa, the illustrious Nīla the earth-lord, Vīradhāman, and the one named Bhūmipāla, O descendant of Kuru —

**1.61.57**  Dantavaktra by name, Durjaya by name, Rukmī the tiger among kings, and King Janamejaya —

**1.61.58**  Āṣāḍha, Vāyuvega, Bhūritejas, Ekalavya, Sumitra, Vāṭadhāna, and Gomukha —

**1.61.59**  The Kārūṣaka kings, Kṣemadhūrti, Śrutāyus, Uddhava, and Bṛhatsena as well —

**1.61.60**  Kṣemogratīrtha, Kuhara the lord of men among the Kaliṅgas, Matimān, and the one renowned as Īśvara, O lord of men —

**1.61.61**  From the Krodhavaśa host there thus arose on earth a multitude of kings, born in ancient times, O great king, of great fame and great strength.

**1.61.62**  He who was the chief lord of the Gandharvas, named Devaka, equal in splendor to the king of the gods, was born on earth as a lord of men.

**1.61.63**  Know, O descendant of Bharata, that Droṇa son of Bharadvāja, not born of a womb, arose from a portion of the divine sage Bṛhaspati of great renown.

**1.61.64**  He who was that Bṛhatkīrti of great radiance, the foremost knower of all weapons among archers, was born here among men, O tiger among kings.

**1.61.65**  Him whom those versed in the Vedas know as the supreme one in the science of archery and in the Veda, who performs deeds like Indra — that Droṇa, the enhancer of his lineage.

**1.61.66**  From the combined essence of Mahādeva and Antaka, from both desire and wrath, O descendant of Bharata, was born that hero, the scourge of foes.

**1.61.67**  Aśvatthāman of great valor, destroyer of the enemy host, that hero with eyes like lotus petals, was a lord of men upon the earth, O king.

**1.61.68**  The eight Vasus were born as sons of Śantanu upon the Gaṅgā, both by the curse of Vasiṣṭha and by the command of Vāsava.

**1.61.69**  The youngest of them, Bhīṣma, the bestower of fearlessness upon the Kurus — wise, versed in the Veda, eloquent, and destroyer of the enemy host.

**1.61.70**  He who was the foremost among all knowers of wisdom, that greatly radiant one, fought with Rāma son of Jamadagni, the great-souled Bhārgava.

**1.61.71**  He who became the brahmarṣi known as Kṛpa upon the earth, O king — know him to have arisen from the host of the Rudras, of surpassing manhood.

**1.61.72**  He who was the great warrior King Śakuni in the world — know him, O king, to have arisen as the Dvāpara age incarnate, the crusher of foes.

**1.61.73**  Sātyaki, true to his word, the exalter of the Vṛṣṇi clan — that crusher of foes was born from a portion of the Marut gods.

**1.61.74**  Drupada too, the royal sage, arose from that same host and was born in this human world, O king, the foremost of all who bear weapons.

**1.61.75**  And know Kṛtavarmā, O king, that lord of people, to have been born as one beyond recompense, the very finest bull among kṣatriya sages.

**1.61.76**  Know the royal sage named Virāṭa, who terrorized the kingdoms of his rivals, to have been born from the host of the Maruts, a crusher of foes.

**1.61.77**  The son of Ariṣṭā widely known as Haṃsa — that chief of Gandharvas was born as an enhancer of the Kuru lineage.

**1.61.78**  Known as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, born also through Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the long-armed, greatly radiant lord of men who sees through wisdom — yet by reason of his mother's fault and the sage's wrath, he was born blind.

**1.61.79**  Know Vidura, born in this world as the most blessed and finest son among those who have sons, to be an incarnation of Atri, the foremost among the wise.

**1.61.80**  From a portion of Kali was born on earth King Duryodhana — of wicked mind, wicked intellect, the one who brought disgrace upon the Kurus.

**1.61.81**  He who was that embodiment of Kali, hated by the whole world, that lowest of men who caused the slaughter of all the earth — through whom the great enmity was kindled that brought destruction to all living beings.

**1.61.82**  All the brothers, sons of Pulastya's lineage, were born among men here — the hundred headed by Duḥśāsana, all of cruel deeds.

**1.61.83**  Durmukha, Duḥsaha, and the others who are not individually named — all those helpers of Duryodhana are sons of Pulastya's line, O bull among the Bharatas.

**1.61.84**  Know King Yudhiṣṭhira to be a portion of Dharma, O king; Bhīmasena a portion of the Wind god; and Arjuna a portion of the king of gods.

**1.61.85**  Likewise Nakula and Sahadeva are portions of the twin Aśvins, peerless in beauty upon earth, captivating the hearts of all the worlds.

**1.61.86**  He who was known as Suvarcā, the mighty son of the Moon god — that Abhimanyu of great fame became the son of Arjuna.

**1.61.87**  Know Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that great warrior, to be a portion of Fire; and know Śikhaṇḍin, O king, who was both woman and man, to be a Rākṣasa.

**1.61.88**  The five sons of Draupadī who were born, O bull among the Bharatas — know them, O king, to be members of the Viśvedeva host, O bull among the Bharatas.

**1.61.89**  Karṇa, that great warrior who was born with armor already upon him — know him to be the incomparable portion of the Sun god, the resplendent deity.

**1.61.90**  He who is known as Nārāyaṇa, the eternal god of gods — his portion among humans was the mighty Vāsudeva.

**1.61.91**  Baladeva of great strength was a portion of the serpent Śeṣa; know Pradyumna, O king, to be the mighty Sanatkumāra.

**1.61.92**  Thus many other portions of the celestials were born as enhancers of Vasudeva's clan, O lord of men.

**1.61.93**  The host of Apsarases which I have enumerated for you, O king — a portion of them was born on earth also by the command of Vāsava.

**1.61.94**  Those sixteen thousand divine women, O lord of men, became in the human world the consorts of Nārāyaṇa.

**1.61.95**  A portion of Śrī was born for the purpose of desire upon the surface of the earth — a blameless maiden arising from the midst of the sacrificial altar in the family of Drupada.

**1.61.96**  Neither too short nor too tall, fragrant as the blue lotus, with long lotus-shaped eyes, lovely hips, and long dark hair —

**1.61.97**  Endowed with all auspicious marks, resembling a vaiḍūrya gem, she was in private the one who bewildered the minds of five lords among men.

**1.61.98**  The two goddesses Siddhi and Dhṛti were born as the mothers of the five — Kuntī and Mādrī; and Mati was born as the daughter of Subala.

**1.61.99**  Thus has been recounted for you, O king, the descent of portions of gods and demons, of Gandharvas and Apsarases, and of Rākṣasas.

**1.61.100**  The kings born on earth, intoxicated with battle, and the great-souled ones born in the vast clan of the Yadus —

**1.61.101**  This account of the descent of portions is auspicious, fame-giving, conducive to offspring, life-extending, and victory-bringing — it should be heard without envy.

**1.61.102**  A wise man who hears this account of the descent of portions of gods, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas, knowing their origin and dissolution, does not sink in times of distress.

**1.62.1**  Janamejaya said: I have heard from you, O brahmin, the full account of the descent of portions of gods, demons, and Rākṣasas, and likewise of Gandharvas and Apsarases.

**1.62.2**  But I wish to hear further from you, O learned one, the lineage of the Kurus from the very beginning, narrated in the presence of this assembly of brahmin sages.

**1.62.3**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The perpetuator of the Paurava lineage was the valorous king named Duḥṣanta, the protector of the four-cornered earth, O foremost of the Bharatas.

**1.62.4**  That lord of men enjoyed a full quarter of the entire earth, and that conqueror in battle also held the ocean-girdled lands.

**1.62.5**  That crusher of foes enjoyed all the lands of the border peoples and forest dwellers, the lands extending to the jewel-bearing sea, inhabited by peoples of the four classes.

**1.62.6**  There was no one who caused the mixing of castes, no one who refused to till the land, no evildoer whatsoever while that king was ruling.

**1.62.7**  Pursuing lawful pleasures, men then attained both righteousness and wealth, O tiger among men, under that lord of the realm.

**1.62.8**  There was no fear of thieves, dear one, not the slightest fear of hunger, and no fear of disease either under that lord of the realm.

**1.62.9**  The castes delighted in their own duties, desireless in their divine observances; having taken refuge in that guardian of the earth, they were free from fear from any quarter.

**1.62.10**  Rain fell in its proper season, crops bore fruit abundantly, and the earth, the treasure-bearer, was rich with all gems at that time.

**1.62.11**  And he, of marvelous great valor, youthful and firm as the thunderbolt, could lift Mount Mandara with his two arms and carry it along with its forest of soma-pressing trees.

**1.62.12**  In archery, in mace combat, in fighting with sword and hilt, on elephant-back, and on horseback, he was fully accomplished.

**1.62.13**  In strength he was equal to Viṣṇu, in splendor like the sun, in imperturbability like the ocean, in forbearance like the earth.

**1.62.14**  That guardian of the earth, honored by all, his city and kingdom contented, dwelt among the people he knew well, with dispositions ever devoted to righteousness.

**1.63.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Once that long-armed one, possessed of abundant troops and vehicles, went into a dense forest, surrounded by hundreds of horses and elephants.

**1.63.2**  He went out surrounded by hundreds of warriors bearing swords and spears, holding maces and clubs in their hands, and carrying lances and javelins.

**1.63.3**  With the lion-roars of the warriors and the sounds of conch-shells and kettledrums, with the rumble of chariot-wheels and the trumpeting of great elephants,

**1.63.4**  Mixed with the neighing of horses and the sounds of war-cries and clapping of arms, a great tumultuous noise arose as the king set forth.

**1.63.5**  Women standing on the upper terraces of the finest palace beheld him, the hero who was the maker of his own glory, resplendent with the full majesty of a king.

**1.63.6**  The groups of women gazing upon that slayer of enemies, who was like Indra himself and was a great elephant against the elephants of his foes, bearing weapons in hand, were filled with wonder.

**1.63.7**  "This is that tiger among men, of wondrous valor in battle — having encountered the might of whose arms, the hosts of enemies survive no more."

**1.63.8**  Thus speaking, those women praised the lord of men with great affection and showered a rain of flowers upon his head.

**1.63.9**  Praised on all sides by foremost brahmins, he departed with great joy into the forest, eager to hunt deer.

**1.63.10**  The townspeople and country-folk followed him a great distance, then turned back when they had been dismissed by the king.

**1.63.11**  Then that lord of the earth, with a chariot swift as Garuḍa, filled the earth and the heavens alike with its thunderous noise.

**1.63.12**  As he traveled, that wise one beheld a forest resembling Nandana, strewn with bel, arka, and khadira trees, and crowded with kapittha and dhava trees.

**1.63.13**  It was uneven with mountain slopes and strewn with rocks, waterless and uninhabited by humans, extending for many leagues, filled with terrifying herds of deer and other creatures of the forest.

**1.63.14**  That tiger among men, Duḥṣanta, together with his retinue and his army and its mounts, roused that forest and slew various kinds of deer.

**1.63.15**  Duḥṣanta struck down many groups of tigers that came within arrow-range, piercing them through with his shafts.

**1.63.16**  That bull among men split those at a distance with arrows, while others that came near he cut down with his sword.

**1.63.17**  He slew certain black deer with his spear, that foremost of the mighty, skilled in the art of wielding the mace in circles, ranging about with boundless valor.

**1.63.18**  He ranged through the forest striking down the wild deer and birds with javelins, swords, maces, clubs, and short swords.

**1.63.19**  The great beasts abandoned the vast forest as it was beaten through by that king of wondrous valor and by his battle-loving warriors.

**1.63.20**  The herds of deer there, their leaders slain and their groups scattered, cried out here and there in their distress.

**1.63.21**  Reaching a dry river, emaciated from the hopelessness of finding water, their hearts exhausted from exertion, they fell senseless to the ground.

**1.63.22**  Overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, weary and fallen to the earth, some among them were devoured there by the hungry tiger-men.

**1.63.23**  Then some forest-dwellers, having kindled fire, properly chopped the flesh and ate it in the prescribed manner.

**1.63.24**  There some mighty elephants, maddened and wounded by weapons, drew in their trunks in fear and fled with great speed.

**1.63.25**  Voiding their dung and urine and streaming much blood, those great wild elephants there trampled many men to death.

**1.63.26**  That forest, thick with buffaloes, with its great animals slain, covered by the king as a cloud of force by its torrents of arrows, shone brilliantly.

**1.64.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having slain thousands of deer, that king with his great army entered yet another forest in pursuit of game.

**1.64.2**  Alone now, that one of supreme strength, afflicted by hunger and thirst, reached the end of the forest and came to a vast barren wasteland.

**1.64.3**  Having crossed even that, the king came to another great forest, endowed with the finest hermitages, delightful to the mind, charming to the eye, and touched by cool breezes.

**1.64.4**  Filled with flowering trees, exceedingly pleasant with lush grass, vast, and resonant with the sweet calls of birds —

**1.64.5**  Covered by trees with great spreading boughs offering cool shade, its vines swayed by bees, endowed with supreme beauty —

**1.64.6**  In that forest, not a single tree was without flowers, not one was without fruit, none had thorns, and none was without its covering of bees.

**1.64.7**  Resounding with birds, adorned most beautifully with flowers, with trees bearing blossoms of every season, exceedingly pleasant and delightful — that great archer entered this finest of forests.

**1.64.8**  There, the flower-laden trees loosened by the wind shed again and again a variegated rain of blossoms.

**1.64.9**  The trees touching the sky, resounding with birds of sweet voices, shone there in their garments of many-colored flowers.

**1.64.10**  On the tender shoots of those trees, bending under the weight of blossoms, the birds cried out softly together with the bees.

**1.64.11**  Beholding many a spot there adorned with heaps of flowers, enclosed by bowers of creepers, filling the heart with joy, that one of great splendor became filled with delight.

**1.64.12**  With trees whose branches intertwined with one another, laden with blossoms, resembling the banner-poles of great Indra, that forest shone magnificently.

**1.64.13**  A breeze, pleasantly cool and fragrant, carrying the pollen of flowers, moved through the forest as if approaching the trees out of a desire to play.

**1.64.14**  The king beheld this forest, endowed with such qualities, beautiful as the Mālini riverbank, resembling a lofty banner.

**1.64.15**  And while he was gazing at that forest filled with joyful birds, he also saw a most charming and lovely hermitage.

**1.64.16**  It was filled with many kinds of trees, its sacred fires blazing brightly, surrounded by ascetics and Vālakhilya sages, attended by troops of holy men.

**1.64.17**  With many fire-shrines, its floor spread with flower offerings, and radiant with large, spacious enclosures, it shone brilliantly.

**1.64.18**  O king, on the banks of the holy Mālinī river with its pleasant waters, crowded with many flocks of birds, the hermitage-grove delightful — beholding there the gentle wild creatures, he was filled with joy.

**1.64.19**  That foremost of chariot-warriors, glorious, arrived at that hermitage, which resembled the world of the gods and was beautiful in every direction.

**1.64.20**  He saw the river intertwined with the hermitage, its waters holy, standing there like a mother to all living creatures.

**1.64.21**  Its sandbars graced with cakravāka birds, flowing with foam and flowers, the home of troops of Kiṃnaras, frequented by monkeys and bears —

**1.64.22**  Resounding with holy recitation, beautified by its sandbars, visited by maddened elephants, tigers, and great serpents —

**1.64.23**  Having seen the river thus joined to the hermitage, and the hermitage itself, that lord of the earth resolved then to enter it.

**1.64.24**  Adorned by the island-graced Mālinī with her lovely banks, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, beautified like the Gaṅgā, resonant with intoxicated peacocks — he entered that great forest.

**1.64.25**  That lord of men, approaching what resembled the garden of Citra-ratha, endowed with manifold excellences and unsurpassed in splendor, then wished to see the great seer Kaṇva, the Kāśyapa, rich in austerities.

**1.64.26**  He stationed his army at the forest gate — chariots, horses crowded together, and masses of infantry — and spoke thus:

**1.64.27**  "I shall go to see the pure sage Kāśyapa, that storehouse of austerities. Remain here until I return."

**1.64.28**  Having entered that forest resembling Nandana, that lord of men, the king, shed his hunger and thirst and was filled with great rejoicing.

**1.64.29**  That lord of men, accompanied by his minister and chaplain, having set aside the marks of kingship, went to that excellent hermitage, wishing to see that undying mass of ascetic merit, the sage.

**1.64.30**  Beholding that hermitage resembling the world of Brahma, resounding with the songs of bees, filled with many groups of brahmins,

**1.64.31**  That tiger among men heard the Ṛgvedic hymns being set in motion by foremost Ṛgvedins with their metrical progressions at the various rites being performed there.

**1.64.32**  The hermitage then shone with those of boundless spirit, well-disciplined, expert in the supplementary sciences of sacrifice, proceeding through their progressions in sequence.

**1.64.33**  Foremost among Atharva-Vedins, honored by assemblies of sacrificers, they chanted the Saṃhitā with its pada and krama recitations.

**1.64.34**  With other brahmins reciting with proper grammatical refinement, that glorious hermitage rang out, gleaming like the world of Brahma.

**1.64.35**  With those expert in sacrificial rites, skilled in sequential recitation training, endowed with the knowledge of logical principles and true meanings, who had crossed to the far shore of the Vedas —

**1.64.36**  Skilled in the synthesis and combination of various textual statements, knowledgeable in special rites, devoted to the dharma of liberation —

**1.64.37**  Those who had attained mastery of establishing propositions, refuting objections, and knowing ultimate truths, together with foremost Lokāyata philosophers — with all of these it resounded on every side.

**1.64.38**  Here and there he saw foremost brahmins, self-disciplined, firm in their vows, devoted to silent recitation and fire offerings — perfected sages. That destroyer of enemy heroes was filled with wonder.

**1.64.39**  Beholding the varied seats adorned with flowers, carefully arranged, that lord of the earth was struck with wonder.

**1.64.40**  Seeing the worship of the divine shrines performed by the brahmins, that best of kings imagined himself to be dwelling in the world of Brahma.

**1.64.41**  He could not satisfy himself gazing at that excellent and auspicious hermitage protected by the austerities of the Kāśyapa, filled with troops of those rich in penance.

**1.64.42**  He, the destroyer of enemies, together with his minister and chaplain, entered the abode of the Kāśyapa, surrounded on all sides by sages of great vows and rich in austerities — a solitary, supremely charming, and auspicious place.

**1.65.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, going forward, that mighty-armed one, having dismissed his ministers, did not see in that hermitage the sage firm in his vows.

**1.65.2**  Not finding that sage and seeing the hermitage empty, he called out loudly, "Who is here?" as if making the forest ring with his voice.

**1.65.3**  Then, hearing that sound of his, a maiden came forth from that hermitage, beautiful as Śrī herself, wearing the garb of an ascetic.

**1.65.4**  She, dark-eyed, upon seeing king Duḥṣanta, at once said "Welcome to you" and honored him with due ceremony.

**1.65.5**  Having honored him with a seat and with water for the feet and the ritual offering, she inquired after the lord of men's health and well-being, O king.

**1.65.6**  Having honored him duly and inquired about his well-being, she said with a gentle smile: "What may be done for you?"

**1.65.7**  Then the king, having been duly honored, spoke to that sweet-spoken maiden with her flawless limbs:

**1.65.8**  "I have come to pay homage to the greatly blessed sage Kaṇva. Where has the venerable one gone, dear lady? Tell me, O lovely one."

**1.65.9**  Śakuntalā said: My father the venerable one has gone from the hermitage to gather fruits. Wait a moment — you shall see him return here.

**1.65.10**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Not seeing the sage, spoken to thus by her, the king, beholding that woman of noble hips, radiant with beauty, and lovely of smile —

**1.65.11**  Shining with her beauty and with asceticism and self-discipline, endowed with form and youth — thus the lord of the earth spoke:

**1.65.12**  "Who are you, O lovely-hipped one? Whose are you? Why have you come to the forest, endowed with such beauty and qualities? Whence are you, O fair one?"

**1.65.13**  "By the mere sight of you, O auspicious one, my heart has been stolen away. I wish to know you — tell me, O lovely one."

**1.65.14**  Thus addressed by the king there in the hermitage, the maiden spoke these words with a smile, in syllables most sweet.

**1.65.15**  "O Dushyanta, I am considered the daughter of the blessed Kanva — the ascetic, the steadfast, the knower of dharma, the illustrious one."

**1.65.16**  Dushyanta said: "The blessed one is of supreme greatness, a practitioner of ūrdhvaretas, worshipped by the world — for even dharma might deviate from its course, but one of sharpened vow does not deviate."

**1.65.17**  "How have you, O fair-complexioned one, come to be his daughter? I have a great doubt in this matter; please resolve it for me here."

**1.65.18**  Shakuntala said: "How this account came to me, and how it came to pass in former times — hear it truly, O king, how I am the daughter of the sage."

**1.65.19**  "A certain seer came here and prompted the account of my birth; the blessed one related it to him — hear it as it is, O lord of the earth."

**1.65.20**  "In former times, so it is said, Vishvamitra was performing great austerities, and greatly afflicted Shakra, the lord of the hosts of gods."

**1.65.21**  "Fearing that this one, whose power blazed with asceticism, might dislodge him from his position, Purandara said this to Menaka:"

**1.65.22**  "'O Menaka, you excel among the apsarases in divine qualities — do me a benefit, O auspicious one; hear what I shall tell you.'"

**1.65.23**  "'That Vishvamitra, radiant as the sun, of great austerity, performing terrible penance — he makes my mind tremble.'"

**1.65.24**  "'O slender-waisted Menaka, this Vishvamitra is your task — he of sharpened soul, most difficult to assail, engaged in fierce austerity.'"

**1.65.25**  "'So that he may not dislodge me from my position, go to him and entice him — create an obstacle to his austerity; do this best favor for me.'"

**1.65.26**  "'With beauty, youth, sweetness, gestures, smiles and speech — captivate him, O shapely one, and turn him away from his austerities.'"

**1.65.27**  Menaka said: "That blessed one is always of great splendor, great in austerity, and wrathful — for even the blessed lord himself knows this about him."

**1.65.28**  "You yourself tremble before his splendor, his austerity, and his wrath — that great-souled one — then how could I not tremble?"

**1.65.29**  "He who deprived the greatly blessed Vasishtha of his beloved sons, and who, though born a kshatriya, became a brahmin by force of will —"

**1.65.30**  "— who, for purposes of purification, created a mighty river with many waters, which people know in the world as the most sacred Kaushiki —"

**1.65.31**  "— where, in a time of difficulty long ago, the righteous royal sage Matanga, gone to the condition of a hunter, supported this great-souled one's wife —"

**1.65.32**  "— where, in a time of famine in the past, the sage returned to his hermitage and the lord then gave the name 'Para' to the river —"

**1.65.33**  "— where he himself, with joyful mind, performed the sacrifice for Matanga, and out of fear of whom, O lord of heroes, you went to drink soma —"

**1.65.34**  "— who, in anger, created new lunar asterisms with richness of stars, surpassing the existing stellar lineages, the constellations beginning with Shravana —"

**1.65.35**  "These are the deeds of him before whom I greatly tremble — command me, O lord, so that when angered he does not burn me."

**1.65.36**  "He could burn the worlds with his splendor, shake the earth with his foot, compress mighty Meru, and quickly set it spinning."

**1.65.37**  "How could a young woman like me touch one such as he — endowed with austerity, blazing like fire, his senses fully mastered?"

**1.65.38**  "He whose face is the sacrificial fire, who blazes, whose eyes are the sun and moon and whose tongue is time itself, O best of gods — how could one like me touch him?"

**1.65.39**  "Yama and Soma and the great seers, the Sadhyas, the Vishvadevas, and all the Valakhilyas — even these tremble before his power; why then should one like me not tremble?"

**1.65.40**  "Being thus commanded by you, O king of gods, how could I not go near the seer? But think of protection for me, O lord of the gods, so that I may act protected for your sake."

**1.65.41**  "Let the wind strip away my garment there while I am at play, O god; and let Manmatha be my helper there in that task, by your divine grace."

**1.65.42**  "And let a sweet-scented wind blow from the forest at that time, as I tempt the sage." Having said 'so be it' and having arranged all this, she then went to the hermitage of Kaushika.

**1.66.1**  Shakuntala said: "Thus addressed by her, Shakra instructed the wind of eternal passage, and Menaka then departed at the appointed time along with the wind."

**1.66.2**  "Then that shapely, timid Menaka saw Vishvamitra performing austerities in the hermitage, his sins burnt away by asceticism."

**1.66.3**  "Having saluted him, she then played before the sage, and the wind carried away her garment, white as the moon."

**1.66.4**  "She, the fair-complexioned one, rushed swiftly to the ground to grab that garment, seemingly smiling with shyness at the wind."

**1.66.5**  "That best of sages then saw Menaka, flustered, clutching her garment, her age and beauty beyond description, her form revealed."

**1.66.6**  "Seeing the excellence of her beauty, that bull among brahmin seers then formed the intent to be with her, falling under the sway of desire."

**1.66.7**  "He invited her, and she, the blameless one, was willing; those two spent a very long time in the forest, delighting together according to their desire as though it were but a single day."

**1.66.8**  "That sage fathered Shakuntala upon Menaka on the lovely slopes of the Himalayas, near the river Malini."

**1.66.9**  "Having delivered the child and abandoned the newborn along the Malini, Menaka, her task accomplished, then quickly went to Shakra's assembly."

**1.66.10**  "Seeing that newborn lying in the desolate forest teeming with lions and tigers, birds surrounded it on all sides."

**1.66.11**  "The flesh-eating, meat-craving predators of the forest did not harm this child — the birds guarded her there, that daughter of Menaka."

**1.66.12**  "I went there to touch the sacred waters, and I saw her lying in the desolate wilderness, surrounded by birds; I then brought her and appointed her as my daughter."

**1.66.13**  "He who made the body, he who gave life, and he whose food one eats — these three in turn are called fathers in the settled teaching of dharma."

**1.66.14**  "And because she was protected by birds in the desolate forest, I gave her the name 'Shakuntala' then and there."

**1.66.15**  "Thus know her as my daughter, O gentle one — Shakuntala — and the blameless Shakuntala considers me her father."

**1.66.16**  "This he related when questioned by the great seer regarding my birth — thus know me as Kanva's daughter, O lord of men."

**1.66.17**  "Not knowing my true father, I consider Kanva my father — thus have I told you, O king, the account as I heard it occurred."

**1.67.1**  Dushyanta said: "It is entirely clear that you are a princess, O auspicious one, speaking as you do — be my wife, O shapely one; tell me, what shall I do for you?"

**1.67.2**  "Gold garlands, garments, earrings, ornaments, beautiful shining cloth from many towns, splendid jewels and gems —"

**1.67.3**  "— all this I shall bring you today, and golden ornaments and animal skins; let the entire kingdom be yours today — be my wife, O lovely one."

**1.67.4**  "Come to me, O timid one, O beautiful one, through the Gandharva form of marriage — for among marriages, the Gandharva is said to be the best, O you with thighs like plantain stems."

**1.67.5**  Shakuntala said: "My father has gone from this hermitage to gather fruits, O king — wait a moment; he will give me to you."

**1.67.6**  Dushyanta said: "I desire you, O shapely one, O blameless one who inclines toward me; know that I am here for your sake — my mind has gone to you."

**1.67.7**  "The self alone is one's own kinsman, the self alone is one's own path, the self alone is one's own refuge — you should give yourself in accordance with dharma."

**1.67.8**  "Eight forms of marriage in total are remembered as sanctioned by dharma: Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya, and also Asura —"

**1.67.9**  "— Gandharva, Rakshasa, and Paishacha as the eighth. Manu Svayambhuva proclaimed the dharmic rules for these in proper order."

**1.67.10**  "Know that the first four are commended for a brahmin; know that for a kshatriya six in order are righteous, O blameless one."

**1.67.11**  "The Rakshasa form is also said to be valid for kings; the Asura is remembered for Vaishyas and Shudras. Of the five, three are righteous; two are remembered as unrighteous here."

**1.67.12**  "The Paishacha and the Asura should never be performed under any circumstance; by this rule one should act — this is remembered as the path of dharma."

**1.67.13**  "The Gandharva and Rakshasa forms are both righteous for a kshatriya — have no fear of them; whether separately or combined, they may be performed — there is no doubt in this."

**1.67.14**  "You who are desirous and I who am desirous — O fair-complexioned one, you deserve to become my wife through the Gandharva form of marriage."

**1.67.15**  Shakuntala said: "If this is indeed the path of dharma, and if I am indeed master of my own giving — then hear my condition, O best of the Pauravas, O lord."

**1.67.16**  "Promise me truly what I shall tell you in private: the son who is born of me shall be your heir after you."

**1.67.17**  "He shall be crown prince, O great king — tell me this truthfully; if it be so, O Dushyanta, let there be union between you and me."

**1.67.18**  Vaishampayana said: "'So be it,' the king replied to her without hesitation, 'and I shall also bring you to my own city, O bright-smiling one — as you deserve, O shapely one; I tell you this truly.'"

**1.67.19**  "Having said this, that royal sage took the hand of that blameless-gaited one according to the rite, and dwelt together with her."

**1.67.20**  "Having reassured her, he departed and said again and again: 'I shall send the four-division army for your sake; with it I shall bring you to my own home, O bright-smiling one.'"

**1.67.21**  "Having thus promised her, O Janamejaya, that king, lord of the earth, departed, pondering in his mind as he went toward Kashyapa."

**1.67.22**  "'What will the blessed one endowed with austerity do upon hearing of this?' — thinking thus, he entered his own city."

**1.67.23**  "After some time had passed, Kanva too returned to the hermitage; but Shakuntala, out of shame, did not go to meet her father."

**1.67.24**  "Then Kanva, of divine knowledge and great austerity, perceived the situation; the blessed one, pleased, spoke having seen all with his divine eye."

**1.67.25**  "'What you have done today, disregarding me, uniting with a man of royal lineage — that union is not a violation of dharma.'"

**1.67.26**  "'For the Gandharva form of marriage is called the best for a kshatriya — performed in private, without mantras, between two who desire each other.'"

**1.67.27**  "'Dushyanta, the best of men, is righteous-souled and great-souled — you have gone to that highest of men as husband with devotion, O Shakuntala.'"

**1.67.28**  "'A great-souled and mighty son shall be born to you in the world — one who shall enjoy this entire earth bounded by the ocean.'"

**1.67.29**  "'And the wheel of that great-souled universal emperor shall roll forward unchecked, ever victorious.'"

**1.67.30**  "Then she washed his feet, and having set down the load and placed the fruits nearby, she spoke to the rested sage."

**1.67.31**  "'The one I have chosen as my husband is that Dushyanta, the best of men — please bestow your grace upon him together with his ministers.'"

**1.67.32**  Kanva said: "I am indeed already pleased with him for your sake, O fair-complexioned one; receive from me the boon you desire on his account."

**1.67.33**  Vaishampayana said: "Then Shakuntala, desiring the welfare of Dushyanta, chose righteous conduct and steadiness in the kingdom for the Pauravas."

**1.68.1**  Vaishampayana said: "After Dushyanta had made his promise and departed, Shakuntala, she of beautiful thighs, gave birth to a son of immeasurable might."

**1.68.2**  When three full years had passed, O Janamejaya, she bore Duḥṣanta's son, blazing with the splendour of a bright flame, endowed with beauty, noble bearing, and every virtue.

**1.68.3**  Kaṇva, foremost among the doers of righteous deeds, then caused the birth-rites and the other purificatory sacraments to be performed for that growing and wise child.

**1.68.4**  With white, peak-like teeth, the frame of a lion, the mark of the wheel on his palm, majestic in bearing, with a great head and immense strength, a boy godlike in radiance — he swiftly grew up there.

**1.68.5**  Even as a boy of only six, around the precinct of Kaṇva's hermitage, he would seize tigers, lions, boars, elephants, and buffaloes —

**1.68.6**  — binding them to trees on every side of the hermitage; the powerful boy would mount them, subdue them, and run about at play.

**1.68.7**  Then the inhabitants of Kaṇva's hermitage gave him his name: 'Let this boy be Sarvadamana — Tamer of All — for he tames everything.'

**1.68.8**  So the prince came to bear the name Sarvadamana, endowed with heroic prowess, brilliant energy, and might.

**1.68.9**  The sage, seeing the prince and his superhuman deeds, declared, 'The time has come for his installation as crown prince,' and so he told Śakuntalā.

**1.68.10**  Recognising that strength, Kaṇva addressed his disciples: 'Lead this Śakuntalā today, without delay, together with her son, from this hermitage to her husband — she who is honoured by every auspicious mark.'

**1.68.11**  For a woman's long sojourn among her kinsmen is not fitting; it destroys reputation, conduct, and righteousness. Therefore take her without further delay.

**1.68.12**  Saying 'So be it,' all of them, those of immeasurable energy, set out placing Śakuntalā together with her son at their head, bound for Hastinapura.

**1.68.13**  Taking with her that lotus-eyed son, radiant as a child of the gods, the fair-complexioned Śakuntalā came forth from the forest that Duḥṣanta had known.

**1.68.14**  Having approached the king and been duly recognised, she was ushered into his presence together with that son of hers who shone with the lustre of the young sun.

**1.68.15**  Having paid him reverence according to due form, Śakuntalā spoke to him: 'O king, let this son whom you fathered be consecrated as crown prince.'

**1.68.16**  For this son, O king, was begotten by you upon me, and he is equal to the gods. Act towards him according to the compact you made, O best of men.

**1.68.17**  Recall, O greatly fortunate one, that compact which was earlier made by you at our meeting in the precinct of Kaṇva's hermitage.

**1.68.18**  Having heard that speech of hers, the king — though he remembered — declared, 'I do not remember. Whose woman are you, O wicked ascetic?'

**1.68.19**  'I recall no connection with you in respect of righteousness, pleasure, or worldly gain. Go, or stay, as you please — do whatever you wish.'

**1.68.20**  Thus addressed, that fair-hipped, proud-spirited woman stood as though shamed, almost insensible with grief, motionless as a post.

**1.68.21**  Her eyes red with fury and indignation, her lips quivering, she looked askance at the king as though burning him with her sideward glances.

**1.68.22**  Concealing her outward expression, stirred by wrath, she restrained at that moment the ascetic energy she had gathered through her austerities.

**1.68.23**  Having reflected for a moment, filled with grief and anger, and gazing steadily at her husband, she spoke these words in fury.

**1.68.24**  'Though you know, O great king, why do you speak thus — "I do not know" — as indifferently as some common, ordinary man?'

**1.68.25**  'Your own heart knows the truth and the untruth here; O auspicious one — you yourself are the witness. Do not demean yourself.'

**1.68.26**  'One who, being otherwise, passes himself off as otherwise — what sin has not been committed by that self-thief, that robber of his own soul?'

**1.68.27**  'You think yourself alone — you do not know the ancient sage dwelling in the heart, who is the knower of every sinful deed; yet it is before him that you commit this wrong.'

**1.68.28**  'He who has done evil thinks "no one knows me," yet the gods know him, and so does the inner Person who dwells within him.'

**1.68.29**  'The sun and the moon, wind and fire, sky, earth, water, the heart, Yama, day and night, and both twilights — and Dharma — all know a man's conduct.'

**1.68.30**  'Yama Vaivasvata exacts the penalty for the evil deeds of that man with whose conduct the witness of deeds, the knower of the field, dwelling in the heart, is displeased.'

**1.68.31**  'But of that wicked-souled man with whom this inner witness is not pleased, Yama exacts retribution for his evil deeds.'

**1.68.32**  'One who demeans himself and behaves contrary to his own nature — the gods do not bestow their grace upon him for whom even his own self is no authority.'

**1.68.33**  'Do not scorn me thus, thinking "she came of her own accord" — I, your faithful wife, I who deserve to be honoured, I who have come before you myself — you do not honour me.'

**1.68.34**  'Why do you look upon me like a common man in this assembly? I am not saying this in private — do you not hear me?'

**1.68.35**  'If you will not heed my plea, O Duḥṣanta, then this very day your head shall split into a hundred pieces.'

**1.68.36**  'Because a husband enters his wife and is born again from her, the ancient sages know the wifeness of a wife as jāyā — she from whom he is born anew.'

**1.68.37**  'The offspring that is born to a man comes from him — it delivers his lineage of deceased fathers and grandfathers who have gone before.'

**1.68.38**  'Because a son delivers his father from the hell called Put, the Self-existent One himself has called him putra — the deliverer.'

**1.68.39**  'She is a true wife who is capable in the home; she is a true wife who bears children; she is a true wife whose life is her husband; she is a true wife who is devoted to her husband.'

**1.68.40**  'A wife is half of a man; a wife is his best companion; a wife is the root of the three aims of life; a wife is the friend of him who is to die.'

**1.68.41**  'Those who have wives can perform rites; together with their wives they are true householders; those who have wives rejoice; those who have wives are endowed with prosperity.'

**1.68.42**  'In solitary moments wives become sweet-spoken companions; in the duties of righteousness they become fathers; to one in distress they become mothers.'

**1.68.43**  'Even in the wilderness a wife is the resting-place for the wayfaring man. He who has a wife is trustworthy; therefore a wife is the highest refuge.'

**1.68.44**  'Even the departed spirit wandering alone through difficult passages — a faithful wife ever follows her husband.'

**1.68.45**  'A wife who dies first waits for her husband after death; or if her husband dies first, the virtuous wife follows him afterwards.'

**1.68.46**  'For this reason, O king, the taking of a wife's hand in marriage is prescribed — for what a husband obtains in his wife belongs to him both in this world and in the next.'

**1.68.47**  'The wise declare that a son is the self begotten by the self; therefore a man should regard his wife as the mother of his son, as he would regard his own mother.'

**1.68.48**  'A father, beholding the son born of his wife — like seeing his own face in a mirror — is gladdened, as if the meritorious man had attained heaven.'

**1.68.49**  'Men afflicted by the burnings of mental grief and by diseases find delight in their wives, as those tormented by the heat find relief in water.'

**1.68.50**  'Even in great anger a wise man should not speak harshly to women, seeing that pleasure, affection, and righteousness are all dependent upon them.'

**1.68.51**  'Women are the sacred, eternal field of one's own birth — what power would even the sages have to create offspring without a woman?'

**1.68.52**  'When a son, who has been running about covered in the dust of the earth, runs up and embraces his father's limbs — what greater joy can there be than that?'

**1.68.53**  'Why then do you disdain this very son who has come to you of himself, who longs for you, and who looks at you with expectant eyes?'

**1.68.54**  'Even ants carry their own eggs and do not break them — how then, knowing righteousness as you do, could you not support your own son?'

**1.68.55**  'The touch of garments, of women, or of water is not as pleasurable as the touch of a small child being embraced — the touch of one's own son.'

**1.68.56**  'A brahmin is the foremost among two-footed beings; the cow is the greatest among four-footed beings; a teacher is the best among elders; a son is the most excellent of all things that can be touched.'

**1.68.57**  'Let this comely son embrace you and touch you — there is no more pleasurable touch in the world than the touch of a son.'

**1.68.58**  'Three full years after I gave birth, O subduer of foes, O lord of kings — I bring you this prince who will put an end to your sorrows.'

**1.68.59**  'O Paurava, a voice from the sky once addressed me at his birth, saying he shall be the performer of a hundred horse-sacrifices.'

**1.68.60**  'Do not men, even when travelling to another village, having first inhaled the fragrance of their sons' heads and marked them with a name-sign out of affection, bid them farewell with blessings?'

**1.68.61**  'The twice-born recite this Vedic declaration at the birth-rite of sons — you too know it likewise:'

**1.68.62**  '"You are born from limb after limb, you spring forth from the heart; you are the self who bears the name of son — so live a hundred autumns."'

**1.68.63**  'My sustenance and my undying lineage depend upon you — therefore, live happily a hundred autumns, my dear child.'

**1.68.64**  'This second man born from a man — born from your limbs — behold your own self as if reflected in a spotless pool, O king; behold my son.'

**1.68.65**  'Just as the Āhavanīya fire is kindled from the Gārhapatya, so has this son been born from you — you being one, you are made twofold.'

**1.68.66**  'For it was you, pursuing game, drawn away by a deer, who found me, a maiden, in my father's hermitage while ranging in the hunt, O king.'

**1.68.67**  'Urvaśī, Pūrvacitti, Sahajanyā, Menakā, Viśvācī, and Ghṛtācī — these six are the foremost of the Apsarases.'

**1.68.68**  'Among them, Menakā by name, the foremost Apsaras sprung from Brahmā's creative power, descending from heaven to earth, bore me by Viśvāmitra.'

**1.68.69**  'That Apsaras Menakā gave birth to me on the slopes of the Himālaya, and having abandoned me there she departed — like a wicked woman casting aside another's child.'
