**1.68.70**  'What inauspicious deed did I commit in a former birth, that I was abandoned by my kin in childhood and now again by you?'

**1.68.71**  'Abandoned by you I shall willingly go back to the hermitage — but you should not abandon this child, your own son born of yourself.'

**1.68.72**  Duḥṣanta spoke: 'I do not acknowledge a son born of you, O Śakuntalā. Women are untruthful in their speech — who would trust your words?'

**1.68.73**  'Your mother Menakā is a merciless harlot — she who cast you away on the slopes of the Himālaya like a discarded garland.'

**1.68.74**  'And that merciless father of yours, Viśvāmitra — born of kṣatriya stock, greedy for brahminhood, entirely given over to lust.'

**1.68.75**  'Menakā is the best of Apsarases and your father is a great sage — the offspring of those two — yet why do you present yourself like a wanton woman?'

**1.68.76**  'Are you not ashamed to speak these unbelievable words, especially in my presence? Go away, O wicked ascetic woman.'

**1.68.77**  'Where stands the great sage, ever terrible, and where the Apsaras Menakā — and where do you stand, so pitiable, wearing the mere garb of an ascetic woman?'

**1.68.78**  'And this son of yours is huge, and even as a child immensely strong — how has he grown up in such a short time, like the trunk of a śāla tree?'

**1.68.79**  'Your origin is very low — you appear to me a wanton woman; for you were born of Menakā by random desire and lust.'

**1.68.80**  'All that you say, O ascetic woman, is unknown to me. I do not recognise you. Go wherever you please.'

**1.69.1**  Śakuntalā spoke: 'O king, you see the faults of others though they be but the size of a mustard seed, yet even when you behold your own faults, though they be the size of a bilva fruit, you do not see them.'

**1.69.2**  Menakā stands high among the thirty gods, and the thirty gods revere Menakā; my birth excels yours, Duḥṣanta, measured from your birth.

**1.69.3**  You roam upon the earth, O king, while I move through the sky — see the distance between us as that between Mount Meru and a mustard seed.

**1.69.4**  I visit the palaces of Mahendra, Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa — behold my power, O king.

**1.69.5**  What I am about to tell you, O sinless one, is a true saying — I speak it as an illustration, not out of hatred; having heard it, you should bear with it patiently.

**1.69.6**  As long as an ugly man does not see his own face in a mirror, he considers himself more handsome than others.

**1.69.7**  But when he looks into the mirror and sees his distorted face, he then knows himself truly — not the other person.

**1.69.8**  One who is supremely gifted in beauty does not belittle anything; but one who talks excessively with harsh words becomes a nuisance in this world.

**1.69.9**  A fool, hearing both good and bad words spoken by people, picks up only the bad words — like a pig that picks up filth.

**1.69.10**  But a wise man, hearing both good and bad words spoken by people, takes only the virtuous word — like a swan that separates milk from water.

**1.69.11**  Just as a good person feels anguish when he speaks ill of others, in the same way a wicked person feels delight when he slanders others.

**1.69.12**  Just as the righteous attain peace by respectfully saluting elders, so a fool attains a perverse contentment by reviling good people.

**1.69.13**  Fools who see no fault in themselves live happily while perceiving faults in others; wherever the virtuous are to be reproached by others, they call those others just such people.

**1.69.14**  There is nothing more laughable in this world than when a wicked man himself calls a virtuous man wicked.

**1.69.15**  From a man fallen from truth and righteousness, enraged, like a venomous serpent, even a non-believer shrinks away — how much more so a believer.

**1.69.16**  Whoever, having himself fathered a son in his own likeness, then disrespects him — the gods destroy his prosperity and he does not enjoy the higher worlds.

**1.69.17**  The forefathers declared a son to be the highest support of family and lineage, the foremost of all sacred duties — therefore one should never abandon a son.

**1.69.18**  Manu declared five kinds of sons: those born of one's own wife, those received as gifts, those purchased, those raised, those begotten on other women, and those adopted.

**1.69.19**  Sons bring righteousness and glory to men, they increase the joy of the heart, and — born as rafts of dharma — they rescue their fathers from hell.

**1.69.20**  Therefore you, O tiger among kings, lord of the earth, lion among rulers, should not abandon your son; protecting yourself, truth, and righteousness, you should not carry deceit in this world.

**1.69.21**  A reservoir is better than a hundred wells; a sacrifice is better than a hundred reservoirs; a son is better than a hundred sacrifices; truth is better than a hundred sons.

**1.69.22**  If a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth are placed in a balance, truth alone surpasses a thousand horse-sacrifices.

**1.69.23**  Mastering all the Vedas and bathing in all the sacred fords — whether these equal speaking truth, O king, or do not equal it, truth is supreme.

**1.69.24**  There is no dharma higher than truth; there is nothing higher than truth; there is indeed nothing more terrible in this world than falsehood.

**1.69.25**  O king, truth is the supreme Brahman; truth is the highest covenant — do not abandon the covenant, O king; let truth be your companion.

**1.69.26**  If you are inclined to falsehood and do not believe in truth yourself, then I am leaving — there is no fellowship with one such as you.

**1.69.27**  Even without you, Duḥṣanta, my son will protect this four-bounded earth adorned with the king of mountains.

**1.69.28**  Vaiśampāyana said: Having spoken these words, Śakuntalā departed. Then, while Duḥṣanta was surrounded by officiating priests, the chief priest, teachers, and ministers, a disembodied voice spoke to him from the sky.

**1.69.29**  The mother is only the bellows; the son belongs to the father from whom he is born. Maintain your son, Duḥṣanta; do not disrespect Śakuntalā.

**1.69.30**  The son of the seed-giver raises him from Yama's realm, O lord of men; and you are indeed the sustainer of this womb — Śakuntalā speaks the truth.

**1.69.31**  The wife bears a son — the self divided into two parts. Therefore, O king Duḥṣanta, maintain your son, the son of Śakuntalā.

**1.69.32**  This is disgrace — who would abandon a living son while himself alive? Maintain the great-souled Śākuntalā, your son Dauḥṣanti, O Paurava.

**1.69.33**  Because he is to be maintained by you, and also by our command, therefore let this son of yours be named Bharata — 'he who is to be maintained.'

**1.69.34**  Hearing the declaration of the heavenly beings, the Paurava king rejoiced and said this to the chief priest and ministers.

**1.69.35**  May you all hear the words of this divine messenger — I too recognize him myself as my own son in exactly this way.

**1.69.36**  If I had accepted him on her word alone, people would have had doubts, and in that way he would not have been certified as pure.

**1.69.37**  Having thus vindicated him through the divine messenger, O Bhārata, the king, filled with joy and delight, accepted his son.

**1.69.38**  He smelled the child's head and embraced him with affection; honored by brahmins and praised by bards, the king experienced the supreme joy born of a son's touch.

**1.69.39**  The king, who knew dharma, honored that wife according to righteousness, and then the king spoke these conciliatory words to her.

**1.69.40**  This union with you was made in secret, away from the world's gaze; therefore, O goddess, I deliberated thus in order to establish your purity.

**1.69.41**  The world might think, on account of you being a woman, that your union with me was improper, and so I accepted this son into the kingdom only after deliberation.

**1.69.42**  And what unpleasant words you, though beloved and devoted to me, spoke to me in great anger — all of that I forgive you, O large-eyed auspicious one.

**1.69.43**  Having spoken thus to her, the royal sage Duḥṣanta honored his beloved queen with garments and food and drink, O Bhārata.

**1.69.44**  Then King Duḥṣanta named his son born of Śakuntalā 'Bharata' and consecrated him as the crown prince.

**1.69.45**  The great-souled Bharata's glorious wheel of conquest began to roll — radiant, divine, unconquered, filling the worlds with its resounding might.

**1.69.46**  He conquered the rulers of the earth and made them submissive; he walked the path of the virtuous and attained unsurpassed glory.

**1.69.47**  That king became a sovereign emperor of the whole earth, blazing with majesty; he performed many sacrifices just as Śakra, the lord of the Maruts, does.

**1.69.48**  Kaṇva caused him to perform a great horse-sacrifice with lavish fees, like Dakṣa; the illustrious one obtained the horse-sacrifice called Govitata, in which Bharata gave Kaṇva a thousand padmas of gold.

**1.69.49**  From Bharata came the glory of the Bharatas, by which this family is called Bhārata; both earlier and later descendants became renowned as Bhāratas.

**1.69.50**  In the lineage of Bharata there were many foremost kings, equal to the gods in power, equal to Brahman in splendor.

**1.69.51**  Their names are beyond count in every respect, O Bhārata; of those most fortunate ones, equal to gods, devoted to truth and uprightness, I shall recite them to you in order of their eminence.

**1.70.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: In the lineage of Dakṣa the Progenitor, Manu Vaivasvata, Bharata, Kuru, Pūru, and Ajamīḍha —

**1.70.2**  — this lineage of the Yādavas and that of the Pāuravas in full, and likewise of the Bhāratas — holy, conferring welfare, meritorious, glory-giving, life-prolonging — I shall recite to you, O sinless one.

**1.70.3**  All blazing with splendor equal to great sages, the ten sons of Pracetas are remembered as the primeval beings — those mighty ones who were burnt by the fire born of clouds.

**1.70.4**  From those ten was born Dakṣa, son of Pracetas; from Dakṣa, O tiger among men, these creatures came into being — he is indeed the grandfather of all the worlds.

**1.70.5**  Dakṣa, the sage son of Pracetas, uniting with Vīriṇī, fathered a thousand sons equal to himself, firm in their vows.

**1.70.6**  Nārada taught Dakṣa's thousand gathered sons the supreme knowledge of liberation, the unsurpassed wisdom of Sāṃkhya.

**1.70.7**  Then Dakṣa the Progenitor, wishing to multiply creation, appointed fifty daughters as his putrikās (daughters treated as sons), O Janamejaya.

**1.70.8**  He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, twenty-seven suited to the passage of time to Indu (the Moon).

**1.70.9**  Of the thirteen wives, the most excellent Dākṣāyaṇī — Kaśyapa, son of Marīci, begat upon her the Ādityas, endowed with might: Indra and the others, and also Vivasvat.

**1.70.10**  From Vivasvat was born the mighty Yama Vaivasvata; and from Yama too, O king, a son was born — Mārtāṇḍa.

**1.70.11**  From Mārtāṇḍa was born the wise and powerful Manu; from Manu this lineage of human beings became celebrated; from Manu were born the Mānavas — brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and the rest.

**1.70.12**  There, O king, brahminhood was united with the warrior order; those Mānavas who were brāhmaṇas studied the Veda together with its ancillary texts.

**1.70.13**  Vena, Dhṛṣṇu, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Ikṣvāku, Karūṣa, Śaryāti, and also Ilā as the eighth —

**1.70.14**  — Pṛṣadhra as the ninth, devoted to the warrior's dharma, and Nābhāgāriṣṭa as the tenth — these are called Manu's mighty sons.

**1.70.15**  Fifty more sons of Manu were likewise born on earth; all of them perished through mutual strife — so we have heard.

**1.70.16**  The learned Purūravas was then born from Ilā — she was both his mother and his father, so we have heard.

**1.70.17**  The greatly glorious Purūravas, though human, consumed thirteen islands of the ocean, surrounded by non-human beings.

**1.70.18**  Purūravas, maddened by his own power, entered into conflict with brāhmaṇas and seized their jewels even as they cried out in protest.

**1.70.19**  Sanatkumāra, O king, came from the world of Brahman and then counseled him; but he did not accept that counsel.

**1.70.20**  Then that lord of men, overcome by greed, drunk on power, having lost all sense, was immediately cursed by the enraged great sages and perished.

**1.70.21**  For he, the sovereign, dwelling in the world of Gandharvas and accompanied by Urvaśī, properly brought the three fires appointed for the rite.

**1.70.22**  Six sons were born from Urvaśī: the wise Āyus, Amāvasu, Dṛḍhāyu, Vanāyu, Śrutāyu — sons of Urvaśī.

**1.70.23**  Nahuṣa, Vṛddhaśarman, Raji, Rambha, and Anenas — born of Svarbhānavī — these are declared to be the sons of Āyu.

**1.70.24**  Nahuṣa, son of Āyu, wise and true in valor, ruled a very great kingdom as lord of the earth by the law of righteousness.

**1.70.25**  Nahuṣa protected the ancestors, gods, sages, brāhmaṇas, Gandharvas, serpents, Rākṣasas, the priestly order, the warrior order, and the merchant class.

**1.70.26**  Having slain hordes of robbers, the mighty Nahuṣa made sages pay tribute and yoked them to carry him on their backs like beasts of burden.

**1.70.27**  He caused himself to hold the position of Indra, having overpowered the dwellers of heaven by his radiance, austerity, valor, and might.

**1.70.28**  Nahuṣa fathered six sons on his beloved wife: Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, the fifth Uddhava, and a sixth.

**1.70.29**  Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, became emperor, true in his valor; he ruled the earth and performed various sacrifices.

**1.70.30**  Honoring the ancestors with supreme power and ever reverently worshiping the gods, the unconquered Yayāti bestowed his grace upon all creatures.

**1.70.31**  His sons, mighty archers endowed with every virtue, O great king, were born of Devayānī and also of Śarmiṣṭhā.

**1.70.32**  Yadu and Turvasu were born of Devayānī; and Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru were born of Śarmiṣṭhā.

**1.70.33**  He, the son of Nahuṣa, ruled his people righteously through endless years, O king, while enduring a terrible old age that was destroying his beauty.

**1.70.34**  Overwhelmed by old age, that king addressed his sons — Yadu, Pūru, Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu — O Bhārata.

**1.70.35**  "I wish to roam in the pleasures of youth and to sport with young women as a young man — help me in this, my sons."

**1.70.36**  Then the elder son born of Devayānī, Yadu, said to him: "What is it that you need from us, and what use is our youth to you?"

**1.70.37**  Yayāti said to him: "Take my old age upon yourself; with your youth let me pursue the objects of pleasure."

**1.70.38**  "Through the curse of the sage Uśanas while I was performing long sacrificial sessions, I have been deprived of the fulfillment of desire, and I grieve because of it, my sons."

**1.70.39**  "Let one of you rule the kingdom with my body, while I, young in a fresh body, attain all pleasures."

**1.70.40**  But Yadu and the others did not accept his old age. Then the youngest, Pūru, of true valor, spoke to him.

**1.70.41**  "O king, roam in the realm of youth with a new body; I, having taken on old age, will remain in the kingdom by your command."

**1.70.42**  Thus addressed, that royal sage, by the power of his ascetic vigor, transferred the old age then to his great-souled son.

**1.70.43**  Taking on the youth of the son of Pūru, the king entered into his prime; and bearing the age of Yayāti, Pūru governed the kingdom.

**1.70.44**  Then, at the end of a thousand years, the unconquered Yayāti, still unsatiated in his desires, spoke to his son Pūru.

**1.70.45**  "Through you I have obtained my inheritance; you are the son who carries on my lineage. The line of Pūru — by this name shall your fame go forth in the world."

**1.70.46**  Then that tiger among kings, having anointed Pūru to the kingdom, passed away to the law of time after a great span of years.

**1.71.1**  Janamejaya said: "Yayāti, our ancestor, who was the tenth from the Lord of Creatures — how did he obtain the daughter of Śukra, she who is supremely difficult to win?"

**1.71.2**  "I wish to hear this in detail, O best of twice-born men; and in due order tell me separately of those who carried on the line of Pūru."

**1.71.3**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Yayāti was a royal sage with the splendor equal to the king of gods. Both Śukra and Vṛṣaparvā chose him in affection in those ancient times."

**1.71.4**  "That I shall fully narrate to you as you ask, O Janamejaya — the union of Devayānī and of Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa."

**1.71.5**  A conflict for supremacy arose between the gods and the demons, throughout the three worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings.

**1.71.6**  Desiring victory, the gods chose the sage Āṅgirasa as their chaplain and sacrificial priest; the others chose Uśanas Kāvya. Those two brahmins were always in fierce rivalry with each other.

**1.71.7**  There, whichever demons were slain by the gods in battle, Kāvya revived them again by resort to the power of his knowledge; and rising again, they fought the gods once more.

**1.71.8**  But those gods whom the demons slew in the thick of battle, Bṛhaspati of great intellect could not revive.

**1.71.9**  For he did not know that knowledge — the life-restoring science — which the mighty Kāvya knew; and so the gods fell into the deepest despair.

**1.71.10**  Then the gods, anxious with fear of Uśanas Kāvya, approached Kaca, the eldest son of Bṛhaspati, and spoke to him.

**1.71.11**  "Favor those who favor you; render us the highest help. That knowledge which resides in the brahmin Śukra of boundless splendor — quickly bring it forth, and you shall share in our portion."

**1.71.12**  "That twice-born one can be found near Vṛṣaparvā; there he protects the demons and does not protect non-demons."

**1.71.13**  "You, in the freshness of your youth, are capable of pleasing that sage, and also Devayānī, the beloved daughter of that great soul."

**1.71.14**  "No one else exists who is capable of winning his favor — not through good conduct, courtesy, sweetness, right behavior, and self-restraint as you are. When Devayānī is pleased, you will surely obtain that knowledge."

**1.71.15**  Saying "So be it," Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, then set out — duly honored by the gods — toward the dwelling of Vṛṣaparvā.

**1.71.16**  Going swiftly, O king, sent forth by the gods, Kaca arrived at the city of the lord of demons, saw Śukra, and spoke these words.

**1.71.17**  "Let your honor accept me as a pupil — the grandson of the sage Āṅgiras, the direct son of Bṛhaspati, known by the name Kaca."

**1.71.18**  "I shall practice the highest celibate studentship under you, the supreme teacher; grant me your approval, O brahmin, for a thousand years."

**1.71.19**  Śukra said: "Kaca, be most welcome; I accept your words. I shall honor you who are worthy of honor, and may Bṛhaspati be honored through you."

**1.71.20**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Kaca, saying 'so be it,' accepted the vow that was prescribed by Śukra Uśanas, the son of the poet, himself."

**1.71.21**  He accepted the prescribed duration of the vow as directed, attending upon his teacher and Devayānī, O Bhārata.

**1.71.22**  Ever intent on pleasing her, that young man, at the threshold of youth, delighted Devayānī with singing, dancing, and playing music.

**1.71.23**  Cultivating the company of Devayānī, the girl who had just come of age, he pleased her with flowers, fruits, and acts of service, O Bhārata.

**1.71.24**  And Devayānī too, that charming woman, singing along with him, attended upon that brahmin who practiced his vows and observances in private at that time.

**1.71.25**  Five hundred years passed thus while Kaca pursued his vow; then the demons, becoming aware of him, turned against Kaca.

**1.71.26**  Finding him alone in the forest tending the cows, in their rage and out of hatred for Bṛhaspati, and to protect the knowledge, they slew him; and having killed him, they ground him to sesame-sized pieces and fed him to wolves.

**1.71.27**  Then the cows returned to their fold without a cowherd. Seeing those cows come back from the forest without Kaca, Devayānī spoke these words at the right moment, O Bhārata.

**1.71.28**  "Your fire-sacrifice has not been offered, and the sun has set, my lord; the cows have come back without a cowherd — father, Kaca is nowhere to be seen."

**1.71.29**  "Clearly Kaca must have been slain or is dead, father; without him I cannot live — I tell you the truth."

**1.71.30**  Śukra said: "By uttering the word 'come here,' I shall revive the dead."

**1.71.31**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Employing the life-restoring knowledge, he called out to Kaca; summoned, Kaca appeared unharmed by virtue of that knowledge, and when questioned by the brahmin's daughter, he told her: 'I was slain.'"

**1.71.32**  Again, urged by Devayānī, the brahmin went to the forest at will to gather flowers; and the demons caught sight of him there.

**1.71.33**  Then the demons slew him a second time, burned him, reduced him to powder, and mixed him into the wine of the brahmin himself.

**1.71.34**  Again Devayānī spoke words to her father: "Kaca who went to gather flowers and run errands, father, is nowhere to be seen."

**1.71.35**  Śukra said: "Daughter, Bṛhaspati's son Kaca has gone the way of the dead. Though revived by the knowledge, he is slain again in this way — what can I do?"

**1.71.36**  "Do not grieve thus, do not weep, Devayānī; one such as you should not mourn a mortal. The gods, the Viśve-devas, and all the world bow before a transformation that has arrived."

**1.71.37**  Devayānī said: "He whose grandfather is the most venerable Āṅgiras, and whose father too is the ascetic-wealthy Bṛhaspati — how should I not grieve, how should I not weep for the son or even the grandson of such a sage?"

**1.71.38**  "He was a celibate student, rich in austerity, ever diligent and skilled in his duties. Father, I shall follow the path of Kaca — I will not eat; for dear to me is the handsome Kaca."

**1.71.39**  Śukra said: "Without doubt the demons hate me — these terrible ones who slay my blameless pupil and wish to make me a non-brahmin; they act toward me as demons have plotted. But there would be an end to this evil here; what person would the guilt of brahmin-slaughter not burn, even Indra himself?"

**1.71.40**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Urged by Devayānī, the great sage Kāvya called out to Bṛhaspati's son Kaca once more, with great intensity."

**1.71.41**  Summoned by the teacher's knowledge and speaking from fear of his guru, a faint voice arose from within the belly. He said to him: "Tell me, brahmin — by what path have you entered, and how do you remain in my belly?"

**1.71.42**  Kaca said: "By your grace, memory does not leave me; I remember everything — what happened and how. But it should not be that there is a waste of my austerity; and so I endure this terrible suffering."

**1.71.43**  "I was given to you in wine by the demons, O Kāvya, after they slew, burned, and ground me to powder. How could the demonic magic ever prevail against the divine magic while you stand firm?"

**1.71.44**  Śukra said: "What shall I do that is pleasing to you today, my son? Kaca could live only at the cost of my death — for Kaca who is inside me, O Devayānī, could be seen only by splitting my belly."

**1.71.45**  Devayānī said: "Two griefs, like fire, would burn me: the destruction of Kaca and harm to you. In the destruction of Kaca there is no peace for me; yet if you are harmed I am unable to live."

**1.71.46**  Śukra said: "You are fully accomplished in form, O son of Bṛhaspati, since the devoted Devayānī cherishes you. Receive this life-restoring knowledge — for if you were not Kaca today, you would be Indra himself in that form."

**1.71.47**  "No one else living would return again from my belly — except a brahmin alone; therefore receive the knowledge."

**1.71.48**  "Becoming my son, sustain me who have sustained you; emerging from this body, my son, consider the righteous regard I have for you — and having received the knowledge from your teacher, be endowed with knowledge."

**1.71.49**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Having received the knowledge from his teacher, the handsome brahmin Kaca burst through the belly and came forth on the right side of the brahmin — like the moon on a full-moon night at the close of the bright fortnight."

**1.71.50**  And seeing that mass of brahmic splendor fallen, Kaca himself raised up the dead man. Having obtained that accomplished knowledge and having paid obeisance, Kaca then addressed him as teacher.

**1.71.51**  "Those who do not revere the teacher who is worthy of worship — the giver of the highest truth, the treasury of treasuries through four lineages — they go to sinful worlds without foundation."

**1.71.52**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Having brought about deception through the drinking of wine and the destruction of consciousness so terrible, and having seen Kaca who had been swallowed in wine by one who was deluded and who was also so handsome —"

**1.71.53**  "— the great-souled one rose up in anger; Uśanas Kāvya himself, wishing to do what was good for brahmins and now deeply troubled about wine-drinking, spoke these words:"

**1.71.54**  "Whatever brahmin henceforth in this world, dull-witted, drinks wine out of delusion — he becomes one fallen from righteousness and also a slayer of brahmins; he shall be censured in this world and in the next."

**1.71.55**  "And this boundary of brahminical law that I have established throughout all the world — let the virtuous brahmins who hearken to their teachers, and let all the gods and all the worlds, hear it."

**1.71.56**  Having spoken thus, that great-souled one — the immeasurable treasury of all treasuries of austerity — summoned those demons whose minds were blinded by fate, and spoke these words to them.

**1.71.57**  "I declare to you — you demons are foolish. Kaca has succeeded and shall remain with me; having obtained the life-restoring knowledge of great import, he is equal in splendor to Brahman and has become Brahman-natured."

**1.71.58**  Having dwelt near his teacher for a thousand years, Kaca, given leave to depart, desired to go to the abode of the thirty gods.

**1.72.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "But as he, his vow completed and released by the teacher, set out toward the dwelling of the thirty gods, Devayānī said this to him."

**1.72.2**  "O grandson of the sage Āṅgiras, you shine by your conduct and birth, and also by knowledge, austerity, and self-restraint."

**1.72.3**  "Just as the sage Āṅgiras is revered and of great renown to my father, so too is Bṛhaspati to me — worthy of reverence and worship above all."

**1.72.4**  "Knowing this, understand what I say to you, O ascetic-wealthy one — understand how I have conducted myself toward you while you were engaged in your vow and observances."

**1.72.5**  "You, now returned with your knowledge, should favor me who am devoted to you; take my hand in the proper manner, with sacred mantras duly preceding."

**1.72.6**  Kaca said: "Just as your venerable father is to be worshipped and revered by me, so too are you, O blameless-limbed one — even more deserving of my veneration."

**1.72.7**  You are dearer than life itself to the great-souled son of Bhṛgu; O noble one, you are by dharma always to be honoured by me as the daughter of my guru.

**1.72.8**  Just as Śukra, your father, is always my revered guru, so too are you, O Devayānī; therefore you ought not to speak to me in this way.

**1.72.9**  Devayānī said: You are indeed the son of a guru's son, but you are not my father's son; therefore you too are honourable and worthy of reverence to me, O best of twice-born.

**1.72.10**  When you were slain again and again by the asuras, O Kaca, recall for yourself the love I bore you from that time forward.

**1.72.11**  You know my supreme devotion in friendship and in love; you ought not, O knower of dharma, to abandon me who am devoted to you and guiltless.

**1.72.12**  Kaca said: You are pressing me into a duty in a matter where I cannot be employed, O you of beautiful vows; be gracious, O fair-browed one — to me you are more revered than even my guru, O auspicious one.

**1.72.13**  Where you dwelt, O wide-eyed one, O moon-faced one, there too did I dwell, O noble one — in the womb of Kāvya himself, O passionate one.

**1.72.14**  You are by dharma my sister; do not speak thus, O beautiful-faced one. I have dwelt at ease, O noble one; there is no anger in me.

**1.72.15**  I take my leave of you and shall go; wish me good fortune on my path. I am to be remembered without violating dharma. Rise ever with diligence and worship my guru.

**1.72.16**  Devayānī said: If you, having been urged, reject me for the sake of dharma and desire, then, O Kaca, this knowledge of yours shall not reach fulfilment.

**1.72.17**  Kaca said: I refuse because you are the guru's daughter, not because of any fault; and I have been released by my guru. Curse me thus if you wish.

**1.72.18**  I speak the ancient law of the seers, O Devayānī; as you have cursed me, I do not deserve this curse — it comes from passion, not from dharma.

**1.72.19**  Therefore the desire you have shall not be fulfilled thus; no son of a seer shall ever take your hand in marriage.

**1.72.20**  The knowledge shall not bear fruit for you — what you said of me shall be so likewise; but I shall teach another, and for him the knowledge shall bear fruit.

**1.72.21**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to Devayānī, Kaca, best of twice-born, quickly departed to the abode of the lord of the thirty gods.

**1.72.22**  Beholding him arrived, the gods with Indra at their head, rejoicing, honoured Bṛhaspati and then spoke these words to Kaca.

**1.72.23**  The most wonderful deed you have done for our benefit — your glory shall never perish; you shall be a sharer of our offerings.

**1.73.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Kaca had mastered his knowledge and returned, the gods, joyful in appearance, having studied that knowledge from Kaca, became fulfilled in their purpose, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.73.2**  All of them assembled together and then spoke to Śatakratu: "Now is the time for your valour; slay your enemies, O Purandara."

**1.73.3**  Thus addressed by the assembled thirty gods, Maghavān then said "So be it" and set forth; and he saw women in a forest.

**1.73.4**  Among the maidens who were playing in that forest resembling Caitraratha's garden, he, having become wind, mixed together all their garments.

**1.73.5**  Then those maidens, rising together from the water, seized those garments in many instances each as they came nearest to hand.

**1.73.6**  There Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, not knowing, took the mixed-up garment of Devayānī.

**1.73.7**  Then a quarrel arose between the two of them there, O king of kings, between Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā on account of it.

**1.73.8**  Devayānī said: Why do you take my garment, having become a pupil of mine, O demoness? It shall not go well with you, being devoid of proper conduct.

**1.73.9**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: Your father praises and salutes my father again and again, whether seated or reclining, standing humbly and submissively.

**1.73.10**  You are the daughter of one who begs, praises, and receives; I am the daughter of one who is praised, who gives and does not receive.

**1.73.11**  Unarmed against one who is armed, empty against one who is full, you stir up trouble, O beggar-girl; you shall find a match to fight you back — I do not count you at all.

**1.73.12**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Śarmiṣṭhā threw Devayānī, who had grown haughty and was clinging to her garment, into a well, and then went home to her city.

**1.73.13**  Thinking "She is dead," Śarmiṣṭhā of wicked resolve departed without looking back toward home, carried away by the force of her anger.

**1.73.14**  Then Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, came to that place, his horses exhausted, his steeds wearied, thirsting, seeking game.

**1.73.15**  He, the son of Nahuṣa, looking about at that waterless well, saw that maiden there, blazing like a flame of fire.

**1.73.16**  Having seen her, that best of kings, with most soothing and gracious words of comfort, questioned that maiden of divine complexion.

**1.73.17**  "Who are you, copper-nailed, dark-complexioned, with well-polished gem-set earrings? You meditate at great length and deeply — why do you sigh so distressed?"

**1.73.18**  "And how have you fallen into this well overgrown with creepers and grass? Whose daughter are you? Tell me everything, O slender-waisted one."

**1.73.19**  Devayānī said: I am the daughter of that Śukra who revives with his knowledge the demons slain by the gods; he surely does not know of me now.

**1.73.20**  This is my right hand, O king, with copper-hued nails on its fingers; take it and lift me up — you are deemed nobly-born in my estimation.

**1.73.21**  For I know you to be self-restrained, valiant, and illustrious; therefore you ought to raise me who have fallen from this well.

**1.73.22**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Recognising her then as a brahmin woman, the son of Nahuṣa took her by the right hand and lifted her up out of that pit.

**1.73.23**  Having quickly raised her from that well, the lord of men Yayāti took his leave of that fair-hipped one and went to his own city.

**1.73.24**  Devayānī said: Go quickly, O Ghūrṇikā, and tell my father everything; for I shall not enter the city of Vṛṣaparvan now.

**1.73.25**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: She quickly went to the demon mansion, found Kāvya, and spoke these words to him, her mind agitated with alarm.

**1.73.26**  "I report to you, O greatly wise one, O greatly fortunate one, that Devayānī has been struck down in the forest by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan."

**1.73.27**  Having heard that his daughter had been struck down there by Śarmiṣṭhā, Kāvya went forth in haste, grieved, searching for his daughter in the forest.

**1.73.28**  Seeing his daughter Devayānī there in the forest, Kāvya embraced her with both arms and, sorrowing, spoke these words.

**1.73.29**  "All beings receive sorrow and happiness through their own faults; I think there must be some misdeed of yours for which this requital has come upon you."

**1.73.30**  Devayānī said: Whether there be a requital for me or not, hear me attentively — what was said to me by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan: and truly she said it — 'You are a singer of the demons.'

**1.73.31**  "Thus does Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, repeatedly speak sharp and harsh words to me, her eyes red with anger."

**1.73.32**  "You are the daughter of one who praises, who begs and receives; I am the daughter of one who is praised, who gives and does not receive."

**1.73.33**  "Thus does Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, speak to me again and again, her eyes flushed red with anger, filled with arrogance."

**1.73.34**  "If I am the daughter of one who praises and receives, then I shall placate Śarmiṣṭhā" — thus was spoken by a companion of mine to me.

**1.73.35**  Śukra said: You are not the daughter of one who praises, O noble one, nor of one who receives; you, O Devayānī, are the daughter of one who does not praise but is praised.

**1.73.36**  Vṛṣaparvan himself knows that, as does king Śakra and Nahuṣa's son; my power is the inconceivable, transcendent, lordly Brahman, beyond all duality.

**1.74.1**  Śukra said: The man who always endures the harsh words of others — know this, O Devayānī: by him all this world is conquered.

**1.74.2**  He who restrains surging anger like a horse — he is called a charioteer by the good, not he who merely hangs on the reins.

**1.74.3**  He who repels surging anger with non-anger — know this, O Devayānī: by him all this world is conquered.

**1.74.4**  He who repels surging anger here with patience, as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin — he is truly called a man.

**1.74.5**  He who restrains wrath, who endures harsh words, and who, though afflicted, does not afflict in return — he is truly a vessel worthy of prosperity.

**1.74.6**  One who sacrifices tirelessly every month for a hundred years, and one who is angered at nothing — of these two, the one without anger is the greater.

**1.74.7**  What enmity mindless boys and girls may stir up — a wise person ought not to follow that course; they do not know the distinction between strength and weakness.

**1.74.8**  Devayānī said: I know, father, even though I am young, the distinction between the paths of dharma here; I also know the difference in strength and weakness in the matter of non-anger and harsh speech.

**1.74.9**  For one who wishes to flourish ought not to tolerate the ungurly conduct of a disciple. Therefore dwelling among those of mixed conduct does not please me.

**1.74.10**  Those men who censure by conduct and by birth — a wise person seeking the highest good ought not to dwell among such evil-minded ones.

**1.74.11**  But those who recognise one's worth by conduct and by birth — among such virtuous ones one ought to dwell; that dwelling is said to be the highest.

**1.74.12**  The ill-spoken, most terrible speech of the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan — I consider nothing harder to bear in all three worlds for one who, of lesser fortune, must attend upon the blazing prosperity of a rival.

**1.75.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kāvya, best of the Bhṛgus, filled with anger, approached Vṛṣaparvan who was seated and spoke to him directly without deliberation.

**1.75.2**  "Unrighteous conduct does not bear fruit at once, O king, like a cow; but if one does not see it in one's own self, it ripens surely in one's sons or grandsons — evil, when swallowed, inevitably bears fruit, as if eaten by a pregnant woman in the womb."

**1.75.3**  "When you caused the brahmin Kaca, the grandson of Aṅgiras, to be slain then — he who was of blameless character, a knower of dharma, devoted to service, content in my house —"

**1.75.4**  "On account of the undeserved killing of him, and on account of the assault on my daughter too, hear this, O Vṛṣaparvan: I shall abandon you along with your kinsmen; I shall not be able to remain in your domain, O king, with you."

**1.75.5**  "Ah, do you regard me, O demon, as one who speaks falsely — that you neither restrain nor heed this fault of your own?"

**1.75.6**  Vṛṣaparvan said: I do not recognise unrighteousness or false speech in you, O Bhārgava; in you dwell both dharma and truth. May you be gracious to us.

**1.75.7**  "If you abandon us, O Bhārgava, and go hence, we shall enter the ocean; there is no other refuge for us."

**1.75.8**  Śukra said: Enter the ocean or flee to the four directions, O asuras; I am not able to bear anything displeasing to my daughter, for she is beloved by me.

**1.75.9**  "Let Devayānī be propitiated; my very life depends on her; I am the guardian of your welfare and security as Bṛhaspati is to Indra."

**1.75.10**  Vṛṣaparvan said: Whatever wealth of the lords of the asuras exists on earth, O Bhārgava, whether elephants, cattle, or horses — of all that you are the master over mine.

**1.75.11**  Śukra said: Whatever treasure of the lords of the daityas there is, O great asura, I am its master; yet let Devayānī be propitiated if it pleases you.

**1.75.12**  Devayānī said: If you are the master of the king's wealth, O father, O Bhārgava, I do not acknowledge that for myself; let the king speak for himself.

**1.75.13**  Vṛṣaparvan said: Whatever desire you desire, O Devayānī, O pure-smiling one, that I shall bestow upon you even if it be hard to obtain.

**1.75.14**  Devayānī said: I desire Śarmiṣṭhā as my maidservant, together with a thousand maidens; let her attend upon me wherever my father shall give me away in marriage.

**1.75.15**  Vṛṣaparvan said: Rise, O attendant-woman, bring Śarmiṣṭhā quickly; and whatever desire Devayānī desires, let her fulfil it.

**1.75.16**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then the nurse went there and spoke these words to Śarmiṣṭhā: "Arise, noble Śarmiṣṭhā, bring happiness to your kinsmen."

**1.75.17**  "The brahmin, urged on by Devayānī, is abandoning his pupils. Whatever desire she holds, that must be fulfilled by you today, O sinless one."

**1.75.18**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Whatever desire she holds, I will fulfill it today. But let not Śukra and Devayānī depart on my account."

**1.75.19**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then, surrounded by a thousand maidens and carried in a palanquin, she swiftly departed from that foremost city by her father's command.

**1.75.20**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "I, along with a thousand maidens, will be your servant and attendant. I will follow you wherever your father gives you in marriage."

**1.75.21**  Devayānī said: "You are the daughter of one who is praised and receives tribute, while I am the daughter of one who praises and renders tribute. How then can you become my servant?"

**1.75.22**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "By whatever means one can bring happiness to afflicted kinsmen — for that reason I will follow you wherever your father gives you in marriage."

**1.75.23**  Vaiśampāyana said: When the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan had thus promised her state of servitude, Devayānī, O best of kings, spoke these words to her father:

**1.75.24**  "I am entering the city, father; I am satisfied, O best of twice-born ones. Your wisdom is unfailing, and your power of learning is immense."

**1.75.25**  Thus addressed by his daughter, that best of twice-born men of great renown entered the city with joy, honored by all the demons.

**1.76.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then, after a long time, O best of kings, the fair-complexioned Devayānī went out to that very forest for sport.

**1.76.2**  Together with that thousand servant-maids and with Śarmiṣṭhā, she reached that very place and wandered there at will, greatly delighted, accompanied by all those companions.

**1.76.3**  All of them were happily sporting, drinking honey-wine, eating various delicacies, and biting into fruits.

**1.76.4**  And once again King Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, arrived at that very spot by chance, seeking game, thirsting for water, and wearied by exertion.

**1.76.5**  He saw Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā and those women drinking and frolicking, adorned with divine ornaments.

**1.76.6**  And he saw the pure-smiling Devayānī seated among those women, incomparable in beauty, the finest of women, being waited upon by Śarmiṣṭhā with foot-massage and other services.

**1.76.7**  Yayāti said: "Each of you is attended by a thousand maidens. I ask you both your family lineages and names."

**1.76.8**  Devayānī said: "I will tell you — receive my words, O lord of men. Śukra is his name, the preceptor of the demons; know me as his daughter."

**1.76.9**  "And this one is my companion and servant, who goes wherever I go — Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, lord of the demons."

**1.76.10**  Yayāti said: "How can this maiden of fair complexion, the daughter of the lord of demons, be your companion and servant, O fair-browed one? I am greatly curious about this."

**1.76.11**  Devayānī said: "Everything follows the ordinance of fate, O tiger among men. Understanding this as decreed by fate, do not weave strange tales about it."

**1.76.12**  "Your form and dress are like a king's, yet you speak with a brahmin's speech. What is your name, where do you come from, and whose son are you? Tell me."

**1.76.13**  Yayāti said: "Through brahmacharya the entire Veda has entered the path of my hearing. I am a king and a king's son, known by the name Yayāti."

**1.76.14**  Devayānī said: "For what purpose have you come to this place, O king — to gather lotus-flowers, or out of desire for game?"

**1.76.15**  Yayāti said: "I came seeking game and water, O noble lady. I have also been much engaged in duties — please grant me leave of that."

**1.76.16**  Devayānī said: "Along with two thousand maidens and with my servant Śarmiṣṭhā, I am dependent on you. Blessings on you — be my companion and husband."

**1.76.17**  Yayāti said: "Know me, O daughter of Uśanas, blessings on you — I am not worthy of you, O passionate one. For kings are not fit to be wedded by those of your father's lineage."

**1.76.18**  Devayānī said: "The brahmin is mingled with the kshatriya and the kshatriya is joined with the brahmin; a seer and a seer's son — O Nāhuṣa, therefore take me in marriage."

**1.76.19**  Yayāti said: "Though the four varṇas are born from one body, O finest of women, they have separate dharmas and separate purities, and among them the brahmin is supreme."

**1.76.20**  Devayānī said: "This rite of taking the hand, O Nāhuṣa, has not been observed by men before — you were the first to take my hand, therefore I choose you."

**1.76.21**  "How could any other man touch my hand — mine, a woman of spirit — after it has been taken by you, a seer's son, or rather by you who are yourself a seer?"

**1.76.22**  Yayāti said: "To a man who knows, a brahmin is more difficult to assail than an enraged venomous serpent or an all-consuming fire."

**1.76.23**  Devayānī said: "Why do you say a brahmin is more difficult to assail than a venomous serpent or an all-consuming fire, O bull among men?"

**1.76.24**  Yayāti said: "A venomous serpent kills one; one can be slain by a weapon — but an enraged brahmin destroys entire kingdoms and their cities."

**1.76.25**  "Therefore a brahmin is more difficult to assail, so I believe, O timid one — and for this reason, O noble lady, I will not marry you without your being given by your father."

**1.76.26**  Devayānī said: "Take me as given by my father, O king — for you have been chosen by me. There is no fear for one who accepts a woman given freely."

**1.76.27**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then Devayānī quickly sent word to her father; and upon hearing it, the descendant of Bhṛgu presented the king before him.

**1.76.28**  Seeing Śukra arrived, Yayāti, lord of the earth, bowed to that brahmin, the descendant of Kavi, standing with folded hands in reverence.

**1.76.29**  Devayānī said: "This king, the son of Nahuṣa, took my hand in an inaccessible place, father. I bow to you — give me to him; I choose no other husband in the world."

**1.76.30**  Śukra said: "You have been chosen as husband by this daughter of mine whom I hold dear, O hero. Take her, given by me as your queen, O son of Nahuṣa."

**1.76.31**  Yayāti said: "Let no great transgression touch me here, O descendant of Bhṛgu — it is due to the sin born of mingling of varṇas that I appeal to you thus, O brahmin."

**1.76.32**  Śukra said: "I release you from the transgression — choose as you desire. Do not despair in this marriage; I remove the sin from you."

**1.76.33**  "Take the slender-waisted Devayānī as your wife according to dharma; together with her you will attain incomparable joy."

**1.76.34**  "And this maiden Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, should always be honored by you, O king — but never summon her to your bed."

**1.76.35**  Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed, Yayāti circumambulated Śukra and departed for his own city with joy, having received leave from that great-souled one.

**1.77.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Yayāti reached his own city, resembling the city of great Indra, and entering the inner apartments, he installed Devayānī there.

**1.77.2**  With Devayānī's consent, he had a house built near the aśoka grove and installed there that daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.

**1.77.3**  Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the asura line, attended by a thousand maidservants, was provided with garments, food, and drink, and treated with great honor.

**1.77.4**  Together with Devayānī, that king, son of Nahuṣa, sported for many years, greatly delighted like a god.

**1.77.5**  When the proper season came, Devayānī, that finest of women, conceived first and gave birth to a son.

**1.77.6**  When a thousand years had passed, Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, reaching the bloom of youth, saw that her season had come and reflected thus:

**1.77.7**  "The season has arrived, and yet I have no husband chosen for me. What has been gained? What must be done? What, if done, would be truly done?"

**1.77.8**  "Devayānī has borne a child, while I, having attained youth, am barren. As she chose her husband, so I too shall choose him."

**1.77.9**  "It is my firm resolve that the king must grant me the fruit of a son. Would that this righteous-souled one might come to me now in private."

**1.77.10**  Then, at that very time, the king came out by chance and encountered Śarmiṣṭhā standing near the aśoka grove.

**1.77.11**  Seeing him alone in a secluded spot, the lovely-smiling Śarmiṣṭhā went forward, made the anjali gesture, and spoke these words to the king:

**1.77.12**  "In the lineage of Soma, Indra, Viṣṇu, Yama, or Varuṇa — or in yours, O Nāhuṣa — who would be worthy to touch a woman?"

**1.77.13**  "For you, O king, have always known me by my beauty, lineage, and conduct. I, propitiating you, ask you — grant me the season's gift, O lord of men."

**1.77.14**  Yayāti said: "I know you as a maiden of the daitya race endowed with good conduct and without reproach; in your beauty I see not even a needle's point of fault."

**1.77.15**  "Yet Uśanas Kāvya told me when he entrusted Devayānī to me: 'This daughter of Vṛṣaparvan must never be summoned to your bed.'"

**1.77.16**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Words spoken in jest do not harm; nor do those spoken to women, O king, nor at the time of marriage, nor when life is at stake, nor when all one's wealth is being taken — these five kinds of untruth are said to be without sin."

**1.77.17**  "But one who speaks falsely when questioned as a witness, or one who is falsely accused — they say, O lord of men, that in a matter rightly and wholly agreed upon, falsehood does not harm the speaker of untruth."

**1.77.18**  Yayāti said: "A king is the measure of all beings; he would perish by speaking falsehood. Even in financial distress I am not inclined to act falsely."

**1.77.19**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "These two are considered equal, O king: a husband and the husband of a companion. Marriage to both is called equal — you have been chosen as husband by my companion, so you are my husband too."

**1.77.20**  Yayāti said: "My vow is established that I must give to those who ask. You are asking me — speak your desire, what shall I do for you?"

**1.77.21**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Protect me from unrighteousness, O king, and establish dharma for me — having offspring from you, I could practice the highest dharma in the world."

**1.77.22**  "There are three who own no wealth, O king: the wife, the slave, and the son — whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong."

**1.77.23**  "I am a maidservant of Devayānī and subject to the descendant of Bhṛgu, and so am I also within your care, O king — therefore take me as one whom you must support."

**1.77.24**  Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed, the king recognized this as true and honored Śarmiṣṭhā, fulfilling dharma for her.

**1.77.25**  Having come together with Śarmiṣṭhā and satisfied their desires, they honored one another and departed each the way they had come.

**1.77.26**  From that union, the fair-browed, lovely-smiling Śarmiṣṭhā first conceived from that best of kings.

**1.77.27**  And in due time, O king, the lotus-eyed one gave birth to a son resembling the offspring of a god, with eyes like lotus petals.

**1.78.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Hearing that a son had been born, the pure-smiling Devayānī became distressed and began to reflect regarding Śarmiṣṭhā, O Bhārata.

**1.78.2**  And approaching Śarmiṣṭhā, Devayānī said: "What is this wrong that you have done, O fair-browed one, overcome by desire?"

**1.78.3**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Some sage of righteous soul, master of the Vedas, came as a guest. He who grants boons was asked by me for the desire in accordance with dharma."

**1.78.4**  "I do not act upon desire unjustly, O pure-smiling one. This offspring of mine is from that sage — this I tell you truly."

**1.78.5**  Devayānī said: "Very well, O timid one, if it is true — then let that brahmin be identified. I wish to know that twice-born man by his lineage, name, and family."

**1.78.6**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Blazing with energy and splendor like the sun — upon seeing him, I had no power to question him, O pure-smiling one."

**1.78.7**  Devayānī said: "If that is so, Śarmiṣṭhā, then I harbor no anger — if you have obtained offspring from a brahmin who is both the eldest and the best."

**1.78.8**  Vaiśampāyana said: Having thus spoken to one another and laughed together, the daughter of Bhṛgu returned home, accepting it as true.

**1.78.9**  King Yayāti begot two sons upon Devayānī — Yadu and Turvasu — who were like Indra and Viṣṇu themselves.

**1.78.10**  From that same royal sage, Śarmiṣṭhā the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan gave birth to three princes — Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.

**1.78.11**  Then on a certain occasion, O king, the fair-smiling Devayānī went out into the great forest accompanied by Yayāti.

**1.78.12**  There she saw boys beautiful as gods playing at their ease, and astonished she said this:

**1.78.13**  "Whose are these children, O king, auspicious and resembling sons of gods? In radiance and form they seem to me like your own."

**1.78.14**  Having questioned the king thus, she then questioned the boys: "What are your names and lineage, little ones? Who is your brahmin father? Tell me truly — I wish to know him."

**1.78.15**  The boys pointed with their forefingers to that very best of kings, and they named Śarmiṣṭhā as their mother.

**1.78.16**  Having spoken so, they went together toward the king; but the king did not welcome them in Devayānī's presence. Then, weeping, the boys ran to Śarmiṣṭhā.

**1.78.17**  Seeing the boys' affection toward the king and understanding the truth of it, the noble lady spoke thus to Śarmiṣṭhā:

**1.78.18**  "Though you were under my authority, why have you done me this wrong? You have followed the ways of the asuras — do you not fear?"

**1.78.19**  Śarmiṣṭhā said: "What was said was that he was a sage — that is the truth, O lovely-smiling one. Acting rightly and in accordance with dharma, I do not fear you."

**1.78.20**  "When the king was chosen by you, he was then chosen by me as well — for a friend's husband is, by dharma, a husband, O beautiful one."

**1.78.21**  "You are my revered and honored elder — a brahmin woman, the most excellent. Yet even above you, the royal sage is most worthy of my veneration — do you not know that?"

**1.78.22**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing her words, Devayānī then said: "O king, I will not stay here any longer — you have done me wrong."

**1.78.23**  Seeing the dark-complexioned woman suddenly rise with tears in her eyes, setting out swiftly toward Kāvya's abode, the king was then distressed.

**1.78.24**  Agitated, the king followed behind her, trying to soothe her — but she, her eyes reddened with anger, did not turn back.

**1.78.25**  Without saying anything to the king, the lovely-eyed woman swiftly arrived at the presence of Kāvya Uśanas.

**1.78.26**  Seeing her father, she paid her respects and stood before him; and thereupon Yayāti also honored the Bhārgava sage.

**1.78.27**  Devayānī said: "Dharma has been defeated by adharma; a descent into wrong has begun. I have been transgressed against by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan."

**1.78.28**  "Three sons have been fathered upon her by this king Yayāti, while upon me, the ill-fortuned one, only two sons — this I tell you, father."

**1.78.29**  "This king, renowned as a knower of dharma, O scion of Bhṛgu, has transgressed the bounds of propriety — this, O Kāvya, I tell you."

**1.78.30**  Śukra said: O great king, though you know righteousness, you performed an unrighteous act for the sake of pleasure. Therefore, old age — unconquerable — will afflict you before long.

**1.78.31**  Yayāti said: O blessed one, when the daughter of the lord of the asuras came to me seeking her season, I went to her with an undivided mind — what I did was in accordance with dharma.

**1.78.32**  O brahmin, the man who has been chosen and yet does not give himself to a woman seeking her season is declared by those who expound sacred learning to be guilty of the sin of killing an embryo.

**1.78.33**  And the man who, when privately solicited by a woman who desires him and who may lawfully be approached, does not go to her — the wise declare him guilty of embryo-slaying in matters of dharma.

**1.78.34**  Weighing these considerations, O scion of Bhṛgu, and trembling with fear of unrighteousness, I went to Śarmiṣṭhā.

**1.78.35**  Śukra said: Surely you should have consulted me — you are under my authority, O king. In matters of dharma, false conduct amounts to theft, O son of Nahuṣa.

**1.78.36**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, was cursed by the enraged Uśanas; forthwith abandoning his former youth, he was instantly overtaken by old age.

**1.78.37**  Yayāti said: O scion of Bhṛgu, I am not yet sated with youth nor with Devayānī — show me your grace, O brahmin; let this old age not enter me.

**1.78.38**  Śukra said: I do not speak falsely in this — you have received old age, O lord of the earth. But this old age you may transfer to another, if you so wish.

**1.78.39**  Yayāti said: O brahmin, whichever son gives me his youth shall be heir to the kingdom, shall partake of merit, and shall also partake of glory — may you sanction this.

**1.78.40**  Śukra said: You will transfer the old age as you wish, O son of Nahuṣa — meditating on me with sincere heart you shall not incur sin.

**1.78.41**  Whichever son gives you his youth, he shall become king — long-lived, glorious, and blessed with many offspring as well.

**1.79.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having obtained old age and having returned to his own city, Yayāti spoke these words to his eldest and most excellent son Yadu:

**1.79.2**  "Old age, wrinkles, and white hairs have overtaken me, my son, by the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, and I am not yet satisfied with youth."

**1.79.3**  "You, Yadu, take up this affliction of old age; with your youth let me enjoy the pleasures of the senses."

**1.79.4**  "When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth to you and resume my own affliction of old age."

**1.79.5**  Yadu said: "With white beard and white hair, wretched, loosened by old age, with wrinkles covering every limb, unsightly, feeble, emaciated —

**1.79.6**  "— incapable of action, scorned by the young and by dependents alike, such old age I do not desire."

**1.79.7**  Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, your progeny, my son, shall not partake of kingship."

**1.79.8**  "Turvasu, take up this affliction of old age; with your youth I will indeed enjoy the pleasures of the senses, my son."

**1.79.9**  "When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth and I myself will resume the affliction of old age."

**1.79.10**  Turvasu said: "I do not desire old age, father — it destroys the enjoyment of desires, it ends strength and beauty, it ruins intellect and vital breath."

**1.79.11**  Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, your lineage, O Turvasu, shall come to complete extinction."

**1.79.12**  "Among those of mixed conduct and dharma, among those who act contrary to social order, among flesh-eaters and outcastes, you fool, shall you be a king."

**1.79.13**  "Among those addicted to their elders' wives, among those fallen into animal wombs, among the sinful who follow the ways of beasts, among the mlecchas, shall you hold sway."

**1.79.14**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus cursed Turvasu, Yayāti spoke these words to his own son Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā:

**1.79.15**  "Druhyu, take up this old age that destroys complexion and form; give me your youth for a thousand years."

**1.79.16**  "When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth and I myself will once again take up the affliction of old age."

**1.79.17**  Druhyu said: "An old man enjoys neither elephant, nor chariot, nor horse, nor woman — his speech too becomes broken. Therefore I do not desire that old age."

**1.79.18**  Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, O Druhyu, your cherished desires shall nowhere be fulfilled."

**1.79.19**  "In a land where crossing is always only by raft and float, without a king, you and your descendants shall bear the name of Bhoja."

**1.79.20**  "Anu, take up this affliction of old age; for one thousand years let me enjoy with your youth."

**1.79.21**  Anu said: "An old man takes food like a child, at unseasonable times, like one impure; he does not offer into the sacred fire at the proper hour. That old age I do not desire."

**1.79.22**  Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, the very fault of old age you have named — that you shall receive."

**1.79.23**  "And your offspring, O Anu, shall perish upon reaching youth; and you yourself shall likewise be devoted to neglecting the sacred fire."

**1.79.24**  "Pūru, you are my beloved son; you shall be the greatest. Old age, wrinkles, and white hair have overtaken me, my son, by the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, and I am not satisfied with youth."

**1.79.25**  "Pūru, take up this affliction of old age; for some time let me truly enjoy the pleasures of the senses with your youthful vigor."

**1.79.26**  "When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth, and I myself will resume the affliction of old age."

**1.79.27**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Pūru replied to his father straightforwardly: "As you have told me, O great king, so I will carry out your words."

**1.79.28**  "I will take up from you the affliction of old age, O king. Take my youth and enjoy desires as you wish."

**1.79.29**  "Covered by old age, bearing your form of age, having given my youth to you, I will conduct myself as you have directed me."

**1.79.30**  Yayāti said: "Pūru, I am pleased with you, my child; and pleased, I give you this: your progeny in the kingdom shall be endowed with fulfillment of all desires."

**1.80.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, with the youth of the Paurava, Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa, delighted, that best of kings, pursued his beloved pleasures.

**1.80.2**  As he desired, with all his energy, in due season and according to his happiness, the lord of kings enjoyed pleasures unopposed to dharma, as was fitting for him.

**1.80.3**  He gratified the gods with sacrifices, and likewise the ancestors with śrāddha offerings; the needy with desired gifts and boons; and the best of the twice-born with desired goods.

**1.80.4**  He honored guests with food and drink, the commoners with protection, the śūdras with kindness, and suppressed bandits with firm restraint.

**1.80.5**  Delighting all his subjects properly with righteousness, Yayāti protected them like a second Indra himself.

**1.80.6**  That king, bold as a lion, youthful, roaming through the field of pleasures, pursued the highest happiness without transgressing dharma.

**1.80.7**  Having obtained auspicious pleasures, satisfied and yet wearied, the lord of men, that ruler of earth, recalled the time — the end of a thousand years.

**1.80.8**  Reckoning up the moments and the divisions of time, that knower of time, that valiant one, judged the period complete and spoke to his son Pūru:

**1.80.9**  "As I desired, with full energy, and in due season, O subduer of foes, pleasures have been enjoyed by me, my son, with your youth."

**1.80.10**  "Pūru, I am pleased with you — blessings upon you. Take back this your own youth, and take also this kingdom — for you are the son who has done me pleasure."

**1.80.11**  Then King Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa resumed old age, and Pūru recovered his own youth once again.

**1.80.12**  When the king wished to consecrate Pūru, his youngest son, the four estates headed by the brahmins spoke these words:

**1.80.13**  "How, O lord, will you give the kingdom to Pūru, passing over the eldest, Yadu — the grandson of Śukra and son of Devayānī?"

**1.80.14**  "Yadu was born your eldest son; after him Turvasu; Śarmiṣṭhā's son Druhyu came next, then Anu, and only then Pūru."

**1.80.15**  "How can the youngest deserve the kingdom, passing over the elders? We set this before you — uphold dharma."

**1.80.16**  Yayāti said: "Let all the estates, headed by the brahmins, hear my words: as to the eldest, the kingdom is in no way to be given by me to him."

**1.80.17**  "My command was not followed by my eldest, Yadu; and he who acts contrary to his father is not considered a son by the righteous."

**1.80.18**  He who obeys the words of his mother and father, who is devoted and beneficial to them — he is a true son; and he who conducts himself toward his parents as a son should.

**1.80.19**  By Yadu I was disrespected, and likewise by Turvasu; by Druhyu and by Anu too, great contempt was shown toward me.

**1.80.20**  My word was fulfilled by Puru, and I was honored by him especially; he is my youngest heir, he who bore my old age — and my desire was accomplished by Puru, who proved himself a true son.

**1.80.21**  And a boon was granted by Shukra himself, the sage Ushanas Kavya: 'The son who obeys you shall be a king, lord of the earth.' Appealing to you on this ground, let Puru be consecrated to the kingdom.

**1.80.22**  The subjects said: A son who is endowed with virtues and is always devoted to the welfare of his mother and father deserves all prosperity, O lord, even if he is the youngest.

**1.80.23**  Puru deserves this kingdom; he is the son who has done what pleases you. By virtue of Shukra's boon, there is no reply that can be made against it.

**1.80.24**  Vaishampayana said: Thus addressed by the satisfied townspeople and country folk, Nahusha's son at that time anointed his own son Puru in the kingdom.

**1.80.25**  Having given the kingdom to Puru and consecrated himself for forest-dwelling, the king departed from the city accompanied by brahmins and ascetics.

**1.80.26**  From Yadu were born the Yadavas; from Turvasu's sons came the Yavanas; from Druhyu's sons came the Bhojas; and from Anu came the tribes of the mlecchas.

**1.80.27**  From Puru came the Paurava lineage, in which you were born, O king — he who was master enough to wield the kingdom for a thousand years.

**1.81.1**  Vaishampayana said: Thus king Yayati, son of Nahusha, having joyfully consecrated his desired son to the kingdom, became a forest-dweller and a sage.

**1.81.2**  And having dwelt in the forest, taking refuge with brahmins, subsisting on fruits and roots, self-restrained and great-souled, he departed from here to heaven.

**1.81.3**  Having gone to the abode of the gods and dwelling there joyfully and happily, after no very great span of time he was cast down again by Shakra.

**1.81.4**  Falling, dislodged from heaven, before he could reach the surface of the earth, he stood suspended in mid-air — so I have heard.

**1.81.5**  And thence he again went to heaven — so goes the tradition — having met, it is said, in an assembly with king Vasumat, with the valiant Ashtaka, with Pratardana, and with Shibi.

**1.81.6**  Janamejaya said: By what deed did that lord of the earth once more attain heaven? I wish to hear all of this fully and truly, O brahmin, as related by you in the presence of the assembly of brahmin-sages.

**1.81.7**  For Yayati, lord of the earth, was equal to the king of the gods; he was the increaser of the Kuru lineage, blazing with a splendor equal to the sun.

**1.81.8**  I wish to hear the conduct of that great-souled one of wide-spread fame and true renown — both in heaven and here on earth, in every regard.

**1.81.9**  Vaishampayana said: Very well, I shall tell you the later story of Yayati — meritorious both in heaven and here on earth, and destructive of all sins.

**1.81.10**  King Yayati, son of Nahusha, having joyfully consecrated his youngest son Puru to the kingdom, then set forth to the forest.

**1.81.11**  Having placed his sons led by Yadu on the frontiers, the king, subsisting on fruits and roots, dwelt for a long time in the forest.

**1.81.12**  With sharpened self, having conquered anger, satisfying the ancestors and the gods, and offering oblations into the sacred fires according to rule, following the ordinances of the forest-dweller stage.

**1.81.13**  The mighty one honored guests with forest oblations, following the practice of gleaning fallen grain, eating only what remained after others were fed.

**1.81.14**  The king maintained this conduct for a full thousand years; for thirty autumns he subsisted on water alone, with restrained speech and mind.

**1.81.15**  Then he became a subsister on air alone for a year without slackening; and for a year the king performed austerities in the midst of the five fires.

**1.81.16**  And he stood on one foot for six months, subsisting on wind; then he of holy fame went to heaven, having pervaded both heaven and earth.

**1.82.1**  Vaishampayana said: That foremost of kings, having gone to heaven, dwelling in the abode of the gods, was honored by the Tridasha gods, the Sadhyas, the Maruts, and the Vasus.

**1.82.2**  Moving from the world of the gods to the world of Brahma, that meritorious, self-controlled guardian of the earth dwelt there for a long time — so goes the tradition.

**1.82.3**  At some point that best of kings, Yayati, came to Shakra; and at the end of their conversation, the lord of the earth was questioned by Shakra.

**1.82.4**  Shakra said: When Puru, O king, bearing your old age in your form, roamed the earth, and when you gave the kingdom to him — what did you say to him? Tell me truly.

**1.82.5**  Yayati said: 'All this territory between the Ganga and the Yamuna is yours; you are king in the middle of the earth — your brothers are rulers of the borderlands.'

**1.82.6**  'The one free from anger is superior to the wrathful; likewise the forbearing is superior to the unfor-bearing; humans are paramount over non-humans; and so the wise man is paramount over the ignorant.'

**1.82.7**  'When reviled, one should not revile in return — the patient man's anger alone burns up the reviler, and he himself gains merit.'

**1.82.8**  'One should not be wounding, nor speak cruelly; one should not seize upon another's weakness. The speech that causes another to tremble — one should not utter that harsh word that leads to evil worlds.'

**1.82.9**  'A man who is wounding, harsh of speech, piercing people with the thorns of his words — know him to be the most inauspicious of people, bearing destruction bound to his mouth.'

**1.82.10**  'One should be honored by the good from the front and protected by the good from behind; one should always forbear the excessive speech of the wicked; and conducting oneself nobly, one should adopt the conduct of the good.'

**1.82.11**  'Word-arrows fly forth from the mouth; struck by them, one grieves through nights and days. When they strike another's vital spots — a wise man should never discharge such words at others.'

**1.82.12**  'Indeed there is no means of winning over others in the three worlds like friendliness toward all beings, giving, and sweet speech.'

**1.82.13**  'Therefore one should always speak gently and never speak harshly anywhere; one should honor those worthy of honor; one should give and never beg.'

**1.83.1**  Indra said: Having completed all your duties, O king, you abandoned your home and went to the forest. This I ask you, O son of Nahusha — with whose austerity are you equal, O Yayati?

**1.83.2**  Yayati said: I see no one equal to myself in austerity — not among gods and men, not among gandharvas and great sages, O Vasava.

**1.83.3**  Indra said: Because you held in contempt those equal to you and even superior to you, not knowing their power — therefore your worlds are now finite; your merit exhausted, you have fallen today, O king.

**1.83.4**  Yayati said: If my worlds are exhausted, O Shakra, by having shown contempt for gods, sages, gandharvas, and men — then I wish, though bereft of the heavenly world, to fall among the good, O king of the gods.

**1.83.5**  Indra said: You have fallen in the presence of the good, O king; having fallen, you will regain your footing once more. Knowing this, O Yayati, do not again despise those equal to you and those superior to you.

**1.83.6**  Vaishampayana said: Then, seeing Yayati falling, having abandoned the blessed worlds cherished by the king of immortals, the foremost royal sage Ashtaka, guardian of the ordinances of right conduct, spoke to him.

**1.83.7**  'Who are you, youthful and equal in form to Vasava, blazing with your own splendor like fire, falling from the sky out of the darkness of rising storm-clouds, like the sun, supreme among sky-travellers?'

**1.83.8**  'Seeing you falling from the path of the sun, your immeasurable radiance like fire and the sun, all of us, speculating what indeed is this that falls, are utterly bewildered.'

**1.83.9**  'And seeing you stationed in the path of the gods, with power equal to Shakra, the sun, and Vishnu, all of us have come forward today to meet you, desiring to know the truth of your fall.'

**1.83.10**  'We did not dare to question you first, and you do not ask us who we are. So we ask you of desirable form: whose son are you? And for what reason have you come?'

**1.83.11**  'But let fear depart from you; abandon grief and confusion quickly, O you of form equal to the lord of gods — for while you remain in the presence of the good, even Shakra, the slayer of Bala, is not able to harm you.'

**1.83.12**  'For the good are truly the foundation for those dislodged from happiness; the good are always like the king of immortals. Those lords of the moving and unmoving are gathered here; you stand firm among the good who are your equals.'

**1.83.13**  'Fire is lord in burning, earth is lord in sustaining, the sun is lord in illuminating — and one who has come to the good is lord.'

**1.84.1**  Yayati said: I am Yayati, son of Nahusha, father of Puru; through contempt for all beings I have been cast down from the worlds of gods, siddhas, and sages; having fallen away, I fall, my merit exhausted.

**1.84.2**  'I am older in age than all of you; therefore I do not offer salutation to you — for he who is elder by learning, austerity, or birth is worthy of worship among the twice-born.'

**1.84.3**  Ashtaka said: If you said that he who is elder in years is the elder, O king, then you should have saluted us in some manner — for he who is truly wise and elder in years is the one worthy of worship among the twice-born.

**1.84.4**  Yayati said: They call sin the course contrary to right action; it dwells in one inclined toward evil worlds. The good do not go along with the wicked in this, like a self that speaks in accordance with what is agreeable to them.

**1.84.5**  'My wealth was immense and great; yet striving I could not retain it. He who, having reflected thus and fixed his mind on his own welfare, conducts himself accordingly — he truly knows how to live.'

**1.84.6**  'Many and various are the states of existence in the world of the living, governed by fate, with their efforts and powers lost. Encountering each such state, the wise man should not be distressed, thinking with steady mind: fate is supreme.'

**1.84.7**  'Whether a creature obtains happiness or suffering, it is under the control of fate, not by its own power. Therefore, holding fate to be supreme, one should neither burn with grief nor ever exult.'

**1.84.8**  'The wise man should not be tormented by sorrow nor exult in happiness; he should always conduct himself with equanimity, thinking fate to be supreme — he should neither burn with grief nor ever exult.'

**1.84.9**  'I am never deluded by fear, O Ashtaka; there is no mental anguish in me whatsoever, thinking: as the Creator ordains my existence in the world, so certainly shall I be.'

**1.84.10**  'Creatures born from sweat, born from eggs, and those that sprout from the earth; reptiles, worms, fish in the waters; stones, grass, and wood — all at the exhaustion of their ordained span return to their own nature.'

**1.84.11**  'Understanding the impermanence of pleasure and pain, why should I, O Ashtaka, indulge in anguish? What shall I do, and having done what shall I not grieve? Therefore, vigilant, I abandon all anguish.'

**1.84.12**  Ashtaka said: What worlds, O foremost of earthly kings, were the chief ones you enjoyed, and for how long, and in what manner? Tell me all of this, O king, exactly as it was — for you speak of dharma like one who knows the field.

**1.84.13**  Yayati said: I was here a universal sovereign of all the earth; then I won great worlds. I dwelt there for just a thousand years; then I advanced to a higher world.

**1.84.14**  Then in the delightful city of Puruhuta — with a thousand gates, extending a hundred yojanas — I dwelt for just a thousand years; then I advanced to a higher world.

**1.84.15**  Then having attained the divine, ageless world of Prajapati, lord of worlds — difficult to reach — I dwelt there for just a thousand years; then I advanced to a higher world.

**1.84.16**  And in the dwelling of god after god, having won the worlds, I dwelt as I pleased, honored by all the Tridasha gods, equal in power and splendor to the lords.

**1.84.17**  And thus I dwelt in Nandana, taking whatever form I desired, for a hundred times ten thousand years, roaming with the apsaras, smelling the sacred fragrances, beholding the flowering trees of beautiful form.

**1.84.18**  When I was stationed there, absorbed in the pleasures of the gods, after a very great time had passed, a messenger of the gods of terrible form cried out loudly three times in a prolonged voice: 'Fall!'

**1.84.19**  This is all that I know, O lion among kings; then I fell from Nandana, my merit exhausted. And I heard the voices of the gods in the sky, lamenting with compassion, O lord of men.

**1.84.20**  'Alas, how painful — Yayati, whose merit is exhausted, he who wrought merit and had a holy name, is falling.' Then I, while falling, said to them: 'How might I fall among the good?'

**1.84.21**  By them was this sacrificial ground of yours pointed out to me; perceiving it, I came here swiftly, guided by the fragrance of the oblations of this sacrificial ground, following the trail of the smoke with confidence.

**1.85.1**  Ashtaka said: When you dwelt in Nandana taking whatever form you desired, for a hundred times ten thousand years — what was the reason, O foremost one of the Krita age, that abandoning that estate you descended to the earth?

**1.85.2**  Yayati said: Just as here a kinsman, friend, or companion is abandoned by people when his wealth is exhausted — so there, when a person's merit is exhausted, the assemblies of gods together with their lords abandon him at once.

**1.85.3**  Ashtaka said: How does their merit become exhausted in that place? My mind is greatly bewildered on this point. What are their characteristics, and to whose abode do they go? Tell me that indeed — you are regarded by me as one who knows the field.

**1.85.4**  Yayati said: They all fall into this earthly hell, O lord of men, lamenting. Exhausted, as food for herons, jackals, and vultures, they go in many directions to grow again.
