**1.85.5**  'Therefore this corrupted and censurable action in the world is to be avoided by a man. All of this has been told to you, O king; say now what more I may tell you.'

**1.85.6**  Ashtaka said: When the birds peck at them — vultures, blue-necked herons, and insects — how do they come to be, how do they come into existence? I hear of no other hell than this earthly one.

**1.85.7**  Yayati said: Rising upward from the body as karma expands, they clearly wander upon the earth; they fall into this earthly hell and do not look back for many, many years.

**1.85.8**  Sixty thousand years they fall through the sky, and then eighty more years besides; as they plummet headlong in their fall, terrible earthbound rākṣasas with sharp fangs torment them.

**1.85.9**  Aṣṭaka said: When those terrible earthbound rākṣasas with sharp fangs torment the falling sinners, how do they come into being, how do they come to exist — in what manner do they become embryonic beings?

**1.85.10**  Yayāti said: Blood, seed, and the essence of flowers and fruits — that which is emitted by the man follows along; that indeed enters the woman's menstrual blood, and becoming an embryo it arrives there.

**1.85.11**  They enter into trees and medicinal plants, into water, wind, earth, and the atmosphere, into all four-footed creatures and two-footed beings as well — in this manner do they become embryonic beings.

**1.85.12**  Aṣṭaka said: Does the embryo fashion a different body here, or does it go of its own will when entering this human womb? Explain this to me — I speak from doubt.

**1.85.13**  And how does the body with its form arise, and by what means does it gain awareness through eye and ear? Tell me all this truth when questioned — for we all regard you, dear one, as one who knows the field.

**1.85.14**  Yayāti said: The wind draws up the embryonic matrix; in the fertile season it is mingled with the essence of seed and flower. There, holding sway through the subtle elements, it gradually nourishes and develops the embryo here.

**1.85.15**  As it is born with its limbs fully formed, the human being is grounded in six modes of cognition; by means of the ears it perceives sound here, and sees all form through the eyes.

**1.85.16**  By the nose it smells fragrance, by the tongue it tastes flavour, by the skin it knows touch, and by the mind it knows inner states — so know, O Aṣṭaka, the accumulation of senses in the body of the great-souled living being.

**1.85.17**  Aṣṭaka said: When a man has died and is burned, or is buried, or is ground to dust — having passed into non-being and reached destruction, by what means does the self become conscious again hereafter?

**1.85.18**  Yayāti said: Having abandoned the vital breaths like one falling asleep, having groaned, having placed merit and demerit before it, it follows at the tip of the wind, O lion among kings, and having left the body it enters another womb.

**1.85.19**  Those who have done good go to an auspicious womb; those who have done evil go to an evil womb — the wicked become insects and moths. I have no desire to say more, O great one.

**1.85.20**  Four-footed creatures, two-footed beings, and six-legged insects — in this way do they become embryonic forms. All this has been told to you in full; what more do you ask, O lion among kings?

**1.85.21**  Aṣṭaka said: By doing what, dear one, does a mortal attain the highest worlds — by asceticism or by knowledge? Being asked, tell me all this truthfully, by what means one may reach the auspicious worlds in due order.

**1.85.22**  Yayāti said: Asceticism, charity, tranquillity of mind, self-restraint, modesty, uprightness, and compassion toward all beings — these always perish in a man when overcome by darkness through arrogance; so say the good.

**1.85.23**  He who studies and fancies himself a scholar yet destroys the reputation of others through his learning — his worlds come to an end, and that sacred knowledge bears no fruit for him.

**1.85.24**  Four acts that should bring fearlessness bring fear instead when performed with arrogance: the agnihotra performed with arrogance, silence practiced with arrogance, learning undertaken with arrogance, and the sacrifice offered with arrogance.

**1.85.25**  One should not take joy when honoured, nor grieve when dishonoured; the good honour the good in this world — the wicked never attain the insight of the virtuous.

**1.85.26**  "Thus shall I give, thus shall I sacrifice, thus shall I study — this is my vow": in such attitude they speak of fearless deeds, yet these very things are to be avoided always when done from egotism.

**1.85.27**  Through that ancient refuge which the wise, devoted equally to honour and dishonour, come to know — attaining that supreme luminous form of the highest good, they reach perfect peace, both here and after death.

**1.86.1**  Aṣṭaka said: How does the householder, pursuing his duties, reach the gods? How does the mendicant? How does the teacher's pupil? And the forest-dweller established on the good path? Many things are now known about this.

**1.86.2**  Yayāti said: He who studies when called upon, who is diligent in the teacher's work without being prompted, who rises first and retires last, who is gentle, restrained, steadfast, and heedful, and devoted to personal study — such a brahmacharī attains success.

**1.86.3**  Having acquired wealth obtained by righteous means, one should sacrifice, give freely, and always feed guests; and one should not take what has not been given by others — this is the ancient secret teaching of the householder.

**1.86.4**  He who lives by his own exertion, who has turned away from sin, who gives to others without tormenting any being — such a sage, dwelling in the forest with regulated food and conduct, attains the highest success.

**1.86.5**  He who lives without a craft, perpetually without a home, with senses conquered, wholly freed from all bonds, who moves from one resting place to another, light and of few wants, wandering through lands alone — he is the true mendicant.

**1.86.6**  The night by which the worlds are won, by which desires are conquered and joys obtained — that very night the wise man, with a disciplined self, should strive to dwell in the forest.

**1.86.7**  Ten ancestors before him, ten relatives after, and himself as the twenty-first — the forest-dweller places them all in the realm of good deeds, releasing the constituent elements of his own body in the forest.

**1.86.8**  Aṣṭaka said: How many kinds of sages are there, and how many kinds of silence are there? Tell us this — we wish to hear.

**1.86.9**  Yayāti said: He for whom the village lies behind while dwelling in the forest, or for whom the forest lies behind while dwelling in the village — that man may be called a sage, O lord of the people.

**1.86.10**  Aṣṭaka said: How is it that when one dwells in the forest the village comes to lie behind, and how is it that when dwelling in the village the forest comes to lie behind?

**1.86.11**  Yayāti said: He who would be a forest-dwelling sage should not make use of village things; in that way, even while dwelling in the forest, the village comes to lie behind him.

**1.86.12**  Without fire, without a fixed dwelling, moving without clan affiliations, the sage should desire clothing only to the extent of a loincloth for covering.

**1.86.13**  He should desire food only to the extent of sustaining the vital breaths — in that way, even while dwelling in the village, the forest comes to lie behind him.

**1.86.14**  But the sage who abandons desires, who has given up action, whose senses are conquered, and who abides in silence — he attains perfection in this world.

**1.86.15**  With teeth washed, nails trimmed, always bathed and adorned, dark in complexion yet established in pure deeds — who would not be worthy to worship such a one?

**1.86.16**  Emaciated by austerity, lean, with flesh, bone, and blood wasted away — when the sage becomes free from the pairs of opposites and abides in silence, then, having conquered this world, he conquers the world beyond.

**1.86.17**  When the sage seeks his food with his mouth alone like a cow, then whatever was his former world becomes fit for immortality.

**1.87.1**  Aṣṭaka said: Which of these two first attains oneness with the gods, as they both race, O king, like the sun and the moon?

**1.87.2**  Yayāti said: The mendicant who is without a fixed home, who is restrained amid householders given over to desire, who dwells in the very village — he of the two has gone ahead.

**1.87.3**  He who has not attained a long life and yet has met with adversity should practise austerity; if he has done that and practises it, let him then proceed to other austerities beyond that.

**1.87.4**  What is cruel they call harmful; he who practises dharma with a mind set on what is not right — even he is without true self-mastery, O king; that uprightness is his concentration, that his nobility.

**1.87.5**  Aṣṭaka said: By whom were you sent as a messenger today, O king — young, garlanded, handsome, radiant? From where have you come, and in which direction are you? Or do you have a royal station?

**1.87.6**  Yayāti said: My merit exhausted, I have been scattered from the sky to enter this earthly hell; having spoken to you, I shall fall at once — the brahmins and the world-guardians urge me on.

**1.87.7**  My fall has been chosen in the presence of the good — they are all assembled here and endowed with virtue. This boon was obtained by me even from Indra — that I should fall upon the earth, O lord of men.

**1.87.8**  Aṣṭaka said: I ask you — do not fall in your fall; if there are worlds belonging to me here, whether stationed in the atmosphere or in the sky, take them — I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.

**1.87.9**  Yayāti said: As many as the cows and horses distributed over the earth, along with the forest animals and mountains — that many worlds of yours are established in the sky. Know it thus, O lion among lords of men.

**1.87.10**  Aṣṭaka said: I give you those worlds of mine — do not fall in your fall; whatever worlds of mine exist in the sky, whether stationed in the atmosphere or established in the heavens, mount them quickly, O destroyer of enemies.

**1.87.11**  Yayāti said: One like me who is not a brahmin, even if learned in the Vedas, does not engage in receiving gifts, O foremost among kings; as what should constantly be given to the twice-born, so did I formerly give, O lord of men.

**1.87.12**  A non-brahmin should never live a wretched life depending on others; likewise a brahmin woman who is the wife of a hero — I am such a one; what good would it be if I were to do what was never done before, when seeking to know the truth?

**1.87.13**  Pratardana said: I ask you, O one of desirable form — I am Pratardana; if there are worlds belonging to me, whether stationed in the atmosphere or established in the sky, I offer them; I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.

**1.87.14**  Yayāti said: Many worlds are yours, O lord of men; even individually they are seven times seven days each — dripping with honey, mixed with clarified butter, free from grief; those boundless worlds await you.

**1.87.15**  Pratardana said: I give you those worlds — do not fall in your fall; whatever worlds are mine, let them truly be yours; whether stationed in the atmosphere or established in the sky, mount them quickly, O one freed from delusion.

**1.87.16**  Yayāti said: One of equal splendour should not desire another's merits; being a king, O king, and meeting with adversity by the decree of fate, the wise man should not act cruelly — for a king should never do so.

**1.87.17**  Contemplating the path of righteousness and honour, a king should act with regard to dharma; one like me, who knows dharma in mind, knowing it, should not act so wretchedly as you describe.

**1.87.18**  I should do what is unprecedented, not done by others — what good is there in that when one is seeking to know the truth? As king Yayāti spoke thus, the most eminent of kings, Vasumanā, addressed him.

**1.88.1**  Vasumanā said: I ask you — I am Vasumanā, son of Rauśadaśva; if there is a world in the sky for me, O lord of men, whether spread through the atmosphere, O great-souled one, I offer it; I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.

**1.88.2**  Yayāti said: What the atmosphere, the earth, the directions, and the radiant sun illuminates with its brilliance — that many worlds are established in the sky for you; those boundless worlds await you.

**1.88.3**  Vasumanā said: I give you those worlds — do not fall in your fall; whatever worlds are mine, let them truly be yours; buy them even for a blade of grass, O king — if the act of receiving a gift is truly corrupted for you.

**1.88.4**  Yayāti said: I do not recall having made a false sale; I would not doubtfully take something obtained in vain from a child, nor would I do what was never done by others — what good is there in that when seeking to know?

**1.88.5**  Vasumanā said: Accept those worlds, O king, given by me; if the purchase is not to your liking, I shall not take them back, O lord of men — let all those worlds truly be yours.

**1.88.6**  Śibi said: I ask you — I am Śibi, son of Uśīnara; if there are worlds for me here as well, dear one, whether in the atmosphere or established in the sky, I offer them — I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.

**1.88.7**  Yayāti said: You, O wise one, have never slighted with word or even with heart those who sought your protection, O lord of men; therefore boundless worlds are established in the sky for you — vast, radiant as lightning, resonant with sound.

**1.88.8**  Śibi said: Accept those worlds, O king, given by me; if the purchase is not to your liking, I shall not take them back now having given them — go to those worlds which you worship, and dwell there.

**1.88.9**  Yayāti said: As you are equal in splendour to Indra, so too are your worlds boundless, O lord of men; yet I take no pleasure today in what has been given by another; therefore, O Śibi, I do not rejoice in the gift.

**1.88.10**  Aṣṭaka said: If you do not accept our worlds one by one, O king, then we shall all go to hell by giving them to you.

**1.88.11**  Yayāti said: Give what is worthy to one who is worthy — you who are good, by the virtue of truth and non-cruelty; but I do not dare to do what was never done by me before.

**1.88.12**  Aṣṭaka said: Whose are these five golden chariots that appear before us, standing high, gleaming, blazing like the flame of fire?

**1.88.13**  Yayāti said: These five golden chariots will carry you — standing high, gleaming, blazing like the flame of fire.

**1.88.14**  Aṣṭaka said: Mount the chariot, O king, stride forth through the sky; we too will follow when the time comes.

**1.88.15**  Yayāti said: Now all must go together — we who have won heaven; this pure, unsullied path to the abode of the gods lies visible before us.

**1.88.16**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: They all mounted the chariots and set forth, those most excellent of kings, ascending to heaven with their radiance, filling both heaven and earth with their dharma.

**1.88.17**  Aṣṭaka said: I think I alone am going ahead — and Indra is my great-souled friend in every way; but why has this Śibi, son of Uśīnara, alone surpassed all others with full speed in his vehicle?

**1.88.18**  Yayāti said: This son of Uśīnara gave to the divine path all the wealth he possessed; therefore Śibi is indeed the best among us.

**1.88.19**  Charity, austerity, truth, dharma, modesty, fortune, forgiveness, O gentle one, and endurance — O king, these virtues of that matchless king, of Śibi of non-cruelty in mind, stand firm. And because he is of such conduct and restrained by modesty — therefore Śibi has indeed surpassed all in his chariot.

**1.88.20**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Aṣṭaka questioned his maternal grandfather once more out of curiosity, that one equal to Indra: "I ask you, O king, tell me truly — from where are you, whose son are you, and whose are you? What you have done, no other doer of that deed exists — no other kṣatriya or brahmin in the world besides you."

**1.88.21**  Yayāti said: I am Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa; I was here as the universal emperor, father of Pūru; I tell you this hidden matter as my own — I am your maternal grandfather, now revealed to you.

**1.88.22**  I conquered all this earth and, having bound it as a package, I gave it to the brahmins; I gave consecrated horses, single-hoofed and well-formed; then the gods became sharers in the merit.

**1.88.23**  I gave the earth to the brahmins — this entire full earth — along with cattle as tribute, gold, and the finest riches; therein were ten billion cows.

**1.88.24**  By my truth, both the sky and the earth-bearing goddess stand firm, and fire blazes among human beings; not one word spoken by me has been in vain — for the good honour truth, as do all the gods, the sages, and the worlds; it is the thought of my mind that the worthy are honoured by truth.

**1.88.25**  Whoever, without envy, recounts to the foremost of the twice-born all of us who have won heaven, exactly as it happened — he shall attain the same world as ours.

**1.88.26**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus that great-souled king Yayāti, the destroyer of foes, was ferried across by his own grandsons. Having abandoned the earth, he whose deeds were supremely noble ascended to heaven, his karmas pervading the whole world.

**1.89.1**  Janamejaya said: Venerable one, I wish to hear about the kings who continued the line of Pūru — what valor they possessed, what manner of men they were, how many there were, and what their prowess.

**1.89.2**  For in this lineage there has never at any time been a king who was lacking in good character, or lacking in valor, or without progeny.

**1.89.3**  O wealth of austerity, I wish to hear in detail the deeds of those kings whose conduct was celebrated and who were endowed with discernment.

**1.89.4**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Well then, I shall tell you what you ask of me — the heroic upholders of Pūru's lineage, whose splendor rivaled that of Indra.

**1.89.5**  Pravīra, Īśvara, and Raudrāśva — three great chariot-warriors — were born to Pūru by Pauṣṭī; of them, Pravīra continued the line.

**1.89.6**  From him was born Manasyu, valiant son of Śyenī, a lord and protector of the earth to its four horizons, with eyes like lotus petals.

**1.89.7**  Subhrū, Saṃhana, and Vāgmī — three sons of Sauvīrī — were born to Manasyu; all were brave great chariot-warriors.

**1.89.8**  Raudrāśva's ten sons by an apsarā were great archers who performed sacrifices, born as brave men with abundant progeny and great learning; all were knowledgeable in every weapon, all were devoted to dharma.

**1.89.9**  They were Ṛcepu, Kakṣepu, the valiant Kṛkaṇepu, Sthaṇḍilepu, Vanepu, and Sthalepuṣa the great chariot-warrior.

**1.89.10**  Tejepu the powerful and wise, Satyepu of Indra-like valor, Dharmepu, Saṃnatepu — the tenth with the prowess of a god — these sons of Anādhṛṣṭi, dear one, all performed the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.

**1.89.11**  After them king Matināra, learned son of Carcepu, was born; O king, Matināra's four sons were of boundless valor: the great Taṃsu, a warrior surpassing even chariot-fighters, and Druhyu of unrivaled brilliance.

**1.89.12**  Of them, Taṃsu of great valor, bearing the Paurava lineage onward, won blazing glory and conquered the earth.

**1.89.13**  The valiant Taṃsu fathered a son named Ilina, and he too conquered this entire earth — foremost among conquerors.

**1.89.14**  O king, Ilina then fathered five sons on Rathaṃtarī — sons comparable to the five elements — headed by Duḥṣanta.

**1.89.15**  They were Duḥṣanta, Śūra, Bhīma, Prapūrva, and Vasu; of them the eldest became king — Duḥṣanta, O Janamejaya.

**1.89.16**  From Duḥṣanta was born Bharata, the wise king son of Śakuntalā; from him the great glory of the Bharata lineage spread wide.

**1.89.17**  Bharata fathered nine sons on three wives, but the king did not rejoice in them, saying, "They do not resemble me."

**1.89.18**  Then Bharata, who had performed great sacrifices, obtained through Bharadvāja a son named Bhumanyu, O Bhārata.

**1.89.19**  Then, knowing himself to be blessed with a son, the delight of the Pauravas consecrated Bhumanyu as crown prince, O best of the Bharatas.

**1.89.20**  Then for that great lord of the earth a son named Vitatha was born; thus Vitatha was the son of Bhumanyu.

**1.89.21**  Suhotra, Suhotā, Suhavi, and Suyaju — sons of Ṛcīka's daughter Puṣkariṇī — were born to Bhumanyu.

**1.89.22**  Of them the eldest, Suhotra, obtained sovereignty over kings of the earth; he performed many sacrifices including the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha.

**1.89.23**  Suhotra enjoyed all the earth girdled by the ocean, full of elephants, cattle, and horses, and teeming with many treasures.

**1.89.24**  The earth seemed to sink under his enormous weight, overflowing with elephants, horses, and chariots, and exceedingly crowded with people.

**1.89.25**  While king Suhotra ruled his subjects according to dharma, the earth was marked with hundreds of thousands of sacrificial stakes and altars; teeming with flourishing people and grain, it shone together with the gods.

**1.89.26**  O Bhārata, Aikṣvākī bore to Suhotra, lord of the earth, three sons: Ajamīḍha, Sumīḍha, and Purumīḍha.

**1.89.27**  Ajamīḍha was the best of them; in him the lineage was established. He in turn fathered six sons on three wives, O Bhārata.

**1.89.28**  Dhūminī bore Ṛkṣa; Nīlī bore Duḥṣanta and Parameṣṭhin; Keśinī bore Jahnu and both called Janarūpiṇau.

**1.89.29**  Thus all the Pāñcālas are descendants of Duḥṣanta and Parameṣṭhin, O king, and the Kuśikas are descendants of Jahnu of boundless splendor.

**1.89.30**  Of the two Janarūpiṇas, the elder Ṛkṣa is called the lord of the people; from Ṛkṣa was born Saṃvaraṇa, O king, the one who continued your lineage.

**1.89.31**  When Saṃvaraṇa son of Ṛkṣa, O king, was ruling the earth, there came about a very great destruction of the people — so we have heard.

**1.89.32**  The kingdom then broke apart through various calamities — struck by famine, death, drought, and disease — and the armies of their enemies assailed the Bharatas as well.

**1.89.33**  Shaking the very earth with his fourfold army, the Pāñcāla king came against him; having swiftly conquered the land, he defeated Saṃvaraṇa in battle with ten akṣauhiṇī armies.

**1.89.34**  Then king Saṃvaraṇa, together with his wives, ministers, sons, and friends, fled from there in great fear.

**1.89.35**  He then dwelt in a thicket on the bank of the great river Sindhu, at the edge of the river region near the mountains; the Bharatas lived there for a long time, having taken refuge in that difficult terrain.

**1.89.36**  After they had lived there for a thousand years, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha came to the Bharatas.

**1.89.37**  Going forth to meet him with great care and paying him homage, all the Bharatas then brought him the guest-offering of arghya, and with due reverence reported everything to the resplendent sage.

**1.89.38**  Having stayed with them for eight years, the king himself then requested him: "Be our purohita — we strive for the kingdom." "So be it" — with this, Vasiṣṭha agreed and accepted the Bharatas.

**1.89.39**  Then he consecrated the Paurava king to imperial sovereignty over all the kṣatriyas, as the foremost of all on earth — so we have heard.

**1.89.40**  He occupied that best of cities previously held by the Bharatas, and made all kings of the earth his tribute-bearers once more.

**1.89.41**  Then, having regained the earth, that mighty descendant of Ajamīḍha performed many great sacrifices with lavish fees.

**1.89.42**  Then Tapatī, daughter of the Sun, bore to Saṃvaraṇa a son named Kuru; all the subjects chose him as their king, calling him "the knower of dharma."

**1.89.43**  By his name the Kurujāṅgala region on earth became celebrated; the great ascetic made Kurukṣetra sacred through his austerities.

**1.89.44**  We have heard that his sons were Aśvavanta, Abhiṣvanta, Citraratha the sage, and the renowned Janamejaya; a noble woman bore these five sons born of the army.

**1.89.45**  From Abhiṣvata came Parikṣit; also born were the valiant Śabalāśva, Abhirāja, Virāja, and the mighty Śalmala.

**1.89.46**  Uccaiḥśravā, Bhadrakāra, and Jitāri the eighth — in the lineage of these men, their descendants became famous for virtues born of their deeds.

**1.89.47**  Janamejaya and six others, and likewise other mighty sons of Parikṣit — seven in all — were all skilled in dharma and artha.

**1.89.48**  They were named Kakṣasena, Ugrasena, the valiant Citrasena, Indrasena, Suṣeṇa, and Bhīmasena.

**1.89.49**  The mighty sons of Janamejaya, renowned on earth, were — Dhṛtarāṣṭra the firstborn, Pāṇḍu, and Bāhlīka.

**1.89.50**  Also Niṣadha of great splendor, the strong Jāmbūnada, Kuṇḍodara, Padāti, and Vasāti the eighth — all were skilled in dharma and artha, all devoted to the welfare of living beings.

**1.89.51**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra then became king; his sons were Kuṇḍika, Hastī, Vitarka, Krātha, Kuṇḍala the fifth, Haviḥśravā, Indrābha, Sumanyu, and Aparājita.

**1.89.52**  O bull of the Bharatas, three sons were born to Pratīpa: Devāpi, Śaṃtanu, and Bāhlīka the great chariot-warrior.

**1.89.53**  Of them, Devāpi retired to the forest in pursuit of dharma; Śaṃtanu obtained the earth, and Bāhlīka became a great chariot-warrior.

**1.89.54**  Many best of kings were born in Bharata's lineage, O king — great chariot-warriors of powerful nature, comparable to divine sages.

**1.89.55**  And likewise other great chariot-warriors comparable to gods were born in the lineage of Manu — those who augmented the Aila line.

**1.90.1**  Janamejaya said: O brahmin, I have heard from you the great origin of my ancestors, and I have now learned of the noble kings in this lineage.

**1.90.2**  But the pleasant narrative, being too brief in content, does not fully satisfy me — so please tell me again in greater detail.

**1.90.3**  This very divine story — the holy birth of those kings from Prajāpati down to Manu — whose heart would it not gladden?

**1.90.4**  Their fame, swelled by the greatness of good dharma and virtue, stands exalted, pervading all three worlds.

**1.90.5**  I am not sated hearing the tale of those endowed with virtue, splendor, valor, energy, strength, and zeal — a tale that tastes like nectar.

**1.90.6**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Listen, O king — hear fully what was properly heard by me from Dvaipāyana long ago, this auspicious account of the entire origin of your own lineage being now recounted.

**1.90.7**  From Dakṣa came Aditi; from Aditi came Vivasvat; from Vivasvat came Manu; from Manu came Ilā; from Ilā came Purūravas; from Purūravas came Āyu; from Āyu came Nahuṣa.

**1.90.8**  Yayāti had two wives: Devayānī, daughter of Uśanas, and Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvā. Here the genealogical succession continues.

**1.90.9**  Devayānī bore Yadu and Turvasu; Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvā, bore Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.

**1.90.10**  Of these, the Yādavas descend from Yadu, and the Pauravas from Pūru.

**1.90.11**  Pūru's wife was named Kausalyā; to her was born his son Janamejaya, who performed three Aśvamedha sacrifices and then, after performing the Viśvajit sacrifice, entered the forest.

**1.90.12**  Janamejaya married Anantā, a Mādhavī princess; to her was born his son Prācinvān, who conquered the eastern direction as far as the sunrise — hence his name Prācinvān.

**1.90.13**  Prācinvān married a princess of the Aśmaka people; to her was born his son Saṃyāti.

**1.90.14**  Saṃyāti married a daughter of Dṛṣadvata named Varāṅgī; to her was born his son Ahaṃpāti.

**1.90.15**  Ahaṃpāti married a daughter of Kṛtavīrya named Bhānumatī; to her was born his son Sārvabhauma.

**1.90.16**  Sārvabhauma carried off by conquest a Kaikeyī princess named Sunandā; to her was born his son Jayatsena.

**1.90.17**  Jayatsena married a Vidarbhā princess named Suṣuvā; to her was born his son Arācīna.

**1.90.18**  Arācīna also married another Vidarbhā princess named Maryādā; to her was born his son Mahābhauma.

**1.90.19**  Mahābhauma married a princess of Prasenajiṭ named Suyajñā; to her was born his son Ayutanāyī, who performed ten thousand Puruṣamedha sacrifices — hence his name Ayutanāyī.

**1.90.20**  Ayutanāyī married a daughter of Pṛthuśravas named Bhāsā; to her was born his son Akrodhana.

**1.90.21**  Akrodhana married a Kāliṅga princess named Karaṇḍu; to her was born his son Devātithi.

**1.90.22**  Devātithi married a Videha princess named Maryādā; to her was born his son Ṛca.

**1.90.23**  Ṛca married an Aṅga princess named Sudevā; to her he fathered a son named Ṛkṣa.

**1.90.24**  Ṛkṣa married a daughter of Takṣaka named Jvālā; to her he gave birth to a son named Matināra.

**1.90.25**  Matināra performed a twelve-year sacrificial session on the banks of the Sarasvatī.

**1.90.26**  When the sacrifice concluded, Sarasvatī herself approached and chose him as her husband; she bore him a son named Taṃsu.

**1.90.27**  Here a genealogical verse occurs.

**1.90.28**  Sarasvatī bore Taṃsu as a son to Matināra; Taṃsu in turn begot his own son Ilina upon Kālindī.

**1.90.29**  Ilina begot five sons on Rathaṃtarī, the eldest of whom was Duḥṣanta.

**1.90.30**  Duḥṣanta married Śakuntalā, the daughter of Viśvāmitra; she bore him Bharata. On this subject two verses are cited.

**1.90.31**  "The mother is but the vessel; the son belongs to his father — he who was begotten is himself the father's own. Acknowledge your son, Duḥṣanta; do not despise Śakuntalā."

**1.90.32**  "The seed-bearer raises his son up from the realm of Yama, O king; you are the maker of this child within the womb — Śakuntalā speaks the truth."

**1.90.33**  From that, his name Bharata is explained.

**1.90.34**  Bharata married Sunandā, called Sārvasenī, a princess of the Kāśī line; she bore him Bhumanyु.

**1.90.35**  Bhumanyु married Jayā, a princess of the Dāśārha line; she bore him Suhotra.

**1.90.36**  Suhotra married Suvarṇā, a princess of the Ikṣvāku line; she bore him Hastī, who founded this city of Hāstinapura — hence its name.

**1.90.37**  Hastī married Yaśodharā, a princess of the Trigarta line; she bore him Vikuṇṭhana.

**1.90.38**  Vikuṇṭhana married Sudevā, a princess of the Dāśārha line; she bore him Ajamīḍha.

**1.90.39**  Ajamīḍha had twenty-four hundred sons by Kaikeyī, Nāgā, Gāndhārī, Vimalā, and Ṛkṣā, each founding separate royal lines — and the chief line-founder among them was Saṃvaraṇa.

**1.90.40**  Saṃvaraṇa married Tapatī, the daughter of Vivasvat; she bore him Kuru.

**1.90.41**  Kuru married Śubhāṅgī, a princess of the Dāśārha line; she bore him Viḍūratha.

**1.90.42**  Viḍūratha married Saṃpriyā, a princess of Magadha; she bore him a son named Arugvān.

**1.90.43**  Arugvān married Amṛtā, a princess of Magadha; she bore him Parikṣit.

**1.90.44**  Parikṣit married Suyaśā, a princess of the Bāhuda line; she bore him Bhīmasena.

**1.90.45**  Bhīmasena married Sukumārī, a princess of Kekaya; she bore him Paryaśravā, who is known by the name Pratīpa.

**1.90.46**  Pratīpa married Sunandā, a princess of the Śibi clan; he fathered three sons upon her: Devāpi, Śaṃtanu, and Bāhlīka.

**1.90.47**  Devāpi entered the forest while still a boy; Śaṃtanu became the king of the earth. A genealogical verse follows here.

**1.90.48**  "Whomsoever he touches with his two hands, the aged one gains ease and becomes young again — therefore they call him Śaṃtanu."

**1.90.49**  That is the explanation of his name Śaṃtanu.

**1.90.50**  Śaṃtanu married the Bhāgīrathī — Gaṅgā herself; she bore him Devavrata, who is known as Bhīṣma.

**1.90.51**  Bhīṣma, desiring to please his father, gave away in marriage Satyavatī — the woman known as Gandhakālī — as his father's bride.

**1.90.52**  She had already conceived before marriage a son by Parāśara — Dvaipāyana; and upon her Śaṃtanu also fathered two sons, Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya.

**1.90.53**  Of the two, Citrāṅgada was slain by a Gandharva before reaching manhood; Vicitravīrya then became king.

**1.90.54**  Vicitravīrya married the two daughters of the king of Kāśī — Ambikā and Ambālikā, born of Kausalyā.

**1.90.55**  But Vicitravīrya passed away without leaving any offspring.

**1.90.56**  Then Satyavatī reflected: "The line of Duḥṣanta's descendant is about to be extinguished."

**1.90.57**  She thought of the sage Dvaipāyana.

**1.90.58**  He stood before her at once and said: "What shall I do?"

**1.90.59**  She said to him: "Your brother Vicitravīrya has gone to heaven leaving no offspring — please beget children upon his wives."

**1.90.60**  Agreeing with the word "so be it," he fathered three sons: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura.

**1.90.61**  There, to king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a hundred sons were born of Gāndhārī by the boon of Dvaipāyana.

**1.90.62**  Among Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, four were pre-eminent: Duryodhana, Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, and Citrasena.

**1.90.63**  Pāṇḍu had two wives — Kuntī and Mādrī — both jewels among women.

**1.90.64**  Now while Pāṇḍu was roaming on the hunt, he saw a sage engaged in intercourse with a doe; even as the sage was thus immersed, still unsatiated and not yet having tasted his desire's sweetness, Pāṇḍu struck him with an arrow.

**1.90.65**  Struck by the arrow, he spoke to Pāṇḍu: "You who call yourself a follower of dharma — because you, knowing better, have struck me down before I tasted the joy of love, you too shall meet this very fate: you shall pass away quickly, deprived of love's pleasure, in this very same condition."

**1.90.66**  Pāṇḍu, his color drained from his face, seeking to avoid the curse, did not approach his wives.

**1.90.67**  And he said: "Through my own rashness I have brought this upon myself; and I have heard that a man without offspring has no worlds hereafter."

**1.90.68**  He said to Kuntī: "Therefore you shall beget sons for my sake."

**1.90.69**  She then bore sons: Yudhiṣṭhira by Dharma, Bhīmasena by the Wind, and Arjuna by Indra.

**1.90.70**  Pāṇḍu said to Kuntī with a joyful countenance: "Your co-wife has no offspring — please arrange for a child to be born of her as well."

**1.90.71**  Kuntī agreed, saying "So be it."

**1.90.72**  Thereupon Nakula and Sahadeva were begotten upon Mādrī by the twin Aśvins.

**1.90.73**  Seeing Mādrī adorned and beautiful, Pāṇḍu was stirred with passion.

**1.90.74**  The very moment he touched her, he passed away.

**1.90.75**  There Mādrī ascended the funeral pyre where he lay.

**1.90.76**  She said to Kuntī: "The noble lady must raise the twins with unwavering care."

**1.90.77**  Then the five Pāṇḍavas, together with Kuntī, were brought to Hāstinapura by the forest ascetics and presented to Bhīṣma and Vidura.

**1.90.78**  There too an attempt was made to burn them in the lac-house, but it could not succeed owing to Vidura's counsel.

**1.90.79**  And having slain Hiḍimba along the way, they went to Ekacakrā.

**1.90.80**  There in Ekacakrā too, having slain the demon named Baka, they proceeded to the city of Pāñcāla.

**1.90.81**  From there they obtained Draupadī as their wife and returned safely to their own realm.

**1.90.82**  They also begot sons: Yudhiṣṭhira fathered Prativindhya, Vṛkodara fathered Sutasoma, Arjuna fathered Śrutakīrti, Nakula fathered Śatānīka, and Sahadeva fathered Śrutakarmā.

**1.90.83**  Yudhiṣṭhira also won at a svayaṃvara a maiden named Devikā, daughter of Govāsana of the Śibi clan, and fathered upon her a son named Yaudheya.

**1.90.84**  Bhīmasena also married Baladhārā, a princess of Kāśī, won by valor, and fathered upon her a son named Sarvaga.

**1.90.85**  Arjuna went to Dvāravatī and married Subhadrā, the sister of Vāsudeva; he fathered upon her a son named Abhimanyu.

**1.90.86**  Nakula married Kareṇuvatī, a princess of the Cedi, and fathered upon her a son named Niramitra.

**1.90.87**  Sahadeva also won at a svayaṃvara Vijayā, herself a Mādrī princess, and fathered upon her a son named Suhotra.

**1.90.88**  Bhīmasena had earlier also fathered upon the demoness Hiḍimbā a son named Ghaṭotkaca.

**1.90.89**  These then are the eleven sons of the Pāṇḍavas.

**1.90.90**  Abhimanyu married Uttarā, the daughter of Virāṭa; the child conceived in her womb was stillborn.

**1.90.91**  Pṛthā received that six-month foetus in her lap, at the command of the supreme Vāsudeva, saying: "I shall restore this one to life."

**1.90.92**  Having revived him, she declared: "Born when the family was brought to ruin, let this one be named Parīkṣit."

**1.90.93**  Parīkṣit married a princess named Mādravatī; she bore him Janamejaya.

**1.90.94**  From Janamejaya and Vapuṣṭamā were born two sons: Śatānīka and Śaṅku.

**1.90.95**  Śatānīka married a princess of Videha; she bore him a son named Aśvamedhadatta.

**1.90.96**  Thus the lineage of Pūru and of the Pāṇḍavas has been recounted; one who hears this line of Pūru is freed from all sins.

**1.91.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a king who sprang from the Ikṣvāku line, lord of the earth, renowned as Mahābhiṣa — truthful in speech and true in valor.

**1.91.2**  With a thousand aśvamedha sacrifices and a hundred vājapeya rites he pleased the lord of gods, Indra, and thereby that powerful king attained heaven.

**1.91.3**  On one occasion the gods assembled to attend upon Brahmā; among them were the royal sages, and king Mahābhiṣa was also present.

**1.91.4**  Then Gaṅgā, the foremost of rivers, came to approach the Grandfather; the wind blew aside her garment, white as moonlight.

**1.91.5**  Thereupon all the hosts of gods suddenly cast their eyes downward — but the royal sage Mahābhiṣa gazed upon the river without hesitation or shame.

**1.91.6**  Mahābhiṣa was censured by the venerable Brahmā, and was told: "You shall be born again among mortals, and then win back these worlds."

**1.91.7**  That king, having reflected among all the ascetic kings, chose Pratīpa — a man of great splendor — as the father he wished to be born from.

**1.91.8**  The best of rivers, seeing that king Mahābhiṣa fall from his composure, turned her mind and heart upon him alone.

**1.91.9**  While going along the path she beheld the Vasus, those celestial gods, their forms wasted away and their vigour crushed by affliction.

**1.91.10**  Seeing them in such a state, the foremost of rivers asked: "Why have your forms thus perished? Are the dwellers of heaven well?"

**1.91.11**  The Vasus, the gods, replied to her: "O great river, we have been cursed by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha in a fit of rage for a trivial offence."

**1.91.12**  "For we all, heedless, once walked right past the foremost of sages, Vasiṣṭha, who was seated in twilight meditation in an unobtrusive spot."

**1.91.13**  "In his anger he cursed us to be born in a womb. What the knower of Brahman has spoken cannot be otherwise undone."

**1.91.14**  "Therefore you, becoming a mortal woman, bear us as sons upon the earth; for we cannot enter the inauspicious womb of ordinary mortal women."

**1.91.15**  Thus addressed, Gaṅgā said "so be it" to those Vasus and then asked: "Who among mortals will be the best of men to act as your father?"

**1.91.16**  The Vasus replied: "The righteous king named Śaṃtanu, son of Pratīpa, will exist in the mortal world; he shall be our father."

**1.91.17**  Gaṅgā said: "O gods of unblemished honour, my mind also agrees with what you have said. I will do what is pleasing to him, and this is your wish as well."

**1.91.18**  The Vasus said: "You should cast our newborn sons into the water, so that our release from the curse may come swiftly, O you who flow through the three worlds."

**1.91.19**  Gaṅgā said: "I will do this. Let there be provided for him a son; his union with me should not be fruitless, for he desires a son."

**1.91.20**  The Vasus said: "Each of us will contribute an eighth part of our own valour; with that valour your son — and his desired heir — will be born."

**1.91.21**  "That son of yours will never beget offspring among mortals; thus he will be without children of his own, though he will be mighty in valour."

**1.91.22**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus made this compact with Gaṅgā, the Vasus departed with joyful hearts, their purpose fulfilled exactly as they had intended.

**1.92.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then that king Pratīpa, devoted to the welfare of all beings, sat for many years on the bank of the Gaṅgā, engaged in prayer.

**1.92.2**  To him came Gaṅgā, endowed with beauty and virtues, like the goddess Śrī made manifest, rising from the water in a form most enchanting to behold.

**1.92.3**  She of divine form and noble spirit, her face radiant as the moon, seated herself on the right thigh of the royal sage as he sat in study, that thigh like the trunk of a śāla tree.

**1.92.4**  The sovereign Pratīpa then spoke to that noble-minded woman: "What may I do for you, fair one? What is it that you desire?"

**1.92.5**  The woman said: "O king, foremost of the Kurus, I desire you — accept me. For the rejection of women who offer themselves in love is condemned by the good."

**1.92.6**  Pratīpa replied: "O lady of excellent complexion, I would not out of desire go to another man's wife, nor to a woman of different caste, O fair one — know this as my sacred vow."

**1.92.7**  The woman said: "I am not unworthy, nor am I one to be avoided or rebuked at any time. Accept me, O king — a maiden, the finest of women, who offers herself to you."

**1.92.8**  Pratīpa replied: "What you urge upon me would overstep the bounds for me. Were I to act otherwise than I have vowed, the violation of dharma would be my ruin."

**1.92.9**  "You have come and seated yourself on my right thigh, O beautiful-limbed one. Know, O timid one, that this is the seat reserved for children and daughters-in-law."

**1.92.10**  "The left side is the place of a beloved wife, but you have not taken that seat. Therefore I shall not engage with you in desire, O beautiful-limbed one."

**1.92.11**  "Become my daughter-in-law, fair one — I choose you for the sake of my son; for you came and took your place on the side belonging to a daughter-in-law, O slender-thighed."

**1.92.12**  The woman said: "So be it then, O knower of dharma — I will be united with your son. Out of devotion to you I will honour the renowned lineage of the Bhāratas."

**1.92.13**  "Among all the rulers of the earth, you are the supreme refuge. Even in a hundred years I could not fully describe the virtues of this line — that peerless excellence which has proceeded from you all."

**1.92.14**  "Your son must not question my lineage, O lord, nor must he ever question whatever I may do — your son should never inquire into any of this."

**1.92.15**  "Dwelling thus with your son, I will bring him joy; and through virtuous, beloved sons your son will attain heaven."

**1.92.16**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said "so be it," she vanished on the spot. The king, expecting the birth of a son, kept her words in his heart.

**1.92.17**  At this very time, O joy of the Kurus, the bull among kṣatriyas, Pratīpa, practised austerities together with his wife for the sake of a son.

**1.92.18**  To that aged pair was born a son — he was Mahābhiṣa; from Śānta was born Saṃtāna, and from him came Śaṃtanu.

**1.92.19**  Constantly remembering the imperishable worlds won by his own deeds in a former life, Śaṃtanu was ever a doer of righteous deeds, O best of Kurus.

**1.92.20**  Then Pratīpa instructed his son Śaṃtanu when he came of age: "Formerly a woman came to me, O Śaṃtanu, for your welfare."

**1.92.21**  "If that woman of lovely complexion — a divine woman full of beauty and desire, seeking a son — comes to you in private, O son, you must not ask her who she is or to whom she belongs."

**1.92.22**  "Whatever she may do that you think should not be done, you must not question her. By my command, honour her who offers herself to you" — so he instructed him.

**1.92.23**  Having thus instructed his son Śaṃtanu, and having consecrated him in his own kingdom, the king Pratīpa then entered the forest.

**1.92.24**  That wise king Śaṃtanu, renowned throughout the earth as a wielder of the bow, became fond of hunting and constantly ranged through the forests.

**1.92.25**  Slaying deer and buffaloes, that best of kings roamed alone along the Gaṅgā, that river frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas.

**1.92.26**  One day, O great king, he beheld a supremely beautiful woman, blazing in her form like the goddess Śrī herself standing before him.

**1.92.27**  She was flawless in every limb, with fine teeth, adorned with divine ornaments, wearing fine garments, standing alone, her radiance equal to the interior of a lotus.

**1.92.28**  Beholding her, the lord of men was filled with delight, his hair standing on end; marvelling at the perfection of her beauty, drinking her in with his eyes, he could not be satisfied.

**1.92.29**  And she too, having seen the king of great splendour as he wandered there, felt affection and tenderness stir within her, and the graceful one could not be satisfied.

**1.92.30**  Then the king spoke to her, addressing her with gentle, soothing words: "Are you a goddess, or a dānavī, a gandharvī, or an apsarā?"

**1.92.31**  "Or a yakṣī, or a nāgakanyā, or a mortal woman, O slender-waisted? Whoever you may be, O radiant as the womb of the gods, become my wife, O beautiful one."

**1.92.32**  Hearing the king's words, soft, gentle, and sweet, that blameless one, remembering the compact of the Vasus, approached him with a smile.

**1.92.33**  And she spoke words that gladdened the king's heart: "I will become your queen, O ruler of the earth, obedient to your will."

**1.92.34**  "But whatever I may do, O king, whether it seems good or ill, I must not be restrained, nor must anything disagreeable be said to me regarding it."

**1.92.35**  "As long as things proceed thus between us, I will dwell with you, O king; but if I am restrained or spoken to disagreeably, I will assuredly leave you."

**1.92.36**  When the king said "so be it," O best of the Bhāratas, she experienced matchless joy upon obtaining that best of kings.

**1.92.37**  Having obtained her, the self-controlled Śaṃtanu enjoyed her as he desired, thinking "she is not to be questioned" — he said nothing at all to her.

**1.92.38**  The lord of the earth was fully pleased by her conduct and character, by her beauty, generosity, and virtues, and by her devoted attentiveness in private.

**1.92.39**  For she, the goddess Gaṅgā, the river flowing through the three paths, that woman of excellent complexion, had assumed a beautiful human form.

**1.92.40**  She had come and presented herself as a wife to Śaṃtanu, that lion among kings, equal in splendour to the king of the gods, whose desire had thus been brought to him by fortune.

**1.92.41**  She delighted the king with loving pleasures and clever arts, with charming coquetry and grace; and as she rejoiced, so did he.

**1.92.42**  The king, absorbed in love and captivated by the qualities of that most excellent of women, did not notice the many years, seasons, and months that passed.

**1.92.43**  Sporting with her as he wished, the lord of men fathered upon her eight sons, each of them radiant as the immortals.

**1.92.44**  Each son as he was born she would cast into the water, O Bhārata, saying "I am gratifying you" as she plunged him into the current of the Gaṅgā.

**1.92.45**  This was not pleasing to king Śaṃtanu, yet the lord of the earth said nothing to her, fearing that she would leave him.

**1.92.46**  But when the eighth son was born, as she made as if to laugh, the king, tormented with grief, spoke to her, longing to keep a son for himself.

**1.92.47**  "Do not kill him! Who are you? Whose are you? Why do you harm your sons? O murderer of children, do not incur so great a sin — stop, O infamous one!"

**1.92.48**  The woman said: "O you who desire a son, best of those who have sons, I am not killing your son. But this agreement I made has now run its course, just as a garment wears out."

**1.92.49**  "I am Gaṅgā, daughter of Jahnu, attended upon by hosts of great sages. I have dwelt with you for the accomplishment of a divine purpose."

**1.92.50**  "These eight are the great and mighty Vasus, the gods; through the fault of Vasiṣṭha's curse they took on human birth."

**1.92.51**  "There is no father for them on earth other than you, nor is there any mortal woman like me who could serve as their mother."

**1.92.52**  "Therefore I took on human form for the purpose of bearing them. By fathering eight Vasus, imperishable worlds have been won by you."

**1.92.53**  "This was the compact of the gods, the Vasus, which was made known to me: 'You shall release each one as he is born from his human birth.'"

**1.92.54**  "Those Vasus have been released from the curse of the great-souled Āpava. Farewell to you — I will depart. Guard this son; he is a keeper of great vows."

**1.92.55**  "This stay with you was arranged in the presence of the Vasus as part of their plan. Know this son, born of me, as Gaṅgādatta — given by Gaṅgā."

**1.93.1**  Śaṃtanu said: "Who indeed is this one called Āpava? And what was the misdeeds of the Vasus, by whose curse they all came to take on a human body?"

**1.93.2**  "And what has been done by this boy, Gaṅgādatta, on account of whose deed he will remain dwelling among mortals?"

**1.93.3**  "Those Vasus who are lords of all the worlds — how did they come to be born among mortals? Tell me this, O daughter of Jahnu."

**1.93.4**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Gaṅgā, the goddess, daughter of Jahnu, then spoke these words to the king, her husband, Śaṃtanu, that bull among men.

**1.93.5**  "The sage named Vasiṣṭha, who was obtained as a son by Varuṇa long ago, O best of the Bhāratas — that sage is also known by the name Āpava."

**1.93.6**  "His holy hermitage, filled with herds of deer and flocks of birds, lies on the flank of Meru, king of mountains, covered with flowers of every season."

**1.93.7**  "There that son of Varuṇa, best among doers of virtuous deeds, performed austerities in that forest, O best of the Bhāratas, which abounded in sweet roots, fruits, and water."

**1.93.8**  "The daughter of Dakṣa, known as Surabhi, exceedingly glorious — that goddess gave birth to a cow from Kaśyapa, O bull of the Bhāratas."

**1.93.9**  "For the benefit of the world that righteous-souled son of Varuṇa received that excellent wish-fulfilling cow, fit to be a sacrificial cow."

**1.93.10**  "That cow, dwelling in that forest of ascetics frequented by sages, wandered freely through the pleasant and sacred woodland, fearless."

**1.93.11**  "Then one day, O bull of the Bhāratas, all the Vasus, with Pṛthu at their head, came to that forest, which was frequented by gods and divine sages."

**1.93.12**  Those Vasus, together with their wives, roamed that forest in all directions and took delight in its charming mountains and woodland groves.

**1.93.13**  There, O hero rivalling Indra, the wife of one of those Vasus—a slender-waisted lady wandering in that forest—caught sight of the cow that was the wish-fulfilling gem of the sage Vasishtha, supreme among all desire-yielding kine.

**1.93.14**  Filled with wonder at the cow's wealth of virtue and beauty, she pointed her out to her husband Dyaus, O bull-eyed one.

**1.93.15**  The cow was deep-uddered, gave milk freely, had a fine tail and a beautiful face, was endowed with every good quality, and possessed a character utterly without equal.

**1.93.16**  The daughter of a Vasu, O lord of kings, O delight of the Pauravas, pointed out that cow, thus endowed with all these qualities, to her husband the Vasu Dyaus long ago.

**1.93.17**  Dyaus, upon seeing that cow, O king, mighty as the lord of elephants, spoke to his goddess-wife, describing the cow's beauty and virtues.

**1.93.18**  "This, O goddess, O dark-eyed one, O fair-hipped lady, is the supreme cow of Varuni's son—that very sage whose this excellent forest is."

**1.93.19**  "Whoever among mortals drinks the sweet milk of this cow, O slender-waisted one, shall live for ten thousand years with unfading youth."

**1.93.20**  Hearing this, O best of kings, that slender-waisted, flawlessly-limbed goddess spoke to her blazingly radiant husband:

**1.93.21**  "In the world of mortals I have a friend, a princess—her name is Jinavati, adorned with beauty and the bloom of youth."

**1.93.22**  "She is the daughter of the royal sage Ushinarathe truthful and wise—and she is renowned throughout the mortal world for the wealth of her beauty."

**1.93.23**  "For her sake, O greatly fortunate one, O best of the immortals, O increaser of merit, quickly bring me this cow along with her calf—she is what I desire."

**1.93.24**  "So that my friend, drinking this cow's milk, may be the one among mortals who is free from old age and disease, O giver of honour."

**1.93.25**  "You, O greatly fortunate one, O blameless one, must do this favour for me, for there is nothing dearer to me than this—nothing at all."

**1.93.26**  Hearing these words of his goddess-wife and wishing to please her, Dyaus then stole that cow together with his brothers led by Prithva.

**1.93.27**  Impelled by that lotus-eyed goddess, Dyaus, O king, was unable to face the fierce austerities of that sage; he stole the cow then and there, and the fall that would follow was not foreseen.

**1.93.28**  Then Vasishtha, son of Varuna, returned to his hermitage bearing fruits, but he did not see the cow with her calf anywhere in that excellent forest.

**1.93.29**  That sage, rich in austerities and of noble intellect, searched for her throughout that forest, yet searching he could not find the cow.

**1.93.30**  Knowing by his divine sight that she had been carried off by the Vasus, he immediately fell under the sway of anger and then cursed those Vasus.

**1.93.31**  "Since the Vasus have stolen my milch-cow with her fine tail, therefore all of them shall without doubt be born among mortals."

**1.93.32**  Thus did the venerable Apava, best of sages, having come under the power of wrath, curse those Vasus, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.93.33**  Having cursed them, that greatly fortunate one turned his mind once again to his austerities. Thus, O king, did that sage of mighty power—that brahmarishi, rich in penance—curse all eight Vasus while filled with wrath against those gods.

**1.93.34**  Then, coming again to that hermitage of the great-souled sage, the Vasus—knowing they had been cursed—approached that rishi.

**1.93.35**  Though the Vasus sought to propitiate that sage, O bull of kings, they could not obtain grace from that best of rishis—from Apava, O tiger among men, who was versed in all the ways of dharma.

**1.93.36**  And that righteous-souled sage said: "Seven of you—Dhara and the rest—will obtain release from the curse within a year."

**1.93.37**  "But this one—Dyaus—on whose account you were cursed by me, shall dwell for a long time in the world of mortals, reaping the fruit of his own deed."

**1.93.38**  "I do not wish to make false what I spoke to you in anger. Yet this high-minded one shall also beget no offspring among mortals."

**1.93.39**  "He shall be righteous-souled, versed in all the scriptures, devoted to what is dear and beneficial to his father, and he shall abstain from the enjoyment of women." Having spoken thus to all the Vasus, the venerable sage departed.

**1.93.40**  Thereupon all those Vasus came to me, O king, and begged a boon of me, and that boon I granted them: "As each of us is born, O Ganga, cast us yourself into the water."

**1.93.41**  Thus, O best of kings, I duly did what was proper for the sake of releasing those who had been cursed—freeing them from the world of mortals.

**1.93.42**  This one alone, O best of kings, O Bharata—Dyaus—shall dwell long in the world of mortals because of that sage's curse.

**1.93.43**  Having narrated all this, the goddess vanished from that very spot; and taking that prince with her, she departed as she wished.

**1.93.44**  That son of Shantanu bore two names—Devavrata and Gangeyaand he surpassed even Shantanu in virtues.

**1.93.45**  And Shantanu, stricken with grief, then returned to his own city. I shall now recount the boundless virtues of Shantanu.

**1.93.46**  And the great good fortune of that glorious Bharata king—the resplendent history of whom is called the Mahabharata.

**1.94.1**  Vaishampayana said: That wise Shantanu—honoured by gods, kings, and sages—was celebrated in all worlds as righteous-souled and true of speech.

**1.94.2**  Self-restraint, generosity, forbearance, wisdom, modesty, steadfastness, and surpassing splendour—these were ever-present in the great-souled Shantanu, bull among men.

**1.94.3**  So endowed with virtues, skilled in dharma and statecraft, that king was the protector of the Bharata lineage and of righteous people.

**1.94.4**  He had a conch-like neck, broad shoulders, and the gait of a lordly rutting elephant; he held firmly to the conviction that dharma stands supreme above desire and material gain.

**1.94.5**  All these qualities dwelt in the great-souled Shantanu, O bull of the Bharatas, and no other kshatriya was his equal in righteousness.

**1.94.6**  Because he abided in his own dharma and was the foremost of all who know dharma, the kings of the earth consecrated him as sovereign over kings.

**1.94.7**  Free from grief, fear, and affliction, waking from pleasant slumber, the kings of the earth rallied to him as protector of the Bharatas.

**1.94.8**  When the world was protected by kings with Shantanu at their head, then by rule the order of all the varnas prevailed with brahminical excellence at the fore.

**1.94.9**  The brahmin order attended upon the kshatriyas; the vaishyas followed the kshatriyas dutifully; and the shudras, devoted to both brahmin and kshatriya, attended upon the vaishyas.

**1.94.10**  Dwelling in lovely Hastinapura, the stronghold of the Kurus, he ruled the earth all the way to the ocean's edge.

**1.94.11**  Comparable to the king of gods, he was a knower of dharma, true of speech, upright of conduct, and endowed with supreme royal glory through the practice of giving, righteousness, and austerity.

**1.94.12**  Free from passion and hatred, he was pleasant to behold as the moon; in splendour he resembled the sun; in swiftness he equalled the wind; in wrath he was like Death himself; and in forbearance he was equal to the earth.

**1.94.13**  When Shantanu was the guardian of the earth, O king, there was no wanton slaughter of cattle, boars, deer, or birds.

**1.94.14**  In a realm where dharma and brahminical order stood supreme, the humble-souled Shantanu ruled all beings equally, free from desire and passion.

**1.94.15**  Rituals were then performed for the sake of gods, sages, and ancestors, and no living creature was slain contrary to dharma.

**1.94.16**  For the unhappy, the unprotected, and those dwelling in animal births—that king became the father of all beings.

**1.94.17**  While that best of Kuru lords, that sovereign of kings, reigned, speech was wedded to truth and the mind rested upon the dharma of giving.

**1.94.18**  For sixteen years, then eight, then four, then eight more—finding no pleasure in women—he roamed the forests.

**1.94.19**  Of such a form, such conduct, such behaviour, and such learning was his son by Ganga—named Devavrata, also called Vasu.

**1.94.20**  Deeply versed in all weapons, both divine and earthly, he was a man of great strength, great fortitude, great valour, and a mighty chariot-warrior.

**1.94.21**  Once, having shot a deer and following the river, king Shantanu saw the Bhagirathi—the Ganga—low in her waters.

**1.94.22**  Seeing this, Shantanu, bull among men, wondered: "Why does this best of rivers not flow today as she did of old?"

**1.94.23**  Then, searching for the cause, that high-minded one beheld a youth—handsome of form, tall, and beautiful to behold.

**1.94.24**  He was wielding divine weapons like the god Indra himself, standing there having covered the whole Ganga with sharp arrows.

**1.94.25**  Seeing the river Ganga thus covered with arrows nearby, the king was filled with astonishment, beholding an act surpassing human capacity.

**1.94.26**  Though Shantanu had seen that son immediately at birth long ago, the wise king could not now recall enough to recognise him as his own child.

**1.94.27**  But that youth, seeing his father, cast a spell of bewilderment upon him with his magic, and having bewildered him, vanished from that very spot.

**1.94.28**  Having witnessed that wonder, king Shantanu, suspecting this to be his son, called out to Ganga: "Show him to me!"

**1.94.29**  Then Ganga, wearing her most beautiful form, showed him that adorned youth, taking him by the right hand.

**1.94.30**  Though Shantanu had seen her before, he did not recognise that faithful one, adorned with jewels and wearing spotless garments.

**1.94.31**  Ganga said: "The eighth son whom you once begat upon me, O king—this is he, O tiger among men. Take him home with you."

**1.94.32**  "He has mastered the Vedas with all their ancillary texts under Vasishtha himself; skilled in arms, an incomparable archer, he equals the king of gods in battle."

**1.94.33**  "He is ever honoured by both gods and demons, O Bharata; whatever scripture Ushanas knows, this one knows it all and completely."

**1.94.34**  "Likewise, the son of Angiras—Brihaspati, adored by gods and demons alike—whatever scripture he knows, all of that too is established fully in this mighty-armed, great-souled son of yours, with every supplement and sub-division."

**1.94.35**  "The mighty sage Rama Jamadagnya, invincible by any foe—whatever weapon-lore he knows, that too is established in this son of yours."

**1.94.36**  "This great archer, skilled in the laws and aims of kingship, O king—this, my own son, a hero—I give to you; O hero, take him home."

**1.94.37**  Vaishampayana said: Thus sent off by her, Shantanu, taking his son who shone like the sun, set out toward his own city.

**1.94.38**  That scion of Puru, arriving at his own city—rivalling the city of Indra, abundant in every desired object—considered himself fulfilled, and then installed his son as crown prince among the Pauravas.

**1.94.39**  The greatly renowned son of Shantanu delighted the Pauravas, his father, and the kingdom by his conduct, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.94.40**  That king of boundless valour thus spent four years rejoicing together with his son.

**1.94.41**  Once, the king went to a forest near the river Yamuna, where he inhaled an indescribably excellent fragrance.

**1.94.42**  Seeking its source, he wandered in all directions and then saw a girl belonging to the fishermen's clan, beautiful as a goddess.

**1.94.43**  Having seen her, he asked that dark-eyed maiden: "Whose daughter are you? Who are you? And what do you intend to do, O timid one?"

**1.94.44**  She replied: "I am the daughter of a fisherman; by my father's command—the great-souled chief of the fishermen, blessings upon you—I ferry people across for the sake of dharma and livelihood."

**1.94.45**  Gazing upon her—endowed with beauty, sweetness, and fragrance, radiant as a goddess—king Shantanu desired that daughter of the fisherman.

**1.94.46**  He went to her father and sought her hand, then questioned her father about his own purposes and conditions.

**1.94.47**  The fisher-king replied to that lord of the earth: "This fair-complexioned girl is mine to give in marriage the moment she is asked; but there is a certain wish in my heart — hear it, O lord of men."

**1.94.48**  "If you desire this girl as your lawful wife, O sinless one, you are known as a speaker of truth — therefore make a solemn compact with me in truth."

**1.94.49**  "Upon a pledge I will give you this maiden, O king; for no bridegroom equal to you shall ever come to me again."

**1.94.50**  Śantanu said: "Having heard your condition, O fisher-man, I will consider whether I can grant it or not. What can be given I will give; what cannot be given I will never give under any circumstances."

**1.94.51**  The fisherman said: "Whatever son is born of her shall be consecrated king and lord of the earth after you — no other, O king."

**1.94.52**  Vaiśampāyana said: Śantanu did not wish to grant that boon to the fisherman, O Bhārata, even though he burned intensely with desire born of the body.

**1.94.53**  That great king, dwelling only in thought on the fisher's daughter, returned to Hāstinapura with his mind struck by grief.

**1.94.54**  Then one day his son Devavrata, approaching his father who was grieving and sunk in brooding thought, spoke these words to him.

**1.94.55**  "All the kings of the earth are subject to your welfare; for what reason then do you grieve here constantly, O sorrowful one? And why, as if lost in meditation, do you say nothing at all, O king?"

**1.94.56**  Thus addressed by his son, Śantanu replied: "Without doubt I am indeed absorbed in brooding, just as you say."

**1.94.57**  "In this great lineage, you alone are our offspring, O Bhārata; and mortal men are impermanent — for this reason I grieve, my son."

**1.94.58**  "Should any misfortune befall you, O son of the Ganges, our lineage is extinct; you alone, without doubt, are worth a hundred sons."

**1.94.59**  "Nor am I willing to take a wife again without purpose; yet for the preservation of the lineage I desire it — may it go well with you. Those who speak of dharma call having only one son the same as being sonless."

**1.94.60**  "The agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, and all the yajñas together with their dakṣiṇās — all these do not equal a sixteenth part of the merit of having offspring."

**1.94.61**  "So it is likewise among men and among all creatures — this is the eternal triad of the ancients and of the best: that offspring is supreme. In this, O greatly wise one, I have no doubt."

**1.94.62**  "And you are a hero, ever proud, ever engaged with weapons, O Bhārata; your death, O sinless one, can come from nowhere other than a weapon."

**1.94.63**  "Thus I am fallen into doubt: should you be at peace, how will it be? I have told you in full, my dear son, the entire cause of my grief."

**1.94.64**  Then, having learned the entire cause in full, Devavrata of great intelligence departed, pondering it deeply.

**1.94.65**  He went quickly to seek the aged minister who was loyal to his father, and approaching him, inquired about the cause of his father's grief.

**1.94.66**  To that chief of the Kurus who asked him properly, the minister recounted in full the boon demanded, naming the maiden in question, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.94.67**  Then Devavrata, accompanied by senior Kṣatriyas, went himself to the fisher-king and sought the maiden on behalf of his father.

**1.94.68**  The fisherman received him according to due rite and honored him, then spoke to him as he sat in the royal assembly, O Bhārata.

**1.94.69**  "You alone are a sufficient guardian for Śantanu, O bull among men; you are the best son among those who have sons — what then shall I say to you?"

**1.94.70**  For who would not grieve upon passing up such a praiseworthy and desirable alliance — this very union — even Indra himself, the performer of a hundred sacrifices?

**1.94.71**  Moreover, this is the offspring of a noble one who is your equal in virtues — from whose seed the illustrious Satyavati was born.

**1.94.72**  By him, dear child, your father has been repeatedly praised; he is worthy of marrying Satyavati among all the kings, O Bharata.

**1.94.73**  Even the divine sage Asita was once refused by me; that foremost of sages had ardently sought Satyavati.

**1.94.74**  But as her father I must speak a little, O bull of the Bharatas: I see only one powerful flaw here — the matter of a rival stepmother.

**1.94.75**  For if you were the rival of anyone — be he a gandharva or an asura — he could never live happily when you are angered, O scorcher of foes.

**1.94.76**  This is the only flaw here; there is no other, O prince. Know this well — good fortune to you — in the matter of giving and receiving, O scorcher of foes.

**1.94.77**  Thus addressed, the son of Ganga replied fittingly, in the hearing of the assembled kings, for his father's sake, O Bharata.

**1.94.78**  "Accept this resolve of mine as true, O best among those who speak truth: neither one born nor yet to be born would dare to speak such words as these."

**1.94.79**  "I will do exactly as you say: whatever son is born of her shall be our king."

**1.94.80**  When he had said this, the fisherman chief spoke to him again, seeking to accomplish a difficult act regarding the kingship, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.94.81**  "You alone are the fitting lord of the immeasurably glorious Shantanu, O righteous soul, and you are the master capable of giving away the maiden."

**1.94.82**  "But hear this word of mine and this matter too, O gentle one; I shall speak it in the manner of those who guard maidens, O subduer of foes."

**1.94.83**  "What you have pledged in the assembly of kings for the sake of Satyavati, O you devoted to truth and righteousness, that is entirely fitting for you."

**1.94.84**  "It cannot be otherwise, O mighty-armed one; there is no doubt about that. But as for offspring that might be born of you — there our doubt is great."

**1.94.85**  Knowing that to be his concern, the one devoted to truth and righteousness then pledged anew, O king, wishing to do what was dear to his father.

**1.94.86**  Devavrata said: "O king of fishermen, O foremost of lords, hear this word of mine which I now speak for my father's sake in the hearing of these assembled kings."

**1.94.87**  "The kingdom I have already renounced before, O lord of men; and now, for the sake of offspring as well, I make this firm resolve."

**1.94.88**  "From this day forward, O fisherman, I shall live in perpetual celibacy; even without a son, imperishable worlds in heaven shall be mine."

**1.94.89**  Vaishampayana said: Hearing these words, his body-hair standing erect with joy, the righteous fisherman replied to him: "I give her."

**1.94.90**  Then the apsaras in the sky, the gods, and the hosts of sages together rained down flowers and cried out: "This one is Bhishma — the Terrible One!"

**1.94.91**  Then, for his father's sake, he said to that illustrious woman: "Mount the chariot, mother; let us go to our own home."

**1.94.92**  Having said this, Bhishma helped that noble lady onto the chariot, came to Hastinapura, and presented her to Shantanu.

**1.94.93**  Kings both assembled together and separately praised that difficult deed of his, and cried out: "This one is Bhishma — the Terrible One!"

**1.94.94**  Seeing that difficult deed done by Bhishma, his father Shantanu, well pleased, himself granted him the boon of death at will.

**1.95.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: After the marriage was concluded, King Śantanu installed that maiden of surpassing beauty in his own home.

**1.95.2**  Then the wise son of Śantanu was born of Satyavatī — the hero named Citrāṅgada, who surpassed all men in valour.

**1.95.3**  Then again the mighty lord begot upon Satyavatī another great archer, Prince Vicitravīrya.

**1.95.4**  While Vicitravīrya had not yet reached youth, O bull of the Bharatas, the wise King Śantanu submitted to the law of time and passed away.

**1.95.5**  With Śantanu gone to heaven, Bhīṣma, abiding by Satyavatī's counsel, established the enemy-taming Citrāṅgada upon the throne.

**1.95.6**  But Citrāṅgada, through his valour, held all other kings in contempt; he considered no human being his equal.

**1.95.7**  As he was thus scorning gods, men, and asuras alike, a powerful Gandharva king bearing the same name came against him; and a mighty battle between them took place on the field of Kurukṣetra.

**1.95.8**  Between those two powerful ones — the Gandharva chief and the chief of the Kurus — the battle raged for three years on the bank of the river Hiraṇvatī.

**1.95.9**  In that tumultuous clash, thick with a rain of weapons, the Gandharva, superior in magical power, slew the foremost of the Kurus.

**1.95.10**  Having slain Citrāṅgada, best of the Kurus, whose bow and arrows were varied and marvelous, the Gandharva then ascended to heaven.

**1.95.11**  When that tiger among kings, of great splendour, was slain, Bhīṣma son of Śantanu performed the funeral rites, O king.

**1.95.12**  And the mighty-armed Bhīṣma then immediately consecrated the child Vicitravīrya, who had not yet come of age, to the Kuru kingship.

**1.95.13**  Vicitravīrya, abiding by Bhīṣma's counsel, then administered the realm that had been his father's and grandfather's, O great king.

**1.95.14**  That king, skilled in the science of dharma, honored Bhīṣma son of Śantanu with righteous conduct, and Bhīṣma in turn protected him.

**1.96.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: When Citrāṅgada was slain, O sinless one, Bhīṣma, abiding by Satyavatī's counsel, administered that kingdom on behalf of his young brother.

**1.96.2**  Seeing that his brother, the best among the wise, had come of age, Bhīṣma resolved to arrange the marriage of Vicitravīrya.

**1.96.3**  Then Bhīṣma heard, O king, that three daughters of the king of Kāśī, equal in beauty to apsarases, were holding a svayaṃvara to choose their own husbands.

**1.96.4**  Then that best of chariot-warriors, clad in armour, set out with a single chariot, with his mother's permission, toward the city of Vārāṇasī.

**1.96.5**  There Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, saw the assembled kings who had gathered from all directions, and the maidens as well.

**1.96.6**  While the names of thousands of kings were being proclaimed, Bhīṣma himself, that mighty lord, then chose those maidens, O king.

**1.96.7**  And Bhīṣma, best of warriors, whose voice was like the roar of a rain-cloud, having placed those maidens on his chariot, addressed the assembled kings, O king.

**1.96.8**  "The gift of maidens after inviting worthy suitors, adorning the bride, and giving wealth according to one's means — this is ordained by the wise as one form of marriage."

**1.96.9**  "Others give a maiden in exchange for a pair of cattle, others for a stated price, others by force, and others by obtaining consent."

**1.96.10**  "Some take a maiden unawares, while others win her by mutual desire — that eighth form, O know well, is named among the sages."

**1.96.11**  "The svayaṃvara is praised and resorted to by Kṣatriyas; but those who speak of dharma declare that a bride seized by force after vanquishing opponents is the highest form of marriage for the warrior class."

**1.96.12**  "These maidens here I intend to carry away by force, O lords of the earth. Exert yourselves to the utmost, whether for victory or otherwise — I stand resolved for battle, O kings."

**1.96.13**  Having thus addressed the kings and the king of Kāśī, the valiant Kaurava placed all the maidens on his chariot, bade farewell to them all, and swiftly departed, the maidens in his possession.

**1.96.14**  Then all those kings sprang up in fury, slapping their own arms and biting their lips.

**1.96.15**  As they rushed forward hastily, removing their ornaments and putting on their armour, there was a great tumult.

**1.96.16**  There was a shower as of falling stars, O Janamejaya, of bright ornaments and coats of armour on all sides.

**1.96.17**  With their armour and ornaments gleaming swiftly in every direction, and with brows furrowed in anger and indignation and eyes red with rage, they stood thus.

**1.96.18**  Mounting their splendid chariots yoked by charioteers, drawn by excellent horses straining at the pole, those heroes equipped with every weapon followed the single Kaurava as he set forth, their weapons raised.

**1.96.19**  Then, O Bharata, there arose a tumultuous and hair-raising battle between him alone and those many kings.

**1.96.20**  They simultaneously let fly ten thousand arrows at him, but Bhishma instantly cut down every one of them before they could reach him.

**1.96.21**  Then all those kings, surrounding him on every side, poured upon him a shower of arrows as storm-clouds rain upon a mountain.

**1.96.22**  He intercepted that rain of shafts with his own arrows from every direction, and then pierced all those earth-lords, each with three arrows in return.

**1.96.23**  Even his enemies marvelled at his superhuman swiftness as a chariot-warrior and at his self-defence in battle.

**1.96.24**  Having utterly vanquished them in battle, that Bharata — skilled in all weapons — departed with the maidens toward the Bharatas.

**1.96.25**  Then, O king, the great chariot-warrior Shalva's king, immeasurable in spirit, attacked Bhishma, son of Shantanu, from behind in battle.

**1.96.26**  Like a bull-elephant, foremost among the strong, who has come upon a cow in heat and strikes a rival bull from behind with his tusks.

**1.96.27**  "O woman-coveter, stand and fight! Stand and fight!" said that king, the great-armed king of Shalva, goaded on by indignation.

**1.96.28**  Then that tiger among men, Bhishma, crusher of enemy forces, stirred by those words, blazed with rage like a smokeless fire.

**1.96.29**  Abiding by the duty of a warrior, free from fear and agitation, that great chariot-warrior turned his chariot back toward Shalva.

**1.96.30**  Seeing him turn back, all those kings became mere spectators at the clash between Bhishma and Shalva.

**1.96.31**  Like two mighty bulls roaring and circling one another over a cow in heat, those two, possessed of great strength and valor, moved against each other.

**1.96.32**  Then Shalva's king, foremost among men, covered Bhishma, son of Shantanu, with hundreds of thousands of swift arrows.

**1.96.33**  Seeing Bhishma thus assailed first by Shalva, those kings were astonished and exclaimed "Well done! Well done!"

**1.96.34**  Witnessing his swiftness in combat, all those lords of the earth, the kings, joyfully honored Shalva with words of praise.

**1.96.35**  Hearing then the words of the assembled warriors, the enraged Bhishma, son of Shantanu — conqueror of enemy cities — cried out, "Stand! Stand!"

**1.96.36**  And in his fury he spoke to his charioteer: "Drive where that king stands, that I may today slay him as the king of birds slays a serpent."

**1.96.37**  Then the Kaurava duly invoked the Varuna weapon, O lord of men, and with it he crushed the four horses of Shalva's king.

**1.96.38**  Warding off the weapons of Shalva's king with his own weapons, that Kaurava Bhishma, O tiger among kings, slew Shalva's charioteer, and with a single weapon further struck down his finest horses.

**1.96.39**  For the sake of the maidens, O best of men, Bhishma, son of Shantanu, having vanquished him, then released that foremost of kings alive; and Shalva departed to his own city, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.96.40**  And those kings who had been present there, wishing to witness the svayamvara, likewise returned to their own kingdoms, O conqueror of enemy cities.

**1.96.41**  Having thus won those maidens, Bhishma, foremost among warriors, proceeded to Hastinapura, where the Kaurava king resided.

**1.96.42**  In no long time, O lord of men, he traversed forests, rivers, and mountains adorned with manifold trees.
