**1.96.43**  Uninjured himself, having destroyed his foes in battle — he whose valor was beyond measure — the son of the river Ganga brought home the daughters of the king of Kashi.

**1.96.44**  That righteous-souled one received them as daughters-in-law, as younger sisters, and as daughters, and escorted them to the Kurus.

**1.96.45**  All of them endowed with virtues, won by his valor — Bhishma, as a brother, gave them to his younger brother Vichitravirya.

**1.96.46**  The righteous Bhishma, knowing the law of the virtuous, having accomplished that superhuman deed, set about arranging the marriage of his brother Vichitravirya, having resolved the matter together with Satyavati, self-possessed as he was.

**1.96.47**  As Bhishma was arranging the marriage, the eldest daughter of the king of Kashi, that virtuous woman, then spoke these words:

**1.96.48**  "The lord of Saubha has already been chosen by me in my heart as my husband, and he too had already chosen me — and this was also my father's wish."

**1.96.49**  "Shalva was to have been chosen by me at that svayamvara. Knowing this, O knower of dharma, do now what is right."

**1.96.50**  Thus addressed by that maiden in the assembly of brahmins, the heroic Bhishma fell into fitting reflection regarding what was to be done in this matter.

**1.96.51**  Having deliberated with brahmins who had crossed to the further shore of the Vedas, the knower of dharma then gave leave to the eldest, Amba, daughter of the king of Kashi.

**1.96.52**  Bhishma gave Ambika and Ambalika as wives to his younger brother Vichitravirya according to the rites prescribed by tradition.

**1.96.53**  Taking the hand of each of them, Vichitravirya, the righteous-souled one, proud of his beauty and youth, became possessed by desire.

**1.96.54**  And they too were tall, dark, with blue curling hair, with reddish and prominent nails, and with full hips and breasts —

**1.96.55**  Certain that they had obtained a husband well-matched to themselves, both honored the auspicious Vichitravirya.

**1.96.56**  And he, resembling the Ashvins in beauty, with the valor and spirit of the gods, became a captivator of the hearts of all women.

**1.96.57**  Sporting with those two for seven years, the young lord of the earth, Vichitravirya, fell ill with consumption.

**1.96.58**  Despite the efforts of his friends and trusted physicians, that Kaurava went to Yama's abode like the sun setting.

**1.96.59**  Acting in accordance with Satyavati's wishes, Bhishma, together with the officiating priests and all the foremost Kurus, duly performed all the funeral rites for King Vichitravirya.

**1.97.1**  Vaishampayana said: Then Satyavati, sorrowful, pitiable, yearning for a son, having performed the funeral duties for her son together with her daughters-in-law, O Bharata —

**1.97.2**  — that honored and greatly blessed woman, reflecting carefully on dharma, the paternal lineage, and the maternal lineage, spoke these words to the son of Ganga:

**1.97.3**  "In you rests the ancestral offering, the fame, and the continuity of Shantanu, the ever-righteous Kaurava of great renown.

**1.97.4**  As ascent to heaven is assured upon doing virtuous deeds, as life is assured in truth, so dharma is assured in you.

**1.97.5**  You know the various duties of dharma both in summary and in detail, O knower of dharma; you know the diverse revealed scriptures and all the Vedas in their entirety.

**1.97.6**  I see in you steadfastness in dharma, adherence to family custom, and conduct in difficult situations like that of Shukra and Angiras.

**1.97.7**  Therefore, O best of those who uphold dharma, I shall set you, greatly reassured, to a task; hear it and you ought to carry it out.

**1.97.8**  My son, your brother, the valiant one who was so dear to you, has gone to heaven even as a boy, without a son, O bull among men.

**1.97.9**  These two queens of your brother, O Bharata — the fair daughters of the king of Kashi, endowed with beauty and youth and longing for sons —

**1.97.10**  — you ought, O greatly blessed one, to beget offspring upon them at my command, for the perpetuation of our lineage; it is your duty to do so here.

**1.97.11**  Be consecrated in the kingdom, govern the Bharatas, take wives according to dharma — do not let our ancestors sink down."

**1.97.12**  Thus addressed by his mother and by his friends, that scorcher of enemies, the righteous-souled one, gave in reply only a righteous answer:

**1.97.13**  "Without doubt, O mother, you have stated a highest duty; and you know well the supreme vow I took regarding offspring.

**1.97.14**  You know what happened in your presence for the sake of the bride-price, O Satyavati; I swear to you the truth again:

**1.97.15**  I would renounce the three worlds, or a kingdom among the gods, or whatever else might surpass even these — but I would never in any way abandon truth.

**1.97.16**  The earth might abandon its smell, water might abandon its own taste, fire might abandon its form, wind might abandon its quality of touch —

**1.97.17**  The sun might cast off its radiance, the comet its heat, space might abandon sound, the moon might cast off its coolness —

**1.97.18**  The slayer of Vritra might abandon his valor, the king of dharma his righteousness — but I could never in any way be resolved to abandon truth."

**1.97.19**  Thus addressed by her son of immeasurable wealth and brilliance, mother Satyavati then spoke again to Bhishma:

**1.97.20**  "I know your supreme steadfastness in truth, O you whose valor is your truth; if you wished, you could by your own power create three other worlds.

**1.97.21**  I know too that what you have spoken is truth, and you spoke it for my sake; but consider the dharma of emergencies — bear the ancestral burden.

**1.97.22**  Act, O scorcher of foes, in such a way that neither the family line nor dharma may come to ruin, and that your friends may rejoice."

**1.97.23**  As she lamented thus, pitiable and yearning for a son, speaking what deviated from dharma, Bhishma spoke once more to her:

**1.97.24**  "O queen, look to the laws of dharma — do not lead us all to ruin; departure from truth is not praised in the codes of dharma for a warrior.

**1.97.25**  I will declare to you, O queen, the eternal warrior dharma by which Shantanu's lineage may endure imperishably on earth.

**1.97.26**  Having heard it, you should act upon it together with the wise men and the priest, who are skilled in the dharma of emergencies and in practical matters, having regard also for the ways of the world."

**1.98.1**  Bhishma said: O greatly blessed one, by Rama son of Jamadagni, who could not endure his father's slaying and was consumed with wrath, the lord of the Haihayas was slain, and the thousand arms of Arjuna were hewn off.

**1.98.2**  And again, taking up his bow and releasing great weapons, conquering the earth with his chariot, he burned the warrior class not just once.

**1.98.3**  Thus, with various high and low weapons, the great-souled Bhargava once made the earth devoid of warriors twenty-one times over.

**1.98.4**  Thereupon, coming together from all directions, those warrior-women had children fathered upon them by self-controlled brahmins.

**1.98.5**  "The son belongs to him who took the hand" — this is established in the Vedas; with that dharma fixed in their minds, those women approached the brahmins; and in the world too this rebirth of the warrior class is seen to have been practiced.

**1.98.6**  Now, there was in ancient times a wise sage known by the name of Utathya, and his wife was named Mamata, held in the highest esteem.

**1.98.7**  But Utathya's younger brother, Brihaspati, the great-souled, the preceptor of the dwellers in the third heaven, approached Mamata with desire.

**1.98.8**  Mamata said to that brother-in-law, foremost among speakers: "I am pregnant by my elder brother-in-law; let it rest — do not proceed."

**1.98.9**  "And this child of mine, O greatly blessed Brihaspati, the son of Utathya, is even now in my womb reciting the Veda together with its six ancillaries here."

**1.98.10**  "Your seed too is never fruitless — you ought indeed to be so; therefore, given all this, you ought today to desist."

**1.98.11**  Though thus properly addressed by her, the great-souled Brihaspati could not restrain his own self, then so given over to desire.

**1.98.12**  Then he, consumed by desire, lay with her who did not desire it; and as he was releasing his seed, the child in the womb spoke to him.

**1.98.13**  O father, I speak as the younger: there is no room here for the two of us. You have infallible seed, and I arrived here first.

**1.98.14**  Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati flew into rage and cursed that one; the venerable seer, rebuking the child of Utathya still in the womb, pronounced his curse.

**1.98.15**  "Because at such a moment, while a thing desired by all beings was taking place, you have spoken such words, therefore you shall enter into prolonged darkness."

**1.98.16**  By reason of that curse the sage was born bearing the name Dīrghatamas — of the far-spreading glory of Bṛhaspati, equal to Bṛhaspati himself in brilliance.

**1.98.17**  That illustrious one then begot sons beginning with Gautama, in order to continue the lineage and increase the family of the sage Utathya.

**1.98.18**  Those sons, Gautama and the rest, overcome by greed and delusion, placed him in a wooden box and cast him into the Gaṅgā.

**1.98.19**  "This one is blind and old and need not be supported by us" — having thought this, those cruel ones turned and went home.

**1.98.20**  Then, O king, the blind sage, floating downstream on that raft, drifted through very many lands.

**1.98.21**  Then a king named Bali, well versed in all duties, saw him as he was sinking, carried near by the current.

**1.98.22**  The righteous Bali, of true valour, rescued him; and recognizing who he was, that bull among men sought a boon from him — the blessing of sons.

**1.98.23**  "O greatly fortunate one, O bestower of honour, for the sake of continuing my line, please beget upon my wives sons who are skilled in dharma and artha."

**1.98.24**  Thus addressed, that splendid sage said "So be it" to him, and the king then sent his own wife Sudeṣṇā to him.

**1.98.25**  But the queen, deeming him blind and old, did not go herself; instead she sent her own handmaid to that aged one.

**1.98.26**  In her — a woman of śūdra birth — that self-controlled, righteous sage begot exactly eleven sons, beginning with Kākṣīvat.

**1.98.27**  Seeing those sons beginning with Kākṣīvat, all engaged in study, the valiant king said to the sage: "These are mine."

**1.98.28**  "No," said the great sage, declaring: "These are mine alone — Kākṣīvat and the rest were begotten by me upon a woman of śūdra birth."

**1.98.29**  "Your chief queen Sudeṣṇā, thinking me blind and old, disrespected me, and the foolish woman gave me a śūdra handmaid instead."

**1.98.30**  Then Bali propitiated that best of sages again, and sent his wife Sudeṣṇā to him once more.

**1.98.31**  Touching the queen with his limbs, Dīrghatamas then said to her: "A prince of great brilliance and truthful speech shall be born to you."

**1.98.32**  There upon Sudeṣṇā was born the royal sage named Aṅga; and in this way other great bowmen — kṣatriyas — were born on earth through brāhmaṇas.

**1.98.33**  Born knowing the highest dharma, endowed with valour and great strength — having heard all this, O mother, do here as you wish.

**1.99.1**  Bhīṣma said: I shall speak once more of a means for the growth of the Bharata lineage and its continuity, O mother — listen as I tell it.

**1.99.2**  Let some virtuous brāhmaṇa be invited with wealth to beget offspring upon the wives who were Vicitravīrya's fields.

**1.99.3**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then Satyavatī, her voice faltering, spoke these words to Bhīṣma with a slight smile tinged with embarrassment.

**1.99.4**  "What you say is true, O great-armed one, O Bhārata. Out of trust in you I shall tell you something for the sake of the family's continuity — a matter of such gravity that it cannot remain untold."

**1.99.5**  "You alone are dharma in our family, you are truth, you are the highest refuge — therefore hear my words and then act accordingly."

**1.99.6**  "O righteous-souled one, my righteous father had a ferry-boat; in my early youth I used to go there to that crossing."

**1.99.7**  "Then the foremost upholder of dharma, the supreme sage Parāśara, wise and intent on crossing the Yamunā river, came to the ferry."

**1.99.8**  "As I was ferrying him across the Yamunā, that best of sages, overcome with desire, approached me and spoke many sweet, coaxing words."

**1.99.9**  "Fearing his curse and fearing my father, O Bhārata, addressed with requests not easily refused, I did not dare to refuse him."

**1.99.10**  "He overpowered me, that child, and brought me under his sway by his ascetic power, shrouding the world in darkness right there on the boat, O Bhārata."

**1.99.11**  "There was once a great fishy smell about me that I found repulsive; removing that, the sage bestowed upon me this pleasing fragrance."

**1.99.12**  "The sage then said to me: once you have delivered my child, you shall remain a virgin on an island in this very river."

**1.99.13**  "That great sage, the great yogin Pārāśarya, was my son born of a virgin — he has from of old been known as Dvaipāyana."

**1.99.14**  "He is the venerable sage who, by his austerity, divided the four Vedas and thereby attained the title of Vyāsa in the world, and the name Kṛṣṇa from his dark complexion."

**1.99.15**  "A speaker of truth, devoted to tranquillity, an ascetic whose sins are burned away — appointed by me and by you, O one of boundless splendour, he will beget auspicious offspring upon your brother's wives."

**1.99.16**  "For he told me there: 'Remember me when there is a task to be done.' I shall summon him to mind, O great-armed Bhīṣma, if you so wish."

**1.99.17**  "With your consent, O Bhīṣma, that mighty ascetic will most certainly beget sons upon the wives of Vicitravīrya."

**1.99.18**  Upon the mention of that great sage, Bhīṣma, joining his palms in reverence, spoke: "One who views the three — dharma, artha, and kāma —

**1.99.19**  "— artha and its consequences, dharma and its consequences, kāma and its consequences, as well as their opposites separately — and who, having pondered them rightly with his intellect, reaches a decision: that person is truly wise.

**1.99.20**  "This that you have proposed is both in accord with dharma and beneficial to our family; what you have declared as the highest good pleases me well."

**1.99.21**  Then, when Bhīṣma had given his consent, O joy of the Kurus, Kālī called the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana to mind.

**1.99.22**  That wise one, who was expounding the Vedas, perceived his mother's thought and appeared before her instantly and unannounced, O joy of the Kurus.

**1.99.23**  She then offered proper worship to her son, embraced him with both arms, sprinkled him with tears, and the daughter of the fisherman shed tears seeing that son after so long.

**1.99.24**  Sprinkling her with water and saluting her, the great sage Vyāsa — the elder-born son — addressed his grieving mother.

**1.99.25**  "I have come to do whatever you intend. Command me, O you who know the true nature of dharma — I shall do what is dear to you."

**1.99.26**  Then the chief priest performed worship for that supreme sage, and he received it duly, with the proper rites and mantras.

**1.99.27**  With him seated, his mother enquired after his welfare; then Satyavatī, gazing at him, spoke the following words.

**1.99.28**  "Sons are born alike of both mother and father, O sage; as a father is their master, so too is a mother — of this there is no doubt."

**1.99.29**  "Ordained by the Creator, you are my first son; Vicitravīrya is my younger son — so too, O brahmarṣi."

**1.99.30**  "Just as Bhīṣma is Vicitravīrya's brother through the father, so are you through the mother — or consider it however you will, my son."

**1.99.31**  "This Śāntanava, maintaining his vow and of true valour, forms no resolve regarding offspring nor indeed regarding the governance of the kingdom."

**1.99.32**  "You, then, out of regard for your brother, for the continuity of the family, at the word and commission of this Bhīṣma, and at my bidding — O sinless one —

**1.99.33**  "— and out of compassion for all beings and for their protection, out of gentleness — what I tell you, you ought to hear and act upon."

**1.99.34**  "Your younger brother's wives — comparable to daughters of the gods, endowed with beauty and youth, and desirous of sons by dharma —

**1.99.35**  "— upon those two you are capable of begetting offspring, my son, fitting for this lineage, for its continuation and for its progeny."

**1.99.36**  Vyāsa said: You know dharma, O Satyavatī, both the higher and the lower, and how your mind, O knower of dharma, is set upon dharma.

**1.99.37**  "Therefore, appointed by you and keeping dharma as my purpose, I shall do what you desire — for this has been seen as the ancient practice."

**1.99.38**  "I shall give sons to your brother comparable to Mitra and Varuṇa — but let those queens observe the vow I prescribe here."

**1.99.39**  "They shall observe it properly for one year; then they will be purified. For no woman without the vow may approach me."

**1.99.40**  Satyavatī said: Arrange it so that the queen may conceive forthwith. In a kingless realm there is no rain, no deities.

**1.99.41**  "How can a kingless kingdom be sustained, O lord? Therefore plant the seed at once; Bhīṣma will nurture the child."

**1.99.42**  Vyāsa said: If a son is to be given by me swiftly, out of season, then let her endure my ugliness — that is the supreme vow required of her.

**1.99.43**  "If she can endure my smell, my form, my dress, and my body, then let Kausalyā conceive an excellent child this very day."

**1.99.44**  Vaiśampāyana said: Having said this in anticipation of the union, the sage vanished. Then she, the queen, approached her daughter-in-law in private and spoke words that were righteous, purposeful, and beneficial.

**1.99.45**  "O Kausalyā, understand what I tell you concerning the thread of dharma. The extinction of the Bharatas has clearly come about through the waning of my fortune."

**1.99.46**  "Seeing me in anguish and the paternal lineage afflicted, Bhīṣma gave me counsel in this matter for the increase of dharma."

**1.99.47**  "That counsel depends on you, my daughter — know this. Raise up once more the Bharata lineage that has perished."

**1.99.48**  "Bear a son, O fair-hipped one, equal in splendour to the king of the gods; for he shall carry the heavy yoke of kingship for our family."

**1.99.49**  She somehow persuaded that righteous woman by appealing to dharma, and caused brāhmaṇas, divine sages, and guests to be fed.

**1.100.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then at the proper time Satyavatī, having settled her daughter-in-law — bathed at the end of her period — upon the bed, gently spoke these words.

**1.100.2**  "O Kausalyā, you have a brother-in-law; he will enter your chamber this night. Remain vigilant and await him — he will come at midnight."

**1.100.3**  Hearing her mother-in-law's words, she lay upon the auspicious bed and thought of Bhīṣma and of the other bulls of the Kuru line.

**1.100.4**  Then the truth-speaking sage, appointed first to Ambikā, entered the bedchamber while the lamps were burning brightly.

**1.100.5**  Seeing his dark form, his reddish matted locks, his blazing eyes, and his tawny beard, the queen shut her eyes.

**1.100.6**  That night the daughter of the Kāśi king, wishing to please her mother-in-law yet seized by fear, could not bring herself to look at him.

**1.100.7**  When he had departed, the mother went to her son and asked: "My son, will a prince of good qualities be born to her?"

**1.100.8**  Hearing his mother's words, Vyāsa of supreme intelligence — knowing what transcends the senses, impelled by fate — spoke.

**1.100.9**  "He shall be born with the strength of ten thousand elephants, a man of learning, the best of royal sages, of great fortune, great valour, and great intelligence."

**1.100.10**  "He shall have a hundred sons, all of great strength — but owing to the failing of his mother, he himself will be blind."

**1.100.11**  Hearing those words of his, the mother then spoke to her son: 'A blind man is not a fitting king of the Kurus, O ascetic treasure.'

**1.100.12**  'You ought to give us another king — a protector of the kinsmen's lineage, an increaser of the ancestral line, a second king of the Kuru dynasty.'

**1.100.13**  He of great austerity promised 'So be it' and departed. And in time Kausalyā gave birth to that blind son.

**1.100.14**  But that blameless lady Satyavatī then instructed her daughter-in-law again and summoned the seer just as before.

**1.100.15**  Then the great seer approached her by the same method. He came to Ambālikā, and she, upon seeing the seer, turned pale as a corpse, crestfallen, O Bhārata.

**1.100.16**  Seeing her frightened, pale as a corpse, and despondent, O king, Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, spoke these words:

**1.100.17**  'Because you turned pale upon seeing my hideous form, therefore this son of yours shall be named Pāṇḍu — pale indeed.'

**1.100.18**  'And that very name shall be his in this world, O fair-faced one.' Having spoken thus, the blessed best of sages departed.

**1.100.19**  Then Satya, watching him depart, spoke to her son. He again reported to his mother the paleness of that child.

**1.100.20**  The mother begged him once more for yet another son. And the great seer replied to that mother, 'So be it.'

**1.100.21**  Then in due time that princess gave birth to the boy Pāṇḍu, endowed with auspicious marks and blazing with glory. From him were born the five Pāṇḍavas, mighty archers all.

**1.100.22**  Then at the fertile season she assigned the eldest daughter-in-law to him again. But that one, like the daughter of a god, reflecting on the seer’s appearance and smell, refused the queen's command out of fear.

**1.100.23**  Then the daughter of the king of Kāśī adorned a maidservant with her own ornaments, making her like an apsaras, and sent her to Kṛṣṇa (Vyāsa).

**1.100.24**  The maidservant went forward to meet the seer as he arrived, greeted him reverently, and, given leave, lay with him and attended him with great care.

**1.100.25**  The seer found satisfaction in pleasure with her; the great seer passed the night dwelling with her, who was joyful.

**1.100.26**  As he rose he said to her: 'You shall no longer be a slave. And this glorious child that has entered your womb, O auspicious one, shall be foremost among all the wise in the world, righteous in soul.'

**1.100.27**  He was born and was named Vidura — son of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, brother of both Dhṛtaraṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, of boundless intelligence.

**1.100.28**  Dharma himself, by the curse of that great-souled Māṇḍavya, was born in the form of Vidura — knowing the truth of meaning, free from desire and anger.

**1.100.29**  Having discharged his debt to Dharma, he (Vyāsa) came once more to his mother and informed her of the birth, then vanished there and then.

**1.100.30**  Thus, in the field of Vicitravīrya, even from Dvaipāyana were born those who shone like the offspring of gods, the increasers of the Kuru lineage.

**1.101.1**  Janamejaya said: 'What deed did Dharma commit by which he incurred a curse? And by whose curse, O Brahma-seer, was he born in a śūdra womb?'

**1.101.2**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'There was a certain brahmin renowned as Māṇḍavya — steadfast, knowing all dharma, abiding in truth and austerity.'

**1.101.3**  He of great austerity stood at the gate of his hermitage at the root of a tree, arms raised, a great yogī, observing the vow of silence.

**1.101.4**  After a long time, while he stood thus in austerity, some robbers carrying stolen goods arrived at that hermitage, pursued by many guards, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.101.5**  They hid the plunder in his dwelling, O best of Kurus, and, having hidden it, crouched in concealment there when the troops arrived in pursuit.

**1.101.6**  With the thieves thus hidden, the force of those guards quickly came there, and those trackers of thieves caught sight of that seer.

**1.101.7**  Then, O king, they questioned that treasure of austerity standing there: 'By which path did the robbers go, O best of twice-born? By that path, O brahmin, let us go with all speed.'

**1.101.8**  But that treasure of austerity, O king, though the guards were speaking thus, said not a word, neither good nor bad.

**1.101.9**  Then those royal servants, searching through that hermitage, found the thieves hidden there, along with the goods themselves.

**1.101.10**  Suspicion then arose among the guards against that sage; they bound him along with the thieves and reported everything to the king.

**1.101.11**  The king ordered him to be executed along with those thieves. And that one of great austerity, unrecognised, was impaled upon a spike by the executioners.

**1.101.12**  Then those guards, having raised that sage on the spike, went back to the king, taking those goods with them.

**1.101.13**  But that righteous soul, though impaled upon the spike, for a long time — without food, even — did not meet death, O brahmin-seer; he sustained his life-breath and drew other sages to him.

**1.101.14**  Through the austerity being performed by that great-souled one on the tip of the spike, the sages were overwhelmed with extreme distress, O scorcher of foes.

**1.101.15**  They became birds at night and gathered round from every side, showing themselves as best they could, and questioned that best of twice-born: 'We wish to hear, O brahmin, what sin you have committed.'

**1.101.16**  Then that tiger among sages replied to those treasures of austerity: 'To what fault shall I trace it? For truly no other has wronged me.'

**1.101.17**  And the king, hearing of that seer, came out with his ministers and then sought to propitiate that best of sages mounted on the spike.

**1.101.18**  'Whatever wrong I did to you out of delusion and ignorance, O best of sages, I beg your forgiveness for that; you ought not be angry with me.'

**1.101.19**  Addressed thus by the king, the sage showed grace. When he had received grace, the king then had him brought down from the spike.

**1.101.20**  Having brought him down from the spike's tip, they tried to pull out the spike. Being unable to extract it fully, they cut it at the base.

**1.101.21**  That sage moved about with the spike still lodged inside him. By that austerity he conquered worlds difficult for others to attain. From then on he is known in the worlds as Aṇīmāṇḍavya — Spike-Māṇḍavya.

**1.101.22**  That brahmin, knowing the supreme truth, went to the abode of Dharma and, seeing Dharma seated there, reproached him, that powerful one.

**1.101.23**  'What evil deed was done by me unknowingly, whose fruit has been visited upon me in such a way? Tell me the truth quickly — see the power of my austerity.'

**1.101.24**  Dharma said: 'You once inserted straws into the tails of insects — the fruit of that deed has fallen upon you, O treasure of austerity.'

**1.101.25**  Aṇīmāṇḍavya said: 'For a trifling offence you have imposed a heavy punishment on me. Therefore, Dharma, you shall be born among men in a śūdra womb.'

**1.101.26**  'I now establish this rule for the world regarding the arising of dharma's fruit: up to the fourteenth year of life there shall be no sin for those who do such things; beyond that it shall indeed be a transgression.'

**1.101.27**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'It was by this offence, by the curse of that great-souled one, that Dharma was born in a śūdra womb in the form of Vidura.'

**1.101.28**  Skilled in dharma and artha, free from greed and anger, far-sighted, devoted to tranquillity, and ever engaged in the welfare of the Kurus.

**1.102.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'When those three princes were born, these three — Kuru-jāṅgala, the Kuru land, and Kuru-kṣetra — all flourished.'

**1.102.2**  The earth bore crops standing tall; the harvests were fruitful; the rain-cloud rained according to the seasons; the trees were laden with many flowers and fruits.

**1.102.3**  The beasts of burden were exhilarated; the deer and birds were joyful; the garlands were fragrant; the fruits were full of flavour.

**1.102.4**  The cities were filled with merchants and artisans; the brave, the learned, and the virtuous all lived happily.

**1.102.5**  There were no robbers, no people inclined to adharma; even in the outlying regions of the realm the Kṛta age prevailed.

**1.102.6**  The people, devoted to giving, righteous action, and dharma, intent on sacrifices and vows, bound to one another with affection, thrived in that time.

**1.102.7**  People were free from pride and anger, rid of greed; they flourished with one another; dharma reigned supreme.

**1.102.8**  That city shone, full like a great ocean, adorned with gateways, arches, and turrets like heaped clouds, crowded with hundreds of palaces, resembling the city of great Indra.

**1.102.9**  People sported joyfully along rivers, in groves, on the banks of ponds and pools, and in pleasant forests.

**1.102.10**  The southern Kurus then ranged about rivalling the northern Kurus and also the Siddhas, sages, and Cāraṇas. There was no wretch, and women were not widowed.

**1.102.11**  In that lovely land many wells, parks, assembly halls, ponds, and brahmin dwellings were built by the Kurus, and everything was guarded on all sides according to the śāstra by Bhīṣma, O king.

**1.102.12**  That land was lovely, marked with hundreds of shrines and sacrificial posts, enlarged by the incorporation of neighbouring kingdoms; the wheel of dharma ordained by Bhīṣma turned in the realm.

**1.102.13**  As the rites for those great-souled princes were being performed, all the citizens and country-folk were in a state of perpetual festival.

**1.102.14**  In the houses of the leading Kurus and of the townspeople, O lord of men, the words 'Give! Eat!' were heard everywhere.

**1.102.15**  Dhṛtaraṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and the great-minded Vidura were all cared for from birth by Bhīṣma as though they were his own sons.

**1.102.16**  Consecrated with all rites, engaged in vows and Vedic study, skilled in exertion and exercise, they came to youth.

**1.102.17**  They became proficient in the science of archery, riding on horseback, fighting with the mace and sword-and-shield, likewise in the training of elephants, and in the science of statecraft.

**1.102.18**  In histories and purāṇas, in various branches of learning, O lord, knowing the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences — they applied themselves diligently in all.

**1.102.19**  Pāṇḍu was surpassingly valiant with the bow, excelling all men; Dhṛtaraṣṭra, lord of the earth, was stronger than all others.

**1.102.20**  In all three worlds there was none equal to Vidura; ever fixed in dharma, O king, he had attained the highest in matters of dharma.

**1.102.21**  Seeing the line of Śaṃtanu, which had seemed lost, once more restored, this saying then spread through the world and all its kingdoms:

**1.102.22**  'Of lands for the sons of heroes, Kuru-jāṅgala; of daughters of Kāśī for knowledge of all dharma; of ancient cities, the Elephant-named city (Hāstināpura) — Bhīṣma has established all these.'

**1.102.23**  But Dhṛtaraṣṭra did not obtain the kingdom on account of his blindness; and Vidura because he was born of a servant woman; Pāṇḍu became lord of the earth.

**1.103.1**  Bhīṣma said: 'This family of ours, renowned and properly furnished with all virtues, holds sovereignty over the earth above all other kings of the earth.'

**1.103.2**  'Protected by kings of old, those great souls who knew dharma, never at any time has our family come to ruin here.'

**1.103.3**  'By me and by Satyavatī, and by the great-souled Kṛṣṇa (Vyāsa), it has been established once more in you, the threads of the lineage.'

**1.103.4**  'This family grows, my son, like the ocean. So it must be furthered by me and especially by you.'

**1.103.5**  'It is heard that a Yādava princess suitable for our family, and likewise the daughter of Subala and the daughter of the lord of Madra —'

**1.103.6**  '— are well-born, beautiful, and possessed of worthy guardians in every way; they are fitting for alliance with us, those bulls among kṣatriyas.'

**1.103.7**  'I think those women should be sought in marriage for the continuation of this family — O best of the wise, or else what do you think, Vidura?'

**1.103.8**  Vidura said: 'You are our father, you are our mother, you are our supreme teacher. Therefore deliberate yourself and do what is beneficial for this family.'

**1.103.9**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then from brahmins he (Bhīṣma) heard of Gāndhārī, daughter of Subala — that she had propitiated the god who grants boons, Hara the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, and that the auspicious Gāndhārī had obtained a boon of a hundred sons.

**1.103.10**  Having truly heard this, Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, thereupon dispatched a messenger to the king of Gandhara, O Bharata.

**1.103.11**  There was hesitation on the part of Subala on account of Dhritarashtra's blindness; but weighing carefully with his intellect the family, the fame, and the conduct of the Kurus, he gave Gandhari, that virtuous woman, to Dhritarashtra.

**1.103.12**  Gandhari too had heard that Dhritarashtra was blind and that she was being given to him by her father and mother, O Bharata.

**1.103.13**  Then that auspicious woman, devoted to her vow of fidelity to her husband, resolved that she would not surpass her lord; she took a strip of cloth, folded it many times, and bound it over her own eyes, O king.

**1.103.14**  Then Shakuni, son of the king of Gandhara, came bringing his sister, endowed with great beauty, to the Kauravas.

**1.103.15**  That hero, having given his sister along with fitting gifts and apparel, returned to his own city, having been honored by Bhishma.

**1.103.16**  Gandhari too, that most excellent woman, through her conduct, deportment, and behavior, gave satisfaction to all the Kurus, O Bharata.

**1.103.17**  Devoted to her vow of chastity, she propitiated them all by her conduct; and firm in her vow, she never praised even in speech any other man.

**1.104.1**  Vaishampayana said: There was a foremost of the Yadus named Shura who was the father of Vasudeva; he had a daughter named Pritha, unequaled in beauty on earth.

**1.104.2**  That mighty hero, having first made a solemn promise to his father's sister's son who was childless, gave to him the first-born of his own offspring.

**1.104.3**  He gave that first-born daughter, whom he had pledged as the foremost gift, to Kuntibhoja, his great-souled friend — given friend to friend.

**1.104.4**  She, appointed in her father's house to the service of gods and guests, attended with devotion a fierce and terrible Brahmin of intense austerity.

**1.104.5**  Him of deep resolve in righteousness, whom they know as Durvasa — that fierce one of sharpened spirit — she pleased by every effort.

**1.104.6**  Considering the dharma applicable in times of difficulty, he gave her a mantra endowed with power to summon, and the sage spoke thus to her.

**1.104.7**  Whichever deity you invoke with this mantra, by that deity's favor a son shall be born to you.

**1.104.8**  Thus addressed by that Brahmin, that virtuous and glorious maiden, out of curiosity, then invoked the sun-god Arka.

**1.104.9**  She saw the sun, the illuminator of worlds, coming toward her; that woman of flawless limbs was filled with wonder upon beholding that great marvel.

**1.104.10**  Then the sun, whose work is to shine, placed his seed in her; she thereupon gave birth to a hero, the foremost of all who bear weapons — born already wearing his armor, splendid, divine in origin, and invested with radiance.

**1.104.11**  Bearing his natural armor and with his face lit by his earrings, was born the son Karna, renowned in all the worlds.

**1.104.12**  That most resplendent one, best among givers, restored her maidenhood to her, and having given thus, ascended to heaven.

**1.104.13**  Concealing that transgression out of fear of her kinsmen, Kunti then cast that auspiciously marked infant into the water.

**1.104.14**  That abandoned child was then adopted as a son by the greatly renowned husband of Radha, a son of a suta, together with his wife.

**1.104.15**  Those two gave a name to that infant: "Since he was born along with wealth, let him be called Vasushena."

**1.104.16**  Growing up and becoming powerful, he applied himself to all weapons; that mighty hero would stand in worship of the sun until the heat touched his back.

**1.104.17**  At the time when that hero of truthful pledge sat muttering prayers, there was nothing that this great-souled one would refuse to give to Brahmins.

**1.104.18**  Indra, the nourisher of all beings and of great splendor, taking the form of a Brahmin, approached him as a suppliant and begged for his earrings and his armor.

**1.104.19**  Karna, though pained, cut off from his own body his armor dripping with blood, and severing his earrings, gave them with joined palms.

**1.104.20**  Shakra, astonished, gave him the Shakti weapon and said: "Among gods, asuras, men, gandharvas, serpents, and rakshasas — at whomever you hurl this in anger, he shall be no more."

**1.104.21**  His former name had been known as Vasushena; thereafter by that deed he became Vaikartana Karna — the cutter of his own flesh.

**1.105.1**  Vaishampayana said: The daughter of Kuntibhoja, endowed with beauty, valor, and virtue, devoted to righteousness and of great vows, was presented by her father at a swayamvara.

**1.105.2**  She chose Pandu — lion-fanged, elephant-shouldered, bull-eyed, and of great might — from among thousands of kings.

**1.105.3**  That joy of the Kurus, of immeasurable good fortune, was united with her, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, as Maghavan was united with Paulomi.

**1.105.4**  By Devavrata's going also to the capital of the Madras, Madri, daughter of the lord of the Madras, renowned in the three worlds, was obtained.

**1.105.5**  She was celebrated among all kings and unequaled in beauty on earth; she was purchased for Pandu's sake with great wealth, and then Bhishma caused the marriage of the great-souled Pandu.

**1.105.6**  Seeing Pandu — lion-chested, elephant-shouldered, bull-eyed, high-minded, that tiger among men — people on earth were filled with wonder.

**1.105.7**  Then Pandu, having wed, endowed with strength and enthusiasm, desiring to conquer the earth, went against enemies on many fronts.

**1.105.8**  Going first against those who had given offence, the Dasharnas were conquered in battle by Pandu, that lion among men, the bearer of the Kauravas' glory.

**1.105.9**  Then Pandu, taking an army bearing banners of many kinds, rich in elephants, horses, and chariots, and teeming with masses of foot-soldiers —

**1.105.10**  — the foe of all heroes, the adversary of all lords of the earth: Darva, the protector of the Magadha realm, was slain at Rajagriha.

**1.105.11**  Then, after taking treasury, conveyances, and forces, Pandu marched to Mithila and conquered the Videhas in battle.

**1.105.12**  Likewise among the Kashis, the Suhmas, and the Pundras, O bull of the Bharatas, by the strength and valor of his own arms he brought glory to the Kurus.

**1.105.13**  Coming against him — that tamer of foes blazing like a great fire with showers of arrows and flames of weapons, that Pandu-conflagration — kings were burned up.

**1.105.14**  Those kings, their forces shattered by Pandu and his forces, were brought into submission and assigned to the works of tribute.

**1.105.15**  By him all those kings of the earth were vanquished; they regarded him alone as the great hero, as the gods regard Purandara.

**1.105.16**  All those lords of the earth came to him with joined palms, bowing low, bearing wealth and various jewels.

**1.105.17**  Gems, pearls, and coral, gold and silver, choice cattle, choice horses, choice chariots, and elephants —

**1.105.18**  — and donkeys, camels, and buffaloes, and whatever sheep and goats there were — all this the king, the lord of Hastinapura, accepted.

**1.105.19**  Taking all that, Pandu set out again with his army rejoicing, intending to gladden his own kingdom and the city of Hastinapura.

**1.105.20**  The fame born of glory that had been lost to Shantanu, that lion among kings, and to the wise Bharata, was raised up again by Pandu.

**1.105.21**  Those who had formerly seized the Kuru kingdoms and the wealth of the Kurus were made tribute-paying by Pandu, the lion of Hastinapura.

**1.105.22**  So spoke the assembled kings and their ministers, their minds filled with satisfaction and joy, together with the townspeople and country folk.

**1.105.23**  All went forth to meet him on his arrival, led by Bhishma; those dwellers of Hastinapura, going as if the road were not far, saw joyfully that the whole world was thronged with many kinds of people.

**1.105.24**  With jewels of high and low quality brought on various vehicles, with choice elephants, horses, and chariots, with cattle, camels, and sheep — the Kauravas together with Bhishma, coming upon it all, could see no end to it.

**1.105.25**  He, the increaser of Kausalya's joy, paid reverence to his father's feet, and duly honored the townspeople and country folk as well.

**1.105.26**  Bhishma, meeting his son who had returned fulfilled in purpose after crushing enemy kingdoms, shed tears of joy.

**1.105.27**  To the great sounds of hundreds of musical instruments and kettledrums, gladdening the citizens on all sides, he entered Hastinapura.

**1.106.1**  Vaishampayana said: With Dhritarashtra's permission, he presented the wealth conquered by his own arms to Bhishma, to Satyavati, and to his mother.

**1.106.2**  Pandu also sent that wealth to Vidura; and that righteous soul fully satisfied his friends with treasure.

**1.106.3**  Then Bhishma satisfied Satyavati and the glorious Kausalya with auspicious jewels won by Pandu, O Bharata.

**1.106.4**  His mother Kausalya rejoiced, embracing that bull among men of matchless splendor, even as Paulomi embraces the victorious Jayanta.

**1.106.5**  With the conquests of that hero, Dhritarashtra performed a hundred horse-sacrifices — great rites with hundreds of thousands in sacrificial gifts.

**1.106.6**  Joined together with Kunti and with Madri, O bull of the Bharatas, Pandu, free from sloth, then became a wanderer of the forests.

**1.106.7**  Abandoning his palace dwelling and his fine beds, he became constantly given to forest life, ever devoted to the hunt.

**1.106.8**  Roaming the lovely southern slopes of the Himalayan mountain, he dwelt on mountain ridges and in forests of great shala trees.

**1.106.9**  Pandu shone in the forest dwelling together with Kunti and Madri, like the splendid elephant of Purandara standing between two she-elephants.

**1.106.10**  The forest dwellers, seeing that Bharata king roaming with his two wives, bearing arrows, sword, and bow, wearing varied armor, a hero and master of weapons supreme, thought him a god.

**1.106.11**  Men, ever diligent and urged on by Dhritarashtra, brought constantly to the forest his desires and enjoyments.

**1.106.12**  Then the son of the Ganga heard of a Parashava maiden, daughter of King Devaka, endowed with beauty and youth.

**1.106.13**  Then that bull among men, having wooed and brought her, caused the marriage of the great-minded Vidura.

**1.106.14**  And Vidura, the joy of the Kurus, begot upon her sons possessed of good breeding, equal to himself in qualities.

**1.107.1**  Vaishampayana said: Then, O Janamejaya, a hundred sons were born to Dhritarashtra through Gandhari, and one more beyond the hundred through a Vaishya woman.

**1.107.2**  To Pandu through Kunti and through Madri were born five great warriors, obtained from the gods for the continuation of the family line.

**1.107.3**  Janamejaya said: How were a hundred sons born to Gandhari, O best of twice-born? And in how much time? And what was their highest lifespan?

**1.107.4**  How did that one son of Dhritarashtra come to be through the Vaishya woman? And how did Dhritarashtra transgress against Gandhari his wife — a woman of righteous conduct equal to himself, living in devotion to him?

**1.107.5**  And how, from Pandu who had been cursed by that great soul, were born five sons, great warriors, from the gods?

**1.107.6**  Knowing all this as it happened, tell it in full, O wealth of austerity; I am not satisfied when my kinsmen are being told of.

**1.107.7**  Vaishampayana said: Gandhari satisfied Dvaipayana when he came, worn out by hunger and fatigue; and Vyasa gave her a boon.

**1.107.8**  She chose a hundred sons equal to her husband and herself; then in time she conceived through Dhritarashtra.

**1.107.9**  Gandhari, childless, bore that planted embryo for two full years; then sorrow overtook her.

**1.107.10**  Hearing that a son of Kunti had been born, blazing in splendor like the morning sun, she reflected upon the steadfastness of her own womb.

**1.107.11**  Unknown to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with great effort and then faint with grief, Gāndhārī caused her own foetus — her very womb-child — to miscarry.

**1.107.12**  Then there issued forth a mass of flesh, hard as an iron ball, that had been carried in the womb for two full years; she set about expelling it.

**1.107.13**  Then Dvaipāyana, having learned of this by his insight, came swiftly; that best of murmurers of mantras beheld the fleshy mass.

**1.107.14**  Then he said to the daughter of Subala: 'What is it you intend to do?' And she truthfully disclosed her own intention to that supreme seer.

**1.107.15**  'Having heard that Kuntī's eldest son was born, radiant as the sun, I caused this womb to be expelled by me out of extreme grief.'

**1.107.16**  'And indeed a hundred sons were granted to me by you before; yet this mass of flesh has been born — truly, as the gift of a hundred sons.'

**1.107.17**  Vyāsa said: 'So it shall be, O daughter of Subala — this can never be otherwise. I have never spoken falsely, not even in jest; how then could it be otherwise?'

**1.107.18**  'Let a hundred pots filled with clarified butter be prepared at once, and sprinkle this solid lump with cold water.'

**1.107.19**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As that solid lump was being sprinkled, it split into a hundred portions at once — each being a separate embryo of the size of a thumb-joint.

**1.107.20**  One hundred and one in full number, O lord of the people — thus, O king, from that mass of flesh, each appeared in due order as time passed.

**1.107.21**  Then he placed those embryos each in its own pot, in well-guarded places, and thereafter arranged their protection.

**1.107.22**  And the blessed one also instructed the daughter of Subala: 'These pots are to be opened again only after this much time has elapsed.'

**1.107.23**  Having said this and having made all the arrangements, the blessed and wise Vyāsa departed for austerities to the Himālaya, that mountain of rocks.

**1.107.24**  Through this process, Duryodhana came to be born as the king among them; yet by birth reckoning, the elder king is Yudhiṣṭhira.

**1.107.25**  The very moment that son was born, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having summoned many Brāhmaṇas and also Bhīṣma and Vidura, spoke thus.

**1.107.26**  'Yudhiṣṭhira, the elder prince and increaser of our lineage, has attained the kingdom by his own merit — we have nothing to say against him.

**1.107.27**  'But will this one, next after him, also become king? Tell me truly what shall certainly come to pass in this matter.'

**1.107.28**  At the end of these words, O Bhārata, in all directions terrifying flesh-eating creatures cried out, and jackals howled their ill omens.

**1.107.29**  Having observed those dreadful portents on every side, O king, the Brāhmaṇas spoke, as did the great-minded Vidura.

**1.107.30**  'Clearly this son of yours shall be the destroyer of the lineage. Peace lies in his abandonment; to keep him thriving is a great wrong.'

**1.107.31**  'Let your sons number one fewer than a hundred, O lord of the earth — secure the welfare of the world and of the lineage through that one act.'

**1.107.32**  'One should abandon one person for the sake of the family; abandon a family for the sake of a village; abandon a village for the sake of a kingdom; abandon the earth for the sake of the Self.'

**1.107.33**  Though thus advised by Vidura and by all those foremost twice-born, the king did not act accordingly, overcome as he was by affection for his son.

**1.107.34**  Then all one hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O king, were born within the space of a single month, and one daughter in addition to the hundred.

**1.107.35**  While Gāndhārī was afflicted by her ever-growing womb, a Vaiśyā woman it is said attended upon the mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

**1.107.36**  In that same year, O king, the greatly renowned and wise Yuyutsu — a Kāraṇa — was born from her by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O ruler of men.

**1.107.37**  Thus were born the hundred sons of the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra — all mighty warriors and heroes — and one daughter, Duḥśalā.

**1.108.1**  Janamejaya said: 'O master, recite in order the names and the seniority — eldest to youngest — of those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.'

**1.108.2**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'Duryodhana, Yuyutsu, and also Duḥśāsana, O king; Duḥsaha, Duḥśala, Jalasaṃdha, Sama, and Saha —

**1.108.3**  Vinda and Anuvinda, Durdharṣa, Subāhu, Duṣpradharṣaṇa, Durmarṣaṇa, Durmukha, Duṣkarṇa, and also Karṇa —

**1.108.4**  Viviṃśati, Vikarṇa, Jalasaṃdha, Sulocana, Citra and Upacitra, Citrākṣa, Ārucitra, and Śarāsana —

**1.108.5**  Durmada, Duṣpragāha, Vivityu, Vikaṭa, Sama, Ūrṇanābha, Sunābha, and likewise Nanda and Upanandaka —

**1.108.6**  Senāpati, Suṣeṇa, Kuṇḍodara, Mahodara, Citrabāṇa, Citravarmā, Suvarmā, and Durvimocana —

**1.108.7**  Ayobāhu, Mahābāhu, Citrāṅga, Citrakuṇḍala, Bhīmavega, Bhīmabala, Balākī, and Balavardhana —

**1.108.8**  Ugrāyudha, Bhīmakarman, Kanakāyu, Dṛḍhāyudha, Dṛḍhavarmā, Dṛḍhakṣatra, Somakīrti, and Anūdara —

**1.108.9**  Dṛḍhasaṃdha, Jarāsaṃdha, Satyasaṃdha, Sadaḥsuvāk, Ugraśravā, Aśvasena, Senānī, and Duṣparājaya —

**1.108.10**  Aparājita, Paṇḍitaka, Viśālākṣa, Durāvara, Dṛḍhahasta, Suhasta, and the pair Vātavega and Suvarcas —

**1.108.11**  Ādityaketu, Bahvāśī, Nāgadanta and Ugrayāyin, Kavacī, Niṣaṅgī, Pāśī, Daṇḍadhāra, and Dhanurgraha —

**1.108.12**  Ugra, Bhīmaratha, Vīra, Vīrabāhu, Alolupa, Abhaya, Raudrakarman, and likewise three others including Dṛḍharatha —

**1.108.13**  Anādhṛṣya, Kuṇḍabhedī, Virāvī, Dīrghalocana, Dīrghabāhu, Mahābāhu, Vyūḍhoru, and Kanakadhvaja —

**1.108.14**  Kuṇḍāśī and Virajā — and Duḥśalā as the one beyond the hundred. This is the full one hundred and one, O king, with one daughter named as well.'

**1.108.15**  'Know the order of birth by the sequence of names, O king. All were atiratha warriors, all heroes, all skilled in battle.

**1.108.16**  All were knowers of the Vedas and versed in the science of kingship; all excelled in the arts of association, adorned by learning and noble birth.

**1.108.17**  Wives befitting every one of them were secured, O lord of the earth, by Dhṛtarāṣṭra in due season, having considered carefully and according to proper rites.

**1.108.18**  At the proper time, O Bhārata, the king gave Duḥśalā to the king of Sindhu, Jayadratha, with the consent of the Subala line.'

**1.109.1**  Janamejaya said: 'The supernal and extraordinary origin of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — transcending the human even among humans — has been narrated by you, O best of those who know Brahman.

**1.109.2**  'Their names too, spoken portion by portion, have been heard by me from you, O Brāhmaṇa. Now recite the birth of the Pāṇḍavas.'

**1.109.3**  'For all of them are great-souled, with the valour of the king of the gods; they themselves were declared by you to be divine portions descended in the chapter on the descent of the divine shares.'

**1.109.4**  'Therefore I wish to hear all about the origin of those whose deeds surpass the human. Recite it fully, O Vaiśaṃpāyana.'

**1.109.5**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: King Pāṇḍu, in a great forest frequented by deer and serpents, came upon the leader of a deer herd at the time of its mating.

**1.109.6**  Then Pāṇḍu pierced both the doe and that stag with five swift, sharp arrows feathered with gold-tipped shafts.

**1.109.7**  And that one, O king, was in truth a great-spirited son of a seer, rich in austerity, a radiant being who had joined with his wife in the form of a deer.

**1.109.8**  While still locked together with that doe, uttering human speech, he fell to the ground in an instant and lamented, his senses distraught.

**1.109.9**  The deer said: 'Even men overcome by desire and anger, even those bereft of the limb of reason, even those addicted to sin — they shun acts of cruelty.

**1.109.10**  'Wisdom does not swallow fate, but fate swallows wisdom; wisdom does not comprehend those ends that have been overturned by fate.

**1.109.11**  'Born in the foremost lineage of those ever devoted to righteousness, O Bhārata — how has your mind been swayed, overpowered by desire and greed?'

**1.109.12**  Pāṇḍu said: 'The same conduct that applies to the slaying of enemies is held to apply to the slaying of deer for kings, O deer — you ought not, out of confusion, reproach me.'

**1.109.13**  'The slaying of deer without disguise and without deceit is indeed desired; that very conduct is the duty of kings — knowing this, why do you reproach me?'

**1.109.14**  'The sage Agastya, while seated at a sacrifice, went out to hunt; having consecrated all the forest-dwelling, divinity-dwelling deer in the great forest —

**1.109.15**  '— according to the dharma seen in scripture, how do you reproach us? Through the oblation-rite of Agastya, your very fat was indeed offered as an oblation.'

**1.109.16**  The deer said: 'Formerly arrows were not released aiming at enemies in the midst of this act — indeed it is the finding of their vulnerable moment that is especially praised as the time of slaying.

**1.109.17**  Pāṇḍu said: 'Whether heedless or heedful, whether exposed or concealed — kings slay powerfully, by stratagems and with sharp arrows. Why then do you reproach me, O deer?'

**1.109.18**  The deer said: 'I do not reproach you for slaying deer, O king, on my own account — but the act of mating should have been awaited by you here, out of non-cruelty.'

**1.109.19**  'At a time cherished and desired by all beings — what wise man would slay a deer engaged in mating in the forest? The dear fruit of the aims of man — that beloved thing you have made fruitless.'

**1.109.20**  'Born in the lineage of the Paurava kings and of those sages of effortless deeds, O Kauravya — this is not fitting for you.

**1.109.21**  'This deed is exceedingly cruel, condemned by all the world, non-conducive to heaven, destructive to fame, and most unrighteous, O Bhārata.

**1.109.22**  'A connoisseur of the pleasures of women, a knower of the true nature of the dharma and artha of the scriptures — you who are like a god should not perform such a deed that shuts the door to heaven.'

**1.109.23**  'By you, O best of kings, those humans who commit cruelty and evil conduct, who are devoid of the three aims of life, ought to be suppressed — not emulated.'

**1.109.24**  'What have you done, O best of men, in slaying me, innocent as I am — a sage subsisting on roots and fruits, wearing the form of a deer, O king, ever dwelling in the forests, wholly devoted to tranquillity?'

**1.109.25**  'Because you have injured me, therefore to you as well, without doubt — you who have acted cruelly toward both of us, who acted helplessly, deluded by desire — the end of life will come in this very same manner.'

**1.109.26**  'For I am the sage Kiṃdama by name, without equal in austerity; being ashamed before humans, I was engaged in mating with my doe.'

**1.109.27**  'Having become a deer, I roam in the dense forest with other deer. Yet this shall not be a brahminicide for you, since you did not know you were slaying me who had taken the form of a deer, deluded thus by desire.'

**1.109.28**  'But you, O fool, shall reap a fruit exactly like this — when you, deluded by desire, are together with your beloved wife, you too in that very condition shall pass to the realm of the dead.'

**1.109.29**  'And the beloved one with whom you shall pass to the realm of Yama, king of the dead — that realm irresistible to all beings — she, out of devotion, O best of the wise, shall follow you there.'

**1.109.30**  'Just as I, in the midst of happiness, have been brought to grief by you — so grief shall come upon you when happiness has arrived.'

**1.109.31**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, afflicted with the greatest pain, that deer was parted from life; and Pāṇḍu too was struck with grief in an instant.

**1.110.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The king, having stepped past that one who had passed away as though it were his own kinsman, together with his wife, afflicted with sorrow and grief, lamented in anguish.

**1.110.2**  Pāṇḍu said: 'Alas — even those born in noble lineages reach misfortune through their deeds, those who have not mastered the self, deluded by the snare of desire.

**1.110.3**  'My father, though born of one ever devoted to righteousness, even as a young man met his end — enslaved by desire, so we have heard.

**1.110.4**  'In the field of that desire-enslaved king, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana — the blessed one himself, restrained of speech — begot me directly.'

**1.110.5**  Now in his calamity this vile resolve has arisen in me — that of one abandoned by the gods through wickedness, a wicked-souled man cast off on the hunt.

**1.110.6**  I resolve upon liberation alone, for bondage is a great affliction. I shall follow that imperishable good conduct of my father, and without any doubt I shall engage myself in the most intense austerities.

**1.110.7**  Therefore, alone, day by day, going from one forest tree to the next, begging alms as a shaven-headed sage, I shall wander over this earth.

**1.110.8**  Covered with dust, taking shelter in empty dwellings or making my abode at the roots of trees, having abandoned all that is dear and all that is not dear.

**1.110.9**  Neither grieving nor rejoicing, treating censure and self-praise as equal, without desire, without bowing to any, free from all pairs of opposites, possessing nothing.

**1.110.10**  Never mocking anyone, never knitting the brow at any time, ever serene of countenance, always devoted to the welfare of all beings.

**1.110.11**  Doing no harm to all four kinds of living beings, moving and stationary, always equal toward all that breathes as toward one's own offspring.

**1.110.12**  Begging alms only at one time of day, visiting two or five households, and when alms are not obtained, practicing fasts as well.

**1.110.13**  Little by little, eating only what is fit to eat, sometimes subsisting on what was obtained before, never exceeding proper measure, filling up seven bites whether gaining or not gaining.

**1.110.14**  If one hacks at one arm with an adze and anoints the other with sandalwood paste, harboring neither ill will nor good will toward either of those two persons.

**1.110.15**  Acting neither as one who desires to live nor as one who desires to die, neither welcoming nor hating death and life.

**1.110.16**  Passing beyond all the prospering actions that can be performed by a living being, remaining established in acts as slight as the blinking of an eye.

**1.110.17**  In all those states, having abandoned all activity of the senses, having wholly relinquished the sense of a dharmic self, with the impurities of the self fully cleansed.

**1.110.18**  Liberated from all sins, having passed beyond all snares, not standing under anyone's sway, sharing the nature of the wind.

**1.110.19**  Wandering continually with this way of life, of such a character, I shall sustain the body, having entered upon the fearless path.

**1.110.20**  I will not delight in the path followed by a dog, fit only for the feeble and pitiable, perpetually straying from one's own duty, bereft of virility.

**1.110.21**  He who, whether honored or dishonored, approaches another livelihood with a miserable eye, driven by desire — he walks the path of dogs.

**1.110.22**  Vaishampayana said: Having spoken thus, the king, afflicted with great grief, sighing deeply, looking at Kunti and Madri, addressed them.

**1.110.23**  Kaushalya, Vidura the Kshattar, the king together with his kinsmen, the venerable Satyavati, Bhishma, and the royal priests —

**1.110.24**  And the great-souled Brahmanas, drinkers of soma, of sharpened vows, and the elders of the Pauravas who dwell there under our protection — all of them are to be propitiated and told: Pandu has gone forth to the forest.

**1.110.25**  Having heard the words of their husband whose mind was resolved upon forest-dwelling, Kunti and Madri both spoke words equal to his own.

**1.110.26**  O bull of the Bharatas, there are also other ashramas that are possible; if we, your two lawful wives, perform great austerities together with you, you will assuredly be rewarded — even as regards heaven, there is no doubt.

**1.110.27**  Restraining the entire host of our senses, devoted to the world of our husband, having abandoned the pleasures of desire, we two shall practice abundant austerity.

**1.110.28**  O greatly wise one, O lord of men, if you abandon us two, this very day we two shall abandon life — of this there is no doubt.

**1.110.29**  Pandu said: If this resolve of yours two is in conformity with dharma, then I shall follow that imperishable way of conduct of my father.

**1.110.30**  Having abandoned the practices and pleasures of village life, performing great austerity, wearing bark garments, eating fruits and roots, I shall wander in the great forest.

**1.110.31**  Offering oblations into the fire at both twilights, touching water at both twilights, lean, taking limited food, wearing rags and hides and matted locks.

**1.110.32**  Enduring cold, wind, and heat, accompanied by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, drying out this body with austerity that is hard to perform.

**1.110.33**  Inclined to solitude, reflecting, subsisting on cooked and uncooked food alike, satisfying the ancestors and gods with forest offerings, with words, and with water.

**1.110.34**  Never performing disagreeable acts even toward forest-dwelling persons and those who dwell in hermitages — how much less toward those who dwell in villages.

**1.110.35**  Thus desiring the fierce, yet fiercer rule prescribed by the forest treatises, I shall abide until this body is extinguished.

**1.110.36**  Vaishampayana said: Having thus spoken to those two wives of his, the king born of the Kaurava lineage then gave the crest-jewel, the neck-ornament, the armlets, the earrings, costly garments, and women's ornaments —

**1.110.37**  Having given all of these to the Brahmanas, Pandu spoke again: Going to Nagapura, it should be announced — Pandu has gone forth to the forest.

**1.110.38**  Having abandoned all wealth, desire, pleasure, and the supreme delight of the self, the bull of the Kurus set out with his wives.

**1.110.39**  Then his retinue and those attendants, hearing the various pitiful words of that lion of the Bharatas, cried out in a terrible, anguished voice: "Alas! Alas!"

**1.110.40**  Shedding hot tears, abandoning that lord of the earth, they went swiftly to Nagapura, carrying all of his message.

**1.110.41**  And having heard from them all that had happened in the great forest, Dhritarashtra, foremost of men, grieved for Pandu alone.

**1.110.42**  The prince of the Kauravas, Pandu, subsisting on roots and fruits, then went together with his wives to the mountain Nagasabha.

**1.110.43**  Reaching the Chaitraratha, passing beyond Varishena, crossing the Himavat, he journeyed on to the Gandhamadana.

**1.110.44**  Protected by the great spirits and by the Siddhas and supreme sages, the king then dwelt in level and uneven places alike.

**1.110.45**  O great king, having reached the lake Indradyumna and passed beyond Hamshakoota, he became an ascetic on the Shatashringa.

**1.111.1**  Vaishampayana said: Even there, engaged in the highest austerity, that mighty one became a beloved sight to the hosts of Siddhas and Charanas.

**1.111.2**  Devoted to service, free from arrogance, self-controlled, his senses conquered, striving to reach heaven through his own prowess, O Bharata.

**1.111.3**  To some he became a brother, to others a friend; and other sages protected him as if he were a son.

**1.111.4**  But after a long time, having attained stainless austerity, Pandu became like a Brahmarishi, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.111.5**  Desiring to cross to the far shore of heaven, he set forth with his wives from Shatashringa, facing north; but the ascetics there spoke to him as they went up and ever further up the king of mountains, facing north.

**1.111.6**  We have seen many impassable regions of this mountain — the playgrounds of the gods and likewise of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.

**1.111.7**  The gardens of Kubera, level and uneven; the banks of great rivers; impassable places and mountain caverns.

**1.111.8**  There are regions of perpetual snow, devoid of trees, beasts, and birds; some places of great downpour; some that are impassable; some that are hard to reach.

**1.111.9**  No bird can cross those places, let alone other animals; only the wind passes through there, and the Siddhas and supreme sages.

**1.111.10**  On this king of mountains, how could these two royal ladies walking there not falter? O bull of the Bharatas, you who do not deserve suffering — do not go.

**1.111.11**  Pandu said: O greatly fortunate ones, the gate to heaven is not declared open for one without offspring. Tormented by that, I who am without offspring — this I tell you.

**1.111.12**  Men are born on earth bound by four debts — the debts owed to ancestors, gods, sages, and men — by the hundreds of thousands.

**1.111.13**  But those who do not discharge these in due time — for them there are no higher worlds: this has been established by those who know dharma.

**1.111.14**  One satisfies the gods through sacrifices, sages through study and austerity, ancestors through sons and funeral rites, and men through kindness.

**1.111.15**  From the debt to sages, gods, and men I am free by dharma; but from the debt to the ancestors I am not free — and by that I am tormented, O you whose wealth is austerity.

**1.111.16**  When the body perishes, the ancestors perish with certainty — this is the settled truth. Therefore the best of men are born here for the purpose of offspring.

**1.111.17**  Just as I was created by that great soul in my father's field, so how indeed might offspring come to be in this field of mine?

**1.111.18**  The ascetics said: O man of dharma, O king, there is indeed auspicious, sinless offspring for you equal to the gods — this we know with divine sight.

**1.111.19**  O tiger among men, bring about here through action what is ordained by fate; a wise man, untroubled, obtains fruit without hardship.

**1.111.20**  When the fruit is thus seen, dear one, you should make the effort; having obtained offspring endowed with virtues, you will attain joy.

**1.111.21**  Vaishampayana said: Having heard those words of the ascetics, Pandu became deeply anxious, knowing that his own capacity for begetting had been destroyed by the curse of the deer.

**1.111.22**  He spoke in private to Kunti, his lawful wife of great renown, deliberating on the means for producing offspring in this difficult situation.

**1.111.23**  Offspring, O Kunti, is indeed the foundation in the worlds, joined to dharma — thus the wise have known from the beginning as the eternal dharma.

**1.111.24**  The sacrifice performed, the gift given, the austerity practiced, the vow duly observed — all of this is said here to bring no purification for the one without offspring.

**1.111.25**  Knowing this, O bright-smiling one, I see clearly, reflecting that I who am without offspring shall not attain the auspicious worlds.

**1.111.26**  My power of begetting has been destroyed by the curse of the deer, O timid one, for me of unrestrained self, a perpetrator of cruelty — destroyed as thoroughly as if it had been shattered.

**1.111.27**  In the view of dharma there are indeed six types of sons who are heirs of kinsmen, and six who are not heirs of kinsmen — hear them from me, O Pritha.

**1.111.28**  The self-born, the appointed, and the purchased son; the son of a remarried woman, the son born before marriage, and he who is born of a woman who goes freely.

**1.111.29**  The given, the bought, the adopted, and he who comes of his own accord; one carried in the womb at the time of marriage, one born from seed already deposited, and one maintained from a low womb.

**1.111.30**  In the absence of the prior and the most prior, understanding this, one should desire to obtain a son; inferior men seek a son from a superior man in adversity.

**1.111.31**  The good obtain the finest offspring that yields the fruit of dharma even from another's seed, O Pritha — so declared Manu Svayambhuva.

**1.111.32**  Therefore today I shall send you out, I myself being deficient in the power of begetting — know the offspring to be your own, O renowned one, from one equal to me or superior.

**1.111.33**  Hear also this story, O Kunti, concerning Sharadandayani, that wife of a hero who was appointed by her elders for the birth of offspring.

**1.111.34**  Purified in her season and bathed, O Kunti, at night at a crossroads, having chosen a perfected twice-born and offered oblations into the fire at the son-producing rite —

**1.111.35**  When that rite was concluded, she dwelt together with him; there she gave birth to three great warriors beginning with Durjaya.

**1.111.36**  In the same way, O auspicious one, by my command, go quickly to a Brahmin distinguished in austerity for the production of offspring.

**1.112.1**  Vaishampayana said: O great king, thus addressed, Kunti spoke to Pandu, that bull of the Kurus, the brave lord of the earth, her husband.

**1.112.2**  O knower of dharma, O lotus-eyed one, you should not speak to me like this in any way — to me your lawful wife who delights in you.

**1.112.3**  Rather, O mighty-armed one, O hero, O Bharata, you yourself shall beget on me offspring endowed with valor, in accordance with dharma.

**1.112.4**  I would go to heaven together with you, O tiger among men; come to me for the sake of offspring, O joy of the Kurus.

**1.112.5**  For I would not approach any other man even in thought apart from you; and who else is there in the world more excellent than you?

**1.112.6**  Now hear this ancient story rooted in dharma from me, O wide-eyed one, which I shall recount — a tale widely celebrated.

**1.112.7**  There was of old a king known as Vyushitashva, supremely devoted to righteousness, the extender of the lineage of Puru.

**1.112.8**  When that righteous and great-souled one was performing sacrifice, the gods together with Indra and the great sages came thither.

**1.112.9**  Indra became exhilarated with soma, and the twice-born with the sacrificial fees, at the great sacrifice of that royal sage Vyushitashva.

**1.112.10**  Then Vyushitashva, O king, shone beyond all mortals, surpassing all creatures as the sun surpasses them at the end of winter.

**1.112.11**  That best of kings, conquering and subduing the monarchs of the east, north, and the middle regions, brought the southern kings to submission.

**1.112.12**  At the great horse sacrifice, the valorous Vyushitashva, that lord of kings, was possessed of the strength of ten elephants.

**1.112.13**  Even now those who know the ancient lore sing this verse about him: Vyushitashva, having conquered this earth up to the shores of the sea, protected all the social orders as a father protects his own sons.

**1.112.14**  Performing great sacrifices, he gave wealth to the brahmins; having collected unlimited riches, he conducted great rites, pressed many soma-libations, and spread out soma ceremonies.

**1.112.15**  He had a wife most highly esteemed, Kakshivati's daughter, named Bhadra, O lord of men, unrivalled in beauty on earth.

**1.112.16**  They two loved each other passionately — so the tradition says; overcome with desire for her, he contracted consumption.

**1.112.17**  Before long he set like the sun, and when that lord of men was dead, his wife was overwhelmed with grief.

**1.112.18**  Childless, the deeply afflicted Bhadra lamented piteously — so we have heard; know this, O lord of men.

**1.112.19**  O best knower of dharma, every woman deprived of a son who lives without her husband does not truly live — she lives in misery.

**1.112.20**  For a woman, death without her husband is better, O bull among Kshatriyas; I wish to follow your path — be gracious and take me with you.

**1.112.21**  Bereft of you I cannot bear to live even a moment; show grace to me, O king, take me swiftly from here.

**1.112.22**  I shall follow behind you, O tiger among men, as you go on without turning back, through level and uneven paths alike.

**1.112.23**  Like a shadow that does not depart, O king, ever devoted to your will, I shall be, O tiger among men, always intent on your welfare and delight.

**1.112.24**  From this day forward, O king, terrible mental agonies that wither the heart will overwhelm me without you, O lotus-eyed one.

**1.112.25**  Surely in my misfortune, O king, unions with companions were severed in previous lives, or associations were broken.

**1.112.26**  And this sorrow born of separation from you has caught up with me now, O king — accumulated in former bodies by sinful deeds.

**1.112.27**  From this day forward, O king, I shall lie on a bed of kusha grass, filled with wretchedness, my whole aim set only upon seeing you again.

**1.112.28**  Show yourself to me, O tiger among men — to me who is wretched, helpless, miserable, and lamenting; be gracious, O lord of men.

**1.112.29**  While she thus lamented in many ways again and again and clasped that corpse, a disembodied voice is said to have spoken.

**1.112.30**  Rise, Bhadra; go — I will grant you a boon here; I shall beget offspring upon you, O fair-smiling one.

**1.112.31**  On my own bed, O fair-limbed one, on the fourteenth or the eighth night after your purifying bath at the appointed season, lie down with me.

**1.112.32**  Thus addressed, that goddess devoted to her husband did exactly as was said; Bhadra, desiring sons, did exactly as instructed.

**1.112.33**  That goddess bore sons by him — the corpse — O lord of men: three Shalvas and four sons of Madra, O best of the Bharatas.

**1.112.34**  In the same way you too, O bull of the Bharatas, are able by the power of austerity and spiritual discipline to beget sons in me by mental resolve alone.

**1.113.1**  Vaishampayana said: Thus addressed by her, the king, that knower of dharma, spoke again to that goddess this most excellent speech in accordance with righteousness.

**1.113.2**  Exactly so did Vyushitashva act in former times, O Kunti, as you have described, O auspicious one — for he was like an immortal.

**1.113.3**  But now I shall speak of this dharma — hear it from me: the ancient usage seen by the great-souled knowers of dharma among the seers.

**1.113.4**  Women were unrestrained in former times, O fair-faced one, roaming freely as they pleased, independent, O lovely-eyed one.

**1.113.5**  When they went to other men from girlhood, apart from their husbands, O blessed one, there was no unrighteousness, O fair-limbed one — for that was the law in ancient times.

**1.113.6**  Even today creatures born in animal wombs follow that ancient law, free from desire and aversion; this dharma as seen by the ancients is still honored by the great seers.

**1.113.7**  Among the Northern Kurus even today that eternal dharma prevails, O Rambhoru, which confers freedom on women.

**1.113.8**  But in this world not long ago this boundary-rule was established, O pure-smiled one — hear from me at length by whom and for what reason.

**1.113.9**  There was a great seer named Uddalaka — so we have heard; his son, the sage who became known as Shvetaketu.

**1.113.10**  This boundary-rule was established by him among humans — so we have heard — out of anger, O lotus-eyed one; hear from me the reason for it.

**1.113.11**  Before Shvetaketu's very eyes, a brahmin took his mother by the hand in his father's presence and said, "Let us go."

**1.113.12**  The son of the seer then became angry and indignant when he saw his mother being led away thus as if by force.

**1.113.13**  Seeing him enraged, his father said to Shvetaketu: "Do not be angry, my son — this is the eternal law."

**1.113.14**  "For the women of all social orders are unrestrained on earth, my son; just as cattle are, so are people, each within their own social order."

**1.113.15**  But the seer's son Shvetaketu could not accept that law, and he established this boundary-rule for men and women on earth.

**1.113.16**  Among humans, O greatly blessed one, but not among other creatures — from that time this rule has been established, so we have heard.

**1.113.17**  From this day forward, for a woman who goes to another man abandoning her husband, the sin shall be equal to the slaying of an embryo — a painful transgression.

**1.113.18**  Likewise for a man who violates a woman who was chaste from girlhood and devoted to her husband, this same sin will apply on earth.

**1.113.19**  And for the wife who is directed by her husband for the purpose of offspring yet refuses to comply, this same sin will befall her as well.

**1.113.20**  Thus in ancient times this righteous boundary-rule was forcibly established, O timid one, by Shvetaketu, the son of Uddalaka.

**1.113.21**  And Madayanti, O Rambhoru, appointed for the production of offspring, went to the seer Vasishtha by Saudasa's direction — so we have heard.

**1.113.22**  From this she received a son named Ashmaka, that beautiful woman, the wife of Kalmashapada, desiring to please her husband.

**1.113.23**  Our own birth is also known to you, O lotus-eyed one — that we were born of Krishna Dvaipayana for the flourishing of the Kuru lineage, O timid one.

**1.113.24**  Considering all these reasons, you ought to carry out this righteous request of mine, O blameless one.

**1.113.25**  "A husband should not be disobeyed by his wife in each fertile season, O princess devoted to your vow" — thus those who know dharma know this law.

**1.113.26**  In all other remaining times, a woman indeed is entitled to independence — good people describe this as the ancient dharma.

**1.113.27**  Whatever a husband commands his wife, O princess, whether righteous or even unrighteous, that must be carried out accordingly — so those who know dharma declare.

**1.113.28**  Especially one who is eager for sons yet is himself lacking in the power of procreation — as I am, O blameless-limbed one, longing to behold a son.
