**1.147.21**  Saying 'Do not weep, father; do not weep, mother; do not weep, sister,' he approached them one by one, seeming almost to smile.

**1.147.22**  Then he picked up a blade of grass and, joyful, spoke again: 'With this I shall slay that man-eating Rakshasa!'

**1.147.23**  Even so, hearing those indistinct words of the child, great joy arose among them who were overcome with grief.

**1.147.24**  Recognizing that the moment had come, Kunti approached them — as if reviving those at the point of death with nectar — and spoke these words.

**1.148.1**  Kunti said: I wish to know the root cause of this grief in truth; and having known it, I would remove it, if it can indeed be removed.

**1.148.2**  The Brahmin said: What you say, O rich in austerity, is fitting for those who are good; yet this grief cannot be dispelled by a human being.

**1.148.3**  Near this city there lives a Rakshasa named Baka, who is the lord of this countryside and of this town, and who is of great might.

**1.148.4**  Nourished on human flesh, evil-minded, a devourer of men, this powerful one perpetually protects this countryside from other demons.

**1.148.5**  Attended by the power of that demon, both the city and the country are protected — because of him we have no fear from enemy armies or from spirits.

**1.148.6**  His appointed wage has been fixed: a cartload of rice, two buffaloes, and a single man — whoever carries that food goes to him.

**1.148.7**  Each family in turn delivers that food; the rotation comes around again only after many years, yet it costs men their lives — a burden impossible to bear.

**1.148.8**  And those men who have anywhere tried to liberate themselves from this — the demon has killed them together with their wives and children and devoured them.

**1.148.9**  The king dwelling in the Vetrakīya house has not adopted a policy here by which the lasting welfare of these people could be assured today.

**1.148.10**  We who live under the dominion of this weak man, constantly full of dread, sheltering under a bad king — we deserve precisely this fate.

**1.148.11**  To whom should brahmins speak, or those who wander as they please? These men of virtue are tamed by their own good qualities, like free-flying birds caught in a snare.

**1.148.12**  One should first find a king, then a wife, then wealth; and when those three are secured, one can then support one's kinsmen and children.

**1.148.13**  But I have acquired all three of these in the wrong order — and having now reached this calamity, we shall suffer greatly.

**1.148.14**  This turn — the destroyer of our family — has now come round to us; I must deliver as his wage one man along with the food.

**1.148.15**  I have no money anywhere to purchase a man, nor can I in any way give a friend; I see no way of escape from that demon.

**1.148.16**  Sunk thus deeply in this vast, uncrossable ocean of grief, I shall go today together with these relatives to the demon — and then that wretched creature will devour all of us together.

**1.149.1**  Kuntī said: You must not give way to despair or to any fear on our account — a means of deliverance from that demon has been perceived here.

**1.149.2**  You have one young son, one ascetic daughter, and your wife — I do not favour the going of any of those three there.

**1.149.3**  I have five sons, O brahmin; one of them shall go on your behalf, carrying the food-offering for that wicked demon.

**1.149.4**  The brahmin said: I will not do this — not for my own life's sake, not under any circumstances — this severing of a brahmin guest from his life for my own benefit.

**1.149.5**  Not even among those of ignoble birth or unrighteous conduct is such a thing found — that one would sacrifice oneself or one's own child for the sake of a brahmin.

**1.149.6**  I hold it my duty to seek my own good; and whether it be the sin of killing a brahmin or the killing of myself, the death of myself is better for me.

**1.149.7**  The killing of a brahmin is the supreme sin, and there is no expiation for it; even if done without prior intent, my own death is better for me.

**1.149.8**  Yet I do not myself desire my own death, O auspicious one — when death is brought about by others, no sin whatsoever falls on me.

**1.149.9**  In the deliberate killing of a brahmin by me I see no expiation; it is both cruel and base.

**1.149.10**  To abandon one who has come to one's house, likewise one who has sought shelter, and to cause the death of one who is supplicating — these are considered the ultimate cruelty.

**1.149.11**  "One should never perform a censurable or cruel act" — so the great-souled men of former times, who knew the dharma of emergencies, have declared.

**1.149.12**  But my own destruction today, together with my wife, is better — I will not in any way consent to the killing of a brahmin.

**1.149.13**  Kuntī said: My own resolve too is firm, O brahmin — brahmins must be protected; nor would a son be unwanted by me even if I had a hundred sons.

**1.149.14**  And that demon is not capable of destroying my son — my son is mighty, accomplished through sacred formulas, and full of blazing energy.

**1.149.15**  He will deliver all that food to the demon and will free himself — such is my firm conviction.

**1.149.16**  For demons — powerful, huge-bodied — have met that hero before and have been seen by him, and many have been slain by him.

**1.149.17**  But this must not be told to anyone at all, O brahmin — for those in pursuit of learning would, out of curiosity, interfere with my sons.

**1.149.18**  "That son of mine who has not been released by his guru should not employ that power" — such is the view of the righteous.

**1.149.19**  Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed by Pṛthā, that brahmin together with his wife, rejoicing, honoured her speech as equal to nectar.

**1.149.20**  Then Kuntī and the brahmin together addressed the son of the Wind: "Do it" — and he answered them: "So be it."

**1.150.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: When Bhīma had pledged "I shall do it," O descendant of Bharata, all the Pāṇḍavas then returned, having collected their alms.

**1.150.2**  Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pāṇḍu, reading the situation from Bhīma's very bearing, sat apart alone and then questioned his mother.

**1.150.3**  "What deed does this Bhīma of terrible valour intend to do? Is this that he wishes to do here done with your consent?"

**1.150.4**  Kuntī said: At my own bidding this scorcher of foes will perform a great deed — for the sake of the brahmin and for the deliverance of the city.

**1.150.5**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: What rash and reckless wrong has been done by you? Good men do not praise the abandonment of a son.

**1.150.6**  How can you wish to abandon your own son for the sake of another's? What you have done by giving up a son is contrary to the practice of the world.

**1.150.7**  Relying on whose arms we all sleep in comfort — it is by relying on them that we hope to win back the kingdom stolen by wicked men.

**1.150.8**  Thinking on whose valour — his, of boundless might — Duryodhana spends all his nights sleepless with grief, together with Śakuni.

**1.150.9**  By the valour of this hero we were freed from the house of lac; and from other wicked men too, and Purоcana was slain.

**1.150.10**  Relying on whose might we think it possible to gain this earth full of riches — after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

**1.150.11**  Resorting to what reasoning have you decided to abandon him? Has your mind perhaps been deranged by grief — have you lost your senses?

**1.150.12**  Kuntī said: Yudhiṣṭhira, you must have no anguish regarding Vṛkodara — nor has this resolve been made by me out of weakness of mind.

**1.150.13**  Here in the brahmin's house, my son, we have dwelt in comfort; this repayment to him has been carefully considered by me. Only so great a person is one in whom a good deed is not lost.

**1.150.14**  Having seen Bhīma's great heroism in the house of lac at that time, and also from the slaying of Hiḍimba — my trust in Vṛkodara is firm.

**1.150.15**  For the strength of Bhīma's arms is great — equal to ten thousand elephants — by which you, resembling great elephants yourselves, were carried out from Vāraṇāvata.

**1.150.16**  There is no other equal to Vṛkodara in strength — there has been none, nor shall there be — who could rise against even the greatest in battle, even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself.

**1.150.17**  Long ago, when he was just born, he fell from my lap onto a mountain — because of the heaviness of his body, the rock was shattered by his limbs.

**1.150.18**  Recalling that, O Pāṇḍava, with discernment — Bhīma's strength — and also the brahmin's need for repayment, I then formed this resolve.

**1.150.19**  This was not decided out of greed, nor out of ignorance, nor out of delusion — my effort for dharma has been undertaken with full deliberation.

**1.150.20**  Two purposes will both be accomplished, Yudhiṣṭhira: repayment for our lodging, and the practice of great dharma.

**1.150.21**  "A kṣatriya who ever renders assistance to a brahmin in his needs attains auspicious worlds" — thus have I heard.

**1.150.22**  A kṣatriya who brings about the liberation from death even of another kṣatriya alone wins great fame in this world and in the next.

**1.150.23**  And a kṣatriya who renders assistance even to a vaiśya in battle will assuredly delight the people in all the worlds.

**1.150.24**  And a king who saves a śūdra who has come seeking refuge — he gains birth here in a family that is prosperous and honoured by kings.

**1.150.25**  So the blessed Vyāsa, that wise man, declared this very clearly long ago, O joy of the Kuru line — therefore this is what I intend to do.

**1.150.26**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: This is fitting, mother — what you have done with full deliberation, out of compassion for a brahmin in distress. Bhīma will certainly return after slaying the man-eater.

**1.150.27**  But the brahmin must be instructed and carefully persuaded in such a way that the townspeople do not come to know of this.

**1.151.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then, when the night had passed, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena took the food and went to the place where that man-eater dwelt.

**1.151.2**  And having reached the forest of that demon, the mighty Pāṇḍava called out to him by name, helping himself to the food.

**1.151.3**  Then that demon, hearing Bhīmasena's words, came in a great rage to where Bhīma stood.

**1.151.4**  Huge-bodied and of immense speed, seeming to cleave the earth, having drawn his brows into a three-peaked frown and biting his lip —

**1.151.5**  — seeing Bhīmasena eating the food, that demon, furious, opened wide his eyes and spoke these words:

**1.151.6**  "Who is this fool of corrupt mind who eats this food prepared for me, before my very eyes — who wishes to go to the abode of Yama?"

**1.151.7**  But Bhīmasena, hearing that, O Bhārata, as if laughing, paid no heed to that demon and ate on, turning his back to him.

**1.151.8**  Then, raising both his arms and uttering a terrible roar, that man-eater charged at Bhīmasena, intending to kill him.

**1.151.9**  Even then, utterly disregarding him and not looking at the demon, Vṛkodara, the Pāṇḍava, slayer of enemy heroes, simply went on eating the food.

**1.151.10**  Filled with wrath, the demon stood behind Kuntī's son and struck him on the back with both his palms.

**1.151.11**  Though struck hard on the back by that powerful being with his palms, Bhīma did not even glance at the demon — he simply went on eating.

**1.151.12**  Then, enraged still further, that mighty demon seized a tree and charged at Bhīma again, intending to strike him.

**1.151.13**  Then Bhīma, that bull among men, finished eating the food at his leisure, sipped water, and stood up in the field of battle, greatly pleased — that mighty-armed one.

**1.151.14**  The valiant Bhīma caught the tree hurled by the enraged demon with his left hand, as if laughing, O Bhārata.

**1.151.15**  Then that mighty one lifted up many more trees of various kinds and flung them at Bhīmasena — and the Pāṇḍava Bhīma flung them back at him.

**1.151.16**  That battle of trees — great, terrible in form, devastating to the forest — took place between Baka and the Pāṇḍava, O great king.

**1.151.17**  Then Baka, shouting his name aloud, rushed at the Pāṇḍava and seized mighty Bhīmasena with both his arms.

**1.151.18**  And Bhīmasena too, great-armed and mighty, threw his arms around that demon and, as he struggled with great force, dragged him away by sheer power.

**1.151.19**  Dragged by Bhīma and dragging the Pāṇḍava in turn, that man-eater was overcome by extreme exhaustion.

**1.151.20**  By their great force the earth trembled, and they pulverised the mighty trees standing around them.

**1.151.21**  But seeing that demon weakening, O bull of the Bharatas, Vṛkodara pressed him down onto the ground with both his hands and struck him.

**1.151.22**  Then pressing down on its back with his knee, he forcibly seized the demon's neck with his right arm.

**1.151.23**  And with his left hand grasping the demon by the waist and garment, the Pandava bent that rakshasa double, while it roared terrifying cries.

**1.151.24**  Then blood poured from the mouth of that fearsome demon, O lord of men, as it was broken apart by Bhima.

**1.152.1**  Vaishampayana said: Terrified by that sound, O king, the household of that demon rushed out of the house together with all its attendants.

**1.152.2**  The mighty Bhima, foremost among warriors, pacified those who were frightened and bewildered, and made them agree to a covenant.

**1.152.3**  "Never again shall you harm human beings here at any time; for those who harm others shall meet swift death just like this," he declared.

**1.152.4**  Hearing those words, O Bharata, those demons said "So be it" to him and accepted that covenant.

**1.152.5**  From that time forward, O Bharata, only gentle demons appeared in that town, seen by the men who dwelt in the city.

**1.152.6**  Then Bhima, taking up that man-eating demon whose life had departed, threw it down at the city gate and departed undetected.

**1.152.7**  Then that Bhima, having slain the demon, went to that brahmin's dwelling and reported to the king everything that had happened, omitting nothing.

**1.152.8**  Then people came out of the city in the early morning and saw the demon lying slain on the ground, drenched in blood.

**1.152.9**  Others went to Ekachakra and spread the news of that demon lying sprawled out, resembling a mountain peak, frightful to behold.

**1.152.10**  Then thousands of people from the city, O king, came there to see Baka — men, women, elders, and children alike.

**1.152.11**  Then all of them, amazed upon seeing that superhuman feat, worshipped the gods, every single one of them, O lord of men.

**1.152.12**  Then they began to reckon whose turn it was that day to supply food; and learning this, all of them came to that brahmin and asked him about it.

**1.152.13**  Questioned thus many times, and still protecting the Pandavas, that foremost of brahmins then spoke these words to all the townspeople.

**1.152.14**  "As I was ordered to provide food and was weeping together with my kinsmen, a certain brahmin of great power, perfected in sacred formulas, saw me."

**1.152.15**  "Having first asked me about my distress and the town's affliction, that best of brahmins consoled me and, smiling slightly, said:"

**1.152.16**  "'I shall deliver this food to that evil-souled one myself; on my account there is no cause for fear,' said that heroic one."

**1.152.17**  "He took that food and went toward the forest of Baka — by him surely this deed has been done for the welfare of the world."

**1.152.18**  Then all those brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras, filled with great wonder and joy, celebrated a festival in honor of the brahmins.

**1.152.19**  Then all the country folk came to the city to see that most wondrous event, while the sons of Pritha continued to dwell there.

**1.153.1**  Janamejaya said: After those tiger-like men had slain the demon Baka, O brahmin, what did the Pandavas do from that time onward?

**1.153.2**  Vaishampayana said: They continued to dwell there, O king, after slaying the demon Baka, studying the highest sacred texts in the brahmin's abode.

**1.153.3**  Then after a few days, a brahmin of sharpened vows came to that brahmin's house seeking lodging.

**1.153.4**  That learned foremost of brahmins, always devoted to the vow of hospitality to all guests, honored him properly and gave him lodging.

**1.153.5**  Then all those Pandavas, bulls among men, together with Kunti, sat in attendance upon that brahmin as he was narrating stories.

**1.153.6**  He spoke of various lands, various sacred pilgrimage sites, various conduct and practices of kings, and various ancient cities.

**1.153.7**  At the end of his narratives there, O Janamejaya, that brahmin described the wondrous swayamvara of Yajnaseni among the Panchalas.

**1.153.8**  He described the birth of Dhrishtadyumna, the birth of Shikhandi, and the womb-less origin of Krishna (Draupadi) at Drupada's great sacrifice.

**1.153.9**  Having heard that most wondrous account of that great-souled man, those bulls among men asked him to tell the story in full detail.

**1.153.10**  "How was the wondrous birth of Drupada's son Dhrishtadyumna from fire? And how was the wondrous birth of Krishna from the midst of the sacrificial altar?"

**1.153.11**  "How did Dhrishtadyumna learn all weapons from the great archer Drona? And how were those two dear friends separated, and by whose doing?"

**1.153.12**  Thus prompted by those bulls among men, O king, that brahmin then narrated everything regarding the birth of Draupadi.

**1.154.1**  The brahmin said: Near the gateway to the Ganga there lived a great sage of great austerities — Bharadvaja, supremely wise and ever firm in his vows.

**1.154.2**  He went to bathe in the Ganga, and there the sage saw the apsara Ghritachi, who had arrived earlier and was bathing.

**1.154.3**  The wind carried away her garment on the river bank at that moment; seeing her with her clothing torn away, the sage was overcome with desire.

**1.154.4**  The mind of that celibate who had practiced chastity from boyhood became attached to her; overcome with rapture, his seed fell — and the sage Drona held it in a vessel.

**1.154.5**  From that, the boy Drona was born of that wise man; he studied the Vedas and all the Vedic auxiliaries in their entirety.

**1.154.6**  Now a king named Prishata was a friend of Bharadvaja; and of him too there was born a son named Drupada at that time.

**1.154.7**  That son of Prishata, bull among kshatriyas, would always go to the hermitage and together with Drona would sport and study.

**1.154.8**  After Prishata passed away, Drupada became king; and Drona heard that Rama was giving away all his wealth.

**1.154.9**  To Rama who was departing to the forest, the son of Bharadvaja said: "Know me, O best of twice-born, as Drona, who has come seeking wealth."

**1.154.10**  Rama said: Only my body alone remains to me now as my possession; choose either my weapons or my body, O brahmin — one or the other.

**1.154.11**  Drona said: You should give me all weapons, together with their means of withdrawal, and the method of application of each and every one of them.

**1.154.12**  The brahmin said: Saying "So be it," the son of Bhrigu thereupon gave them to him; having received them, Drona then considered his purpose accomplished.

**1.154.13**  Overjoyed in heart, having received from Rama the most excellent Brahmastra, he became superior to all men.

**1.154.14**  Then the powerful son of Bharadvaja, tiger among men, approached Drupada and said: "Know me as your friend."

**1.154.15**  Drupada said: A non-vedic scholar cannot be the friend of a vedic scholar; a non-chariot-warrior cannot be the friend of a chariot-warrior; nor can a non-king be the friend of a king — what does this former friendship matter?

**1.154.16**  The brahmin said: Having decided in his mind, that wise man set out toward Panchala and went to the city of the chief Kurus, called Nagasahvaya (Hastinapura).

**1.154.17**  Bhishma, upon his arrival, gave the wise Drona his grandsons along with various riches, as pupils.

**1.154.18**  Then the learned Drona, having assembled all his pupils, spoke these words for the purpose of bringing grief to Drupada:

**1.154.19**  "Something in the way of a teacher's fee turns over in my heart; when you have mastered weapons, that should be given — tell me truly, O sinless ones."

**1.154.20**  And when all the Pandavas had mastered weapons and completed their training, Drona spoke these words again regarding the teacher's fee:

**1.154.21**  "Let the kingdom of Drupada, son of Prishata, ruler of Chatravati, be swiftly seized and given to me."

**1.154.22**  Then the five sons of Pandu, having defeated Drupada in battle, brought him bound together with his ministers before Drona.

**1.154.23**  Drona said: "I desire friendship with you once again, O lord of men; for it is said that a non-king cannot deserve to be friend to a king."

**1.154.24**  "Therefore I have striven in your kingdom, O Yajnasena; you are king of the southern bank of the Bhagirathi, and I of the northern."

**1.154.25**  The brahmin said: That great insult never left the king's heart even for a moment; downcast in mind, he grew thin.

**1.155.1**  The brahmin said: King Drupada, burning with resentment, wandered through many brahmin hermitages seeking twice-born men accomplished in ritual action.

**1.155.2**  Desiring the birth of a son, his mind stricken with grief, he would always brood: "I have no excellent offspring."

**1.155.3**  In his despair he would curse even his born sons, saying "Shame on my kinsmen," and he was given over to sighing, desiring to requite Drona.

**1.155.4**  Reflecting on Drona's might, discipline, training, and conduct, and on his own kshatriya strength, that best of kings, O Bharata, could find no way to requite him despite his efforts.

**1.155.5**  Wandering on the banks of the Kalmashin near the Ganga, that lord of the earth came upon a holy brahmin hermitage.

**1.155.6**  There was no one who had not completed his studentship, no twice-born without a vow, and likewise none without high merit; and he saw two who were firm in their vows.

**1.155.7**  The son of Prishata saw the two brahmin-sages Yaja and Upayaja, who were at rest, engaged in the study of the sacred collection, both belonging to the Kashyapa lineage.

**1.155.8**  Those two best of sages, fit brahmins for conducting a rite of passage, he addressed with all manner of desirable things, tirelessly.

**1.155.9**  Perceiving the power and intelligence of both, he took the younger aside privately and approached Upayaja, who was firm in his vows, pleasing him with gifts.

**1.155.10**  Engaged in the service of his feet, speaking sweetly, giving him all his desires, he honored Upayaja duly and spoke to him:

**1.155.11**  "O brahmin, O Upayaja, by whatever rite a son might be born to me for the death of Drona — for that performed, I shall give you ten million cows."

**1.155.12**  "Or whatever else, O best of twice-born, may be deeply pleasing to your mind — all of that I shall give you; there is no doubt about this."

**1.155.13**  Thus addressed, the sage replied "Not I" — and Drupada, wishing to propitiate him, attended upon him again.

**1.155.14**  Then at the end of a year, that best of twice-born, Upayaja, spoke to Drupada, O king, at the right moment in a sweet voice:

**1.155.15**  "My elder brother, while wandering by a forest stream, picked up a fruit that had fallen to the ground whose purity was uncertain."

**1.155.16**  "I observed that improper action of my brother following him along, and I thought: he would never show discrimination in taking something impure."

**1.155.17**  "Seeing only the fruit, he did not notice the faults that attend it; one who does not discriminate purity — how could he do so in other matters?"

**1.155.18**  "He who, while studying the sacred texts and dwelling in his teacher's household, always eats the leftover alms-food of others, ever and again praising the merits of food and without shame —"

**1.155.19**  "I consider my brother to be one who seeks mere material fruit, by the eye of reasoning; go to him, O king — he will perform the sacrifice for you."

**1.155.20**  The king, though feeling a certain repugnance, reflected on this in his mind; having heard Upayaja's words, that king who knew all dharma duly honored the worthy sage Yaja and spoke to him:

**1.155.21**  "I shall give eighty thousand cows — perform the sacrifice for me, O lord; you ought to gladden me who am scorched by enmity toward Drona."

**1.155.22**  For he is the foremost among those who know the Brahman, and peerless in the Brahma-weapon as well; it was for this reason that Droṇa defeated me in that conflict with my friend.

**1.155.23**  There is no warrior anywhere on earth who is his equal, no one who stands foremost — that wise Bhāradvāja, the chief preceptor of the Kauravas.

**1.155.24**  Droṇa's volleys of arrows strip away both life and body, and his bow — six cubits long — appears vast and without equal.

**1.155.25**  That great-souled great archer Bhāradvāja, with the force of a Brahmin, checks without doubt the force of the warrior class.

**1.155.26**  Stationed like Jāmadagnya, he is ordained for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas; his terrible power of arms is indeed irresistible by men on earth.

**1.155.27**  Pouring forth Brahmic energy like a fire fed with oblations, he consumes the warrior class in battle with the Brahman going before him; and when Brahmin and Kṣatriya power are ranged against each other, Brahmic energy prevails.

**1.155.28**  I, fallen short in the power of the warrior class and seeking Brahmic energy, have come to you — superior even to Droṇa and the most learned of those who know the Brahman.

**1.155.29**  I wish to obtain a son who will be Droṇa's death-in-battle, unconquerable in war — perform this rite for me, O Yāja; I will give you a hundred million cows.

**1.155.30**  Yāja agreed, saying 'so be it,' and prepared for the sacrifice on behalf of the patron; for the teacher's sake he also urged Upayāja, who was unwilling; and Yāja thus pledged himself for Droṇa's destruction.

**1.155.31**  Then the great ascetic Upayāja explained to that lord of men the sacrificial rite that would yield a son as its fruit.

**1.155.32**  "The son you desire — O king, one of great heroism, great energy and great strength — shall be just such a one as you wish."

**1.155.33**  With the intention of obtaining the slayer of Bhāradvāja's son, king Drupada had all of that duly carried out for the success of the rite.

**1.155.34**  Then at the end of the oblation Yāja called out to the queen: "Come to me, O queen Pṛṣatī — a pair is ready awaiting you."

**1.155.35**  The queen said: "My face is anointed, O Brahmin, and I bear sacred fragrances upon me; I am detained on account of my desire for a son — wait for me, O Yāja, my dear."

**1.155.36**  Yāja said: "The oblation has been cooked by Yāja and consecrated by Upayāja — how can it fail to fulfil your wish? Come, O Brahmin lady, or stay as you will."

**1.155.37**  The narrator said: When Yāja had spoken thus, and the oblation had been poured and duly sanctified, a boy resembling a god arose from that fire.

**1.155.38**  Flame-colored, of terrible aspect, wearing a diadem and bearing the finest armor, sword in hand, arrow-equipped, bow in hand, he roared again and again.

**1.155.39**  He mounted a splendid chariot and set out in it; then the Pāñcālas shouted in delight, "Excellent! Excellent!"

**1.155.40**  "This prince, dispeller of fear, bringer of glory to the Pāñcālas, dispeller of the king's grief — he is born truly for the slaying of Droṇa!" — so said a great invisible being that moved through the sky at that time.

**1.155.41**  A maiden of Pāñcāla also arose from the midst of the sacrificial altar — lovely, beautiful of limb, slender-waisted, and delightful.

**1.155.42**  Dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals, curling dark hair, she bore a human form yet was visibly of celestial beauty.

**1.155.43**  From her wafted the fragrance of a blue lotus, perceptible from a league away; she bore supreme beauty for which there was no comparison on earth.

**1.155.44**  And as she of lovely hips was born, a bodiless voice spoke: "This Kṛṣṇā, foremost of all women, will bring about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas."

**1.155.45**  "This slender-waisted one will in time accomplish the work of the gods; on her account a great terror will arise among the Kṣatriyas."

**1.155.46**  Hearing this, all the Pāñcālas roared like a pride of lions; the earth could not bear those who were filled with such joy.

**1.155.47**  Seeing the two, Pṛṣatī — who had desired children — approached Yāja, saying: "Let these two know no other mother than me."

**1.155.48**  Yāja said "so be it" to her, wishing to please the king; and the twice-born, their hearts full of joy, gave names to the two.

**1.155.49**  "Because of his boldness and exceeding audacity, and because he arose from the sacred fire's brilliance, let this boy of Drupada be called Dhṛṣṭadyumna."

**1.155.50**  They called the girl Kṛṣṇā, for she was dark of complexion. Thus that twin pair was born at Drupada's great sacrifice.

**1.155.51**  Taking Dhṛṣṭadyumna of Pāñcāla into his own residence, the powerful Bhāradvāja trained him in the use of weapons.

**1.155.52**  The great-minded Droṇa, understanding that what is destined cannot be escaped, did this nonetheless — to preserve his own glory.

**1.156.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, the sons of Kuntī became as if pierced by lances, and those great warriors were all unsettled in mind.

**1.156.2**  Then Kuntī, seeing her sons distraught and out of their senses, spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira — she who ever speaks the truth.

**1.156.3**  "We have lodged here for a long time in the dwelling of the Brahmin, taking our pleasure in this delightful city and obtaining our alms, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**1.156.4**  All the lovely forests and groves here have been seen again and again, O subduer of enemies.

**1.156.5**  Seen again and again, they no longer delight us as before; and alms too are not obtained as they were, O hero, O joy of the Kurus.

**1.156.6**  Let us go to Pāñcāla — if you think it good; we shall see things never seen before, my son, and it will be delightful.

**1.156.7**  The Pāñcālas are said to be prosperous, O you who wear down enemies, and that king Yajñasena too we have heard is devoted to Brahmins.

**1.156.8**  Long dwelling in one place is not good, and is not my view; let us go there to Pāñcāla — if you think so, my son."

**1.156.9**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Whatever you consider should be done is our highest good; as for my younger brothers, I know not whether they will go or not."

**1.156.10**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kuntī spoke of the journey to Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the twins, and they too said "so be it" at that time.

**1.156.11**  Then, O king, Kuntī took leave of that Brahmin and set out together with her sons for the lovely city of the great-souled Drupada.

**1.157.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While those great-souled Pāṇḍavas were dwelling in disguise, Vyāsa the son of Satyavatī came to see them.

**1.157.2**  Seeing him arrive, those scorchers of enemies went forward to meet him, bowed down to him and greeted him, and then stood with hands joined in reverence.

**1.157.3**  Having given them all leave to be seated, the sage, pleased and honored by the sons of Pṛthā, spoke these words with affection.

**1.157.4**  "Are you conducting yourselves according to dharma and the scriptures, O scorchers of enemies? Is your reverence toward the Brahmins who deserve reverence not diminishing?"

**1.157.5**  Having spoken words full of righteousness and purpose, and various other stories, that blessed sage then spoke again as follows.

**1.157.6**  "In a forest of asceticism there was once the daughter of a great-souled sage — slender-waisted, lovely-hipped, with beautiful brows, endowed with every virtue.

**1.157.7**  Yet through deeds done by herself she became ill-fated; that virtuous and beautiful maiden found no husband.

**1.157.8**  Unhappy, she then undertook to practice austerities for the sake of a husband, and with severe asceticism she propitiated Śaṃkara.

**1.157.9**  The blessed god, pleased with her, spoke to that ascetic woman: 'Choose a boon, fair one — good fortune to you; I am the giver of boons.'

**1.157.10**  Then she spoke to the Lord what was beneficial for her: 'I desire a husband endowed with every virtue' — she said this again and again.

**1.157.11**  Then the Lord, the best of speakers, replied to her: 'Five husbands shall be yours, O auspicious one' — so said Śaṃkara.

**1.157.12**  As she replied 'Give me one husband, O Śaṃkara,' he said to her once again these excellent words, O god:

**1.157.13**  'You have said to me five times \"give me a husband\"; when you have passed into another body, what I have said shall come to pass.'

**1.157.14**  'That maiden of divine appearance, born in Drupada's family — the blameless Kṛṣṇā Pārṣatī — is appointed as your wife.'

**1.157.15**  'Therefore enter the city of Pāñcāla, O men of great might; having obtained her you will be happy — there is no doubt.'

**1.157.16**  Having spoken thus, that most blessed grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas, the great ascetic, took leave of the sons of Pṛthā and Kuntī and departed.

**1.158.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those bulls among men, scorchers of enemies, set out with their mother placed in front, following level northward roads as directed.

**1.158.2**  Traveling for a day and a night, those tigers among men, the sons of Pāṇḍu, reached the Somaśravāyaṇa ford on the Gaṅgā.

**1.158.3**  Lifting up a firebrand, the greatly famous Dhanaṃjaya went in front of them — to give light and for protection.

**1.158.4**  There, in the lovely waters of the Gaṅgā in a secluded spot, the jealous king of Gandharvas had come for water-sports, sporting with women.

**1.158.5**  He heard the sound of them approaching the river; possessed by that sound, that powerful one became extremely angry.

**1.158.6**  Seeing the Pāṇḍavas there together with their mother, those scorchers of enemies, he twanged his terrible bow and spoke these words.

**1.158.7**  "The terrible twilight that glows red at the coming of the early night — that moment, they say, is lacking eighty truṭas of the full period.

**1.158.8**  That time is ordained for the free movement of Yakṣas, Gandharvas and Rākṣasas; what remains besides is remembered here as the time for men to move at will.

**1.158.9**  Those foolish men who out of greed roam about at those hours — together with the Rākṣasas we seize and restrain those who transgress.

**1.158.10**  Those who know the Brahman censure all men who approach the water at night — even the powerful, even kings.

**1.158.11**  Stand far off — do not approach near to me! Why do you not recognize me who has come to the waters of the Bhāgīrathī?

**1.158.12**  Know me to be the Gandharva Aṅgāraparṇa, one who relies on his own strength; I am proud and jealous, and the beloved friend of Kubera.

**1.158.13**  This forest of mine is known as Aṅgāraparṇa — the beautiful one along the Gaṅgā and the Vākā — where I dwell.

**1.158.14**  Neither ghosts nor horned beasts, neither gods nor human beings approach this place — why then do you approach it?"

**1.158.15**  Arjuna said: "On the ocean, on the slopes of Himavat, or on this river, O wicked-minded one — whose domain is established for the night, the day, or the twilight?

**1.158.16**  We are endowed with power and do not fear you even at an improper time; it is those who are powerless that honor you in a moment of danger.

**1.158.17**  "Of old this Gaṅgā issued forth from Himavat's golden peak, and flowing to the ocean's waters divides itself into seven streams.

**1.158.18**  And again, flowing pure as one stream through the sky, this Gaṅgā attains among the gods, O Gandharva, the form of the Alakanandā.

**1.158.19**  In the same way, for the ancestors she becomes the Vaitaraṇī, impassable by those of wicked deeds, O Gandharva — as Dvaipāyana has declared.

**1.158.20**  This unobstructed, auspicious divine river that leads to heaven — how do you wish to block it? This is not eternal dharma.

**1.158.21**  How should we not touch at will the sacred waters of the Bhāgīrathī, which cannot be stopped and is unobstructed — how can your words prevent us?"

**1.158.22**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that, Aṅgāraparṇa in fury bent his bow and discharged blazing arrows like venomous serpents.

**1.158.23**  Swiftly whirling the firebrand and raising his excellent shield, Dhananjaya — the Pandava — deflected every single arrow of his.

**1.158.24**  Arjuna said: O gandharva, this terror of yours is not deployed against those who know the science of weapons; when directed at those who do know it, it dissolves like foam.

**1.158.25**  I regard all gandharvas as surpassing ordinary men, O gandharva; therefore I shall fight with a divine weapon, and not with illusion.

**1.158.26**  Long ago, O gandharva, Brihaspati — son of the guru of Shatakratu — bestowed this fire weapon upon Bharadvaja.

**1.158.27**  From Bharadvaja it passed to Agnivesha, and from Agnivesha to my guru; that foremost of brahmanas, Drona, gave it to me.

**1.158.28**  Vaishampayana said: Having spoken thus, the Pandava, filled with wrath, released the blazing fire weapon at the gandharva, and it set his chariot ablaze.

**1.158.29**  That mighty gandharva was left without a chariot, utterly undone, bewildered by the brilliance of the weapon, and fell forward face downward.

**1.158.30**  Dhananjaya seized him by his garlanded hair and dragged him — rendered senseless by the fall of the weapon — toward his brothers.

**1.158.31**  His wife, named Kumbhinasi, seeking refuge and desiring to save her husband, threw herself before Yudhishthira as a suppliant.

**1.158.32**  The gandharva woman said: Save me, O great king, and release this husband of mine! I am a gandharva woman who has come to you for refuge — I am named Kumbinasi, O lord.

**1.158.33**  Yudhishthira said: Who indeed would slay an enemy who has been conquered in battle, stripped of glory, whose wife is his master, and who is no longer a warrior? O slayer of foes, release him.

**1.158.34**  Arjuna said: Take him back, O gandharva woman — go and do not grieve. The Kuru king Yudhishthira grants you safety today.

**1.158.35**  The gandharva said: I have been defeated; I relinquish my former name Angaraparna. Henceforth I shall not boast of my strength or my name in any gathering of people.

**1.158.36**  It is well indeed that I have gained this gain — that I, who wished to fight with gandharva illusion against one who wields divine weapons and is superior to me in age and valor.

**1.158.37**  My magnificent chariot has been burned by the fire of that weapon; I who was once Chitraratha have now become Dagdharatha — the one with the burnt chariot — in name.

**1.158.38**  This knowledge was gathered by me through austerities long ago; today I shall present it to this great-souled one who has given me back my life.

**1.158.39**  He who reunites with life an enemy who was overpowered by force, defeated, and has come seeking refuge — does he not deserve every good fortune?

**1.158.40**  This knowledge is called Chakshushi — that which Manu gave to Soma; Soma gave it to Vishvavasu, and Vishvavasu gave it to me.

**1.158.41**  This guru-given knowledge, if it reaches a coward, is lost; I have described its origin — now hear from me its power.

**1.158.42**  Whatever one wishes to see with the eye in the three worlds, one can see it; and in whatever form one wishes to see it, one is able to behold it in that very form.

**1.158.43**  One who remains established in the vow for six months will obtain this knowledge; I myself will conduct this knowledge to you once the vow is observed.

**1.158.44**  By this knowledge, O king, we gandharvas are distinguished above men, yet we fall short of the gods, being moved by their power.

**1.158.45**  I shall give, O best of men, one hundred horses born of gandharvas each separately to your five brothers — a hundred for each.

**1.158.46**  These are the mounts of the gods and gandharvas, of divine fragrance, traveling at the speed of thought; though they may tire and tire again, their swiftness never diminishes.

**1.158.47**  Long ago, the thunderbolt of Mahendra, fashioned for the slaying of Vritra, was shattered tenfold and a hundredfold upon the head of Vritra.

**1.158.48**  Those portions were then distributed among the gods, and the share of the thunderbolt is worshipped in the world; whatever in the world serves as a means of power — that is said to be the body of the thunderbolt.

**1.158.49**  A brahmin is the thunderbolt in the hand; the kshatriya is said to be the thunderbolt of the chariot; the vaishyas are the thunderbolt of giving, and the youngest class the thunderbolt of action.

**1.158.50**  Horses are the thunderbolt of the kshatriya; horses are declared to be inviolable; a mare gives birth to the wheel of the chariot, and those considered chariot-drivers are among horses.

**1.158.51**  Of any color one desires, born as one desires, appearing at one's will — these horses born of gandharvas will fulfill your every wish.

**1.158.52**  Arjuna said: Whether given out of affection or when one's life was in danger — knowledge, wealth, or learning — I do not desire that, O gandharva.

**1.158.53**  The gandharva said: Fellowship indeed brings joy, as is seen in all assemblies; delighted by the gift of my life, I give you this knowledge.

**1.158.54**  From you I shall receive the supreme fire weapon in return, and likewise an enduring friendship, O Bibhatsu, O bull among the Bharatas.

**1.158.55**  Arjuna said: In exchange for the weapon I choose the horses from you; let our union be eternal, O friend. Tell me, O gandharva, what it is that would free you from fear.

**1.159.1**  Arjuna said: Tell me the reason, O gandharva — what was it by which we were assailed — we who were traveling, knowing the Vedas, virtuous, all of us, at night, O subduer of enemies?

**1.159.2**  The gandharva said: You were without fire, without offerings made into fire, and not accompanied by a brahmin in the lead — therefore you were assailed by me, O joy of the Pandavas.

**1.159.3**  Yakshas, rakshasas, gandharvas, pisachas, serpents, and men — all these tell at length of the glory of your illustrious Kuru lineage.

**1.159.4**  And from Narada and other divine sages I have heard, O hero, them recounting the virtues of your wise forebears.

**1.159.5**  And I myself have seen, as I wandered across this entire earth girdled by oceans, the power of your own lineage.

**1.159.6**  I recognize, O Arjuna, your teacher in the Veda and in archery — the illustrious Bharadvaja's son, renowned in the three worlds.

**1.159.7**  I know Dharma, Vayu, and Shakra, likewise the Ashvins, and Pandu — these six, O tiger among Kurus, O Partha, these fathers, foremost among gods and men, who increased your lineage.

**1.159.8**  You brothers are of divine nature, great-souled, the foremost of all who bear weapons, heroic, all of you observing vows of noble conduct.

**1.159.9**  Yet knowing your sublime mind and intellect, O Partha, knowing you to be souls of disciplined spirit — I nevertheless committed this assault upon you here.

**1.159.10**  In the presence of women, O Kauravya, no man who relies upon the wealth of his arms ought to endure an insult to himself when he sees it.

**1.159.11**  And at night our strength increases even further; that is why wrath came upon me together with my wife, O son of Kunti.

**1.159.12**  Yet I have been defeated by you here in battle, O enhancer of the lineage of Tapati; learn from me by what means this glory is to be proclaimed.

**1.159.13**  Brahmacharya — celibate discipline — is the supreme dharma, and that too is established in you; it is for this reason, O Partha, that I was conquered by you in this battle.

**1.159.14**  Whatever kshatriya, O scorcher of foes, is governed by desire and fights in battle at night — he cannot survive under any circumstances.

**1.159.15**  But a king who is even governed by desire, O descendant of Tapati, can conquer all night-roaming beings in battle — provided he is guided by a purohita at the helm.

**1.159.16**  Therefore, O descendant of Tapati, in whatever action men here seek their highest good, self-controlled purohitas should be engaged for that undertaking.

**1.159.17**  Those who are devoted to the Veda with its six limbs, who are pure, truthful in speech, righteous in soul, and disciplined in self — such men should be the purohitas of kings.

**1.159.18**  Victory is certain for a king, and heaven follows thereafter, whose chief priest is learned in dharma, eloquent, of noble character, and pure.

**1.159.19**  To gain what has not yet been gained, and to protect what has already been gained, a king should appoint a purohita endowed with virtuous qualities.

**1.159.20**  A king who wishes to obtain this entire earth, adorned by Meru as its crest jewel and girdled in all directions by ocean, should abide by the counsel of his purohita.

**1.159.21**  For no king, lacking brahmin support, can ever conquer the earth by valor alone or by noble birth alone — not anywhere.

**1.159.22**  Therefore understand this, O increaser of the Kuru lineage: a kingdom with brahmins at its head is alone capable of being sustained for a long time.

**1.160.1**  Arjuna said: The word 'Tapatya' that you have addressed to me here — I wish to understand the definitive meaning of 'Tapatya.'

**1.160.2**  Who is this Tapati on account of whom we are called Tapatyas? We are the sons of Kunti, O good one — I wish to know the truth.

**1.160.3**  Vaishampayana said: Thus addressed, the gandharva caused Dhananjaya, the son of Kunti, to hear a tale renowned throughout the three worlds.

**1.160.4**  The gandharva said: Come then — I shall tell you this delightful tale in full and exactly as it happened, O Partha, O best of those who uphold dharma — a righteous tale.

**1.160.5**  The word by which I addressed you as 'Tapatya' — that I shall narrate to you now. Listen to me with an undivided mind.

**1.160.6**  He who pervades heaven with his seat and pervades the sky with his radiance — to him was born a daughter named Tapati, matchless in form.

**1.160.7**  She was the daughter of Vivasvat, O son of Kunti, the younger sister of Savitri, O lord, renowned in the three worlds, and endowed with the heat of ascetic power.

**1.160.8**  She was not a goddess, nor an asuri, nor a yakshi, nor a rakshasi, nor an apsara, nor a gandharvi — no one possessed a form equal to hers.

**1.160.9**  Her limbs were well-proportioned and flawless; her eyes were dark and wide; she was virtuous in conduct, righteous, beautifully dressed, and resplendent.

**1.160.10**  Savitar found no one in the three worlds equal to her, O Bharata — no one worthy to be her husband in beauty, character, lineage, and learning.

**1.160.11**  Seeing his daughter who had reached the bloom of youth, ready to be given in marriage, he found no peace as he pondered to whom to bestow her.

**1.160.12**  The son of Riksha and Artha, O son of Kunti — Samvarana, the bull among the Kurus, powerful king — always worshipped the Sun.

**1.160.13**  The king, ever steadfast, worshipped with offerings of water and garlands, with vows, fasts, and various austerities.

**1.160.14**  Devoted in service, free of arrogance, pure — the joy of the Paurava clan — he worshipped with devotion the radiant one rising with his rays.

**1.160.15**  Then the Sun regarded Samvarana — grateful, learned in dharma, matchless in form on earth — as a worthy husband for Tapati.

**1.160.16**  He then wished to give his daughter to that Samvarana, O Kauravya — that foremost of kings, of illustrious lineage.

**1.160.17**  Just as the bright-rayed sun illumines the sky with his radiance, so did Samvarana shine upon the earth with his own brilliance.

**1.160.18**  Just as the knowers of Brahman worship the rising Aditya, so did the people — brahmins and lower orders alike — worship Samvarana, O Partha.

**1.160.19**  That glorious king surpassed the moon in beauty and the sun in radiance — even in the eyes of enemies, not only of friends.

**1.160.20**  For a king of such qualities and such conduct, O Kauravya, the Sun himself resolved to give Tapati.

**1.160.21**  Then one day that glorious king, of wide renown upon the earth, went hunting, O Partha, in the forest on a mountain — so it is said.

**1.160.22**  As he ranged in the hunt, his peerless horse — worn out by hunger, thirst, and fatigue — died on the mountain, O son of Kunti.

**1.160.23**  His horse dead, the king wandered on the mountain on foot alone, O Partha, and he saw a maiden with wide eyes, matchless in the world.

**1.160.24**  He, the crusher of enemies, the tiger among kings, approaching that solitary maiden alone, stood still, gazing at her with unblinking eyes.

**1.160.25**  The king surmised her to be Shri herself in form, then surmised again that she was like the radiance of the sun fallen to earth.

**1.160.26**  The mountain slope on which she stood, her eyes bright as a white blossom, glowed as though fashioned of gold — trees, shrubs, and all.

**1.160.27**  Beholding her, the king deemed her form surpassing that of every living creature; and he felt that his eyes had at last gained their true reward.

**1.160.28**  From the day of his birth the great king had seen many things, yet he reflected that he had never beheld any beauty comparable to hers.

**1.160.29**  His mind and eyes were bound by the cords woven from her virtues; he stirred not from that spot, and knew nothing of what passed around him.

**1.160.30**  "Surely," he thought, "the Creator churned the whole world — gods, asuras, and men alike — and brought forth this form of the wide-eyed one."

**1.160.31**  Thus did King Saṃvaraṇa reason to himself, marvelling at the treasure of her beauty, a maiden unequalled anywhere in the world.

**1.160.32**  That king of noble lineage, having gazed upon the auspicious maiden, fell into deep anxious thought, tormented by the arrows of desire.

**1.160.33**  Burning fiercely in the fire of Kāma, the bold king, though she was reticent, spoke to that renowned maiden.

**1.160.34**  "Who are you, O round-thighed one? Whose are you? For what purpose do you stand here? And how, O pure-smiling one, do you roam alone in this deserted forest?"

**1.160.35**  "You are blameless in every limb, adorned with every ornament; and yet you seem yourself to be the desired ornament of all these ornaments."

**1.160.36**  "I take you for neither a goddess nor an asura-woman, neither a yakṣī nor a rākṣasī, neither a serpent-princess of Bhogavatī, nor a gandharva-maiden, nor a mortal."

**1.160.37**  "Of all the beautiful women I have ever seen or heard of, I do not consider you the equal of any of them, O woman whose eyes are full and intoxicating."

**1.160.38**  Thus did the king address her; but she, in that solitary forest, did not reply a single word to the love-stricken man.

**1.160.39**  Then, as the king entreated her further, the large-eyed one vanished on that very spot, like a flash of lightning amid clouds.

**1.160.40**  Seeking her, the king wandered through that forest, eyes like lotus petals, roaming about like one who had lost his wits.

**1.160.41**  Not finding her, and having lamented greatly in that place, the foremost of the Kauravas stood motionless for a while, all movement ceased in him.

**1.161.1**  The Gandharva said: When she vanished from sight, the king, deluded by desire — he who was the feller of enemy hosts — fell to the ground.

**1.161.2**  When he had fallen upon the earth, that lovely-smiling, full and shapely-hipped woman revealed herself to the king once more.

**1.161.3**  Then the auspicious one spoke in a sweet voice to that king, founder of the Kuru line, whose mind was struck down by desire.

**1.161.4**  "Arise, arise! May fortune be yours! O subduer of foes, O tiger among kings, you ought not to yield to such delusion, lying exposed upon the earth."

**1.161.5**  Thus addressed by her sweet voice, the king looked up and saw her — broad-hipped and fair — standing directly before him.

**1.161.6**  Then the lord of men, his soul consumed by the fire of Kāma, spoke to her of dark-tinged eyes in a voice uncertain and faltering.

**1.161.7**  "O dark-eyed one, O woman with full and bright eyes, favour me who am tormented by desire and who devotedly seeks you — for life is departing from me."

**1.161.8**  "For your sake, O wide-eyed one, O woman bright as the interior of a lotus, Kāma pierces me with his sharp arrows and does not abate."

**1.161.9**  "I am seized by the great serpent of desire and there is none to hear my cry, O fortunate one — O full-hipped, auspicious-faced woman, rescue me."

**1.161.10**  "My life depends entirely on you, O woman whose voice is like the song of a kiṃnara, whose every limb is beautiful and blameless, whose face resembles both the lotus and the moon."

**1.161.11**  "Without you, O timid one, I cannot sustain my life. Therefore, O wide-eyed woman, O graceful one, show compassion toward me."

**1.161.12**  "O dark-eyed one, you must not abandon me who am devoted to you. You have the power to save me with the bond of love, O passionate woman."

**1.161.13**  "Come, O timid one, beautiful woman, take me in the Gāndharva form of marriage — for of all marriage rites, O round-thighed one, the Gāndharva is said to be the highest."

**1.161.14**  Tapatī said: I am not mistress of my own person, O king — I am a maiden who has a father. If you truly love me, then go and ask my father.

**1.161.15**  "Just as you say your life has been seized by me, O lord of men, know too that at the very sight of you you have likewise taken away my life."

**1.161.16**  "Yet I am not free to dispose of my own body; therefore, O best of kings, I cannot draw near you — women are not independent."

**1.161.17**  "What maiden in all the worlds would not desire a king of celebrated lineage as her lord and husband, one who is kind and devoted to those who love him?"

**1.161.18**  "Therefore, in this situation, go and entreat my father, the sun-god Āditya, with prostrations, austerities, and observances."

**1.161.19**  "If he wishes to give me to you, O crusher of foes, then, O king, I shall forever be obedient to you."

**1.161.20**  "I am Tapatī by name, the younger sister of Sāvitrī, daughter of Savitṛ — of the sun who is the lamp of the world — O bull among kṣatriyas."

**1.162.1**  The Gandharva said: Having spoken thus, the blameless one swiftly rose upward; and the king fell once more upon the ground on that very spot.

**1.162.2**  The minister who had accompanied him found him in the great forest, fallen to the ground like the banner of Indra that has been cast down.

**1.162.3**  Seeing that great archer horseless and fallen to earth, the minister was as though set ablaze by fire.

**1.162.4**  He hastened to him with the agitation that love brings, and raised up the king who was dazed by desire.

**1.162.5**  Like a father lifting a fallen son from the ground, that minister — aged in wisdom, years, fame, and self-restraint — raised up the lord of earth.

**1.162.6**  Having raised the king, the minister's own anguish faded; and he spoke to him who had just risen, with auspicious, sweet words: "Fear not, O tiger among men; may good fortune be yours, O sinless one."

**1.162.7**  He surmised that the king — he who fells enemies in battle — had fallen to the ground overcome by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion.

**1.162.8**  He then sprinkled the king's head with very cool water fragrant as the white lotus, taking care not to disturb the royal crown.

**1.162.9**  When the powerful king had recovered his life-breath, he dismissed the entire army, retaining only that one minister.

**1.162.10**  By the king's command, the great army marched away; and the king sat down once more upon that mountain slope.

**1.162.11**  Then, on that excellent mountain, he became ritually pure, joined his palms in supplication, and stood upon the ground with arms raised, desiring to propitiate the sun.

**1.162.12**  And in his mind, King Saṃvaraṇa — the slayer of foes — turned also to Vasiṣṭha, the best of seers, his own household priest.

**1.162.13**  As the lord of the people remained thus in that solitary place through nights and days alike, the seer among brāhmaṇas came to him on the twelfth day.

**1.162.14**  That great and cultivated-souled seer, knowing by divine means that the king's heart had been taken by Tapatī, understood all.

**1.162.15**  That righteous-souled one then addressed the best of kings, who had been disciplining his self thus, desiring to accomplish his purpose.

**1.162.16**  While the lord of men watched, the blessed seer, radiant as the sun himself, ascended upward to behold the sun.

**1.162.17**  Standing before the thousand-rayed one with joined palms, Vasiṣṭha gladly made himself known, saying: "I am Vasiṣṭha."

**1.162.18**  Vivasvān, of great splendour, then said to the best of sages: "Welcome to you, O great seer — speak freely of whatever you wish."

**1.163.1**  Vasiṣṭha said: This daughter of yours named Tapatī, the younger sister of Sāvitrī — I ask you for her hand on behalf of Saṃvaraṇa, O Vibhāvasu.

**1.163.2**  "For that king Saṃvaraṇa is of great fame, learned in dharma and wealth, of noble mind — a fitting husband for your daughter, O one who roams the sky."

**1.163.3**  The Gandharva said: Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, Savitā the day-maker, resolved to give her, welcomed the seer and replied.

**1.163.4**  "Saṃvaraṇa is the best among kings; you are the best among sages, O muni; Tapatī is the best among women — what reason could there be for refusal?"

**1.163.5**  Then Tapana himself gave the blameless Tapatī — resplendent as fire — for Saṃvaraṇa's sake to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha; and the great seer accepted that maiden Tapatī.

**1.163.6**  Vasiṣṭha, having been sent off, came back again to the place where that bull of the Kurus of celebrated fame was waiting.

**1.163.7**  That king, who had been possessed by Kāma and whose inner self had dwelt entirely on her, seeing that goddess-daughter, the lovely-smiling Tapatī, coming with Vasiṣṭha, was filled with exceeding joy.

**1.163.8**  When the king's twelve nights of arduous vigil had been completed, the pure-souled, blessed seer Vasiṣṭha arrived.

**1.163.9**  Having propitiated through austerities the boon-granting god, the lord and master of the cattle of the sky, Saṃvaraṇa obtained his wife by the very power of Vasiṣṭha.

**1.163.10**  Then on that most excellent mountain, frequented by gods and gandharvas, that bull among men took Tapatī's hand according to the rites.

**1.163.11**  Permitted by Vasiṣṭha, that royal seer desired to dwell on that same mountain range in the company of his wife.

**1.163.12**  Thereupon the lord of earth gave command over the city, the realm, the transport, and the armies to that same minister.

**1.163.13**  Vasiṣṭha then took his leave of the king and departed; and the king too sported on that mountain, like one equal to an immortal.

**1.163.14**  For twelve years the king took his pleasure on that mountain, in its forests and waters, together with his wife alone.

**1.163.15**  During those twelve years, throughout that king's city and throughout all his realm, the thousand-eyed Indra sent no rain whatsoever.

**1.163.16**  That city then, with its people tormented by hunger, joyless, and reduced to the state of corpses, looked like the city of the king of the dead, crowded with ghosts.

**1.163.17**  Seeing the city in such a state, that same blessed seer — righteous-souled Vasiṣṭha — went to the best of kings.

**1.163.18**  He brought that tiger among kings back to his city — O king — together with Tapatī, after his having sojourned twelve years away.

**1.163.19**  Then, as that tiger among kings re-entered his city, the slayer of the enemies of the gods — Indra — caused rain to fall there as in former times.

**1.163.20**  Then that city, together with the whole kingdom, rejoiced with the greatest joy, enlivened by that foremost of kings, himself of enlivened soul.

**1.163.21**  Thereafter the lord of men performed sacrifice for twelve more years together with his wife Tapatī, just as Śakra the lord of the Maruts does.

**1.163.22**  Such was she — the greatly blessed Tapatī of ancient times, daughter of Vivasvat — O Pārtha; and it is from her that you are known as Tāpatya.

**1.163.23**  King Saṃvaraṇa begot upon Tapatī the ancestor Kuru, O best of those who blaze with splendour; from her descent you are called Tāpatya, O Arjuna.

**1.164.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of the gandharva, Arjuna, O bull of the Bharata line, shone with the greatest delight, like the full moon.

**1.164.2**  And that great archer, best of the Kurus, deeply curious about the power of Vasiṣṭha's austerity, spoke to the gandharva.

**1.164.3**  "This name of the seer 'Vasiṣṭha' that you have uttered — I wish to hear the full account of it. Tell me truly."

**1.164.4**  O lord of the Gandharvas, who was this one who served as the family priest of our ancestors? Tell me of him — who indeed is this venerable sage?

**1.164.5**  The Gandharva said: He whose two feet were forever massaged by desire and anger — both of them conquered by his austerity, those two who are ever unconquerable even by the immortals —

**1.164.6**  who, though of noble spirit, did not bring about the destruction of the Kushikas despite Vishvamitra's offense, even while bearing the greatest wrath within —

**1.164.7**  who, though powerful and lordly and tormented by the calamity of his sons, did not choose the terrible deed of destroying Vishvamitra —

**1.164.8**  who, even to bring back his dead sons from Yama's realm, did not transgress fate, just as the great ocean does not transgress its shore —

**1.164.9**  having obtained whom — that self-conquered, great-souled one — the Ikshvaku kings, those guardians of the earth, won this world —

**1.164.10**  having obtained Vasishtha, the best of household priests, the foremost of sages, those kings performed sacrifices, O joy of the Kurus —

**1.164.11**  for that brahmarshi presided over the sacrifices of all those foremost kings, O best of the Pandavas, just as Brihaspati does for the immortals —

**1.164.12**  therefore a brahmin who is foremost in righteousness, who knows the dharma of the Vedas, who is sought-after and endowed with virtues — some such one should be carefully chosen as your priest.

**1.164.13**  For a man born as a kshatriya who desires to conquer the earth must first appoint a household priest, O Partha, for the increase of his kingdom.

**1.164.14**  A king who desires to conquer the earth must place a brahmin at the fore; therefore let some virtuous twice-born one be your household priest.

**1.165.1**  Arjuna said: What was the cause of the enmity between Vishvamitra and Vasishtha as they dwelt in their holy hermitage? Tell us all of that fully.

**1.165.2**  The Gandharva said: This ancient tale of Vasishtha is told throughout all the worlds, O Partha. Learn it fully from me.

**1.165.3**  In Kanyakubja there was a great king, O bull among Bharatas, known in the world as Gadhi — devoted to truth and righteousness.

**1.165.4**  This righteous king's son, possessed of abundant forces and mounts, became known as Vishvamitra, the crusher of foes.

**1.165.5**  He roamed the hunt with his ministers through dense forest, piercing deer and boars in the pleasant sandy tracts.

**1.165.6**  Worn thin by exertion, eager for game and overcome with thirst, he came, O foremost of men, toward the hermitage of Vasishtha.

**1.165.7**  Seeing him arrive, Vasishtha the sage, foremost in good fortune, received Vishvamitra, that foremost of men, with full honor.

**1.165.8**  With water for the feet, the guest-offering, water for sipping, and a warm welcome, O Bharata, he received him likewise with forest oblations.

**1.165.9**  Then the wish-granting cow of great-souled Vasishtha, told to yield all desires, duly milked them forth.

**1.165.10**  She milked herbs both domestic and wild, and milk itself, and the six tastes, and the nectar-like juice, the unsurpassed elixir of life.

**1.165.11**  Foods to be eaten, liquids to be drunk, various delicacies to be chewed, lickable things akin to ambrosia, and things to be sucked — all of these, O Arjuna.

**1.165.12**  Honored with all those desires fully provided, that lord of the earth together with his ministers and army was greatly pleased, that king.

**1.165.13**  With six elongated parts, fine flanks and thighs, three broad parts and five contracted ones, frog-like eyes, perfect form, and full udder — blameless —

**1.165.14**  with a handsome tail, spike-shaped ears, beautiful horns, and a lovely form, with well-nourished, elongated head and neck — gazing at her in wonder —

**1.165.15**  delighted by Nandini, Vasishtha's milk-cow, Vishvamitra, greatly pleased, spoke to the sage:

**1.165.16**  "Give me Nandini, O brahmin, in exchange for ten million cows, or else for my kingdom — enjoy my kingdom, O great sage."

**1.165.17**  Vasishtha said: For the sake of the gods, guests, and ancestors, and for clarified butter offerings, this milk-cow Nandini is not to be given away by me, even for your kingdom, O sinless one.

**1.165.18**  Vishvamitra said: I am a kshatriya; you are a brahmin whose means are austerity and Vedic study. Where does valor reside in brahmins, who are tranquil and self-controlled?

**1.165.19**  "Since you will not give me what I desire even for ten million cows, I will not abandon my own duty — I shall take your cow by force."

**1.165.20**  Vasishtha said: You stand in power; you are a king; you are a kshatriya of mighty arm. Do quickly as you wish — do not deliberate.

**1.165.21**  The Gandharva said: Thus addressed, O Partha, Vishvamitra then seized by force that cow Nandini, who resembled a swan or the moon.

**1.165.22**  Struck by whips and staffs, driven this way and that, lowing aloud, that auspicious Nandini of Vasishtha —

**1.165.23**  turned back and stood facing him, O Partha, her face turned toward her lord; though beaten hard, she did not leave the hermitage.

**1.165.24**  Vasishtha said: I hear your cry, dear one, as you call out again and again. You are being carried off by force, O Nandi — but I am a brahmin, and forbearance is my nature.

**1.165.25**  The Gandharva said: But Nandini, overpowered by the force of those forces, O bull among Bharatas, terrified of Vishvamitra, came to Vasishtha.

**1.165.26**  The cow said: O lord, why do you ignore me as though I have no protector — me, who am being beaten with stones and staffs, crying out, beset by the terrible forces of Vishvamitra?

**1.165.27**  The Gandharva said: Even as she was thus afflicted, O Partha, the great sage did not agitate, nor did he waver from his composure, firm in his vow.

**1.165.28**  Vasishtha said: The strength of kshatriyas is their energy; the strength of brahmins is forbearance. Forbearance attends me — so go, if you please.

**1.165.29**  The cow said: Have I been abandoned by you, lord, that you speak to me thus? I have not truly been abandoned by you, O brahmin — I cannot be taken away by force.

**1.165.30**  Vasishtha said: I do not abandon you, O auspicious one. Stay, if you are able. They have bound your calf with strong rope and are carrying it off by force.

**1.165.31**  The Gandharva said: Hearing those words "Stay!" from Vasishtha, his milk-cow raised her head and neck upward and blazed forth, terrible to behold.

**1.165.32**  That cow, with eyes red with fury and a dense thunderous bellow, scattered Vishvamitra's entire army in every direction.

**1.165.33**  Struck by the tips of whips and staffs, driven here and there, her eyes blazing with wrath, she gathered yet more wrath within her.

**1.165.34**  She blazed, her body lit with fury like the midday sun, repeatedly raining down a great shower of embers from her tail.

**1.165.35**  From her tail she created the Pahlavas; from her dung she created Shabaras and Shakas; maddened with rage, from her urine she created the Yavanas.

**1.165.36**  From her foam she created Pundras, Kiratas, Dravidians, Sinhalese, Barbaras, and likewise Daradas and other barbarians.

**1.165.37**  By those created hosts, bands of various barbarians clad in varied armor and bearing varied weapons, the great army of Vishvamitra was overwhelmed as he looked on.

**1.165.38**  Each warrior was surrounded by five or seven, and the army of Vishvamitra, driven by a great rain of weapons, was shattered on all sides, terrified, as he watched.

**1.165.39**  Yet none of those soldiers of Vishvamitra were separated from their lives by the enraged forces of Vasishtha, O bull among Bharatas.

**1.165.40**  The army of Vishvamitra, driven back three yojanas, crying out, seized with fear, found no protector.

**1.165.41**  Seeing that great wonder born of brahmanic splendor, Vishvamitra, disillusioned with the nature of the kshatriya, spoke these words:

**1.165.42**  "Shame on the strength of the kshatriya! The strength of brahmic splendor is true strength. Having weighed strength against strength, I conclude that austerity alone is supreme strength."

**1.165.43**  Renouncing his flourishing kingdom, that blazing royal glory, and leaving all pleasures behind, he turned his mind solely to austerity.

**1.165.44**  Having attained perfection through austerity, pervading the worlds with his splendor, blazing in energy he scorched all beings and won brahminhood; and that Kaushika drank the soma juice together with Indra.

**1.166.1**  The Gandharva said: There was a king known as Kalmashapada in this world, O Partha — born of the Ikshvaku lineage, unmatched on earth in his splendor.

**1.166.2**  Once that king, crusher of enemies, went out from his city into the forest for the hunt, piercing deer and boars as he roamed.

**1.166.3**  That king, afflicted by thirst and hunger, was travelling alone on a narrow path when he encountered great-souled Vasishtha, the foremost of sages.

**1.166.4**  That unconquered-in-battle king saw coming toward him a sage named Shakti — highly blessed, the delight of Vasishtha's line, the eldest among the hundred sons of great-souled Vasishtha.

**1.166.5**  "Leave our path!" — thus spoke the king. And the sage spoke back to him, calming him with gentle words.

**1.166.6**  But the sage did not step aside, standing firm on that path of dharma; nor did the king move away, out of pride toward the sage and also out of anger.

**1.166.7**  That best of kings, in delusion, then struck with a whip the sage who would not yield the path — struck him as though he were a demon.

**1.166.8**  Struck by the blow of the whip, that foremost of sages, Vasishtha's son, overcome with rage, cursed that best of kings:

**1.166.9**  "Because you strike an ascetic like a demon, O lowest of kings, from this day forward you shall become a man-eater."

**1.166.10**  "Addicted to human flesh, you shall roam this earth" — thus spoken to by Shakti, that Shakti of mighty power, "Go, O vilest of kings!"

**1.166.11**  Now the enmity between Vishvamitra and Vasishtha had arisen over the matter of whose sacrificial client the king was — and Vishvamitra followed that king.

**1.166.12**  As these two were thus in conflict, the sage Vishvamitra of fierce austerity, O Partha, the illustrious one, drew near.

**1.166.13**  Then that best of kings afterward recognized the sage — the son of the sage Vasishtha, equal to Vasishtha himself in splendor.

**1.166.14**  Vishvamitra too, O Bharata, concealing himself, approached both of them, wishing to do what was pleasing to himself.

**1.166.15**  The best of kings, thus cursed by Shakti, went to seek refuge with Shakti, worthy of placating him.

**1.166.16**  Knowing the king's intention, O joy of the Kurus, Vishvamitra then directed a demon against the king.

**1.166.17**  By the curse of that brahmin-sage and by the command of Vishvamitra, a demon named Kinkara then entered into the king.

**1.166.18**  Knowing that the king had been seized by the demon, that sage Vishvamitra then withdrew from that place, O crusher of enemies.

**1.166.19**  Then that wise king, guarding himself by his own self, was powerfully tormented even so by the demon that had entered within him.

**1.166.20**  A certain brahmin saw that king setting out again, and, being hungry, begged from him food along with meat.

**1.166.21**  The royal sage Mitrasaha then spoke to that brahmin, placating him: "Stay here for just a moment, O brahmin."

**1.166.22**  "When I return I shall give you food as you desire" — so saying, the king departed, and that best of brahmins waited.

**1.166.23**  The brahmin's words had meanwhile entered within the king's mind; and that lord of men entered his inner apartments and retired.

**1.166.24**  Then at midnight the king arose, quickly summoned the cook, and spoke, remembering what he had promised the brahmin:

**1.166.25**  "Go — in that place a brahmin waits for me, seeking food. You must supply him with food together with meat."

**1.166.26**  Thus instructed, the cook, unable to find any meat anywhere, reported this to the king in distress.

**1.166.27**  But the king, possessed by the demon, addressed the cook without any anxiety, saying again and again: 'Feed him with human flesh.'

**1.166.28**  Saying 'So be it,' the cook then went swiftly to the place where the executioners lived, took human flesh without fear.

**1.166.29**  He prepared it properly, mixed it with other food, and quickly served it to that hungry brahmin ascetic.

**1.166.30**  That best of twice-born sages, seeing the food with his spiritually perfected sight, said 'This is unfit to eat,' his eyes clouded with rage.

**1.166.31**  "Since that lord of men gives me food unfit to eat, therefore the craving for this very thing shall afflict that fool himself."

**1.166.32**  "Addicted to human flesh, as Shakti previously declared, he shall roam this earth as a terror to all living beings."

**1.166.33**  When the curse was spoken twice over the king, it became powerful; possessed by the force of the demon, he became bereft of his senses.

**1.166.34**  Then that best of kings, his senses overwhelmed by the demon, having seen Shakti before him, spoke to him thus, O Bharata:

**1.166.35**  "Since you have inflicted upon me this undeserved curse, I shall begin with you to devour human beings."

**1.166.36**  Having said this, he immediately deprived Shakti of his life and devoured him, as a tiger devours a desired prey.

**1.166.37**  Seeing Shakti slain, Vishvamitra then directed that same demon against the remaining sons of Vasishtha.

**1.166.38**  Enraged, it devoured those hundred surviving sons of the great-souled Vasishtha, as a lion devours small animals.

**1.166.39**  Vasishtha, hearing that his sons had been slain by Vishvamitra, bore that grief as a great mountain bears the earth.

**1.166.40**  That best of sages resolved to destroy himself, but that foremost of the wise did not contemplate the annihilation of the Kushika line.

**1.166.41**  The venerable sage threw himself from the peak of Mount Meru, and his body fell upon the rocks below as if upon a heap of cotton.

**1.166.42**  When he did not die from that fall, O Pandava, the venerable one kindled a fire and entered it in the great forest.

**1.166.43**  Yet even though blazing fiercely, the fire did not burn him; O slayer of enemies, the fire became cool.

**1.166.44**  The great sage, overcome with grief, went to the ocean, tied a heavy rock around his neck, and plunged into its waters.

**1.166.45**  But the force of the ocean's waves cast the great sage back onto dry land; dejected, he turned back toward his hermitage.

**1.167.1**  The gandharva said: Then, seeing the hermitage bereft of those sons, the sage, overwhelmed with deep grief, departed once more from the hermitage.

**1.167.2**  He saw a river full with fresh waters in the rainy season, carrying along many kinds of trees that grew on its banks, O Partha.

**1.167.3**  Then a thought again came to him, O scion of the Paurava line: 'I shall submerge myself in the waters of this river,' filled with sorrow.

**1.167.4**  Then the great sage, binding himself tightly with cords, plunged into the waters of that great river, deeply distressed.

**1.167.5**  But the river cut through those cords, O crusher of enemy forces, and released the sage upright, free of bonds.

**1.167.6**  Having emerged, freed from the cords, the great sage then named that river Vipasha — 'freed from bonds' — and so the great sage named it.

**1.167.7**  He then set his mind again upon ending his grief, and did not stay in one place; he wandered to mountains, rivers, and lakes.

**1.167.8**  Then that sage came again to a Himalayan river full of fierce crocodiles, and cast himself into its current.

**1.167.9**  That best of rivers, reflecting upon that brahmin who was equal to fire, split into a hundred streams; hence it became known as Shatadru — 'flowing in a hundred streams.'

**1.167.10**  Seeing himself deposited on dry land even there, he said to himself, 'Death is not possible for me,' and returned once more to his hermitage.

**1.167.11**  Followed by his daughter-in-law Adrishyanti, walking toward the hermitage, he suddenly heard from behind the sound of Vedic recitation, complete with its six auxiliary disciplines, full of meaning.

**1.167.12**  'Who is this that follows me?' he asked. His daughter-in-law replied: 'I am Adrishyanti by name — the wife of Shakti, O great one, a devoted ascetic.'

**1.167.13**  Vasishtha said: 'O daughter, whose is this sound of the recitation of the Veda with its limbs? I heard it long ago from Shakti, reciting the Veda with its limbs.'

**1.167.14**  Adrishyanti said: 'This is the embryo of Shakti, your son, arisen in my womb; for twelve years, O sage, he has been here practicing the Vedas.'

**1.167.15**  The gandharva said: Thus spoken to, Vasishtha, that sage of the highest fortune, rejoiced, and saying 'The lineage endures,' he turned back from death, O Partha.

**1.167.16**  Then, having turned back, he and his daughter-in-law saw Kalmashapada sitting in a deserted forest, O sinless one.

**1.167.17**  As soon as the king saw him, O Bharata, he rose up in rage, possessed by the fierce demon, and intended to devour him.

**1.167.18**  Adrishyanti, seeing that cruel-actioned one before them, spoke these words to Vasishtha in a voice trembling with fear:

**1.167.19**  'That terrible demon approaches here, O venerable one, like death itself, bearing a raised club of wood.'

**1.167.20**  'There is no one else on earth today able to restrain him, except you, O great one, best among all who know the Vedas.'
