**1.167.21**  'Protect me, O venerable one, from this terrible-looking evil — the demon surely intends to devour us both here.'

**1.168.1**  Vasishtha said: 'Fear not, O daughter — you need have no fear whatsoever of a demon. The terror you see approaching is not a demon.'

**1.168.2**  'This is King Kalmashapada, renowned on earth for his valor; it is he who dwells in this region of the forest in this terrible form.'

**1.168.3**  The gandharva said: Seeing him rushing forward, the venerable and radiant sage Vasishtha restrained him with a mere thunder-sound, O Bharata.

**1.168.4**  Then, sprinkling him again with water sanctified by mantras, he truly liberated that best of kings from the dreadful demon.

**1.168.5**  For twelve years he had been possessed — held by the power of Vasishtha himself — as the sun is eclipsed at a sacred juncture.

**1.168.6**  Freed from the demon, the king illumined that great forest with his splendor, as the sun illumines the twilight clouds.

**1.168.7**  Having regained his senses, the king bowed with joined palms and spoke in proper form to Vasishtha, that best of sages:

**1.168.8**  'I am Saudasa, O great one, your sacrificial patron, O best of twice-born; tell me now what you desire — what shall I do for you?'

**1.168.9**  Vasishtha said: 'All this has come to pass as was fated. Go and rule your kingdom; and never, O lord of men, disrespect the brahmins.'

**1.168.10**  The king said: 'I shall never disrespect the best of brahmins, O brahmin; abiding by your instruction, I shall always honor the twice-born.'

**1.168.11**  'But I wish to receive from you, O best of twice-born, that boon by which I may be freed from debt to the Ikshvaku lineage, O best among those who know the Vedas.'

**1.168.12**  'Please go to my beloved queen, who is endowed with virtue, beauty, and fine qualities, to beget the offspring I desire, for the growth of the Ikshvaku line.'

**1.168.13**  The gandharva said: 'So I shall give it,' replied Vasishtha to that king there — Vasishtha, best of twice-born, firm in his pledges.

**1.168.14**  Then in due course the lord of men returned, accompanied by Vasishtha, to Ayodhya, that most celebrated city in the world, O sinless one.

**1.168.15**  All the people, rejoicing, came forth to welcome him — that great-souled one now free from sin — as the celestials welcome their lord.

**1.168.16**  Without delay that lord of men, accompanied by the great-souled Vasishtha, entered the city renowned for its righteous deeds.

**1.168.17**  Then the citizens of Ayodhya saw him, O king, like the sun risen in due season together with the Pushya constellation.

**1.168.18**  For he, the best among the prosperous, filled that Ayodhya with splendor, as the cool-rayed moon fills the sky when it rises in the autumn season.

**1.168.19**  That excellent city, with its roads sprinkled and swept clean, adorned with raised banners, gladdened his heart.

**1.168.20**  Filled with contented and prosperous citizens, that city shone with him at its center, O joy of the Kurus, as Amaravati shines with Indra.

**1.168.21**  Then, after that king of kings had entered the city, the queen, by the king's command, approached Vasishtha.

**1.168.22**  At the proper season, the great seer Vasishtha, that sage of the highest fortune, united with the queen according to divine rite.

**1.168.23**  When the embryo was conceived in her, that best of sages, having been saluted by the king, departed again to his hermitage.

**1.168.24**  When the queen, having carried the embryo for a long time, did not deliver it, she then struck her own womb with a stone.

**1.168.25**  Then in the twelfth year he was born, O bull among men — the royal sage named Ashmaka, who founded the city of Potana.

**1.169.1**  The gandharva said: Then Adrishyanti, dwelling at the hermitage, gave birth to a son who would perpetuate Shakti's line — a second Shakti, O king.

**1.169.2**  The venerable best of sages himself performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies for his grandson, O best of the Bharatas.

**1.169.3**  And since Vasishtha had been saved from death by him even while still in the womb, that one became known in the world as Parashara.

**1.169.4**  That virtuous soul regarded Vasishtha as his father from birth, and conducted himself toward him just as toward a father.

**1.169.5**  He addressed the brahmin-seer Vasishtha as 'Father' in the presence of his mother Adrishyanti, O Kaunteya, O scorcher of foes.

**1.169.6**  Hearing that sweet word 'Father,' spoken with full meaning, Adrishyanti, with eyes full of tears, spoke to him:

**1.169.7**  'No, child — do not say "Father, Father" — this great sage is not your father. Your father, child, was devoured by a demon in the forest.'

**1.169.8**  'The one you think of as father — he is not your father, O sinless one. This honored one is the father of your father, that great-souled man.'

**1.169.9**  Thus addressed, that great-minded, truthful best of sages was afflicted with grief, and resolved to destroy all the worlds.

**1.169.10**  Vasishtha, that great ascetic, restrained the great-souled one thus resolved, by the reason you shall now hear.

**1.169.11**  Vasishtha said: 'There was a king on earth known as Kritavirya, that bull among kings, the sacrificial patron of the Bhrigus and of those who know the Vedas.'

**1.169.12**  'He, lord of the people, gratified those foremost ones, dear child, with great stores of grain and wealth at the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice.'

**1.169.13**  'When that tiger among kings had gone to heaven, a need for property arose at some point among his descendants.'

**1.169.14**  'Learning of the wealth of the Bhrigus, all those kings went as supplicants to those best of the Bhrigu lineage, dear child.'

**1.169.15**  Some of the Bhṛgus buried their imperishable wealth in the earth, while others gave it to twice-born men, knowing the danger from the kṣatriyas.

**1.169.16**  Yet other Bhṛgus gave those kṣatriyas their wealth as the kṣatriyas desired, O dear one, having seen another motive behind their actions.

**1.169.17**  Then, O dear one, as a certain kṣatriya was digging the ground by chance, the wealth that had been buried in a Bhārgava household was discovered; all the assembled bull-like kṣatriyas saw it.

**1.169.18**  Then, overcome with rage and scorning those Bhṛgus who had sought refuge, those mighty bowmen slew them all with sharpened arrows, cutting down even the unborn in the womb, and they roamed across the earth.

**1.169.19**  Then, as the Bhṛgus were being exterminated in this manner out of fear, O dear one, the wives of the Bhṛgus fled to the Himālaya mountain.

**1.169.20**  Among them, one Brahmin woman, in fear, bore a radiant embryo concealed in her left thigh for the propagation of her husband's lineage; those kṣatriyas saw that Brahmin woman blazing with her own splendor.

**1.169.21**  Then that embryo burst through the Brahmin woman's thigh and issued forth, blinding the sight of the kṣatriyas like the midday sun; and those, now deprived of sight, wandered bewildered in the mountain fastnesses.

**1.169.22**  Then those bull-like kṣatriyas, their plans foiled and stricken with fear, took refuge with that blameless Brahmin woman for the sake of their sight.

**1.169.23**  And those kṣatriyas, bewildered and deprived of light, tormented by suffering like fires with extinguished flames, spoke to that illustrious woman.

**1.169.24**  "By the grace of Your Holiness, may the kṣatriya class regain its sight; and may we, having desisted from our evil deeds, depart together as one."

**1.169.25**  "You, together with your son, should bestow grace on all of us; by restoring sight you should rescue these kings."

**1.170.1**  The Brahmin woman said: "I do not take your sight from you, O dear ones; I am not filled with anger. But this Bhārgava who was born from the thigh is surely angered with you today."

**1.170.2**  "By him, that great-souled one, your sight has surely been seized in his rage, as he remembers his kinsmen who were slain — of this there is no doubt."

**1.170.3**  "When you were slaying even the embryos of the Bhṛgus, O sons, it was then that I bore this embryo in my thigh for a hundred years."

**1.170.4**  "The entire Veda with its six ancillaries entered this child even while he was still in the womb, desiring to do what is most pleasing to the lineage of Bhṛgu."

**1.170.5**  "This one now wishes to slay you in his rage over his father's murder; it is by whose divine energy your eyes have been stripped away."

**1.170.6**  "Entreat him, O dear ones — Aurva, my most excellent son; pleased by your prostration, he will release your sight."

**1.170.7**  The Gandharva said: Thus addressed, all those kings then spoke to him who had been born from the thigh, saying "Be pleased," and he thereupon showed them his grace.

**1.170.8**  And by this very fact he became renowned by that name throughout the worlds — that best of men, the brahmin seer Aurva, born by bursting through the thigh (ūru).

**1.170.9**  Having recovered their sight, the kings then departed; but the Bhārgava sage resolved upon the destruction of all the worlds.

**1.170.10**  That great-minded one, O dear one, turned his mind entirely and utterly toward the destruction of all the worlds.

**1.170.11**  That best of the Bhṛgus, wishing to exact retribution for the Bhṛgus, magnified by his great austerities, turned his mind toward the destruction of all the worlds.

**1.170.12**  He tormented the worlds, including gods, asuras, and humans, with his fierce great austerities, intent on gladdening his ancestral fathers.

**1.170.13**  Then his ancestral fathers, O dear one, recognizing that best of the Bhṛgus, all came from the world of the ancestors and spoke these words to him.

**1.170.14**  "Aurva, we have witnessed the power of your fierce austerity, dear son. Show grace to the worlds; restrain your wrath."

**1.170.15**  "For at that time, O dear one, the slaughter by those kṣatriyas who were doing violence was deliberately overlooked by all those Bhṛgus of cultivated soul, who were not powerless."

**1.170.16**  "For when, having lived to a very great age, weariness entered us, it was then, O dear one, that we ourselves desired to be slain by the kṣatriyas."

**1.170.17**  "Indeed that wealth buried in a certain Bhārgava household was deposited there precisely in order to create enmity, by those who wished to provoke the kṣatriyas to anger. What use is wealth to us, O best of twice-born, who are longing for heaven?"

**1.170.18**  "But when Death was utterly unable to take us, then this means was seen and approved by us, O dear one."

**1.170.19**  "And a man who kills himself, O dear one, does not attain the auspicious worlds; therefore, having considered this, we did not destroy ourselves by our own hand."

**1.170.20**  "Nor is this pleasing to us, dear one — what you wish to do now. Restrain this mind from the sin of destroying all the worlds."

**1.170.21**  "For no kṣatriyas and no seven worlds, O son, can taint our austerities and our splendor. Abandon this wrath that has arisen."

**1.171.1**  Aurva said: "The vow I made in my wrath back then, O ancestors, for the destruction of all the worlds — that must not go unfulfilled for me."

**1.171.2**  "For I am not able to live on as one whose wrathful vow goes in vain; the unfulfilled wrath would burn me like fire burns kindling-wood."

**1.171.3**  "The man who endures wrath that has arisen for just cause is not capable of properly protecting the three aims of life."

**1.171.4**  "Wrath is justly employed by kings who desire heaven, as a restrainer of the undisciplined and a protector of the disciplined."

**1.171.5**  "I heard, lying in the thigh, resting in the womb-bed, the outcry of the company of mothers at the slaughter of the Bhṛgus by the kṣatriyas."

**1.171.6**  "When the utter extermination of the Bhṛgus, down to the unborn in the womb, by the lowest of kṣatriyas was endured by the worlds together with the gods, then wrath seized me."

**1.171.7**  "My mothers and fathers, it seems, overflowing with power, did not find a refuge in any of the worlds out of fear."

**1.171.8**  "When no one then came to the aid of those wives of the Bhṛgus, it was then that this auspicious one bore me alone in her thigh."

**1.171.9**  "When a restrainer of evil exists in the worlds, then an evildoer finds no foothold in all the worlds."

**1.171.10**  "But when the evildoer finds no restrainer anywhere, then many in the world persist in evil deeds."

**1.171.11**  "And he who, though knowing evil and capable, does not restrain it, even though he is the lord — he too becomes implicated in that very deed."

**1.171.12**  "If my fathers, though able, could not be protected by kings and lords — counting life here as desirable —"

**1.171.13**  "— therefore I am enraged against them; being today the lord of the worlds. Yet your words I am not able to simply transgress."

**1.171.14**  "And for me too, as an existing lord, this would be a great thing — again to have fear of sin from overlooking the worlds."

**1.171.15**  "And this fire born of my wrath, which wishes to devour the worlds — if suppressed, it would burn me myself with its own energy."

**1.171.16**  "I know your desire for the welfare of all the worlds. Therefore, O lords, ordain what is best for the worlds and for me."

**1.171.17**  The ancestral fathers said: "This fire born of your wrath that wishes to devour the worlds — release it into the waters; good fortune to you, for the worlds are established in water."

**1.171.18**  "All flavors are water-born, the entire world is water-born; therefore release this fire of wrath into the waters, O best of twice-born."

**1.171.19**  "Let this fire of your wrath remain, O brahmin, in the great ocean if you so wish, burning the waters — for the worlds are declared to be water-born."

**1.171.20**  "Thus this vow of yours will be fulfilled, O sinless one, and the worlds together with the gods will not come to destruction."

**1.171.21**  Vasiṣṭha said: Then Aurva, O dear one, released that fire born of wrath into the abode of Varuṇa; and that fire indeed uses the waters, dwelling in the great ocean.

**1.171.22**  Becoming a great horse's head — which those who know the Veda know of — it continually drinks the waters of the great ocean, vomiting forth that fire from its mouth.

**1.171.23**  "Therefore you too, good fortune to you, should not desire to destroy the worlds, O Parāśara; knowing the highest dharmas, O best among the wise."

**1.172.1**  The Gandharva said: Thus addressed by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, that brahmin seer restrained his own wrath from destroying all the worlds.

**1.172.2**  And that son of Śakti, the greatly resplendent Parāśara, best among those who know all the Vedas, performed a rākṣasa-sacrifice.

**1.172.3**  Then that great sage, remembering the murder of Śakti, burned both aged and young rākṣasas in that extended sacrifice.

**1.172.4**  For Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him from the slaughter of the rākṣasas, out of the firm resolve: "I must not break his vow a second time."

**1.172.5**  That great sage in that sacrifice stood before the three blazing sacred fires like a fourth fire.

**1.172.6**  By that pure sacrifice being offered in the proper manner, the sky was illuminated, like by the sun at the end of the rainy season.

**1.172.7**  All the sages there, led by Vasiṣṭha, regarded him, blazing in the sky with his splendor, as a second sun.

**1.172.8**  Then Atri, that sage of noble intellect, wishing to bring to completion that sacrifice which was supremely difficult for others to complete, approached him.

**1.172.9**  Likewise Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu also approached that great sacrifice, O slayer of enemies, desiring life for the rākṣasas.

**1.172.10**  Then Pulastya, O bull of the Bharatas, O Pārtha, spoke these words to Parāśara the tamer of enemies, to stop the slaughter of those rākṣasas.

**1.172.11**  "I hope you are without impediment, dear one; I hope you find joy, O son — not in the slaughter of all these rākṣasas who are ignorant and without fault."

**1.172.12**  "This total extermination of a lineage, O best among soma-drinkers — you, being among the highest, are doing what is most unrighteous, O Parāśara. And King Kalmāṣapāda now desires to ascend to heaven."

**1.172.13**  "And those sons of the great sage Vasiṣṭha who were superior to Śakti — they all rejoice with delight, together with the gods. All this is known to Vasiṣṭha, O great sage."

**1.172.14**  "And the extermination of these ascetic rākṣasas — you, O son of Vasiṣṭha's joy, have been the instrument of it in this sacrifice. Release this sacrifice; good fortune to you — let this be concluded."

**1.172.15**  Thus addressed by Pulastya and the wise Vasiṣṭha, that son of Śakti, Parāśara, then brought the sacrifice to a close.

**1.172.16**  The sage released the fire that had been gathered for the universal rākṣasa-sacrifice on the northern slope of the Himālayas, in the great forest.

**1.172.17**  That fire is seen there even today, consuming rākṣasas, trees, and very rocks, always at each and every new moon and full moon.

**1.173.1**  Arjuna said: "For what reason was the wife appointed to that teacher, the best among knowers of Brahman, by King Kalmāṣapāda?"

**1.173.2**  "And why did the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, knowing the highest dharma and worldly propriety, approach one who was unapproachable? That great-souled one did so in the past — you should tell me everything, as I ask."

**1.173.3**  The Gandharva said: "Listen to this, O Dhanaṃjaya, that which you ask me about — regarding Vasiṣṭha the invincible and likewise the king who endured his enemies."

**1.173.4**  "I have told you earlier, O best of the Bharatas, how that king was cursed by Śakti, the great-souled son of Vasiṣṭha."

**1.173.5**  "But that king, having fallen under the power of the curse, his eyes overwhelmed with fury, departed from the city together with his wife, O scorcher of enemies."

**1.173.6**  "Having gone to the uninhabited forest, he wandered together with his wife through it — teeming with many herds of deer, crowded with many creatures."

**1.173.7**  "Dense with thickets of various shrubs and vines, covered with various trees, that forest resounding with dreadful sounds — he, seized by the curse, roamed through it."

**1.173.8**  "One day, seized with hunger, searching for food for himself, greatly afflicted, he came upon a certain forest stream and saw a Brahmin woman and a Brahmin man who had come together for the purpose of union."

**1.173.9**  Seeing those two, frightened and having not achieved their purpose, they fled; but as the two ran away, the king seized the brahmin by force.

**1.173.10**  Seeing her husband seized, the brahmin woman then spoke: "Listen, O king, to the words I will speak to you, O virtuous one."

**1.173.11**  "You are indeed born of the lineage of the Sun, celebrated throughout the world, ever-vigilant, established in righteousness, and devoted to the service of your teacher."

**1.173.12**  "You have received a curse, O unconquerable one — you ought not to commit sin. The fertile season having arrived, I have today come together with my husband."

**1.173.13**  "I have not yet attained my purpose with my husband, and my longing for offspring is great. Be pleased, O best of kings — let this husband of mine be released."

**1.173.14**  Even as she cried out thus, that doer of terrible deeds devoured her husband as a tiger devours a coveted deer.

**1.173.15**  The tears that fell to the ground from her, overcome with rage, became a blazing fire and lit up that very place.

**1.173.16**  Then she, tormented by grief and afflicted by the calamity of losing her husband, that brahmin woman cursed the royal sage Kalmāṣapāda in fury.

**1.173.17**  "Because, O wretch, you have cruelly devoured before my eyes my lord and husband of great glory, while I had not yet achieved my purpose —"

**1.173.18**  "Therefore you too, O evil-minded one, struck by my curse, shall instantly give up your life the moment you approach your wife in her fertile season."

**1.173.19**  "The sons of that seer Vasiṣṭha were destroyed by you; having united with him, your wife shall bear a son — that son who perpetuates your lineage shall be born, O most vile of kings."

**1.173.20**  Having thus cursed the king, that auspicious woman of Āṅgirasa descent entered the blazing sacred fire right there in his presence.

**1.173.21**  And the highly blessed Vasiṣṭha witnessed all of this, O scorcher of foes, through the power of great knowledge and his austerities.

**1.173.22**  After a great length of time the royal sage was released from the curse; and when at the fertile season he approached Madayantī, he was restrained by her.

**1.173.23**  The king, bewildered by the curse, did not recall that curse; but upon hearing the queen's words, that best of kings, recollecting the curse, was then greatly tormented.

**1.173.24**  For this reason the king, afflicted by the fault of the curse, engaged Vasiṣṭha with his own wife, O best of the Bharatas.

**1.174.1**  Arjuna said: "Indeed, tell us, O Gandharva, who would be a suitable purohita for us — one learned in the Vedas. All is known to you."

**1.174.2**  The Gandharva said: "The younger brother of Devala practices austerity in the forest — Dhaumya, at the ford called Utkocaka. Choose him if you wish."

**1.174.3**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then Arjuna duly gave the Āgneya weapon to the Gandharva, and pleased, spoke these words to him.

**1.174.4**  "Let the horses remain with you for now, O best of Gandharvas; I will take them when the time for their use arrives" — and he also said: "May you fare well."

**1.174.5**  They honoured one another, and then the Gandharva and the Pāṇḍavas departed as they wished from the pleasant bank of the Bhāgīrathī.

**1.174.6**  Then, going to the ford of Utkocaka and to Dhaumya's hermitage, the Pāṇḍavas chose Dhaumya for the office of purohita, O Bhārata.

**1.174.7**  Dhaumya, the foremost among those who know all the Vedas, received them with water for the feet and with fruits and roots, and also took on the office of purohita for them.

**1.174.8**  Then the Pāṇḍavas, placing that brahmin foremost, hoped to obtain prosperity and kingdom, and also the svayaṃvara of the Pāñcālī.

**1.174.9**  Those bulls among the Bharatas, together with their mother — six of them — united with that teacher, then considered themselves as though they had a protector.

**1.174.10**  For that noble-minded one, knowing the true import of the Vedas, became their teacher; by him, who was learned in righteousness and all knowledge, the Pārthas were made fit to be officiated for in sacrifice.

**1.174.11**  He regarded those heroes as having attained kingship by their own duty, endowed with intelligence, heroism, strength, and enterprise — like other gods.

**1.174.12**  Having had the auspicious rites performed for them by him, those lords of men then resolved together to go to the svayaṃvara of the Pāñcālī.

**1.175.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Then those five brothers, tigers among men, the Pāṇḍavas, set out to see Draupadī and that great festival equal to the gods.

**1.175.2**  Those tigers among men, scorchers of foes, as they set out together with their mother, saw on the road many brahmins going with their groups.

**1.175.3**  The brahmins, O king, spoke to those Pāṇḍavas who appeared as celibate students: "Where are you gentlemen going, and from where have you come?"

**1.175.4**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Know us, O seers of the divine, as brothers come from Ekacakrā, travelling together with our mother."

**1.175.5**  The brahmins said: "Go today itself to the Pāñcāla lands, to the dwelling of Drupada — a great svayaṃvara with enormous riches will take place there."

**1.175.6**  "We too are travelling in the same caravan and heading there; for a great festival of wondrous appearance will take place there."

**1.175.7**  "The daughter of Yajñasena, the great-souled Drupada, born from the midst of the sacrificial altar, her eyes resembling the petals of a lotus —"

**1.175.8**  "— beautiful to behold, with faultless limbs, tender, spirited, the sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna the powerful, enemy of Droṇa —"

**1.175.9**  "— who was born, the great-armed one, clad in armour, bearing sword, arrows and bow, from the well-kindled sacred fire, blazing like fire itself —"

**1.175.10**  "— the sister of that one, the faultless-limbed Draupadī of slender waist, whose fragrance, equal to that of a blue lotus, wafts from a league away —"

**1.175.11**  "— to see her, the daughter of Yajñasena, for whom the svayaṃvara occasion has been arranged, and that great festival equal to the gods, we are going."

**1.175.12**  "Kings and princes, performers of sacrifice with lavish gifts, devoted to Vedic study, pure, great-souled, firm in their vows —"

**1.175.13**  "— young, handsome, come from various lands, great warriors, skilled in arms — these lords of the earth will assemble there."

**1.175.14**  "Those lords of men will give there various gifts for the sake of winning — wealth, cows, and all manner of food and provisions."

**1.175.15**  "Having received all of that, and having seen the svayaṃvara, and having enjoyed the festival, we shall go as we desire."

**1.175.16**  "Actors, bards, dancers, sūtas and māgadhas, and mighty wrestlers will assemble there from various lands."

**1.175.17**  "Having thus gratified your curiosity, and having seen and received gifts, O great-souled ones, you shall return with us."

**1.175.18**  "And having seen all of you, handsome as gods, as you stand there, Kṛṣṇā might by chance choose one among you as her chosen lord."

**1.175.19**  "This brother of yours, glorious, handsome, and mighty-armed — competing, he might by chance win great wealth."

**1.175.20**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Most certainly, sirs, we shall go, all of us together with you, to see that great festival equal to the gods and the svayaṃvara of that maiden."

**1.176.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed, the Pāṇḍavas set out, O Janamejaya, to the southern Pāñcāla lands protected by king Drupada.

**1.176.2**  Then, O king, the Pāṇḍavas saw on the road that great-souled one, the pure-souled and sinless Dvaipāyana.

**1.176.3**  Having honoured him duly, being comforted by him, and at the end of their conversation receiving his permission, they proceeded to the abode of Drupada.

**1.176.4**  Beholding the charming forests and lakes, resting here and there, those great warriors went slowly.

**1.176.5**  Devoted to Vedic study, pure, gentle and sweet-spoken, the Kuru princes arrived in due order in the Pāñcāla country.

**1.176.6**  The Pāṇḍavas, having seen the city and the encampment, then took up lodging in the workshop of a potter.

**1.176.7**  There they collected alms, living by the way of a brahmin; no one anywhere recognised those heroes who had arrived.

**1.176.8**  But the wish of Yajñasena was always: "May I give Kṛṣṇā to the Pāṇḍava, the diadem-wearer" — yet he did not reveal this.

**1.176.9**  The Pāñcāla king, O Janamejaya, O Bhārata, searching for the Kaunteyās, had a mighty bow made that was impossible to string.

**1.176.10**  He also had made an artificial machine in the sky, and along with that machine the king had a golden target made.

**1.176.11**  Drupada said: "He who, having strung this bow and with these arrows from it, passes through the machine and strikes the target — he shall win my daughter."

**1.176.12**  Vaiśampāyana said: Thus king Drupada had it proclaimed everywhere; hearing it, all the kings, O Bhārata, gathered there.

**1.176.13**  And great-souled sages, wishing to witness the svayaṃvara, as well as the Kurus headed by Duryodhana and accompanied by Karṇa, O king —

**1.176.14**  — and greatly blessed brahmins came from various lands; those groups of kings were honoured by the great-souled Drupada.

**1.176.15**  Then all the townsfolk, with a roar like that raised by the ocean, reached the city of Śiśumāra; those kings too took up residence there.

**1.176.16**  To the northeast of the city, on a level and auspicious plot of ground, the festival arena shone, surrounded on all sides by pavilions.

**1.176.17**  Enclosed with a wall and moat, adorned with gate-arches, covered everywhere with a variegated canopy —

**1.176.18**  — filled with hundreds of bands of musical instruments, perfumed with the finest aguru incense, sprinkled with sandalwood water, and adorned with garlands and festoons —

**1.176.19**  — firmly built, enclosed on all sides with well-constructed tall palaces that resembled the peaks of mount Kailāsa and scraped the sky —

**1.176.20**  — covered with golden lattice-work, adorned with gem-set floors, with stairs easy to ascend, furnished with great seats and coverings —

**1.176.21**  — spread with garments fit for the non-rustic, fragrant with the finest aguru, white as swans, many of them, their perfume carrying for leagues —

**1.176.22**  — with hundreds of unobstructed doors, beautified with beds and seats, their bodies studded with many minerals — like the peaks of the Himālaya —

**1.176.23**  There all the kings, splendidly adorned, vying with one another, took their seats in the various kinds of royal pavilions.

**1.176.24**  There they saw seated those lions among kings, of great spirit and valour, greatly blessed, adorned with black aguru paste.

**1.176.25**  Greatly gracious, devoted to the brahmins, protectors of their own kingdoms, dear to all the world through their good deeds and auspicious actions.

**1.176.26**  On the most excellent galleries the townspeople and country-folk sat down everywhere, eager for the delight of seeing Kṛṣṇā.

**1.176.27**  The Pāṇḍavas too, together with the brahmins, sat down, beholding the unsurpassed prosperity of the king of Pāñcāla.

**1.176.28**  Then that assembly grew, O king, over many days, filled with the giving of gems, and beautified by actors and dancers.

**1.176.29**  While the assembly was in progress, on the charming sixteenth day, having bathed, dressed in fine garments, adorned with all ornaments —

**1.176.30**  — taking up the hero's bronze vessel that was ornamented with gold, Draupadī then descended into the arena, O bull of the Bharatas.

**1.176.31**  The purohita of the Somakas, a brahmin learned in mantras, pure, having spread the ritual grass, then poured oblations of clarified butter into the fire according to the rite.

**1.176.32**  He, having satisfied the blazing fire and having pronounced blessings upon the brahmins, then caused all the musical instruments on every side to cease.

**1.176.33**  When silence had been made there, O lord of men, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, standing in the centre of the arena, proclaimed loudly in a voice deep as a thundercloud these words — smooth, meaningful, and excellent.

**1.176.34**  "Here is the bow, here the target, and here the arrows — let all the kings hear me: passing through the aperture of the machine, strike the target with five arrows."

**1.176.35**  "Whoever shall accomplish this supremely difficult feat, endowed with noble birth, handsome form, and strength — his wife this Kṛṣṇā, my sister, shall become today. I speak no falsehood."

**1.176.36**  Having thus addressed them, Drupada's son then spoke to Draupadī, proclaiming the names, lineages, and deeds of all those assembled kings.

**1.177.1**  Dhṛṣṭadyumna said: Duryodhana, Durviṣaha, Durmukha, Duṣpradharṣaṇa, Viviṃśati, Vikarṇa, Saha, and Duḥśāsana —

**1.177.2**  Yuyutsu, Vātavega, Bhīmavegadhara, Ugrāyudha, Balākī, Kanakāyu, and Virocana —

**1.177.3**  Sukuṇḍala, Citrasena, Suvarcās, Kanakadhvaja, Nandaka, Bāhuśālī, Kuṇḍaja, and Vikaṭa —

**1.177.4**  These and many other mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with Karṇa — valiant warriors, a hundred in number, great-souled and renowned bulls among kṣatriyas — have come here for your sake.

**1.177.5**  Śakuni, Bala, Vṛṣaka, and Bṛhadbala — all these sons of the king of Gāndhāra have assembled here.

**1.177.6**  Aśvatthāmā and Bhoja, the foremost of all weapon-bearers, two great-souled ones, have come together adorned for your sake.

**1.177.7**  Bṛhanta, Maṇimān, the mighty Daṇḍadhāra, Sahadeva, Jayatsena, and Meghasaṃdhi the Māgadha —

**1.177.8**  Virāṭa together with his two sons Śaṅkha and Uttara, Vārdhakṣemi, Suvarcās, and king Senābindu —

**1.177.9**  Abhibhū with his son, Sudāman and Suvarcas, Sumitra, Sukumāra, Vṛka, and Satyadhṛti —

**1.177.10**  Sūryadhvaja, Rocamāna, Nīla, Citrāyudha, Aṃśumān, Cekitāna, and the greatly powerful Śreṇimān —

**1.177.11**  The glorious Candrasena son of Samudrasena, Jalasaṃdha, the father-and-son pair Sudaṇḍa and Daṇḍa —

**1.177.12**  Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, the mighty Bhagadatta, Kaliṅga, Tāmralipta, and the lord of harbours —

**1.177.13**  The king of Madra, Śalya the great chariot-warrior together with his son, along with the hero Rukmāṅgada and Rukmaratha —

**1.177.14**  The Kaurava Somadatta and his three heroic mahāratha sons assembled together: Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala —

**1.177.15**  Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, Dṛḍhadhanvā the Kaurava, Bṛhadbala, Suṣeṇa, and Śibi of Uśīnara —

**1.177.16**  Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, the mighty son of Rukmiṇī, Sāmba, Cārudeṣṇa, Sāraṇa, and Gada —

**1.177.17**  Akrūra, Sātyaki, the mighty Uddhava, Kṛtavarmā the son of Hṛdika, Pṛthu, and Vipṛthu —

**1.177.18**  Viḍūratha, Kaṅka, Samīka, Sāramejaya, the valiant Vātapati, Jhillī, Piṇḍāraka, and the mighty Uśīnara — these Vṛṣṇis have been proclaimed.

**1.177.19**  Bhagīratha, Bṛhatkṣatra, the Saindhava Jayadratha, Bṛhadratha, Bāhlika, and the mahāratha Śrutāyu —

**1.177.20**  Ulūka, the Kaitava king, Citrāṅgada, Śubhāṅgada, the steadfast Vatsarāja, and the lord of Kosala —

**1.177.21**  These and many other lords of various peoples, O fortunate one — kṣatriyas renowned on earth — have come for your sake.

**1.177.22**  These valiant men will attempt this supreme target for your sake. Whichever one strikes this target, O auspicious one, choose him today."

**1.178.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those adorned, earringed young men, gathered and rivalling one another, each deeming himself supreme in weapons and strength, all sprang up with pride.

**1.178.2**  Swelling with pride in their beauty, valour, lineage, righteousness, and youth, swept up by the surge of intoxication, they were like lordly elephants from the Himālayas in rut.

**1.178.3**  Gazing at one another in rivalry, their bodies overwhelmed by desire born of thought, each saying "This Kṛṣṇā is mine," they rose suddenly from their royal seats.

**1.178.4**  Those kṣatriyas who had entered the arena, assembled and eager to win Drupada's daughter, shone like the hosts of gods gathered around Umā, the daughter of the mountain king.

**1.178.5**  Their bodies pierced by the arrows of Kandarpa (the god of love), their hearts already gone to Kṛṣṇā, those lords of men who had descended into the arena for Drupada's daughter made even friends into enemies there.

**1.178.6**  Then the hosts of gods arrived in their celestial cars — the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, all the Sādhyas and the Maruts — with Yama and Dhaneśvara (Kubera) leading them.

**1.178.7**  The Daityas, the Suparṇas, the great serpents, divine sages, Guhyakas, Cāraṇas, Viśvāvasu, Nārada and Parvata, and the chief Gandharvas together with the Apsarases —

**1.178.8**  Halāyudha and Keśava were there too, and the foremost among the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas watched; those bulls of the Yadu clan stood abiding by Kṛṣṇa's judgment.

**1.178.9**  Seeing those Pārthas — like lordly elephants in rut, like five lordly elephants of highest excellence, like fires whose bodies are covered with ash — that foremost hero of the Yadus pondered.

**1.178.10**  He whispered to Rāma identifying Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Jiṣṇu (Arjuna), and the twin heroes; and having observed them slowly and carefully, Rāma looked at Janārdana with a delighted mind.

**1.178.11**  Other princes and grandsons of kings, their eyes and minds naturally drawn to Kṛṣṇā, straining with effort, watched her moving about — their faces copper-red as they bit their lips.

**1.178.12**  Likewise the broad-armed Pārthas and those two majestic twin heroes — all of them, beholding Draupadī at that moment, were struck by the arrows of Kandarpa.

**1.178.13**  That space was crowded with divine sages and Gandharvas, frequented by Suparṇas, Nāgas, Asuras, and Siddhas, filled with divine fragrance and strewn with divine garlands —

**1.178.14**  — and with the great reverberating sounds of kettledrums, the sky became crowded; it grew dense with celestial cars on all sides, resonant with flutes, vīṇās, and paṇava drums.

**1.178.15**  Then those assemblies of kings, striving one after another for Kṛṣṇā's sake, O king, were unable even by force to string that powerful bow.

**1.178.16**  Those lords of men, straining and being flung away by the rigid, quivering bow, lay writhing on the ground — they appeared pitiful, their spirits broken.

**1.178.17**  With cries of despair, their armlets and earrings crushed and shattered by that unyielding bow, their confidence for Kṛṣṇā's sake exhausted — the circle of kings was in distress then.

**1.178.18**  But while the assembly was in turmoil and those lords of men had given up the attempt, Jiṣṇu, the son of Kuntī, that hero, desired to string that bow and take up the arrows.

**1.179.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the kings had desisted from the task of stringing the bow, then Jiṣṇu of noble mind rose up from the midst of the brāhmaṇas.

**1.179.2**  The chief brāhmaṇas cried out, waving their deerskins, upon seeing Pārtha advance — he who was as radiant as Indra's banner.

**1.179.3**  Some were despondent; some were filled with joy; and some among them — the sharp-witted men who live by their intellect — spoke to one another:

**1.179.4**  "That which was not bent by powerful kings world-renowned and devoted to the science of archery — Karṇa, Śalya, and others at their head —

**1.179.5**  — how can that bow be strung, O brāhmaṇas, by one who has not mastered weapons, who is more feeble than those alive, who is merely a young student?"

**1.179.6**  "The brāhmaṇas will become a laughingstock before all kings if this deed is not accomplished and we entered it rashly without reflection."

**1.179.7**  "If he has set out to seize the bow out of pride or boldness, or out of the fickleness of a brāhmaṇa youth, it would be well to stop him — let him not go."

**1.179.8**  "We shall not become objects of ridicule, nor shall we be placed in a position of lightness, nor shall we incur the hostility of the kings of the earth."

**1.179.9**  Others said: "He is a young man of splendour, like the trunk of the king of elephants, with broad shoulders and mighty arms, and in steadfastness like the Himālaya —"

**1.179.10**  "This feat seems possible in him, and from his enthusiasm his great ability may be inferred — for one who is incapable would not go forward of his own accord."

**1.179.11**  "And there is no deed whatsoever in the worlds that would be unachievable for brāhmaṇas who dwell and move in the three states."

**1.179.12**  "Living on water, living on air, or subsisting on fruit alone, firm in their vows, the brāhmaṇas are indeed stronger than the strong by the blazing power of brahman."

**1.179.13**  "A brāhmaṇa is not to be despised, whether he conducts himself well or ill — whether the deed that has come to him be pleasant or painful, great or small."

**1.179.14**  While the brāhmaṇas were thus lamenting with these various words, Arjuna stood near the bow, immovable as a mountain.

**1.179.15**  He circumambulated the bow, then performed the reverential pradakṣiṇa (clockwise circuit), bowed his head in obeisance with delight, and grasped it — he the scorcher of foes.

**1.179.16**  In the twinkling of an eye he strung it; he took up five arrows, pierced the target, and it fell — suddenly shot through via the aperture, falling to the ground.

**1.179.17**  Then a sound arose in the sky and a great roar in the midst of the assembly; the gods rained divine flowers upon Pārtha's head — he who destroys his enemies.

**1.179.18**  The people waved their garments everywhere and cried out in wonder; showers of flowers fell from the sky on all sides.

**1.179.19**  A hundred musical instruments were played by musicians; gatherings of Sūtas and Māgadhas praised him there with sweet voices.

**1.179.20**  Seeing this, Drupada the destroyer of enemies was filled with joy; and he, together with his army, desired to come to Pārtha's aid.

**1.179.21**  But when that great sound had risen, Yudhiṣṭhira, the most excellent among those who uphold dharma, quickly went back to their dwelling together with the two foremost of men, the twins.

**1.179.22**  But Kṛṣṇā, having fully observed the target struck and gazing upon Pārtha who was equal to Indra, took up a white bridal garland and went to the son of Kuntī with a smile.

**1.179.23**  He, having won her and taking her, being honoured by those twice-born ones, departed from the arena — he of inconceivable deeds — followed by that wife of his.

**1.180.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As he sought to give the maiden to that great-souled brāhmaṇa, anger arose among the kings as they looked at one another nearby.

**1.180.2**  "Passing over us and treating us who are assembled here as worthless as grass, he wishes to give Draupadī — the most excellent of women — to a brāhmaṇa."

**1.180.3**  "Let us slay this wicked-souled one who has no regard for us — he deserves no respect, nor does he merit the customary honour by virtue of any qualities."

**1.180.4**  "Let us slay him along with his son — this man of evil conduct, hostile to kings — for having invited all the lords of men, honoured and well-feasted them, he now despises them afterwards."

**1.180.5**  "In this assembly of kings, like the gathering of gods, has he truly not seen any king who is his equal?"

**1.180.6**  "And the brāhmaṇas have no right regarding the choice — the svayaṃvara belongs to kṣatriyas: this is the well-known scriptural injunction."

**1.180.7**  "Or if this maiden does not wish for anyone here, let us cast her into the fire and depart to our kingdoms, O kings."

**1.180.8**  "But if a brāhmaṇa has done this disagreeable thing out of youth or greed, this one must not be slain under any circumstances —"

**1.180.9**  "— for our kingdoms, our lives, our riches, our sons and grandsons, and whatever other wealth we possess all exist for the sake of brāhmaṇas."

**1.180.10**  "Out of fear of disgrace and for the protection of our own dharma, and so that other svayaṃvaras do not end thus — let this not be the outcome."

**1.180.11**  Having thus spoken, those tiger-like kings — joyful, with arms like iron bars — took up their weapons and rushed upon Drupada to seize him.

**1.180.12**  Seeing those kings — bows and arrows in hand, furious, charging — Drupada, seized with terror, took refuge among the brāhmaṇas.

**1.180.13**  But those two sons of Pāṇḍu, the greatly valiant and enemy-taming pair, stood forth to meet those kings charging with fury like elephants in rut.

**1.180.14**  Then those kings leapt up with weapons raised, their fingers bound with finger-guards, intent on killing the two sons of the Kuru king, inflamed with rage at Arjuna and Bhimasena.

**1.180.15**  Then Bhima, that hero of wondrous valor in battle, mighty as a thunderbolt, that lone champion, uprooted a tree with his two arms and stripped it of its branches, as a lordly elephant would do.

**1.180.16**  Taking that tree like Yama grasping his terrible staff, the slayer of foes — that Partha of broad and long arms — stood close beside the bull among men, Arjuna.

**1.180.17**  Witnessing that feat which surpassed human comprehension — the deed of Jishnu together with his brother — Damodara of inconceivable acts spoke these words to his brother of fierce valor, Halaayudha.

**1.180.18**  "He who moves like a rutting bull and draws that great bow measuring a palm-tree's height — he is Arjuna; there is no doubt about this. If I am Vasudeva, O Sankarshana."

**1.180.19**  "And he who, having swiftly uprooted that tree at the tumult of the kings, has now turned back — he is Vrikodara; no other among mortal men on this earth would be capable of that today."

**1.180.20**  "He who stands foremost with lotus-wide eyes, slender, with the gait of a great lion, composed, fair-complexioned, with a long, gleaming and beautiful nose — he who has stepped forth, O Achyuta, is the Dharmaraja."

**1.180.21**  "Those two who appear like a pair of young Karttikeyas — they are the two sons of the Ashvins, so I surmise; for I have heard that the sons of Pandu and Pritha escaped from the burning of the house of lac."

**1.180.22**  Halaayudha, radiant as pure water, glad and confident, spoke to his younger brother: "I am delighted, for by fortune our father's sister Pritha has been freed together with the foremost of the Kauravas."

**1.181.1**  Vaishampayana said: Shaking their antelope skins and water-pots, those foremost among twice-born ones spoke to him: "Have no fear — we shall fight the enemies."

**1.181.2**  Arjuna, as if smiling, spoke to those brahmins who were saying this: "You stand to the side as spectators."

**1.181.3**  "I shall hold back these enraged ones by scattering hundreds of straight-tipped arrows upon them, as mantras hold back venomous serpents."

**1.181.4**  Having said this, that great warrior took up the bow won as the bride-price and stood together with his brother Bhima, immovable as a mountain.

**1.181.5**  Then those two fearless ones charged against those angry kshatriyas led by Karna who had risen up in fury, as two bull-elephants charge against rival elephants.

**1.181.6**  And those kings, intent on killing, spoke harsh words: "Even the slaying of a twice-born man in battle is justified when he desires to fight."

**1.181.7**  Then Karna, the son of Vikartana, went with full force toward Arjuna seeking battle, as an elephant goes toward a rival elephant for the sake of a cow in rut.

**1.181.8**  The mighty Shalya, lord of the Madras, went against Bhimasena, while Duryodhana and the others, in conflict with the brahmins, fought gently and without effort in that battle.

**1.181.9**  Then wise Arjuna, drawing his bow with full strength, shot back at the onrushing Karna, son of Vikartana, with three arrows.

**1.181.10**  Stunned by the force of those sharp arrows blazing with fierce energy, Radheya strove with all effort and pressed after him.

**1.181.11**  Both of them, incomparable in swiftness, foremost among conquerors, fought with fierce intensity, each striving for victory over the other.

**1.181.12**  "See stroke met with counterstroke — see the might of my arms!" — with such warrior-proud words they addressed each other in turn.

**1.181.13**  Then Karna the son of Vikartana, recognizing the incomparable valor of Arjuna's arms, fought on enraged, matching him blow for blow.

**1.181.14**  Deflecting those swift arrows launched by Arjuna, Karna then roared aloud, and the soldiers honored him with acclaim.

**1.181.15**  Karna said: "I am pleased with you, O foremost of brahmins, with the strength of your arms in combat, with your undaunted spirit, and with your mastery of both weapons and missile-lore."

**1.181.16**  "Are you Dhanurveda incarnate, or Rama himself, O best of brahmins? Or are you perhaps Indra of the bay horses in person, or Vishnu the Infallible in bodily form?"

**1.181.17**  "Concealing your true identity and relying on the strength of your arms, you have assumed this brahmin form and then fight me."

**1.181.18**  "No man other than the lord of Shachi himself or the diademed Pandava would be capable of fighting me in battle when I am enraged."

**1.181.19**  Vaishampayana said: To Karna speaking thus, Phalguna replied there: "I am not Dhanurveda, O Karna, nor am I the glorious Rama. I am a brahmin, the foremost in battle, the best among all who bear weapons."

**1.181.20**  "I am accomplished in both the Brahma and Pauramdara weapon-sciences by the teaching of my guru. I stand here today in battle to conquer you. Stand firm, O hero."

**1.181.21**  Thus addressed, Radheya Karna withdrew from the battle, that great chariot-warrior deeming the brahminic energy arrayed against him unconquerable.

**1.181.22**  O king, Shalya and Vrikodara, both mighty, intoxicated with pride and strength, engaged in combat simultaneously, rival in their rivalry.

**1.181.23**  Challenging each other like two great maddened elephants, they struck one another with fists and with knees, and for a moment they dragged each other about on the battlefield.

**1.181.24**  Then Bhima, foremost among the strong, lifted Shalya with both arms in the midst of battle and hurled him down; thereupon the brahmins laughed.

**1.181.25**  There the bull among men, Bhimasena, performed a wonder — though mighty himself, he did not strike the mighty Shalya as he lay fallen on the ground.

**1.181.26**  With Shalya thrown down by Bhimasena and Karna intimidated, all the frightened kings surrounded Vrikodara.

**1.181.27**  And they said to one another: "These are certainly foremost among brahmins. Let it be known where they were born and where they dwell."

**1.181.28**  "Who indeed would be capable of fighting Radha's son in battle other than Rama, or Drona, or Kripa son of Sharadvat,

**1.181.29**  or Krishna the son of Devaki, or Phalguna the scorcher of foes? And who would be capable of fighting back against Duryodhana in battle,

**1.181.30**  and likewise against Shalya the king of the Madras, best among the strong — no one but Baladeva the hero, or the Pandava Vrikodara?"

**1.181.31**  "Let withdrawal be made from this battle combined with brahmins; then, once we have identified them here, we shall fight them again."

**1.181.32**  Krishna, observing that feat of Bhima and growing suspicious about those two sons of Kunti, restrained those kings, appeasing them all with the argument that she had been lawfully won.

**1.181.33**  Those foremost of kings, skilled in battle, having thus been turned back from the fight, all departed to their own lodgings in amazement.

**1.181.34**  "The arena has been dominated by a brahmin; the Panchali princess has been chosen by brahmins" — saying this, all who had assembled there departed.

**1.181.35**  Bhimasena and Dhananjaya, covered with disguise by brahmins wearing robes of black-deer hide, with difficulty made their way back.

**1.181.36**  Free from the press of the crowd, scratched by enemies, followed by Krishna, those two heroes among men shone brilliantly there.

**1.181.37**  Their mother anxiously thought of many forms of destruction as the appointed hour for alms-gathering passed by and her sons had not yet returned.

**1.181.38**  "Might the bulls of the Kurus have been slain by the sons of Dhritarashtra, knowing who they are, or by Rakshasas endowed with illusion, those greatly terrifying and implacable foes?"

**1.181.39**  "Has even the prediction of the great-souled Vyasa turned out contrary?" — thus Pritha meditated, filled with maternal love for her sons.

**1.181.40**  Then in the late afternoon, Jishnu entered there, surrounded by brahmins, like the sun veiled by clouds, with brahmins preceding him.

**1.182.1**  Vaishampayana said: Going to that workshop of the Bhargava smith, the two Parthas of great majesty reached Pritha and joyfully announced to that daughter of Yajna-sena and those foremost of men: "We have received alms."

**1.182.2**  She, having entered the hut without looking at her sons, said "Share it equally among you all." But afterwards Kunti, looking closely at the maiden, said: "Alas, what a thing I have said!"

**1.182.3**  Afraid of unrighteousness and ashamed, Kunti took that greatly noble daughter of Yajnasena by the hand, approached Yudhishthira, and spoke these words:

**1.182.4**  "This maiden is the daughter of King Drupada, entrusted to me by your younger brothers, O son. Through inadvertence I too spoke the fitting word, O king: 'Share it equally among you all.'"

**1.182.5**  "How can what I said today not become a falsehood, O bull of the Kurus? Tell me. Yet neither should unrighteousness befall the daughter of the Panchala king — something unprecedented."

**1.182.6**  King Yudhishthira of highest valor, the foremost of the Kurus, having pondered for a moment, reassured his mother Kunti and spoke these words to Dhananjaya:

**1.182.7**  "By you, O Pandava, was Yajnaseni won; by you will this princess be pleased. Let fire be kindled and the oblation poured — take her hand in accordance with the rites."

**1.182.8**  Arjuna said: "Do not make me, O king of men, a partaker in unrighteousness; this is not the dharma desired by others. You should be wedded first, then this long-armed Bhima of inconceivable deeds,

**1.182.9**  then I, then Nakula next to me, then Madri's son Sahadeva the youngest. O king, Vrikodara, I, and the twins — this maiden and all of us are yours to command."

**1.182.10**  "Given this situation, reflect on what is to be done here that is righteous and honorable, and what would please the Panchala king. Speak — we all stand ready at your command."

**1.182.11**  Vaishampayana said: All of them, seeing the glorious Krishna standing there, looked at one another as they sat and held her in their hearts.

**1.182.12**  For all of them of boundless valor, upon seeing Draupadi, desire arose, churning through all their senses.

**1.182.13**  For the Panchali's lovely form had been fashioned by the Creator himself, surpassing all other women, captivating the hearts of all beings.

**1.182.14**  Yudhishthira, son of Kunti and knower of their outward signs and inner states, fully recalling the words of Dvaipayana, O bull among men,

**1.182.15**  that king, fearing discord among them, spoke to his brothers: "The auspicious Draupadi shall be the wife of all of us."

**1.183.1**  Vaishampayana said: All the sons of Pandu, having considered those words of their eldest brother, then of boundless energy, held that very matter in their minds and sat there.

**1.183.2**  But the foremost of the Vrishnis, together with the son of Rohini, being apprehensive about the foremost of the Kurus, went to that workshop of the Bhargava smith where those foremost of men were sitting.

**1.183.3**  There Krishna together with the son of Rohini saw the long and broad-armed Ajatashatru seated, with those others surrounding him, seated nearby, blazing like fires.

**1.183.4**  Then Vasudeva approached and, pressing the feet of the best among upholders of dharma, said: "I am Krishna" — the feet of King Yudhishthira of the Ajamidha lineage.

**1.183.5**  Likewise the son of Rohini did the same after him; and the Kurus rejoiced and welcomed them. Also the foremost of the Yadus grasped the feet of their father's sister, O chief of the Bharatas.

**1.183.6**  And Ajatashatru, the foremost of the Kurus, after reporting his own welfare, asked Krishna: "How, O Vasudeva, were all of us known to you while we were living here in disguise?"

**1.183.7**  Vasudeva replied with a smile: "Even hidden fire is perceived, O king. Who else among men is to be found who could perform that feat which surpasses the Pandavas?"

**1.183.8**  "By good fortune all of you Pandavas, conquerors of enemies, have been freed from that fire. By good fortune the wicked son of Dhritarashtra along with his minister has not had his desire fulfilled."

**1.183.9**  "May what is hidden in the cave be auspicious for you. Grow strong like a fire being kindled. Let no kings here discover you." Having thus been granted leave by the Pandava, Krishna of undying glory swiftly departed together with Baladeva toward the camp.

**1.184.1**  Vaishampayana said: Dhrishtadyumna the Panchala prince followed behind those two delights of the Kurus as they went to the dwelling of the Bhargava.

**1.184.2**  He, remaining unrecognized, posted men all around and himself settled at a distance within the Bhargava's dwelling.

**1.184.3**  Then in the evening, Bhima the crusher of enemies, Jishnu, and the twins of great majesty, those of undaunted spirit, having gathered alms, presented them to Yudhishthira.

**1.184.4**  Then Kunti the bountiful spoke in proper time to that daughter of Drupada: "Take of it first, dear girl, set aside an offering, and give alms to the brahmin."

**1.184.5**  "To those who desire food, give to them — the people who have gathered all around. Then, having divided the remainder swiftly, give half for the four and for myself."

**1.184.6**  "And give the other half to Bhima, dear girl — he who resembles a bull in rut, that dark young man of powerful frame; for this hero is always a great eater."

**1.184.7**  That princess, her face filled with joy, accepting her words without hesitation as right and proper, the virtuous one carried out exactly as instructed; and all of them partook of the food.

**1.184.8**  Sahadeva, the swift son of Madri, made his bed upon the ground with kusha grass; and all the heroes, spreading their own antelope hides, slept upon the earth.

**1.184.9**  Their heads, those best of the Kurus, faced the direction governed by Agastya; Kunti lay before them and Krishna lay crosswise at their feet.

**1.184.10**  She lay upon the ground alongside the sons of Pandu, made as if a footrest on the kusha; yet she felt no sorrow there, nor did those bulls among the Kurus disrespect her.

**1.184.11**  Those heroes there began to converse, telling varied tales befitting warriors in command of armies — divine weapons, chariots and war-elephants, swords, maces, and battle-axes.

**1.184.12**  As those tales were being recounted, the son of the Panchala king heard them, and also saw Krishna seated there; and all the people saw them too.

**1.184.13**  Prince Dhrishtadyumna, having heard everything that had transpired and all that was said that night, went in haste to report it all in full to King Drupada.

**1.184.14**  The king of Panchala, his face cast down and unable to identify those Pandavas, questioned Dhrishtadyumna, that great-souled one: "Where has Krishna gone, and by whom was she taken?"

**1.184.15**  "Has she not been taken by a Shudra, or a man of low birth, or a Vaishya tributary? Has my head not been pressed underfoot? Has the garland not fallen in the cremation ground?"

**1.184.16**  "Is the man foremost of his own caste, or perhaps of a higher varna? Or has a left foot today been placed upon my head, my son, by the one who has touched Krishna?"

**1.184.17**  "Shall I worship with supreme confidence, having secured the bull among men, the Partha? Tell me truly, O great-spirited one — who is he who has won my daughter today?"

**1.184.18**  "Do the sons of Vichitravirya, those heroes among the Kurus, yet survive? And was the bow taken up and the target struck down today by the younger Partha?"

**1.185.1**  Vaishampayana said: Thus questioned, his face filled with joy, the prince Dhrishtadyumna, foremost of the Somakas, reported to his father what had happened and by whom Krishna had been taken.

**1.185.2**  "That young man with large reddish eyes, wearing a black antelope skin, equal in beauty to a god — it was he who strung the foremost bow and brought the target crashing to the earth."

**1.185.3**  "Unimpeded, he went swiftly, surrounded and honored by the foremost twice-born, moving among the sons of Diti like Indra with his thunderbolt, honored by all the gods and sages."

**1.185.4**  "And Krishna, taking hold of the antelope hide, followed him with joy, as an elephant cow follows her mate, even as the kings of men, refusing to accept it, charged furiously at him there."

**1.185.5**  "Then another, uprooting a great tree from the earth in the midst of those royal lords, drove back the flood of kings like Death himself, enraged, driving back the living."

**1.185.6**  "Those two foremost of men, O lord of kings, took Krishna away before the very eyes of all the kings, shining like the sun and moon, to the workshop of Bharadvaja's son outside the city."

**1.185.7**  "Seated there, blazing like a flame of fire, is, I conjecture, their mother; and seated near her are three other foremost of men, equal in splendor to fire."

**1.185.8**  "Those two then bowed at her feet, said to Krishna 'pay your respects,' and having presented Krishna there, those foremost of men went out to beg alms."

**1.185.9**  "Krishna received their alms, made the customary offering, gave a portion to the brahmins, served that elder woman and those foremost of men, and herself ate as well."

**1.185.10**  "All of them, O king, then slept, while Krishna became a footrest at their feet; their bed was upon the earth, furnished with a spread of the finest darbha grass and antelope hides."

**1.185.11**  "They roared like dark monsoon clouds as they told their varied tales; those heroes spoke no tales fit for a Vaishya or a Shudra, nor indeed of twice-born men."

**1.185.12**  "They are without doubt bulls among Kshatriyas, O king, for they speak of battle as warriors do; indeed our hope is now clearly fulfilled, for we hear the Parthas have escaped the fire."

**1.185.13**  "As the target was struck down and the bow forcefully strung by him, and as they speak among themselves — undoubtedly those Parthas move about in disguise."

**1.185.14**  Then King Drupada, filled with joy, dispatched his priest there, with the words: "We would know who you are — are you the great-souled sons of Pandu?"

**1.185.15**  The king's priest, having received his instructions, went and greeted them with praise, then delivered the king's message completely and in proper order, he who knew the right procedure.

**1.185.16**  "The lord of the earth, King Drupada of Panchala, desires to know who you are, O worthy ones; having seen this striker of the target, he finds no limit to his joy."

**1.185.17**  "Therefore declare your lineage and family in order; set your foot upon the heads of your enemies; and gladden my heart and that of King Drupada with his retinue."

**1.185.18**  "For King Pandu was the beloved friend of King Drupada, equal to himself; and it was his desire that this daughter of mine might become a daughter-in-law of the Kaurava."

**1.185.19**  "And this desire has ever dwelt in the heart of King Drupada, O you of blameless limbs — that Arjuna, with his broad and long arms, might win my daughter by righteous means."

**1.185.20**  The king, hearing the priest speak thus and seeing him standing there humbly, commanded Bhima who stood nearby: "Let water for washing the feet and the gift of honor be given to him."

**1.185.21**  "The priest of King Drupada is worthy of honor; for him an especially great worship must be offered." Bhima did exactly so, O lord of men; and having received that honor,

**1.185.22**  when that priest was seated comfortably, Yudhishthira addressed him as a brahmin: "The daughter has been given away by King Drupada of Panchala in accordance with his own dharma, as he pleased."

**1.185.23**  "The bride-price was fixed by King Drupada; by this hero it was fulfilled accordingly; no distinction was made regarding varna, occupation, family lineage, or clan."

**1.185.24**  "By the stringing of the bow and the striking of the target was she awarded; and thus by this great-souled one was Krishna here won in the midst of the assembly of kings."

**1.185.25**  "Things being thus, the son of Somaka, the king, should not today grieve to his displeasure; and that desire which King Drupada harbored — that too shall be fulfilled for the lord of the earth."

**1.185.26**  "For I deem it right, O brahmin, that this princess is one hard to obtain; that bow could not be strung with its bowstring by one of feeble strength — nor could such a target be struck down by one untrained in weaponry or of low birth."

**1.185.27**  "Therefore King Panchala does not deserve to grieve today on account of his daughter; nor indeed could that feat of striking the target otherwise have been accomplished by any mortal on earth."

**1.185.28**  Even as Yudhishthira was speaking thus, another man arrived quickly from the vicinity of the Panchala king to announce that the meal was ready.

**1.186.1**  The messenger said: "Food has been prepared by King Drupada for the occasion of the wedding; come, receive it now that all arrangements are complete; and Krishna should not delay there any longer."

**1.186.2**  "These chariots, adorned with golden lotuses and yoked with good horses, fit for lords of the earth — mount them all and proceed to the palace of King Panchala."

**1.186.3**  Vaishampayana said: Then those bulls among the Kurus set out, sending the priest ahead first, mounting those great vehicles; and Kunti and Krishna went along together.

**1.186.4**  Hearing the words which Dharmaraja had spoken, O Bharata, and wishing to learn more about those foremost Kurus, Drupada gathered together many kinds of goods.

**1.186.5**  Fruits and garlands finely prepared, hides and armor and seats, cattle, O king, and also ropes and other implements for agriculture —

**1.186.6**  and whatever there might be in the various crafts, all of it completely arranged and ready, and also those things intended for sport — all of this the king assembled there.

**1.186.7**  Gleaming chariots, horses and armor, great swords and splendid horse-drawn vehicles, foremost bows and principal arrows, lances and javelins adorned with gold —

**1.186.8**  javelins, bhuśuṇḍi weapons and battle-axes, and likewise all manner of war equipment; beds and seats of the finest quality — all these too were arranged variously there.

**1.186.9**  Kunti, taking the virtuous Krishna with her, entered the inner apartments of Drupada; and the women, of noble spirit, received and honored that wife of the Kaurava king.

**1.186.10**  Beholding those foremost of men — with the gait of lion's valor, with the eyes of great bulls, wearing antelope hides as upper garments, with shoulders hidden, with arms as long and thick as the bodies of great serpents —

**1.186.11**  the king and all the king's ministers, the king's sons and friends likewise, and all the servants without exception, O king, were filled with the greatest joy there.

**1.186.12**  Those heroes, those foremost of men, without any hesitation and without showing wonder, took their seats in order of seniority upon the excellent thrones with their footstools, as was their due.

**1.186.13**  Male and female servants in fine attire, and cooks too, brought food fit for kings — varied and of high and low rank — served in vessels of gold and silver.

**1.186.14**  Those foremost of men ate there as they wished and were greatly satisfied; then, passing over all the goods arranged there, those heroic men chose the weapons of war.

**1.186.15**  Noticing this, Drupada's son and the king, together with all his chief ministers, came forward joyfully and honored the sons of Kunti as princes and heirs of kings.

**1.187.1**  Vaishampayana said: Then the Panchala king, of great splendor, summoned prince Yudhishthira and drew him close with a brahminical embrace.

**1.187.2**  He of undepressed spirit questioned the radiant son of Kunti: "How are we to know of you — are you Kshatriyas, or Brahmins,

**1.187.3**  "or Vaishyas endowed with virtues, or those born of Shudra stock, or perfected beings ranging in all directions, having taken up a form of illusion?"

**1.187.4**  "Come from the heavens to behold us, having arrived here for the sake of Krishna — tell us the truth; our doubt in this matter is great."

**1.187.5**  "If at the end of our uncertainty a satisfaction might enter the mind here, and if our good fortune might prove auspicious — O scorcher of enemies."

**1.187.6**  "Tell the truth willingly; truth is becoming in kings; likewise by religious sacrifice and meritorious deeds — and falsehood must not be spoken."

**1.187.7**  "For having heard your words, O one equal to the immortals, O subduer of foes, I shall certainly proceed to the conducting of the marriage according to the prescribed rites."

**1.187.8**  Yudhishthira said: "Do not be downcast, O king of Panchala; let there be joy for you — your desired wish is certainly fulfilled, without doubt."

**1.187.9**  "We are indeed Kshatriyas, O king, sons of the great-souled Pandu; know me as the eldest, Kunteyaka; these are Bhimasena and Arjuna, by whom, O king, your daughter was won in the royal assembly."

**1.187.10**  "And the twins are there where Krishna has taken her place; let the grief depart from your mind — we are Kshatriyas, O bull among men; your daughter has gone from one lake to another, like a lotus."

**1.187.11**  "Thus truthfully, O great king, I tell you all of this; you are indeed our highest elder and supreme refuge."

**1.187.12**  Vaishampayana said: Then King Drupada, his eyes stirred with joy, was unable at that moment to make a fitting reply to Yudhishthira.

**1.187.13**  But with effort suppressing that joy, the scorcher of foes, the king, then replied fittingly to Yudhishthira.

**1.187.14**  The righteous-souled king asked him how they had fled before; and the Pandava told him everything in full sequence.

**1.187.15**  Hearing the words of the son of Kunti, King Drupada then censured Dhritarashtra, lord of the people.

**1.187.16**  And Drupada, foremost of speakers, reassured the son of Kunti, Yudhishthira, and pledged his support for their restoration to the kingdom.

**1.187.17**  Then Kunti and Krishna, Bhimasena and Arjuna, and the twins, as directed by the king, entered the great palace.

**1.187.18**  There they resided, O king, honored by Yajnasena; and then the king, together with his sons, spoke to them when they were at ease.

**1.187.19**  "Let the joy of the Kurus take her hand today itself according to the prescribed rite; on an auspicious day let the mighty-armed Arjuna choose the moment."

**1.187.20**  Then king Yudhishthira, son of Dharma, said to him: "A marriage alliance must first be made for me as well, O lord of the people."

**1.187.21**  Drupada said: "Either you yourself take my daughter's hand according to the prescribed rite, or, O hero, assign Krishna to whomever you think fit."

**1.187.22**  Yudhishthira said: "Draupadi shall be the queen of all of us, O king; for thus it was spoken before by my mother, O lord of the people."

**1.187.23**  "And I have not yet married, nor has Bhimasena the Pandava; she was won by Partha, and your daughter is a jewel among women."

**1.187.24**  "This is our compact, O king — to share a jewel in common; and we do not wish to abandon that compact, O best of kings."

**1.187.25**  "By dharma, Krishna shall be the queen of all of us; in order of seniority let each of us take her hand by the sacred fire."

**1.187.26**  Drupada said: "Many queens are ordained for one man, O joy of the Kurus; but never is one woman ordained for many men at any time."

**1.187.27**  You, O son of Kuntī, who are righteous and pure, ought not to commit an act contrary to worldly usage and the Vedas. Why do you have such a mind?

**1.187.28**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Dharma is subtle, O great king; we do not know its course. We follow the path trodden in succession by the ancients.

**1.187.29**  My speech does not speak untruth, nor does my mind dwell on adharma. Mother speaks thus, and it accords with my own heart's resolve.

**1.187.30**  This is a fixed dharma, O king — follow it without hesitation. Let there be no doubt in your mind about this in any way, O lord of the earth.

**1.187.31**  Drupada said: You, O son of Kuntī, and Kuntī, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna my son — let all discuss what is to be done. We shall act at the proper time tomorrow.

**1.187.32**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all of them came together and were conversing, O Bhārata, when Dvaipāyana arrived there by chance, O king.

**1.188.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all the Pāṇḍavas and the greatly renowned son of Pāñcāla, rising to receive him, worshipped that great-souled Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana upon seeing him.

**1.188.2**  Having welcomed them all and enquired after their welfare in full, that great-minded one took his seat on a bright golden throne.

**1.188.3**  Then, permitted by Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendour, all those foremost among men seated themselves on their respective splendid seats.

**1.188.4**  Then, after a moment, the lord of the Pāñcālas — the son of Pṛṣata — addressed that great soul in sweet words and asked him about the matter of Draupadī.

**1.188.5**  How can one woman be the wife of many, and how would there be no confusion of dharma? Let the revered one explain all this to us as it truly is.

**1.188.6**  Vyāsa said: In this matter of dharma that is disputed and opposed to worldly usage and the Vedas, I wish to hear whatever opinion each one holds.

**1.188.7**  Drupada said: In my view this is adharma, contrary to both worldly usage and the Vedas; for one wife for many men is not known to exist, O best of the twice-born.

**1.188.8**  Nor has this dharma been practised by the great-souled ones of the past. And an eternal dharma shared among many is not to be followed.

**1.188.9**  Therefore I shall not carry out such a resolution in action; for this seems to me shrouded in doubt and uncertainty regarding dharma.

**1.188.10**  Dhṛṣṭadyumna said: How, O bull among the twice-born, O brahmin, could an elder brother, being of good conduct and a storehouse of austerity, approach the wife of a younger brother?

**1.188.11**  Yet because of the subtlety of dharma we cannot in any way know its course. Nor can a determination be made as to what is adharma and what is dharma.

**1.188.12**  This cannot be resolved by persons like us, O brahmin. Therefore I am in no way able to determine that Kṛṣṇā should be the chief queen of five men.

**1.188.13**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: My speech does not speak untruth; my mind does not dwell on adharma. My heart inclines in this direction — this is in no way adharma.

**1.188.14**  For even in ancient legend it is heard that Jaṭilā, the daughter of Gautama, dwelt with seven seers who were upholders of dharma, O best among the righteous.

**1.188.15**  They say that the word of one's teacher is dharma, O best among those who know dharma; and among all teachers the mother is the supreme teacher.

**1.188.16**  And she too spoke the words 'Let it be enjoyed like alms.' Therefore I consider this to be dharma, O foremost among the twice-born.

**1.188.17**  Kuntī said: It is exactly as Yudhiṣṭhira, that follower of dharma, has said. My fear of untruth is intense — how could I be freed from untruth?

**1.188.18**  Vyāsa said: You will be freed from untruth, O blessed one, and this is indeed the eternal dharma. But I shall not speak of it before all; O Pāñcāla, hear from me yourself.

**1.188.19**  As this dharma has been ordained, and as it is eternal, and as the son of Kuntī has declared it — so it is dharma, without any doubt.

**1.188.20**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the revered lord Vyāsa Dvaipāyana rose, and taking the king by the hand, entered the royal palace.

**1.188.21**  And the Pāṇḍavas, Kuntī, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata remained there with bewildered minds, awaiting those two.

**1.188.22**  Then Dvaipāyana related to that great-souled lord of men how one wife for many is indeed dharma.

**1.189.1**  Vyāsa said: Long ago the gods performed a sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest, O king. There Vaivasvata Yama then acted as the slaughterer.

**1.189.2**  Then Yama, consecrated in that sacrifice, O king, did not cause the death of any living being. Thereupon the creatures multiplied greatly, freed from death through the passage of time.

**1.189.3**  Then Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Vasus, and the Aśvins, together with other gods, came to Prajāpati, the guide of the worlds.

**1.189.4**  Then, assembled together, they addressed the teacher of the worlds: 'We have intense fear from the multiplication of humans. Trembling from that fear, all of us who seek happiness come to you as our refuge.'

**1.189.5**  Brahmā said: What fear have you of mortals, you who are all immortals? Let there never be any fear for you from the presence of mortal beings.

**1.189.6**  The gods said: The mortals have become as immortals — there is no distinction whatsoever. Troubled by this lack of distinction, we have come here seeking distinction.

**1.189.7**  Brahmā said: Vaivasvata is occupied with the sacrifice; that is why these humans do not die. When his single-pointed attention is finished with that task, the time of their end will come.

**1.189.8**  And the body of Vaivasvata, made mighty and set in motion by your collective power — that shall be their end at the time of their ending; for that body shall become the force of death among men.

**1.189.9**  Vyāsa said: Then the gods, having heard the words of the elder god, went to where the gods were performing the sacrifice. Seated together, those mighty ones saw a lotus on the Bhāgīrathī.

**1.189.10**  Seeing it, they were filled with wonder. Indra the heroic one went there among them, and he saw a woman of blazing splendour where the Gaṅgā ever flows forth.

**1.189.11**  That woman, weeping and longing for water, plunged into the goddess Gaṅgā and stood there. A teardrop of hers fell into the water, and from it arose that golden lotus.

**1.189.12**  Seeing that wonder, the wielder of the thunderbolt then approached near and asked that woman: 'Who are you? Why do you weep and for what reason? I desire you to speak the truth here.'

**1.189.13**  The woman said: You will come to know who I am here, O Śakra, and the reason why I, the ill-fortuned one, weep. Come, O king, I will go before you — you shall see that for the sake of which I weep.

**1.189.14**  Vyāsa said: He followed her as she went, and then from a distance he saw a handsome young man seated on a lion-throne with a young woman as his companion, playing at dice on the summit of the king of mountains.

**1.189.15**  The king of gods addressed him angrily: 'Know that this entire world is under my power — I am the lord.' So he spoke with indignation, seeing him wholly absorbed in dice.

**1.189.16**  But the god, looking steadily at the wrathful Śakra, laughed, and gazed at Śakra calmly. Then the king of gods became paralysed, looked upon by him, and stood stiff as a post.

**1.189.17**  When at last his play here was completed, he addressed that weeping goddess: 'Let this one be brought from where I came — so that arrogance may not enter him again.'

**1.189.18**  Then Śakra, merely touched by her, fell to the ground with limbs gone limp. The revered one of fierce splendour addressed him: 'Do not act thus again, O Śakra, in any way.'

**1.189.19**  Roll open this great mountain king, and behold your own immeasurable strength and might. Having opened it, enter its interior, where others like you, blazing like the sun, are seated.

**1.189.20**  He opened that peak of the great mountain and saw four others equal in splendour. Gazing upon them he became grieved: 'Shall I too become like these?'

**1.189.21**  Then the god Giriśa, opening his eyes, addressed the wielder of the thunderbolt in anger: 'Enter this cave, O Śatakratu — because in your childishness you disrespected me before.'
