**1.189.22**  Thus addressed by the mighty one, the king of gods trembled violently with anguish, his limbs gone limp, like an aśvattha leaf driven by the wind on the summit of the mountain king.

**1.189.23**  He, with folded hands and bowed face, trembling, suddenly so addressed, spoke to the many-formed and terrible one: 'You, O revered one, will today be the witness of the remainder.'

**1.189.24**  The wielder of the fierce bow laughed and said to him: 'Those of such character do not attain a remainder here. These too shall be thus hereafter. Therefore enter this cave and remain.'

**1.189.25**  The remainder of your time will also be thus — there is no doubt. All of you shall enter a human womb. There, having performed irresistible deeds and having brought many others to destruction—

**1.189.26**  —you shall return again to Indra's realm, that great and worthy abode won previously by your own deeds. All this has been spoken by me as it is. Other things of various purposes are also to be done.

**1.189.27**  The former Indras said: We shall go from the world of gods to the human world where the ordained liberation is hard to attain. But let the gods place us in a mother's womb — Dharma, Vāyu, Maghavan, and the Aśvins.

**1.189.28**  Vyāsa said: Hearing these words, the wielder of the thunderbolt addressed the best of gods again: 'I will give, through my power and for the purpose of this task, a fifth man to them, born from myself.'

**1.189.29**  The revered wielder of the fierce bow granted their desire, giving what was sought through divine release as spoken. And that woman beloved of the world, Śrī herself, he ordained as their wife among men.

**1.189.30**  Then that god went together with those very ones to the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa. He too ordained all of it. Thereupon all of them were born upon the earth.

**1.189.31**  And Hari plucked two hairs from himself — one white and one black. Those two hairs entered two women of the Yadu clan, Rohiṇī and Devakī. From them, one became Baladeva, and the second became Kṛṣṇa Keśava.

**1.189.32**  Those who previously, bearing Indra's form, were confined in that cave of the northern mountain — they are here the mighty Pāṇḍavas. The Pāṇḍava Savyasācī is a portion of Indra.

**1.189.33**  Thus these Pāṇḍavas were born, O king — those who were formerly Indras. And Lakṣmī herself was earlier ordained for them; this Draupadī of divine form is their wife.

**1.189.34**  For how else could a woman arise from the earth at the end of a ritual act other than through divine dispensation — she whose beauty shines like the moon and sun, and whose supreme fragrance wafts a league away?

**1.189.35**  And this other boon I give you gladly, O lord of men — a most wonderful one: divine sight. See the sons of Kuntī endowed with their blessed and divine former bodies.

**1.189.36**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Vyāsa, that brahmin of supremely noble deeds, pure through his austerity, bestowed divine sight on the king. The king saw all of them as they truly were in their former bodies.

**1.189.37**  Then he saw them divine, wearing golden crowns and garlands, resembling Indra, of the colour of fire and sun, wearing bound diadems, handsome and youthful, broad-chested, of the height of a palm tree.

**1.189.38**  Adorned most brilliantly with divine spotless golden garments and finest garlands, they were like the Three-eyed one himself, or the divine Vasus, or the Ādityas possessed of every virtue. Seeing those former Indras so handsome, king Drupada was delighted and full of wonder.

**1.189.39**  And having attained that immeasurable divine māyā, the lord of earth saw her too — that foremost one, like Śrī incarnate, worthy of them by her beauty, splendour, and fame — their glorious wife.

**1.189.40**  Having seen that great and wondrous form, he clasped the feet of the son of Satyavatī. With serene mind he addressed him: 'This is no marvel for you, O supreme seer.'

**1.189.41**  Vyāsa said: In a hermitage forest there was once a daughter of a great-souled seer. That maiden, though beautiful and virtuous, could not find a husband.

**1.189.42**  She propitiated Śaṃkara with fierce austerity. The Lord, well pleased, personally told her: 'Choose your boon.'

**1.189.43**  Thus addressed, the maiden said to the god, the granter of boons, the Lord: 'I desire a husband endowed with every virtue' — saying this again and again.

**1.189.44**  The lord of gods, Śaṃkara, joyfully granted her that boon then: 'Five noble husbands shall be yours.'

**1.189.45**  She, still entreating the god, spoke again: 'I deserve one husband endowed with virtue from you.' Then the god of gods, with joyful heart, spoke again an auspicious word to her.

**1.189.46**  'Five times you have said to me: give me a husband — again. So shall it be, O fortunate one; may good come to you. When you have gone to another body, what was spoken shall come to pass for you.'

**1.189.47**  She is this very one who was born as Drupada's daughter, of divine form. The blameless Kṛṣṇā, daughter of Pṛṣata, has been ordained as wife to five.

**1.189.48**  The glory of heaven, born in a great sacrifice for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas — having here performed fierce austerity, she has come to be your daughter.

**1.189.49**  This resplendent goddess, beloved of the gods, is one wife for five by her own past deed — she herself created as wife of the gods by the Self-born. Having heard, O king, do what Drupada desires.

**1.190.1**  Drupada said: Without having heard such words from you, O great seer, I had earlier striven in this matter. Indeed what has been ordained cannot be averted — the very same ordinance has come to pass.

**1.190.2**  The knot of destiny is not to be undone; nothing here is ordained by one's own action alone. Indeed what was brought about as the cause for the one boon — that very thing has now come to pass for many.

**1.190.3**  Just as Kṛṣṇā previously said 'Let the revered one grant me not many husbands,' and he too replied to her with the boon thus — the god indeed knows what is supreme in this matter.

**1.190.4**  If this has been ordained by Shankara, whether it be dharma or adharma, the fault is not mine. Let these men take her hand in the prescribed manner; for Krishnaa has indeed been destined for them as they desire.

**1.190.5**  Vaishampayana said: Then the blessed one spoke to Dharmaraja: 'Today is an auspicious day, O Pandaveya. Today the moon enters the Pushya constellation. You must be the first today to take Krishnaa's hand.'

**1.190.6**  Then King Yajnasena with his son brought together the many excellent items required for the wedding ritual, and also his daughter Krishnaa, having bathed her and adorned her with numerous jewels.

**1.190.7**  Then all his friends, ministers, and counselors assembled there, full of great delight, to witness the wedding, along with twice-born priests and townspeople according to their rank.

**1.190.8**  That palace of his, made beautiful by the assembled guests, with its courtyard adorned with scattered lotuses and blue water-lilies and decorated with heaps of priceless gems, shone like the sky studded with bright stars.

**1.190.9**  Then those princes of the Kuru royal line, adorned with earrings, youthful, wearing magnificent garments, anointed with fine sandalwood paste, having performed the ceremonial bath and the auspicious rites—

**1.190.10**  —together with the family priest Dhaumya, resplendent as fire, and in accordance with the prescribed rites, O lord, all of them entered that assembly hall in order, rejoicing like great bulls entering a cow-pen.

**1.190.11**  Then that master of the Vedas, having kindled the fire, offered oblations into the blazing flame with sacred mantras; and the knower of mantras, having led Yudhishthira forward, joined him together with Krishnaa.

**1.190.12**  That master of the Vedas caused the two of them, with joined hands, to circumambulate the fire. Then the family priest, having given his blessing to that radiant champion, departed from the king's house.

**1.190.13**  In this same manner those sons of kings, great warriors who enhanced the glory of the Kuru lineage, each assuming the most handsome form day after day, took the hand of that noble woman.

**1.190.14**  And the brahmin-sage there declared this supreme marvel, surpassing human understanding: that the great-souled, slender-waisted one became a virgin again with each passing day.

**1.190.15**  After the wedding was completed, Drupada gave manifold and excellent gifts to the great chariot warriors: a hundred chariots adorned with fine gold ornaments, drawn by four horses each, with golden bridles and garlands.

**1.190.16**  Also a hundred elephants bearing lotus emblems, resembling mountains with golden peaks; and likewise a hundred maidservants in the prime of youth, wearing costly attire, ornaments, garments, and garlands.

**1.190.17**  Separately and individually, the son of Sumaka gave, with fire as witness, wealth amounting to ten thousand pieces each, along with garments and jewels of great magnificence and immense value.

**1.190.18**  After the wedding was completed, the mighty Pandavas, resembling Indra, having thus obtained that prosperity filled with abundant riches, rejoiced in the city of the Panchala king.

**1.191.1**  Vaishampayana said: For Drupada, who had now gained alliance with the Pandavas, there arose no fear whatsoever, not even from the gods.

**1.191.2**  Those women of the great-souled Drupada approached Kunti, chanting her name in praise, and touched her feet with their foreheads.

**1.191.3**  And Krishnaa, clad in linen, having performed the auspicious wedding rituals, having paid her respects to her mother-in-law, stood with bowed head and folded hands.

**1.191.4**  Pritha spoke with love the words of blessing to her daughter-in-law Draupadi, who was endowed with beauty and auspicious marks, and possessed of excellent character and conduct.

**1.191.5**  'As Indrani is to Indra, as Svaha is to Agni, as Rohini is to the moon, as Damayanti was to Nala—

**1.191.6**  —as Bhadra is to Vaishravana, as Arundhati is to Vasishtha, as Lakshmi is to Narayana, so may you be to your husbands.

**1.191.7**  May you be a mother of long-lived sons, a mother of heroes, O auspicious one, endowed with great happiness, fortunate, blessed with enjoyments, a worthy partner in sacrifices, devoted to your husband.

**1.191.8**  May your years always pass in duly honoring guests who arrive, the virtuous, children, elders, and teachers according to what is right.

**1.191.9**  In the chief kingdoms and cities, foremost among which is Kurujangala, may you be consecrated as queen alongside a king devoted to dharma.

**1.191.10**  The earth conquered by valor by your mighty husbands—may you dedicate it entirely to the brahmins at the great Ashvamedha sacrifice.

**1.191.11**  Whatever gems of quality exist on the earth—O virtuous one, may you obtain them all, and may you live happily for a hundred autumns.'

**1.191.12**  'As I welcome you today, O daughter-in-law, clad in linen, so shall I again welcome you, a virtuous mother of sons, adorned with excellence.'

**1.191.13**  Then Hari sent to the sons of Pandu, now that they had taken their wife, golden ornaments adorned with pearls and vaidurya gems,

**1.191.14**  and Madhava sent also the most costly garments from many lands, fine woolen blankets, precious skins, pleasant to the touch and auspicious.

**1.191.15**  And various large couches, seats, and conveyances, decorated with vaidurya and diamond ornaments, and hundreds of vessels—

**1.191.16**  —and maidservants endowed with beauty, youth, and skill, well adorned, Krishna gave by the thousands, from many different lands.

**1.191.17**  And trained and auspicious elephants, well-caparisoned fine horses, and tamed chariots decorated with auspicious golden banners—

**1.191.18**  —and gold by the tens of millions in its raw and refined forms: the immeasurable-souled Madhusudana sent all of this to them.

**1.191.19**  All of this King Yudhishthira received, filled with supreme joy, out of his desire to please Govinda.

**1.192.1**  Vaishampayana said: Then the news was brought to the kings by their trusted spies: that the auspicious Draupadi had been won by the Pandavas and united with her husbands.

**1.192.2**  That great-souled one who, drawing that bow, had hit the target—he was Arjuna, the best among the victorious, the greatest bearer of arrows and bow.

**1.192.3**  And that mighty one who had lifted Shalya the king of Madra and whirled him about, and who in fury had terrified men in battle with a tree—

**1.192.4**  —and there had been no confusion whatsoever in that great-souled one: he was Bhima, terrible to touch, the destroyer of enemy armies.

**1.192.5**  Hearing that the sons of Pandu's king, the sons of Kunti, had been disguised in brahmin form, amazement arose among the lords of men.

**1.192.6**  For Kunti along with her sons had formerly been reported burned in the house of lac. 'They have been reborn,' thought all the kings with wonder.

**1.192.7**  Uttering curses then upon Bhishma and Dhritarashtra the Kaurava for the most cruel deed done by Purochana—

**1.192.8**  —after the svayamvara was over, all those kings departed the way they had come, having learned that the Pandavas had been chosen.

**1.192.9**  Then King Duryodhana, downcast in spirit, along with his brothers, with Ashvatthaman, with his maternal uncle, with Karna, and with Kripa—

**1.192.10**  —having turned back, seeing Arjuna of the white horses chosen by Draupadi, Duhshasana, full of shame, spoke to him slowly and haltingly:

**1.192.11**  'Had he not been disguised as a brahmin, he would not have won Draupadi. For truly, O king, no one recognized Dhananjaya for who he really was.'

**1.192.12**  'I believe fate is supreme and human effort is futile. Shame on our prowess, dear friend, seeing how the Pandavas flourish here.'

**1.192.13**  Speaking thus and cursing Purochana, they entered Hastinapura, wretched and dispirited.

**1.192.14**  Frightened, their resolve gone, having seen the sons of Pritha of great power, having seen that they had escaped from the fire and were now allied with Drupada—

**1.192.15**  —and reflecting on Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandi and the other sons of Drupada, all skilled in every kind of warfare—

**1.192.16**  Then Vidura, hearing that the Pandavas had been chosen by Draupadi and that the sons of Dhritarashtra had returned ashamed and broken in pride—

**1.192.17**  —then the delighted Kshatta, full of wonder, spoke to Dhritarashtra, O lord of the people: 'By good fortune, the Kurus prosper!'

**1.192.18**  And the son of Vichitraveerya, the king, hearing that from Vidura, spoke with supreme delight: 'By good fortune! By good fortune!' — O Bharata.

**1.192.19**  For the king whose eyes are wisdom, through ignorance believes it is his eldest son Duryodhana who has been chosen by the daughter of Drupada.

**1.192.20**  Then he commanded his son Duryodhana: 'Let the many ornaments of Draupadi be brought here — bring Krishnaa!'

**1.192.21**  But then afterward Vidura explained to him that the Pandavas had been chosen, that all the heroes were well and had been honored by Drupada, and also that they had many other powerful relatives.

**1.192.22**  Dhritarashtra said: 'Just as Pandu's sons are mine as well, so too this is greater cause for delight; this growth is greater in my view, O Vidura — that those heroic Pandavas are well and have gained allies.'

**1.192.23**  'For who, O Kshatta, having gained Drupada as an ally together with his kinsmen, would not prosper? Even a king who had lost his fortune and was in need would flourish.'

**1.192.24**  Vaishampayana said: Vidura replied to him who spoke thus: 'May this wisdom of yours remain firm, O king, for a hundred years.'

**1.192.25**  Then Duryodhana and the son of Radha, O lord of the people, approached Dhritarashtra and spoke these words to him at that time:

**1.192.26**  'In Vidura's presence, O king, we are unable to speak to you. We wish to speak to you in private. What is your intention in this matter?'

**1.192.27**  'O dear father, best among men, you consider the growth of your enemies to be your own growth, and you praise it in Kshatta's presence.

**1.192.28**  'When one course of action is called for, O blameless king, you do another. The undermining of their strength is what must always be done, dear father.

**1.192.29**  'We should deliberate upon and plan a timely course of action so that they may not devour us along with our sons, armies, and kinsmen.'

**1.193.1**  Dhritarashtra said: 'I too think about this in the very same way as you two. But I do not wish to betray my intentions in my manner before Vidura.

**1.193.2**  'That is why I praise their virtues specifically — so that Vidura would not understand my true intentions from my gestures and signs.

**1.193.3**  'What you consider the right course of action — speak it, O Suyodhana. And you too, O son of Radha, tell me what you consider the right course of action.'

**1.193.4**  Duryodhana said: 'Today let us sow division among the sons of Kunti and the two sons of Madri, the Pandavas, through skilled brahmins — trustworthy men who carry out their tasks well.

**1.193.5**  'Or else King Drupada along with great hoards of wealth — and his sons and all his ministers — should be tempted and won over.

**1.193.6**  'Let them be persuaded to abandon King Yudhishthira the son of Kunti, or alternatively, let those men encourage the Pandavas to remain there itself.

**1.193.7**  'Let them describe, each separately, the faults and disadvantages of living here, so that the Pandavas, being divided, may set their minds on remaining there only.

**1.193.8**  'Or else let some skillful men, expert in the use of gifts, sow discord among the sons of Pritha from one to another by exploiting their mutual affections.

**1.193.9**  'Or let them turn Krishnaa against them — that is easy given the plurality of husbands. Or alternatively let them create dissension between the Pandavas regarding her, and through her, divide them.

**1.193.10**  'Or, O king, let the death of Bhimasena be arranged through men skilled in stratagems, working in secret — for he is the greatest in strength among them.

**1.193.11**  'For when he has been slain, O king, their enthusiasm will be crushed, their energy broken — they will no longer strive for the kingdom. He is indeed their chief support.

**1.193.12**  'For Arjuna is invincible in battle when Vrikodara is guarding his back. Without Phalguna, in battle Radheya does not even reach his feet.

**1.193.13**  'Knowing their great weakness without Bhimasena, and knowing us to be the stronger party, they who are weaker will not prevail against us.

**1.193.14**  'When the sons of Pritha have come here and are subject to our authority, O king, we shall proceed as we see fit to crush them.

**1.193.15**  'Or alternatively let each son of Kunti there be seduced by beautiful women, and then let Krishnaa become disillusioned with them.

**1.193.16**  'Or let the son of Radha be sent to bring them here; and then, once they have been lured in with bribes, let them be slain by trusted agents.

**1.193.17**  'Of all these strategies, whichever you consider to be free of fault — proceed to employ it. The time is passing; do not delay.'

**1.193.18**  As long as Draupadī has not yet placed her full trust in Drupada, the bull among kings, for so long only are they now capable of being overpowered — not beyond that point.

**1.193.19**  This is my counsel, dear friend, aimed at their suppression — whether it be right or wrong. But what do you think, O son of Rādhā?

**1.194.1**  Karṇa said: Duryodhana, in my opinion your reasoning is not sound. The Pāṇḍavas cannot be subdued by stratagem, O joy of the Kuru line.

**1.194.2**  Indeed, you tried previously to overpower them with subtle stratagems, O hero, yet even then you were not able to restrain them.

**1.194.3**  Even when they were right here, near you, O king, still children without fully-grown wings, you were simply unable to harm them.

**1.194.4**  Now they are fully fledged, dwelling abroad, grown powerful in every way — the sons of Kuntī cannot be overcome by stratagem; this is my settled conviction, O Acyuta.

**1.194.5**  Nor can they be ensnared in misfortune, for fate itself protects them; they are ever vigilant and they are earnestly seeking the throne of their fathers and forefathers.

**1.194.6**  Nor can dissension be sown among them, for those who are devoted to a single wife do not split against one another.

**1.194.7**  Nor indeed can Kṛṣṇā be separated from them by enemies — she chose them when they were reduced to destitution, so how much less now when they are resplendent with glory.

**1.194.8**  The quality most desired by a lone woman — to have many husbands — Kṛṣṇā has obtained; she is therefore not easily divided from them.

**1.194.9**  And the king of Pāñcāla is of noble conduct; he is no lover of mere wealth. He will certainly not abandon the sons of Kuntī even for the gift of a kingdom.

**1.194.10**  Likewise his son is virtuous and deeply attached to the Pāṇḍavas. Therefore I hold that they cannot by any means be overcome by stratagem.

**1.194.11**  But this is what is now fitting for us to do, O bull among men, O lord of the earth: while the sons of Pāṇḍu have not yet struck deep roots, for so long they are to be struck — let your valour be exercised.

**1.194.12**  As long as our side is great and the Pāñcāla force is weak, for so long let their destruction be carried out — do not hesitate.

**1.194.13**  As long as they have not yet gathered abundant mounts and numerous allies, O son of Gāndhārī, act swiftly and strike now.

**1.194.14**  As long as the king of Pāñcāla, together with his sons of great valour, has not yet set his mind to exertion, strike swiftly now.

**1.194.15**  As long as Vārṣṇeya — Kṛṣṇa — has not yet arrived, drawing the Yādava host in support of the sons of Pāṇḍu's claim to the kingdom, strike swiftly now.

**1.194.16**  Wealth, varied pleasures, and the kingdom itself — there is nothing that Kṛṣṇa would not abandon for the Pāṇḍavas' sake, O lord of the earth.

**1.194.17**  By valour did the great-souled Bharata win this earth; by valour did Pākaśāsana — Indra — conquer all three worlds.

**1.194.18**  Valour is celebrated as a kṣatriya's virtue, O lord of the earth; for valour is the inherent duty of heroes, O bull among kings.

**1.194.19**  With our great four-limbed army, O king, let us quickly overpower Drupada and bring the Pāṇḍavas here.

**1.194.20**  For the Pāṇḍavas cannot be brought to submission by conciliation, nor by gifts, nor by sowing dissension; therefore vanquish them by valour alone.

**1.194.21**  Having conquered them by valour, enjoy this whole earth; I see no other means of accomplishing this end, O lord of men.

**1.194.22**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the speech of the son of Rādhā, the illustrious Dhṛtarāṣṭra, after honouring it, spoke these words in reply.

**1.194.23**  Such a speech, filled with valour, is fitting for you, O greatly wise son of the charioteer, who is accomplished in weaponry.

**1.194.24**  But let Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Vidura, as well as the two of you, together form a counsel such as will bring happiness to us.

**1.194.25**  Then, having summoned all those counsellors, the greatly illustrious Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O great king, deliberated with them.

**1.195.1**  Bhīṣma said: A conflict with the sons of Pāṇḍu does not please me in any way. Just as Dhṛtarāṣṭra is to me, so without doubt is Pāṇḍu.

**1.195.2**  Just as the sons of Gāndhārī, so too the sons of Kuntī are regarded by me; and as they are to be protected by me, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, so likewise by you.

**1.195.3**  Just as they are to me and to the king, so too to Duryodhana, and so to all the Kurus and to others as well, O descendant of Bharata.

**1.195.4**  This being so, I do not favour conflict with them. Let peace be made with those heroes and the land be given to them today; this kingdom too belongs to their great-grandfathers and to their father among the foremost of Kurus.

**1.195.5**  Duryodhana, just as you, my dear, regard this kingdom as your patrimony, so likewise do the Pāṇḍavas regard it.

**1.195.6**  If the suffering Pāṇḍavas have not received a kingdom, then whence would even you have a claim to it — or the lineage of Bharata, or anyone else?

**1.195.7**  But if you have obtained the kingdom by right, O bull of the Bharata line, then they too had obtained the kingdom previously — this is my conviction.

**1.195.8**  Therefore, in friendliness alone, let half the kingdom be given to them; this is indeed for the good of all people, O tiger among men.

**1.195.9**  If it is done otherwise, it will not be for our good; and for you too, complete disgrace will certainly ensue — there is no doubt.

**1.195.10**  Hold fast to the protection of your reputation, for reputation is the highest strength; the life of a man who has lost his reputation is held to be fruitless.

**1.195.11**  As long as a man's reputation does not perish, O Kaurava, for so long he lives, O son of Gāndhārī; but one whose reputation is lost is truly dead.

**1.195.12**  Embrace this duty befitting the Kuru family, O mighty-armed one; act in accordance with your ancestors and with your own nature.

**1.195.13**  By good fortune those heroes survive; by good fortune that Pṛthā lives; by good fortune that wicked Purocana, whose intent was their destruction, has met his end.

**1.195.14**  Ever since that time, O son of Gāndhārī, I have been unable to look any living being in the face in this world, having heard that Kuntī was brought to such a condition.

**1.195.15**  Nor does the world attribute that guilt to Purocana as it attributes guilt to you, O tiger among men.

**1.195.16**  Therefore this — their survival — and the sight of the Pāṇḍavas must be pondered as the means of washing away your sin, O great king.

**1.195.17**  Nor indeed can the paternal share of those living heroes be taken away, O joy of the Kurus — not even by the wielder of the thunderbolt himself.

**1.195.18**  For they all stand firm in righteousness, all are of one mind, and they were driven out unjustly from a kingdom that was equally theirs.

**1.195.19**  If you are to act according to dharma, if you wish to do what is dear to me, and if well-being is to be sought, then let half be given to them.

**1.196.1**  Droṇa said: I have heard, O king, that those summoned to counsel who are well-wishers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra should speak what is righteous, wholesome, and conducive to glory.

**1.196.2**  My counsel too, dear friend, is the same as that of the great-souled Bhīṣma: the sons of Kuntī must be given their share — this is the eternal law.

**1.196.3**  Let some pleasant-spoken man be sent at once to Drupada, bearing abundant jewels for their benefit, O descendant of Bharata.

**1.196.4**  And let him go bearing much in the way of mutual gifts, and let him speak of the supreme advantage that would arise from that alliance.

**1.196.5**  Let him speak of you as greatly pleased, O king, and likewise of Duryodhana — repeatedly, to Drupada and to Dhṛṣṭadyumna as well, O descendant of Bharata.

**1.196.6**  And let him describe the appropriateness and dearness of the union, and again and again let him speak reassuringly to the sons of Kuntī and the sons of Mādrī.

**1.196.7**  And let him present, on your word, O lord of kings, many bright golden ornaments to Draupadī.

**1.196.8**  And likewise to all the sons of Drupada, O bull of the Bharata line, and to all the Pāṇḍavas, and to Kuntī — whatever is fitting for each.

**1.196.9**  Having thus spoken to Drupada and the Pāṇḍavas with words of conciliation, the envoy should thereafter address them regarding their return.

**1.196.10**  When the heroes have given their consent, let a fine escort proceed; let Duḥśāsana and Vikarṇa bring the Pāṇḍavas here.

**1.196.11**  Then they, O foremost of kings, constantly honoured by you and with the assent of the subjects, will abide in their paternal position.

**1.196.12**  Such conduct, O great king, toward them and your sons alike I consider appropriate — together with Bhīṣma's counsel, O descendant of Bharata.

**1.196.13**  Karṇa said: These two, bound close by considerations of wealth and honour, second to none in every matter — that they do not deliberate for your benefit, what is more remarkable than this?

**1.196.14**  One who speaks of welfare but harbours a corrupt inner mind, concealing his true soul — how could such a person act in accordance with the counsel of the righteous?

**1.196.15**  Friends are not for welfare or the opposite in times of material difficulty; for by the law of fate, both sorrow and joy come to all in their proper course.

**1.196.16**  Whether wise or unwise, whether young or old, whether attended by allies or alone — a man finds everything, everywhere, in its appointed time.

**1.196.17**  For it is heard that long ago there was a certain king known as Ambuvīca, a ruler of the Māgadha lords, in Rājagṛha.

**1.196.18**  He was bereft of all his faculties, that king, living by breathing alone; in all affairs he was wholly dependent on his ministers.

**1.196.19**  His minister Mahākarṇi became the sole master of power; thinking himself to have gained strength, he grew contemptuous.

**1.196.20**  That fool then seized for himself the king's women, his gems and wealth — everything — and the sovereignty as well.

**1.196.21**  And having taken that, greed from gain grew greater in the greedy man; having thus taken everything, he then desired to seize the kingdom itself.

**1.196.22**  But though he strove, he could not seize that kingdom from the king who, though bereft of all his faculties and living by breathing alone, retained it — so we have heard.

**1.196.23**  What else could account for that man's lordship but destiny? If the kingdom is destined for you, O lord of the earth, it will be yours.

**1.196.24**  Before the eyes of all the world it will certainly remain with you. But if destiny has willed otherwise, you will not obtain it even by striving.

**1.196.25**  Knowing this, discern the good and bad qualities of your ministers; the words of the corrupt and of the uncorrupt alike must be understood.

**1.196.26**  Droṇa said: We know why you say this, driven by a fault in your own disposition. Corrupted by your enmity toward the Pāṇḍavas, you reveal our fault to us.

**1.196.27**  But I speak what is supremely beneficial for the growth of the Kuru line, O Karṇa. If you think it is wrong, then speak what you consider supremely beneficial.

**1.196.28**  If what I declare to be supremely beneficial is done otherwise, the Kurus will perish before long — this is my firm conviction.

**1.197.1**  Vidura said: O king, you must certainly be counselled by your kinsmen for your own good — but advice does not take hold in those who are unwilling to listen.

**1.197.2**  That speech which Bhīṣma, son of Śāṃtanu, the best of Kurus, has spoken is indeed for your welfare, O king — and yet you do not accept it.

**1.197.3**  Likewise Droṇa has spoken at length what is supremely beneficial; and Karṇa, the son of Rādhā, holds that too as not being for your good.

**1.197.4**  And reflecting upon it, O king, I do not see among your true well-wishers anyone who could surpass these two lions among men in wisdom.

**1.197.5**  For these two are aged in years, in wisdom, and in learning; and they are equally disposed toward you, O lord of kings, and toward the sons of Pāṇḍu.

**1.197.6**  In righteousness and in truthfulness they are inferior to none, O king, O descendant of Bharata — not to Rāma the son of Daśaratha, not to Gaya — there is no doubt.

**1.197.7**  They have never before counselled what was harmful, nor is any wrongdoing by them toward you discernible.

**1.197.8**  How could these two tiger-like men, whose valour rests on truth, fail to counsel your welfare when you have done no wrong toward them, O king?

**1.197.9**  These two foremost of men are wise in this world, O lord of men; for your sake they will speak nothing crooked — such is my settled conviction, O joy of the Kurus.

**1.197.10**  Those two who know righteousness will not speak in favour of any party out of self-interest; this they regard as your supreme good, O Bhārata.

**1.197.11**  O king, just as Duryodhana and the rest are your sons, so too are the sons of Pāṇḍu your sons — of this there is no doubt.

**1.197.12**  If your counsellors were to advise anything harmful toward them out of foolishness, those advisors do not truly perceive what is good for you.

**1.197.13**  And if in your heart, O king, there lurks some distinction between them, those who reveal that inner bias will certainly not serve your welfare.

**1.197.14**  It is for this reason, O king, that those two great-souled and radiant ones have said nothing openly — for that is not yet your settled resolve.

**1.197.15**  And what those two bulls among men have declared to be unachievable against the Pāṇḍavas — so it truly is, O tiger among men; may good come to you.

**1.197.16**  For how could the glorious Pāṇḍava Savyasācī, the scorcher of foes, be conquered in battle, O king — not even by Indra himself?

**1.197.17**  How could the mighty long-armed Bhīmasena, whose strength equals ten thousand elephants, be defeated in battle even by the immortal gods?

**1.197.18**  And likewise, those two accomplished twins, like sons of Yama himself in battle — how could anyone wishing to live endure them on the battlefield?

**1.197.19**  He in whom steadfastness, compassion, forbearance, truth, and valour are ever-present — the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas — how could he be defeated in battle?

**1.197.20**  Rāma champions their cause, Janārdana is their counsellor, and Sātyaki stands on their side — what could be unconquerable in battle for them?

**1.197.21**  Drupada is their father-in-law, and their brothers-in-law are the Pārṣatas — the heroic sons of Drupada led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**1.197.22**  Having understood their invincibility above all else, O Bhārata, and recognising their right of inheritance by law, conduct yourself rightly toward them.

**1.197.23**  This great and indelible disgrace wrought by Purocana — wash yourself of it today, O king, by showing them favour.

**1.197.24**  Drupada too is a great king, and one who was formerly our enemy; winning him over, O king, is the strengthening of your own side.

**1.197.25**  The Dāśārhas are powerful and numerous, O lord of the people; where Kṛṣṇa is, there they will be — and where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.

**1.197.26**  When a matter can be accomplished by conciliation alone, O king, who but one cursed by fate would pursue it through conflict instead?

**1.197.27**  The townspeople and the country folk, having heard that the Pārthas live, yearn keenly to see them — O king, do what pleases them.

**1.197.28**  Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala are given to unrighteousness, evil-minded, and childish — do not follow their counsel.

**1.197.29**  I have said this to you before, O king — by the transgression of Duryodhana this people will perish.

**1.198.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The learned Bhīṣma son of Śāntanu, and the venerable sage Droṇa, and you yourself — all speak to me what is supremely beneficial and true.

**1.198.2**  Just as those heroic great warriors, the sons of Kuntī, are the sons of Pāṇḍu, so by right are they all my sons — of this there is no doubt.

**1.198.3**  Just as this kingdom is ordained for my sons, so too is this kingdom ordained for the sons of Pāṇḍu — of this there is no doubt.

**1.198.4**  Go, Kṣattṛ, bring them here, well honoured, along with their mother and together with that goddess-like Kṛṣṇā, O Bhārata.

**1.198.5**  By good fortune the Pārthas live; by good fortune Pṛthā lives; by good fortune those great warriors have won the daughter of Drupada.

**1.198.6**  By good fortune we all prosper; by good fortune Purocana has been quieted; by good fortune my great grief has been taken away, O greatly glorious one.

**1.198.7**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Vidura, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, went to Yajñasena and to the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata.

**1.198.8**  Having gone there, that knower of righteousness, learned in all the scriptures, attended upon Drupada in proper form, O king, joining him as was appropriate.

**1.198.9**  And Drupada too received Vidura in due form, and together they exchanged, as was fitting, the customary inquiries after one another's welfare.

**1.198.10**  He saw the Pāṇḍavas there and Vāsudeva as well, O Bhārata; embracing them with affection, he then inquired about their health.

**1.198.11**  And he of boundless intellect was duly honoured by them in proper order, repeatedly with affection, at the bidding of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

**1.198.12**  He inquired after the welfare of those sons of Pāṇḍu, O king, and also bestowed upon them various gems and riches.

**1.198.13**  For the Pāṇḍavas and Kuntī, for Draupadī, O lord of the people, and for the sons of Drupada, gifts were given as was given by the Kauravas.

**1.198.14**  And he of boundless wisdom spoke humbly and with courtesy to Drupada in the presence of the sons of Pāṇḍu and of Keśava.

**1.198.15**  O king, hear my words together with your ministers and sons — Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his sons, ministers, and kinsmen...

**1.198.16**  ...inquires after your welfare, O king, again and again with joy; and he is deeply gladdened by the alliance with you, O lord of men.

**1.198.17**  Likewise Bhīṣma son of Śāntanu, greatly wise, together with all the Kauravas, inquires after your welfare in every respect.

**1.198.18**  Droṇa the son of Bharadvāja, the great archer and your dear friend, approaches you in a close embrace and inquires after your welfare.

**1.198.19**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Pāñcālya, considers himself fulfilled in having obtained alliance with you, and so do all the Kauravas.

**1.198.20**  Their gaining a kingdom is not considered to bring them as much joy as obtaining this alliance with you, O Yajñasena.

**1.198.21**  Knowing this, may you dispatch the Pāṇḍavas; for the Kauravas are greatly eager to see the heirs of Pāṇḍu.

**1.198.22**  These bulls among men have been away for a long time, and Pṛthā too will be eager to see the city.

**1.198.23**  And all the noble ladies of the Kurus are eagerly awaiting to see Kṛṣṇā the Pāñcālī, as well as our city and realm.

**1.198.24**  May you, without delay, instruct the sons of Pāṇḍu to depart together with their wives — this is the message I bring.

**1.198.25**  When you have sent forth the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, O king, I shall then dispatch Dhṛtarāṣṭra's swift messengers; the sons of Kuntī will come, and Kuntī together with Kṛṣṇā.

**1.199.1**  Drupada said: O greatly wise Vidura, it is even as you say to me today; I too feel supreme joy at this alliance having been made, O lord.

**1.199.2**  And their going home would indeed be proper; yet it is not for me to say so myself in my own words just now.

**1.199.3**  When the heroic Yudhiṣṭhira son of Kuntī thinks fit, and Bhīmasena and Arjuna, and the twins who are bulls among men,

**1.199.4**  and also Rāma and Kṛṣṇa who know righteousness — then let the Pāṇḍavas go; for these two tiger-like men are devoted to what is dear and beneficial to them.

**1.199.5**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: O king, we all along with our followers are subject to you; whatever you will say to us with affection, so shall we do.

**1.199.6**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Vāsudeva said: Departure pleases me, or whatever King Drupada, the knower of all righteousness, may think.

**1.199.7**  Drupada said: Whatever the heroic Dāśārha, the best of men, the long-armed one, regards as timely — that judgment is my settled conviction.

**1.199.8**  For just as the greatly blessed sons of Kuntī are now mine, so too are the sons of Pāṇḍu Vāsudeva's — of this there is no doubt.

**1.199.9**  The son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira born of Dharma, does not contemplate for them what Keśava the tiger among men contemplates for their good.

**1.199.10**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, given leave by the great-souled Drupada, the Pāṇḍavas and Kṛṣṇa and the great-minded Vidura

**1.199.11**  took Draupadī Kṛṣṇā and the illustrious Kuntī and journeyed in ease and comfort to the city named after the serpent — Hastināpura.

**1.199.12**  And Dhṛtarāṣṭra the Kaurava, hearing that the heroes were approaching, sent the Kauravas to receive the Pāṇḍavas.

**1.199.13**  He sent Vikarṇa the great archer and Citrasena, O Bhārata, and Droṇa the supreme archer and Kṛpa the son of Gautama.

**1.199.14**  Surrounded by them, those heroic and resplendent great warriors then slowly entered the city of Hastināpura.

**1.199.15**  The city seemed to burst with excitement as those tiger-like men — who dispel grief and sorrow — entered.

**1.199.16**  Then the Pāṇḍavas, who touched the heart, heard high and low voices of welcome uttered by those wishing to show them affection.

**1.199.17**  "This tiger among men, the knower of righteousness, returns — he who protects us with righteousness as though we were his own heirs."

**1.199.18**  "Today great King Pāṇḍu has returned as though from the forest, he who loves the forest — come to do what is dear to us; of this there is no doubt."

**1.199.19**  "What has not been done today that is supremely dear to all of us — for the heroic sons of Kuntī, our lords, have returned?"

**1.199.20**  "If we have given gifts, if we have offered oblations, if we have performed austerities — by that merit, may the Pāṇḍavas dwell in the city for a hundred autumns."

**1.199.21**  Then they paid reverence at the feet of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the great-souled Bhīṣma and of the others who were worthy of such honour.

**1.199.22**  Having exchanged greetings with the entire city, they entered their quarters by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

**1.199.23**  After resting for some time, those great-souled and mighty men were summoned by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and by the son of Śāntanu.

**1.199.24**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O son of Kuntī, hear these words of mine together with your brothers — let there be no conflict between you again; enter Khāṇḍavaprastha.

**1.199.25**  And no one will be able to trouble you while you dwell there, protected by Pārtha as the thirty gods are protected by the wielder of the thunderbolt; having obtained half the kingdom, enter Khāṇḍavaprastha.

**1.199.26**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Accepting that command and bowing to the king, those bulls among men departed thence toward that formidable forest, and having obtained half the kingdom, they entered Khāṇḍavaprastha.

**1.199.27**  Then those Pāṇḍavas, unfailing, went there with Kṛṣṇa at their head and adorned that city, making it like heaven itself.

**1.199.28**  Then those great warriors, in that holy and auspicious place, having performed the peace rite, laid out the city with Dvaipāyana at their head.

**1.199.29**  It was adorned with moats resembling the ocean, and furnished with a rampart that seemed to touch and cover the sky.

**1.199.30**  Gleaming like white clouds and like a mass of snow, that finest of cities shone with its serpents just as Bhogavatī does.

**1.199.31**  It was guarded by gateways fearsome in appearance, resembling Garuḍa with wings spread, and protected by gatehouse towers resembling piled clouds, like Mount Mandara.

**1.199.32**  Well guarded and covered with various weapons thrust in firmly, and encircled by spears like two-tongued serpents, furnished with regular watch-platforms, it shone with warriors as its guard.

**1.199.33**  Adorned with sharp elephant-goads, śataghni machines, and a network of war-engines, and further with great iron wheels, that finest of cities shone resplendent.

**1.199.34**  With its broad avenues well laid out, free from the affliction of evil spirits, and brilliant with various magnificent white mansions, it blazed forth in glory.

**1.199.35**  That Indraprastha shone like the heaven of the gods, even as a great mass of clouds in the sky swells and is encircled with lightning.

**1.199.36**  There, in that delightful and auspicious place, the dwelling of the Kauravya prince shone, filled with wealth, resembling the abode of Kubera, the lord of riches.

**1.199.37**  There, O king, came brahmins who were the foremost among all knowers of the Vedas, and they were pleased to take up residence there — men who were also versed in all languages.

**1.199.38**  Merchants too came there from all directions seeking wealth, and all manner of artisans came to settle in that land at that time.

**1.199.39**  And charming gardens spread all around the city, with mango trees, hog-plum trees, kadamba trees, aśoka trees, and campaka trees —

**1.199.40**  — with puṃnāga and nāgapuṣpa trees, lakuca and jackfruit trees, śāla, tāla and kadamba trees, bakula and saketaka trees,

**1.199.41**  — with lovely flowering trees bowed down under the weight of their fruits, with old āmalaka trees, lodhra trees, and aṅkola trees in full bloom,

**1.199.42**  — with rose-apple trees, pāṭalā trees, kubjaka and atimuktaka creepers, karavīra and pārijāta trees, and many other trees of diverse kinds —

**1.199.43**  — always bearing flowers and fruits, filled with flocks of birds of many species, resounding with the cries of intoxicated peacocks and ever-joyful cuckoos.

**1.199.44**  The gardens were adorned with houses as pure and clear as mirrors, with various arbours of climbing plants, with charming painted pavilions and raised terraces like little hills, and with various step-wells brimming with the finest water.

**1.199.45**  There were also most delightful lakes fragrant with lotuses and blue water-lilies, filled with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks and graced by cakravāka birds.

**1.199.46**  There were various charming lotus-ponds surrounded by groves, and beautiful tanks — both large and great.

**1.199.47**  As those Pāṇḍavas dwelt in that great realm filled with virtuous people, O great king, their joy continuously increased.

**1.199.48**  There, with the establishment of righteousness brought about by Bhīṣma and the king, the Pāṇḍavas became the settled inhabitants of Khāṇḍavaprastha.

**1.199.49**  Graced by those five mighty archers who were like Indra himself, that finest of cities shone just as Bhogavatī shines graced by the nāgas.

**1.199.50**  Having settled them there, that hero Keśava then departed for Dvāravatī together with Rāma, O king, with the consent of the Pāṇḍavas.

**1.200.1**  Janamejaya said: O treasure of asceticism, having thus obtained that kingdom at Indraprastha, what thereafter did those great-souled Pāṇḍavas do?

**1.200.2**  All those great-souled men who were the forebears of my grandfather — how did Draupadī, the lawful wife, conduct herself toward them?

**1.200.3**  How was it that those five lords of men, all sharing the one Kṛṣṇā, though greatly blessed, did not become divided against one another?

**1.200.4**  I wish to hear all of this in full detail, O treasure of asceticism — their conduct toward one another while they were united with that Kṛṣṇā.

**1.200.5**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Permitted by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, those tiger-men among men, the Pāṇḍavas, scorchers of foes, having obtained their kingdom, took their delight together with Kṛṣṇā.

**1.200.6**  Having obtained the kingdom, the greatly resplendent Yudhiṣṭhira, true to his word, governed the earth righteously together with his brothers.

**1.200.7**  Having vanquished their enemies, those greatly wise sons of Pāṇḍu, devoted to truth and righteousness, dwelt there having attained the highest joy.

**1.200.8**  Performing all duties toward the citizens, those bulls among men took their seats on magnificent royal thrones.

**1.200.9**  Then, while all those great-souled men were seated thus, the divine sage Nārada arrived of his own accord. Yudhiṣṭhira offered his own beautiful seat to him.

**1.200.10**  Once the divine sage had taken his seat, the wise Yudhiṣṭhira himself offered him the arghya guest-gift according to due rite and presented his kingdom to him.

**1.200.11**  Having accepted that worship, the sage became glad at heart. After blessing him with benedictions he said to him: "Be seated."

**1.200.12**  Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, given leave, sat down, and sent word to Kṛṣṇā that the venerable one had arrived.

**1.200.13**  On hearing this, Draupadī too, having purified herself and composed her mind, went to where Nārada was sitting with the Pāṇḍavas.

**1.200.14**  She who walks in the path of righteousness, the daughter of Drupada, bowed to the feet of the divine sage, stood with joined palms, well-veiled in her garment.

**1.200.15**  That righteous-souled, truth-speaking best of sages, Nārada, pronounced various blessings upon her, the princess, and the venerable one said to that blameless lady: "You may go."

**1.200.16**  Then, after Kṛṣṇā had gone, the venerable sage spoke privately to all the Pāṇḍavas with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head.

**1.200.17**  "The glorious Pāñcālī is the one lawful wife of you all. A rule must be established among you so that no dissension arises here.

**1.200.18**  The two asuras Sunda and Upasunda were brothers who stood together — both invincible to all others, renowned in the three worlds.

**1.200.19**  They shared one kingdom, one house, one bed, seat, and food — yet on account of Tilottamā those two killed each other.

**1.200.20**  Therefore let a mutual friendship be safeguarded between you. Do what is necessary so that no division arises among you, O Yudhiṣṭhira."

**1.200.21**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: O great sage, whose sons were the asuras Sunda and Upasunda? How did the division arise among them, and how did they kill each other?

**1.200.22**  Was Tilottamā an apsarā or a daughter of the gods? Whose was she, maddened by desire for whom those two killed each other?

**1.200.23**  We wish to hear all of this exactly as it happened, and in full detail, O treasure of asceticism — for our curiosity is very great, O brahmin.

**1.201.1**  Nārada said: Hear from me in full this ancient tale exactly as it happened, O Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira, together with your brothers.

**1.201.2**  In the lineage of the great asura Hiraṇyakaśipu there was of old a lord of the daityas named Nikumbha, full of energy and great in strength.

**1.201.3**  His two sons were born of great valour and terrible might. They ate together, each with the other, and never went anywhere without the other.

**1.201.4**  Each was devoted to the pleasure of the other, each spoke words dear to the other; alike in character and conduct, they were as though one being divided into two.

**1.201.5**  Those two, grown great and mighty, with a single resolve even in their undertakings, took a single firm resolution: to conquer the three worlds.

**1.201.6**  Taking the rite of consecration, they went to the Vindhya mountain and there performed fierce austerities. After a long time they became fully absorbed in tapas.

**1.201.7**  Exhausted by hunger and thirst, wearing matted locks and bark-cloth garments, with all their limbs encrusted with dirt, they became subsisting on air alone.

**1.201.8**  Offering oblations of their own flesh, standing balanced on the tips of their big toes, arms raised upward, eyes unblinking, they maintained their vow for a long time.

**1.201.9**  By the power of their austerities, the Vindhya mountain, scorched for a long time, began to emit smoke — and that seemed like a wonder.

**1.201.10**  Then the gods became frightened on seeing their fierce austerities, and the gods created obstacles for the purpose of disrupting their tapas.

**1.201.11**  They repeatedly tempted the two with jewels and women, again and again — but those two, so mighty in their vow, did not break their vow.

**1.201.12**  Then the gods devised another illusion for those two great-souled ones — their sisters, mothers, wives, and their retinue of attendants,

**1.201.13**  — being chased in terror by a demon holding a trident, their ornaments and hair dishevelled, their garments slipping from their bodies,

**1.201.14**  — all running toward them crying "Save us! Save us!" Yet those two, so mighty in their vow, did not break their vow.

**1.201.15**  When neither of the two was moved to agitation or distress, those women and all that apparition vanished away entirely.

**1.201.16**  Then the Grandfather himself, Brahmā the grandfather of all worlds, approached those two great asuras in person and offered them a boon of their choosing.

**1.201.17**  Then those two brothers, Sunda and Upasunda, firm in their valour, on seeing the divine Grandfather, stood with joined palms.

**1.201.18**  And then those two spoke together to the divine Lord: "If the Grandfather is pleased with this our austerity —

**1.201.19**  — may we both be masters of illusion, masters of weapons, mighty, able to assume any form at will, and both immortal — if the Lord is pleased with us."

**1.201.20**  The Grandfather said: Except for immortality, everything else you have asked shall be granted. Choose instead a manner of death equal to that of the immortals.

**1.201.21**  "The great austerity you two have undertaken with the aim of doing this — on account of that very purpose, immortality cannot be ordained.

**1.201.22**  "The austerity has been undertaken by you two for the purpose of conquering the three worlds — on this account, O lords of the daityas, I cannot grant you that wish."

**1.201.23**  Sunda and Upasunda said: May we have no fear from anything whatsoever — whether movable or immovable — in the three worlds, except from each other, O Grandfather.

**1.201.24**  The Grandfather said: This boon that you have asked for and stated — this wish I grant you both. And this manner of death shall indeed come to pass for you as ordained.

**1.201.25**  Nārada said: Then the Grandfather, having granted them that boon and caused them to cease their austerities, departed to the world of Brahmā.

**1.201.26**  Having obtained all the boons, those two lords of the daityas, now invincible to all the worlds, returned to their own dwelling.

**1.201.27**  Seeing those two great asuras who had obtained their boons and fulfilled their desire, all their circle of friends and kinsmen rejoiced greatly on their account.

**1.201.28**  Then those two, discarding their matted locks, became adorned with crowns, decked with the most precious ornaments, and wearing spotless garments.

**1.201.29**  Those two lords of the daityas, supremely delighted, held an out-of-season moonlit festival fulfilling every desire, as did their circle of friends.

**1.201.30**  "Eat! Feast! Make merry! Sing! Drink! Give!" — such were the cries that rang out in house after house.

**1.201.31**  Here and there, with great drinking bouts resounding with the sound of clapping and cymbals, the entire city of the daityas became full of gladness and merriment.

**1.201.32**  Through those many and various diversions of the daityas who could assume any form at will, years passed in play for them as though they were but a single day.

**1.202.1**  Nārada said: But as soon as the festival was over, those two who longed to conquer the three worlds took counsel and then gave orders to the army.

**1.202.2**  Sent off with the blessings of their friends and the elder daitya counsellors, having performed the departure rites, they set out at night under the Maghā constellation.

**1.202.3**  They set out accompanied by a great daitya army, bearing maces and paṭṭiśa blades, armed with tridents and hammers in hand.

**1.202.4**  Praised by bards with auspicious hymns and victory songs, those two marched forth with the greatest joy.

**1.202.5**  Those two daityas, both able to go wherever they willed, rose up into the sky and made their way toward the very dwelling of the gods, intoxicated with the desire for battle.

**1.202.6**  Learning of their coming and of that boon granted by the Lord, the gods thereupon abandoned heaven and departed to the world of Brahmā.

**1.202.7**  Those two, fierce in their valour, conquered the realm of Indra and likewise the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, and vanquished even the sky-moving beings.

**1.202.8**  Those two great asuras then conquered the serpents dwelling within the earth, and vanquished all the barbarian peoples who dwelt by the ocean.

**1.202.9**  Then, determined to conquer the whole earth, those two of terrible command assembled their soldiers and addressed them in sharp words.

**1.202.10**  "The royal sages through great sacrifices, and the twice-born through oblations to gods and ancestors, increase the might, strength, and prosperity of the gods.

**1.202.11**  Therefore all those enemies of the asuras, as they thus grow powerful, must be slain by us all together with every means at our disposal."

**1.202.12**  Having thus commanded all their forces, and having resolved upon a cruel course, the two set out from the eastern shore of the great ocean, marching in every direction.

**1.202.13**  Whoever performed sacrifices, and whatever twice-born priests officiated at sacrifices — the mighty pair, upon seeing them all, struck them down by force.

**1.202.14**  In the hermitages, the sacred fires of the self-purified sages were seized by their soldiers acting without fear and hurled into the waters.

**1.202.15**  Even the curses pronounced in anger by great-souled sages rich in austerities could not take hold of the two, for they were protected by the boon they had received.

**1.202.16**  When curses fell off like arrows loosed against stone, the twice-born, abandoning their vows, fled in all directions.

**1.202.17**  Those on earth who were perfected through austerity, self-restrained and devoted to tranquility, fled in fear of the two just as serpents flee from Garuda.

**1.202.18**  With hermitages churned up and shattered, with sacred vessels and ladles scattered about, the whole world became desolate, as if struck down by time itself.

**1.202.19**  With royal sages and sages nowhere to be seen, the two great asuras, resolved and bent upon slaughter, wreaked havoc freely.

**1.202.20**  Taking the form of elephants in rut with ichor streaming from their temples, the two dragged those hiding even in inaccessible places to the abode of Yama.

**1.202.21**  Becoming lions, then tigers, then vanishing altogether, the two cruel ones, upon sighting sages, slew them through these and various other means.

**1.202.22**  Sacrifices and Vedic recitation ceased; kings and brahmin priests disappeared; festivals and solemn rites fell into disuse — thus the earth became at that time.

**1.202.23**  Full of wailing, stricken with fear, with markets and shops closed, with rites to the gods discontinued, and bereft of auspicious marriage celebrations.

**1.202.24**  Agriculture and cattle-tending ceased; cities and hermitages were demolished; the earth became scattered with bones and skeletons — a terrible sight to behold.

**1.202.25**  The rites for the ancestors were abandoned, and the auspicious vaṣaṭ-call fell silent; the world took on a fearful appearance and became difficult to look upon.

**1.202.26**  The moon and the sun, the planets, the stars, the constellations, and the dwellers of heaven all fell into despair upon witnessing the deeds of Sunda and Upasunda.

**1.202.27**  Having thus conquered all the quarters through cruel deeds, the two asuras, now without rivals, established their encampment at Kurukshetra.

**1.203.1**  Nārada said: Then all the divine seers and the perfected supreme sages fell into great distress upon witnessing that vast slaughter.

**1.203.2**  Those who had conquered anger, conquered the self, and conquered the senses then went, out of compassion for the world, to the dwelling of the Grandfather.

**1.203.3**  There they beheld the Grandfather seated together with the gods, surrounded on all sides by perfected ones and brahmin sages.

**1.203.4**  There was the great god Mahādeva, there was Agni along with Vāyu, the Moon and the Sun, Dharma, Parameṣṭhī, and Budha as well.

**1.203.5**  The Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, the forest-dwellers, those who live on rays of light, the unborn, the undeluded, the sages who carry fire within them, the ascetics — all these sages were attending upon the Grandfather.

**1.203.6**  Then, approaching together, all the great sages reported in full everything that Sunda and Upasunda had done.

**1.203.7**  What had been done, and in what manner it had been done, and in what sequence — they reported all of this in its entirety to the Grandfather.

**1.203.8**  Then all the hosts of gods and those supreme sages, placing that very matter before him, urged the Grandfather to act.

**1.203.9**  The Grandfather, having heard the words of all, reflected for a moment and determined what needed to be done.

**1.203.10**  With a view to their destruction, he summoned Viśvakarmā; and seeing Viśvakarmā before him, the Grandfather of great austerity commanded: "Let a woman be created here, one to be sought after."

**1.203.11**  Viśvakarmā, having bowed to the Grandfather and praised his words, pondered carefully and then fashioned a divine woman with great effort.

**1.203.12**  From whatever existed in all three worlds, whether moving or stationary, he gathered with great care each and every beautiful thing.

**1.203.13**  He set into her body tens of millions of jewels and created her composed of an accumulation of gems — a woman divine in form.

**1.203.14**  She, fashioned with great effort by Viśvakarmā, became in beauty unrivaled among all women in the three worlds.

**1.203.15**  There was not the smallest part of her body that was not endowed with the perfection of beauty, nor any place where the gaze of those who looked upon her did not become fixed.

**1.203.16**  She was as if Śrī herself had taken bodily form — lovely in appearance, glorious of figure — and she stole the eyes and minds of all beings.

**1.203.17**  Because she was fashioned by gathering jewels particle by particle — sesame-seed by sesame-seed (tila by tila) — the Grandfather gave her the name Tilottamā.

**1.203.18**  The Grandfather said: "Go, Tilottamā, to the asuras Sunda and Upasunda; with your irresistible beauty, dear one, bring about their temptation."

**1.203.19**  "Bring it about that merely by seeing you and through the perfection of your beauty, discord arises between the two of them against each other — arrange things thus."

**1.203.20**  Nārada said: She, promising "so be it" and bowing to the Grandfather, performed a circumambulation of the assembled wise ones there.

**1.203.21**  The venerable one sat facing east, Maheśvara was to the south, the gods sat to the north, and the sages were on every side.

**1.203.22**  As she performed that circumambulation there, Indra and the venerable Sthāṇu remained steadfast through fortitude.

**1.203.23**  As she passed to his side, for Brahmā who was exceedingly desirous of seeing her, another face emerged — a southern face with curved lashes.

**1.203.24**  As she moved behind him, a western face emerged; as she passed to the northern side, a northern face emerged.

**1.203.25**  For the great Indra too, a thousand of those wide eyes with reddened corners spread on every side — to his flanks, his back, and his front.

**1.203.26**  Thus Sthāṇu, the great god, became four-faced in ancient times; and thus the Slayer of Bala, Indra, came to have a thousand eyes.

**1.203.27**  Likewise, from all the hosts of gods and from the sages in every direction, faces turned whichever way Tilottamā went.

**1.203.28**  The gaze of those great-souled ones fell upon her body — the gaze of all of them for the most part, excepting only the divine Grandfather.

**1.203.29**  As she departed then, all the gods and the supreme sages deemed the task accomplished by reason of her perfection of beauty.

**1.203.30**  When Tilottamā had departed, the sustainer of the worlds dismissed all the gods and those hosts of sages.

**1.204.1**  Nārada said: Having conquered the earth, the two asuras, without rivals, free from anxiety, having rendered the three worlds undisturbed, felt their purpose accomplished.

**1.204.2**  Having seized all the jewels of the gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, kings, and rākṣasas, the two attained the highest satisfaction.

**1.204.3**  When there were none left anywhere to oppose them, the two became free of exertion and sported like immortals.

**1.204.4**  With women, with garlands and fragrances, with abundant food and delicacies to eat, and with various delightful beverages, the two attained the highest pleasure.

**1.204.5**  In the inner apartments, in forest gardens, in mountain groves and woodland retreats — in whatever places they desired — the two sported like immortals.

**1.204.6**  Then one day the two came to sport on the flat stone surface of the Vindhya's crest, amid the sāla trees whose tops were in full bloom.

**1.204.7**  With all divine desirable things brought there, the two sat down with great delight upon excellent seats, together with their women.

**1.204.8**  Then women attended upon the two with instrumental music and dance, and came forward with songs mingled with praises to give them pleasure.

**1.204.9**  Then Tilottamā, gathering flowers in that forest, donned a provocative garment of a single red cloth.

**1.204.10**  She, slowly gathering the karṇikāra flowers that grew on the riverbanks, moved quietly toward the place where the two great asuras sat.

**1.204.11**  The two, having drunk excellent wine with reddened and intoxicated eyes, were overcome with agitation the very moment they saw that woman of beautiful hips.

**1.204.12**  The two leapt up, abandoning their seats, and went to where she stood; both, maddened with desire, both besought her.

**1.204.13**  Sunda seized the fair-browed one by her right hand; Upasunda too grasped Tilottamā by her left hand.

**1.204.14**  Intoxicated by the boon they had been granted, and by their own bodily strength, and by their intoxication with wealth and jewels, and by the intoxication of wine —

**1.204.15**  Maddened by all these intoxications, frowning at each other, seized by the madness of desire, the two then spoke to one another.

**1.204.16**  "She is my wife; to you she is an elder" — thus Sunda addressed him. "She is my wife; to you she is a daughter-in-law" — thus Upasunda addressed him.

**1.204.17**  "She is not yours, she is mine" — at this, fury entered the two; and on her account both of them seized their terrible iron clubs.

**1.204.18**  Grasping those terrible clubs and deluded by desire for her, shouting "I am first! I am first!" at each other, the two struck one another down.

**1.204.19**  The two terrible ones, struck down by the clubs, fell to the surface of the earth with their bodies smeared in blood — like two suns fallen from the sky.

**1.204.20**  Then those women fled, and the entire host of asuras retreated to the underworld, every one of them trembling with despair and fear.

**1.204.21**  Then the Grandfather of pure soul came there together with the gods and great sages, desiring to honor Tilottamā.

**1.204.22**  She, invited by Brahmā to choose a boon, chose simply joy itself; and the pleased Grandfather then addressed her there.

**1.204.23**  "You shall roam the worlds that the sun traverses, O radiant one; and because of your brilliance, no one will be able to look at you directly."

**1.204.24**  Having thus bestowed the boon upon her, the lord Grandfather of all the worlds entrusted the three worlds to Indra and departed to Brahmaloka.

**1.204.25**  Thus those two, who had been united and of one resolve in all matters, became enraged with each other over Tilottamā and slew one another.

**1.204.26**  "Therefore I tell you out of affection, O best of the Bharatas all: arrange things so that no discord arises among you all on account of Draupadī. Do so, may it be well with you — if you wish what is dear to me."

**1.204.27**  Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed by the great sage Nārada, those great-souled ones, O king, came together with one another and made a compact in the very presence of that divine seer Nārada of boundless might.

**1.204.28**  "Whoever among us finds another sitting with Draupadī shall live as a celibate student in the forest for twelve years on our behalf."

**1.204.29**  When that compact had been made by the Pāṇḍavas who walked in righteousness, the great sage Nārada also departed, well pleased, to whatever abode he desired.

**1.204.30**  Thus was the compact previously made by them at Nārada's instigation; and all of them were never divided against one another from that time forth, O Bhārata.

**1.205.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Having thus made their compact, the Pāṇḍavas dwelt there, bringing other rulers of the earth under their sway through the might of their weapons.

**1.205.2**  Kṛṣṇā became obedient to all of those five sons of Pṛthā, those lions among men of immeasurable might.

**1.205.3**  And she, together with those five heroic husbands, was supremely content, like the Sarasvatī amid its elephants.

**1.205.4**  While the great-souled Pāṇḍavas conducted themselves righteously, all the Kurus thrived, free from fault and full of happiness.

**1.205.5**  Then, O lord of the people, O best of kings, after a long time, some thieves stole the cattle of a certain brahmin.

**1.205.6**  As his wealth was being carried off, the brahmin, swooning with rage, came to Khāṇḍavaprastha and cried out loudly to the Pāṇḍavas.

**1.205.7**  "My cattle are being carried off by base, cruel, and uncontrolled wretches! Rush out from your domain and pursue them, O Pāṇḍavas!"

**1.205.8**  "The oblation of the heedless brahmin is plundered by crows; a jackal invades the empty cave of the tiger."

**1.205.9**  "While a brahmin's property is stolen by thieves, while the purpose of righteousness is violated, while I weep aloud — let your weapons be taken up!"

**1.205.10**  The Pāṇḍava, Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, heard those words of the weeping brahmin close by.

**1.205.11**  Hearing this, the mighty-armed one said to the brahmin, "Fear not." But where the weapons of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas were kept, King Yudhiṣṭhira the dharmarāja was there together with Kṛṣṇā.

**1.205.12**  Unable to enter and unable to go away, the Pāṇḍava was urged again and again by the brahmin's words of distress. There, amid that outcry, the son of Kuntī pondered, filled with grief.

**1.205.13**  "As the wealth of that ascetic brahmin is being carried away, it is my duty to wipe away his tears" — so he resolved.

**1.205.14**  "The sin of negligent inaction would be very great for a ruler of the earth if today I do not protect this weeping man at my very door."

**1.205.15**  "And disbelief in all of us would become established in this world if we fail to protect, and unrighteousness would also be ours."

**1.205.16**  "And if I go without asking the king, without doubt it will displease King Ajātaśatru as well as me."

**1.205.17**  "But if I enter the king's chamber, I shall have to go to the forest. Let there be great unrighteousness, or let me die in the forest — even at the cost of my body's destruction, dharma alone prevails."

**1.205.18**  Having thus resolved, Dhanañjaya son of Kuntī entered, took leave of the king, O lord of the people,

**1.205.19**  and, taking up his bow with joy, spoke to the brahmin: "Come quickly, O brahmin, while those who seek another's wealth still have not gone far."

**1.205.20**  "Those wretches have not gone far — let us go together now, so that today I may recover your wealth from the hands of the thieves."

**1.205.21**  The mighty-armed one, bearing his bow, armored, mounted on his chariot with his banner, pursued them, scattered the thieves with his arrows, and conquered that wealth.

**1.205.22**  Having restored it to the brahmin and having drunk deep of glory, the heroic Pāṇḍava Savyasācī, scorcher of foes, returned to the city.

**1.205.23**  He saluted all the elders, and being greeted by them in return, he said to Dharmarāja: "Let the vow be prescribed for me."

**1.205.24**  "The compact has been transgressed by me by my coming into your presence; I shall go to the forest, for this is the agreement we made."

**1.205.25**  When thus addressed, Dharmarāja was suddenly struck by this unwelcome word; and Yudhiṣṭhira, grieved and with faltering speech, said "How so?" to Guḍākeśa — one brother to the other, the steadfast one.

**1.205.26**  "If I am an authority for you, hear my word, O sinless one. Whatever displeasure you caused me, O hero, by entering — I pardon all of it; it is not a grievance in my heart."

**1.205.27**  "For a younger brother's entry into the elder's presence is no offence; it is the younger one's entry that violates the rule for the eldest."

**1.205.28**  "Turn back, O mighty-armed one, and obey my word; there is no breach of dharma for you, nor has any offence been done to me."

**1.205.29**  Arjuna said: "I have heard from you that one should not practise dharma under a pretext. I will not swerve from truth — by truth I take up my weapon."

**1.205.30**  Vaiśampāyana said: Having obtained the king's permission, he was initiated into the vow of celibacy and came to dwell in the forest for twelve years.

**1.206.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: As the mighty-armed glory of the Kauravas set out, great-souled brahmins who had mastered the Vedas followed him.

**1.206.2**  Those learned in the Vedas and their ancillaries, as well as thinkers on the self, the pure and those devoted to the Lord, bards and those versed in the Purāṇas,

**1.206.3**  other storytellers, O king, ascetic forest-dwellers, and brahmins who sweetly recite celestial narratives —

**1.206.4**  by these and many other companions with pleasing speech, the son of Pāṇḍu was surrounded and proceeded like Vāsava amid the Maruts.

**1.206.5**  Pleasant and varied forests, lakes, rivers, oceans, and regions too, O Bhārata,

**1.206.6**  and holy pilgrimage sites he saw, O bull of the Bharatas; reaching Gaṅgādvāra, the lord set up his camp.

**1.206.7**  Hear from me, O Janamejaya, the wonderful deed that the pure-souled foremost charioteer of the Pāṇḍus performed there.

**1.206.8**  When the son of Kuntī had settled there, O Bhārata, those brahmins kindled their sacred fires many times over.

**1.206.9**  While those fires were being kindled, blazing, and fed with oblations, flower-offerings having been made, the brahmins having gone to the bank of the ford,

**1.206.10**  with the learned ones having bathed, disciplined and established on the good path — that Gaṅgādvāra shone exceedingly, O king, with those great souls.

**1.206.11**  As that encampment was thus filled with activity, the son of Pāṇḍu, the son of Kuntī, descended into the Gaṅgā for his ritual bath.

**1.206.12**  Having bathed there and satisfied the ancestors, and wishing to ascend from the water in order to perform the fire-rite, O king,

**1.206.13**  the mighty-armed one was drawn beneath the water, O great king, by Ulūpī, the daughter of the serpent king, who was overcome with desire.

**1.206.14**  There the Pāṇḍava beheld fire burning clearly and well-tended in the highly honored dwelling of that serpent of the Kauravya line.

**1.206.15**  There Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, performed his fire-rite; offered without hesitation, the fire was pleased with him.

**1.206.16**  Having performed the fire-rite, the son of Kuntī then spoke this word to the daughter of the serpent king, smiling as it were:

**1.206.17**  "What is this bold deed you have done, O timid one, O beautiful lady? What is this charming place? And who are you, whose daughter?"

**1.206.18**  Ulūpī said: "A serpent born in the Airāvata lineage, named Kauravya — I am his daughter, O Pārtha; I am the serpent maiden named Ulūpī."

**1.206.19**  "When I saw you, O son of Kuntī, descending into the river for your bath, I was at once overcome by Kandarpа, the god of love."

**1.206.20**  "Me, thus tormented by the bodiless one on your account, O joy of the Kurus — I who have come to you and to no other — gladden today by giving yourself to me in private."

**1.206.21**  Arjuna said: "This twelve-year vow of celibacy has been enjoined upon me by Dharmarāja; I am not my own master, O fortunate one."

**1.206.22**  "And I wish to do what is pleasing to you as well, O dweller in the water; I have never spoken an untruth at any time."

**1.206.23**  "How then might that not be untruth and yet what is pleasing to you might also come about, and my dharma might not be harmed — tell me how to act so, O serpent maiden."

**1.206.24**  Ulūpī said: "I know, O son of Pāṇḍu, how you wander the earth, and how your preceptor enjoined this celibacy upon you."

**1.206.25**  "Whichever of you, heedlessly, were to intrude upon the other in the presence of Drupada's daughter — he was to observe celibacy in the forest for twelve years: this is the compact you made."

**1.206.26**  "This exile from one another was made for the sake of Draupadī, for the purpose of dharma — in this matter dharma is not violated."

**1.206.27**  "And the rescue of those in distress is a duty, O large-eyed one; by rescuing me, your dharma is not diminished."

**1.206.28**  "And even if there were the slightest transgression of this dharma, that too would be dharma for you — by giving me life, O Arjuna."

**1.206.29**  "Cherish me who am devoted to you, O Pārtha; this is the view of the good, O lord. If you do not act thus, know me as dead."

**1.206.30**  "By the gift of life practise the highest dharma, O mighty-armed one; I have come to you for refuge today, O best of men."

**1.206.31**  "O son of Kuntī, you always protect the wretched and the unprotected; I come to you for shelter and I cry out in grief."

**1.206.32**  "I beg you, being desirous of you; therefore do what is pleasing to me. You — you are the one who should fulfil my desire by giving yourself."

**1.206.33**  Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed by the daughter of the serpent king, the son of Kuntī did all of that, citing dharma as the reason.

**1.206.34**  That valiant one, having spent that night in the serpent's dwelling, rose at sunrise and departed from the abode of Kauravya.

**1.207.1**  Vaiśampāyana said: Having narrated all that to the brahmins, O Bhārata, the son of the wielder of the thunderbolt then journeyed to the slopes of the Himālaya.

**1.207.2**  Reaching the Agastya-banyan tree, the mountain of Vasiṣṭha, and the heights of Bhṛgu, the son of Kuntī performed his purification.

**1.207.3**  He gave thousands of cattle and also dwellings to the twice-born at the sacred fords and shrines — that best of Kurus gave.

**1.207.4**  And bathing at the ford of Hiraṇyabindu, that best of men beheld the finest mountains and the sacred shrines.

**1.207.5**  Descending with the brahmins, O Bhārata, that best of men, bull of the Bharatas, set out with the intention of reaching the eastern direction.

**1.207.6**  The best of Kurus visited the pilgrimage sites in due order, and the lovely river Utpalinī, towards the Naimiṣa forest.

**1.207.7**  The Nandā, the Aparanandā, the celebrated Kauśikī, the great river, Gayā, and the Gaṅgā as well, O Bhārata.
